title: Sudan Situation: UNHCR Monthly External Update #122 - August 2026
content:
Highlights

▪ Sudan: Persistent clashes, airstrikes and drone activity across the Blue Nile, Kordofan and Darfur States triggered further displacement, disrupted access to services and heightened humanitarian needs and protection risks. In North Kordofan, nearly 10,000 people were displaced by insecurity in and around Kazgeil, while intensified hostilities in Geisan and Al Kurmuk localities in Blue Nile displaced more than 12,000 people. In Darfur, intercommunal tensions, criminality, arbitrary arrests and detention further compounded protection risks and constrained humanitarian operations.

▪ Central African Republic (CAR): The National Commission for Refugees (CNR) and UNHCR met with local government authorities and heads of public services in Birao. The engagements provided an opportunity to present UNHCR’s operational priorities, strengthen institutional dialogue and reinforce collaboration with local authorities in support of refugees, returnees, internally displaced people and host communities.

▪ Chad: Insecurity, criminal incidents in some refugee sites, and heavy seasonal rains continued to affect humanitarian operations, disrupting access and damaging refugee shelters and critical infrastructure across eastern Chad.

▪ Egypt: On 21 August, the executive regulations of Asylum Law No. 164/2024 took effect, initiating the transition of asylum registration and refugee status determination from UNHCR, which has performed these functions under the 1954 agreement, to the Government’s Permanent Committee for Refugee Affairs.

▪ Ethiopia: In the Amhara Region, the security situation remained tense and volatile, with armed clashes and criminal activity continuing to pose risks to humanitarian personnel and operations. In Benishangul-Gumuz, Ura refugee site and Sherkole refugee camp remained calm and stable, while the situation at Kurmuk Transit Centre and along the Ethiopia-Sudan border remained unpredictable amid intensified fighting in neighboring Sudan’s Blue Nile State. Reception and registration of new arrivals at Kurmuk Transit Centre remained suspended.

▪ Libya: Libya’s operating environment remained sensitive in August. While large-scale demonstrations declined, calls for renewed mobilization and opposition to UNHCR’s presence persisted, continuing to affect the operational environment, particularly in western Libya. In eastern and southern Libya,
UNHCR and partners continued to deliver activities and assistance to refugees.

▪ South Sudan: Due to severe funding constraints, WFP food assistance to refugees is expected to be discontinued from 1 October 2026. During August, UNHCR, WFP and the Commission for Refugee Affairs (CRA) engaged government authorities and coordinated across field locations to support the transition and ensure consistent communication with refugees, host communities and local authorities.
UNHCR and WFP also issued a joint press release explaining the planned discontinuation of assistance and the underlying funding constraints.

▪ Uganda: On 19 August, the Office of the Prime Minister reinstated prima facie refugee status for asylum-seekers from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), South Sudan and Sudan, following a policy review confirming continued instability in these countries. The decision took immediate effect and comes amid continued Ebola-related border restrictions, particularly along the DRC and South Sudan borders.

title: Sudan Situation: UNHCR Monthly External Update #123 - September 2026
content:
Highlights

▪ Sudan: In September, intensified conflict across the Blue Nile, Kordofans and Darfur States, including ground clashes, drone strikes and intercommunal tensions, drove further displacement and disrupted humanitarian operations. Severe weather further compounded humanitarian needs by damaging shelters and essential infrastructure, while continued attacks on civilians and humanitarian operations into October underscored the deteriorating security environment and constraints on aid delivery.

▪ Central African Republic (CAR): During the reporting period, the security situation in Vakaga Prefecture remained fragile, with movements of non-state armed groups, political tensions and insecurity along major roads. In Birao, reports of potential attacks heightened tensions and triggered population movements.

▪ Chad: On 28 and 29 September, a high-level joint donor mission visited Ennedi Est and the Ouré Cassoni refugee-hosting site to assess humanitarian needs and advocate for increased support. The delegation included government representatives, the Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator, ambassadors and representatives of development and humanitarian partners and UN agencies including OCHA, UNFPA, UNICEF, UNHCR, and WFP.

▪ Egypt: UNHCR recorded 6,052 file closures by Sudanese nationals in September, the highest monthly figure to date, bringing the total to 33,286 between January and 3 October 2026. The increase coincided with greater cross-border movements and changes in travel procedures between Egypt and Sudan. Preliminary interviews suggest that some closures may be linked to regularising departure and facilitating future travel or re-entry, pointing to potentially circular movements. UNHCR continues to monitor these trends.

▪ Ethiopia: Insecurity persisted in the Amhara region and along the Ethiopia–Sudan border in Benishangul-Gumuz region, amid armed clashes, criminal activity and continued fighting in Sudan’s Blue Nile State. No major security incidents directly affecting refugees or humanitarian personnel in Aftit site in Amhara were reported.

▪ Libya: Libya’s protection environment deteriorated amid renewed anti-refugee rhetoric and intensified security measures. Sudanese refugees reported heightened fear and uncertainty following online threats, hate speech and calls for violence against refugees, migrants and other foreign nationals.

▪ South Sudan: Insecurity persisted, with clashes in Amiet Common Market, in Abyei Administrative Area near the border with Sudan, resulting in at least 40 deaths and over 100 injuries. In Maban, the discontinuation of targeted food assistance raised concerns over spontaneous returns to Sudan, while funding shortfalls threatened the continuity of essential health services for refugees and host communities.

▪ Uganda: Heavy winds and rainfall on 22 September damaged shelters in Kiryandongo, leaving more than 300 families without adequate shelter. New arrivals, single women and persons with disabilities were particularly affected, while limited resources constrained families’ ability to repair or upgrade temporary shelters.

title: Caribbean Real-Time Food Security Monitoring Report | World Food Programme
content:
Food consumption was acceptable for 89.5 percent of households, leaving 10.5 percent with poor or borderline consumption. However, this comparatively favourable consumption picture coexisted with considerably higher levels of stress across other indicators: 12.5 percent of households were in rCSI Phase 3+, 29.5 percent experienced moderate or severe food insecurity according to FIES, and 29.4 percent used crisis or emergency livelihood coping strategies. The divergence between current consumption and these broader measures suggests that many households were able to maintain food consumption while experiencing significant pressure on access and livelihoods.
The quarterly pattern points to a particularly difficult period in Q4 2025. Poor or borderline FCS rose sharply from 5.8 percent in Q3 to 15.3 percent in Q4, while rCSI Phase 3+ increased from 10.8 to 18.1 percent and moderate/severe FIES reached 31.8 percent, up from 26.7 percent. Conditions subsequently improved: poor/borderline FCS fell to 12.3 percent in Q1 2026 and 8.9 percent in Q2, while FIES declined to 28.8 and 27.7 percent, respectively. However, affordability pressures persisted. Reported food-price increases, which declined from 66.5 percent in Q3 2025 to 57.9 percent in Q4, subsequently rose again to 60.7 percent in Q1 and 63.8 percent in Q2 2026.
Country differences were substantial, but they need to be interpreted in context. Poor/borderline FCS was highest in Jamaica, at 14.4 percent, and Saint Lucia, at 13.8 percent. Jamaica also recorded some of the highest values across FIES, rCSI, LCSI, income disruption and market access. Importantly, these findings overlap with the impacts and recovery period following Hurricane Melissa, meaning Jamaica's elevated annual outcomes should not be interpreted simply as reflecting the same structural conditions observed elsewhere in the Caribbean. The hurricane shock also provides important context for interpreting the regional deterioration observed in Q4 2025, although the regional trend reflects conditions across all ten monitored countries.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 93, as of 10 November 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • In the south-east of the country, humanitarian partners are strengthening Ebola virus disease prevention efforts.
  • Mbomou: 357 households affected by heavy rainfall received emergency shelter kits and non-food items.
  • In Vakaga, insecurity continues to restrict humanitarian movements and access to affected populations.

GENERAL CONTEXT

Vakaga Prefecture – North-East

  • Armed clashes reported since 30 October in the areas surrounding Birao, Boromata, Tiringoulou and Am-Dafock continue to affect the operational environment. Ongoing insecurity has resulted in severe restrictions on humanitarian movements, particularly in the Boromata area, limiting humanitarian actors’ access to affected populations. The security situation has also forced communities to reduce their movements and has disrupted agricultural activities. In addition, transhumance-related concerns remain significant amid the onset of cross-border livestock movements, which could further exacerbate local tensions.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Multisectoral

Nana-Gribizi Prefecture – Centre

  • On 4 November, a joint mission conducted by CIAUD, EDA, UNICEF, URU and OCHA to the Lazaret IDP site in Kaga-Bandoro highlighted a deterioration in living conditions for the 4,443 internally displaced persons (1,085 households) residing on the site since 2017 and wishing to integrate into the local community. Priority needs include protection, particularly freedom of movement and gender-based violence (GBV) prevention and response, as well as access to safe drinking water, shelter, education, healthcare and food assistance. Only two of the site's 13 water points are currently functional, while many shelters are in an advanced state of deterioration. Access to healthcare has also declined following the withdrawal of humanitarian organizations, with financial constraints limiting the use of available services. Despite some livelihood support initiatives, food insecurity remains a major concern. For the displaced population, the main priority remains the implementation of a durable local integration solution to end their displacement. Without such a solution, humanitarian needs are likely to persist, requiring continued assistance to affected populations.

Health

Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

  • No confirmed cases of Ebola virus disease (EVD) have been recorded in the Central African Republic (CAR). However, the ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to pose a risk of importation, particularly in border areas of the south-east of the country. On 6 November, a joint mission was deployed to Béma, a locality bordering Yakoma in the DRC, where confirmed cases have been reported. The mission aimed to support preparedness and prevention efforts against a potential introduction of the disease into CAR. An assessment conducted by the World Health Organization (WHO), the World Food Programme (WFP) and OCHA found that community awareness of EVD was generally good, owing to the activities of the local communication committee. In addition, Red Cross volunteers trained in infection prevention and control are available in the area. Several priority actions remain urgent, including strengthening surveillance at all points of entry along the Mbomou River, deploying screening personnel at informal crossing points, completing the two isolation centres under construction in Béma, and operationalizing the rapid response team. WHO has provided the Ouango-Gambo Health District with preparedness and response equipment, including beds, tents, sprayers, stretchers, personal protective equipment (PPE) and chlorine solutions. WFP organized a two-day training session for community health workers on the nutritional management of patients in isolation.

title: TZA: Flood - 11-2026 - Mbeya Nzonvwe Flood Response (Report Date: 2026-11-05)
content:
Description

On 3 November 2026, heavy rainfall triggered flooding in Nzovwe Ward, Mbeya City Council, Mbeya Region, Tanzania. The flooding caused extensive damage to residential properties and resulted in significant displacement, with preliminary reports indicating that approximately 125 houses were destroyed and around 300 households displaced.

The disaster has severely disrupted the lives and livelihoods of affected families, leaving many without adequate shelter and essential household belongings. While some displaced households have sought temporary accommodation with relatives and host communities, others have been left homeless and face urgent humanitarian needs, particularly in shelter, food, non-food items (NFIs), safe water, sanitation and psychosocial support.

In response to the emergency, the Tanzania Red Cross Society (TRCS), in collaboration with government authorities, local leaders and other humanitarian stakeholders, has supported the provision and distribution of food and essential non-food items to affected households in need. Families whose houses were destroyed or rendered uninhabitable and who have no alternative accommodation have been relocated to a nearby school, which is currently being used as a temporary emergency shelter.

Community reports suggest that ongoing road maintenance and four-way road construction activities may have affected existing drainage systems, contributing to the accumulation and diversion of rainwater into neighbouring residential areas. The flooding also affected sections of the Tanzania–Zambia Highway (TANZAM Road), raising concerns about road accessibility, public safety and potential disruption to transportation and movement.

Rainfall was still ongoing at the time of reporting, increasing the risk of further flooding, additional property damage and displacement. No fatalities had been reported at the time of the initial assessment.

As part of the ongoing emergency response, TRCS deployed 50 volunteers to support search and rescue operations, provide First Aid to affected individuals and deliver Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) to affected households and communities. TRCS continues to coordinate closely with government authorities, local leaders and relevant stakeholders to assess emerging humanitarian needs, support affected families and identify appropriate response measures to address the immediate needs of displaced populations.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: No

NS Requests International Assistance: Yes

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by National Society

General

  • Search & Rescue
  • Food aid
  • Health
  • Shelter
  • Camp management
  • Psychosocial support services
  • Evacuation
  • First Aid

Summary:

Since the onset of the emergency, the Tanzania Red Cross Society (TRCS) has mobilised its response teams and deployed 50 trained volunteers to support affected communities in Nzovwe Ward, Mbeya City Council. The response is being implemented in close coordination with government authorities, local leaders and relevant humanitarian stakeholders to address the immediate needs of affected households and displaced populations. The following activities have been undertaken: 1. First Aid (FA) TRCS deployed volunteers to provide First Aid services to individuals affected by the flooding. The volunteers are supporting the identification of people requiring immediate medical attention and providing basic emergency care while facilitating referrals to appropriate health facilities where necessary. 2. Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) TRCS volunteers are providing Mental Health and Psychosocial Support to affected individuals and families, particularly those who have experienced distress, loss of homes and displacement. These interventions aim to promote emotional well-being, reduce psychological distress and strengthen the coping capacities of affected communities. 3. Search and Rescue TRCS deployed 50 volunteers to support search and rescue operations in the affected areas, working alongside relevant local authorities and emergency response actors. The teams are supporting efforts to reach affected households, assist individuals in need and ensure that vulnerable people are safely moved away from flood-affected areas. 4. Evacuation In collaboration with government authorities and local leaders, TRCS has supported the evacuation of affected households from flood-prone and severely damaged residential areas. Families whose houses were destroyed or rendered uninhabitable have been assisted to move to safer locations. Displaced households without alternative accommodation have been accommodated at a nearby school, which has been designated as a temporary emergency shelter. 5. Shelter and Camp Management TRCS is working with local government authorities and relevant stakeholders to support the management of the temporary emergency shelter established at the nearby school. Efforts are focused on identifying the needs of displaced households, supporting safe and dignified living conditions, and facilitating access to essential services. Particular attention is being given to the protection and specific needs of women, children, older persons and persons with disabilities. 6. Food and Non-Food Items (NFI) Distribution In collaboration with government authorities, local leaders and other humanitarian stakeholders, TRCS has supported the distribution of food and essential non-food items to affected households requiring immediate humanitarian assistance. The assistance aims to address urgent food needs and help families who have lost their homes and household belongings meet their basic daily needs with dignity. 7. Coordination TRCS is actively participating in emergency coordination with government authorities, local leaders and other relevant humanitarian stakeholders to strengthen information sharing, identify emerging needs, avoid duplication of assistance and facilitate a coordinated response. The coordination also supports the identification of priority households, management of displacement and planning for additional humanitarian interventions as the situation evolves.

Actions taken by RCRC

General

  • Other

Summary: -

Actions taken by Federation

Summary:

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), through the Juba Cluster, deployed Daniel Mutinda, Disaster Management Delegate, as surge support to strengthen the Tanzania Red Cross Society's (TRCS) emergency response operations. The surge deployment is providing technical and operational support in key areas, including: 1. Emergency Coordination: Supporting the National Society in strengthening coordination of the ongoing response, ensuring effective communication, information sharing and collaboration with relevant stakeholders. 2. Resource Mobilisation: Providing support and technical guidance on resource mobilisation to facilitate access to the financial, material and logistical resources required to address the growing humanitarian needs. 3. Technical Support and Operational Guidance: Providing hands-on disaster management technical support to strengthen the National Society's response capacity, facilitate smooth implementation of planned activities and ensure that response operations are conducted effectively and in line with established humanitarian standards. 4. Warehouse and Stock Assessment: Conducting a visit to the TRCS warehouse to assess the availability and status of pre-positioned emergency stocks, including essential relief items. This assessment is intended to establish available stock levels, identify potential gaps and inform timely replenishment and mobilisation of additional relief supplies to support the continuation and scaling up of humanitarian assistance. 5. National Society Strengthening: Working alongside TRCS management and response teams to identify operational challenges, provide technical guidance and ensure that the National Society receives the necessary support to deliver humanitarian services efficiently and without unnecessary operational constraints. Overall, the IFRC surge deployment aims to strengthen the operational readiness and response capacity of TRCS, facilitate resource mobilisation and ensure timely, coordinated and effective delivery of humanitarian assistance to flood-affected communities.

Actions taken by others

The Government of Tanzania, through the Mbeya Regional Commissioner’s Office and the relevant local government authorities, has taken the lead in coordinating the emergency response since the onset of the flooding in Nzovwe Ward, Mbeya City Council. The following actions have been undertaken by government authorities and other relevant stakeholders: 1. Emergency Coordination and Leadership: The Regional Commissioner’s Office, working closely with local government authorities and other relevant stakeholders, is leading and coordinating the overall emergency response to ensure timely assistance reaches affected communities and that response activities are implemented in a coordinated manner. 2. Security and Public Safety: Government authorities have facilitated security arrangements in the affected areas to protect affected populations, safeguard property and support the safe implementation of emergency response operations, including search and rescue and evacuation activities. 3. Emergency Shelter and Evacuation: The government has facilitated the provision of temporary emergency shelter for displaced households whose homes were destroyed or rendered uninhabitable. A nearby school has been designated as a temporary shelter to accommodate families with no immediate alternative accommodation. 4. Food and Non-Food Assistance: In collaboration with relevant stakeholders, government authorities have supported the provision and distribution of food and essential non-food items to affected households to address their immediate humanitarian needs. 5. Infrastructure Rehabilitation and Flood Mitigation: The government is facilitating efforts to rehabilitate and restore damaged infrastructure, including reviewing and addressing drainage-related challenges and other infrastructure vulnerabilities. These interventions aim to improve water drainage, reduce future flood exposure and minimise the risk of similar incidents recurring in the affected communities. 6. Stakeholder Engagement: Government authorities continue to engage relevant stakeholders, including humanitarian organisations and local leadership structures, to identify priority needs, mobilise resources and support ongoing relief and recovery interventions. Overall, the Government of Tanzania, through the Regional Commissioner’s Office and local government authorities, is providing leadership in emergency coordination, security, temporary shelter, relief assistance and recovery planning, while working with Tanzania Red Cross Society and other stakeholders to address the humanitarian consequences of the flooding and strengthen community resilience against future flood risks.

DREF: Requested

title: PAK: Drought - 09-2026 - Drought Situation in Tharparkar District, Sindh Province, Pakistan – 2026 (2026-11-09)
content:
Sources for data marked as Other

Dawn. (08 November 2026). “Sindh CM declares Tharparkar drought-hit, orders relief measures.” The Express Tribune. (08 November 2026). “Thar declared drought-hit as 90% of crops perish.”

Description

Tharparkar District in Sindh Province is experiencing severe drought conditions following inadequate and unevenly distributed rainfall during the 2026 monsoon season. The situation has affected all seven talukas of the district, resulting in significant agricultural losses and increasing concerns over water availability, livestock and the livelihoods of communities dependent on rain-fed agriculture and livestock rearing.

According to the Agriculture Extension Department, approximately 90% of cultivated crops have been destroyed or rendered unproductive, with only 10–15% reportedly surviving. Rainfall was particularly low during September 2026, ranging between 1 mm and 36 mm across the district, contributing to the drying of crops and natural vegetation.

On 07 November 2026, the Chief Minister of Sindh officially declared Tharparkar a drought-affected district and directed relevant government departments to take immediate measures to ensure drinking water supplies, restore non-functional water facilities and arrange fodder to protect livestock.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: No

NS Requests International Assistance: No

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by National Society

Summary:

As of 09 November 2026, PRCS, NHQ in coordination with the Sindh Branch, is closely monitoring the evolving drought situation in Tharparkar. Coordination and information sharing are ongoing to obtain an initial understanding of the extent of the impact, identify affected communities and assess emerging humanitarian needs. PRCS Sindh Branch, in coordination with relevant district authorities, will facilitate further assessment to determine priority needs and inform potential response interventions. Updates on assessment findings and planned response activities will be shared as further information becomes available.

Actions taken by Federation

Summary:

The IFRC CD, is maintaining close coordination with the NS to monitor the evolving situation, facilitate information sharing and assess potential humanitarian support requirements. IFRC will continue to engage with NS to identify priority needs and explore appropriate technical and operational support, as required, based on the findings of the assessment.

Actions taken by others

The Government of Sindh declared Tharparkar a drought-affected district on 07 November 2026. Through the District Administration and relevant provincial departments, the government is leading the response by coordinating relief measures, restoring water supply facilities, ensuring drinking water availability and arranging emergency fodder for livestock.

title: WFP Kenya Country Brief September 2026
content:
• WFP assisted 678,887 people in August through food and cash assistance and resilience-building interventions.
  • WFP continued preparations for anticipated El Niño impacts, including pre-positioning supplies and strengthening operational readiness in ASAL and refugee-hosting areas.
  • WFP strengthened local food systems and market access for smallholder farmers, with farmer groups in Turkana supplying more than 112 MT of green grams to WFP during the reporting period.
  • Through increased utilization of the Mombasa Corridor, WFP is projected to reduce Kenya Corridor transport rates from USD 32.81/MT to USD 19.40/MT, generating efficiencies for regional humanitarian operations.

title: WFP Mozambique Country Brief October 2026
content:
• Mozambique is entering a critical period where early action can make the greatest difference. Conflict, the lean season and El Niño are converging, increasing pressure on already vulnerable communities.
  • The response is increasingly about getting ahead of crises, not only responding to them. Government-led anticipatory action is being expanded, alongside climate preparedness and pre-arranged financing, to protect lives and livelihoods before shocks escalate.
  • From Cabo Delgado to climate-affected communities across the country, WFP is combining lifesaving assistance with livelihoods and resilience support, nutrition and school meals, helping communities meet immediate needs while strengthening their ability to withstand future shocks.

title: UNRWA Situation Report #238 on the Humanitarian Crisis in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem) [EN/AR]
content:
Highlights

The Gaza Strip

  • Over the reporting period, UNRWA recorded several significant armed incidents affecting its personnel and displaced people inside UNRWA schools-turned-shelters. At least six displaced people, including an UNRWA student and an UNRWA staff member, were injured, and at least one displaced person was killed inside the yard of a school-turned-shelter. An UNRWA Job Creation Programme worker was also reportedly killed due to an airstrike by Israeli forces in an open area.
  • Security threats continued to affect UNRWA operations. Over the reporting period, Israeli forces issued shelter-in-place instructions affecting five UNRWA installations in Nuseirat, followed by a reported strike in their vicinity. Separately, militia activity in eastern Maghazi and southern Rafah led to the temporary suspension of activities at Maghazi Health Centre and UNRWA temporary learning spaces in the area.
  • UNRWA’s stock of lubricant oil has been completely depleted for several weeks, leading to progressive deterioration of equipment and prolonged suspension of operations. Generators at several UNRWA facilities have been out of service for more than two months, and staff transportation is also constrained by the lack of lubricant oil.
  • Despite such challenges, UNRWA continues efforts to restore and expand essential services. Additional classrooms at the Rehabilitation Centre for the Visually Impaired in Gaza City are being established to increase education capacity. Rehabilitation work is also ongoing to establish a health facility at the Gaza Training Centre to enhance and consolidate health service delivery in Northern Gaza.
  • UNRWA’s latest site sweep assessed winterisation needs across 113 displacement sites and identified 18 Designated Emergency Shelters as unsafe, including four at very high risk of collapse, six at high risk, and eight at medium risk. UNRWA joined inter-agency efforts to identify alternative shelter options and is working with humanitarian partners to secure tents for the voluntary relocation of affected families. Priority is being given to 270 households currently living in sections of four premises assessed as being at very high risk of collapse.
  • Since 25 October, a protest by former UNRWA staff at the Khan Younis Training Centre (KYTC), a key UNRWA logistics and operational hub, has disrupted UN humanitarian operations. Access to vehicles, warehouses, and other facilities has been restricted, affecting the movement and distribution of humanitarian supplies, staff transport, and other activities.

1. Key points

The Gaza Strip

Fatalities and Injuries

  • Between 7 October 2023 and 30 October 2026, according to the Ministry of Health, as reported by the Health Cluster, 74,594 Palestinians were killed in the Gaza Strip and another 175,834 were injured. This includes 1,580 fatalities and 5,873 injuries between the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025 and 30 October 2026.
  • UNRWA has recorded 395 colleagues killed in the Gaza Strip since the start of the war (311 UNRWA personnel and 84 persons who were supporting UNRWA[2] ), as of 4 November. Health crisis • Acute respiratory infections increased ahead of the winter season, with a further increase expected in the coming weeks.

Wash, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) needs

  • According to the WASH Cluster’s Light Touch Monitoring Survey, completed in September, 84 per cent of the population of the Gaza Strip are experiencing frequent, unpredictable disruptions in access to safe, clean, and reliable water for daily drinking, cooking, and hygiene. Water insecurity thus remains a significant concern, despite signs of improvement - 91 per cent of the population reported water insecurity in the previous round.
  • Access to basic hygiene supplies also remained severely constrained, with 89 per cent of households reporting insufficient access to essential hygiene items.

Displacement, site management

  • UNRWA continues to monitor the movement of displaced persons and displacement sites. A total of 113 UNRWA collective emergency shelters host approximately 60,000 internally displaced persons.

Shelter needs

  • According to the Shelter Cluster’s classification, based on surveys conducted between 14 and 28 June, an estimated 1.98 million people, representing 94 per cent of the population of the Gaza Strip, require shelter and non-food item assistance (NFI). The assessment also suggests that 58 per cent of the population is facing critical or catastrophic shelter needs, meaning severe deficiencies in shelter conditions or lack of access to essential services and NFIs that expose them to serious health, safety, and dignity risks.

Operational implications and humanitarian response

  • Around 10,500 Palestinian UNRWA personnel continue to provide services and assistance to people in the Gaza Strip. In the occupied West Bank, UNRWA also plays a central role with around 4,500 of the Agency’s Palestinian personnel providing education, healthcare, and other services to Palestine Refugees.
  • All UNRWA international staff are prevented from entering the Occupied Palestinian Territory - the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem. This follows the implementation of laws passed by the Israeli parliament on 28 October 2024[3] that purport to prohibit UNRWA’s operations in areas that Israel considers its sovereign territory, including occupied East Jerusalem, and seek to bar any contact by Israeli officials with UNRWA. The Israeli authorities have not granted the Agency’s international staff visas or permits to enter the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including Gaza, since the end of January 2025.
  • Since March 2025, the Israeli authorities have been blocking UNRWA from directly bringing humanitarian personnel and aid into the Gaza Strip. Despite the huge needs on the ground, UNRWA was therefore unable to distribute the aid it had pre-positioned outside Gaza, which included enough food parcels, flour, and shelter supplies for hundreds of thousands of people.

The occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem

  • According to OCHA, between 7 October 2023 and 23 October 2026, 1,145 Palestinians – at least 250 of them children – were killed in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem. Ninetyeight of them have been killed since the beginning of 2026.
  • Following a fatal shooting attack on Israeli soldiers on 23 October, Israeli forces imposed severe security conditions on the city of Hebron in the southern West Bank. More than 2,000 Palestinians were reportedly forcibly displaced from their homes as part of the large-scale operation, which also included extensive demolitions of houses and private property. The Director of UNRWA Affairs in the West Bank released a statement expressing grave concern at the situation. On the evening of 1 November, Israeli forces concluded the operation.
  • The annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank continued despite persistent settler violence and harassment targeting participating Palestinians, as well as movement obstacles imposed by Israeli forces preventing Palestinians from accessing their agricultural land. October marked the worst month to date in 2026 for settler violence and harassment, in a year which has already surpassed preceding years for Palestinian casualties associated with settler violence.
  • Heightened security restrictions were in place in the occupied West Bank in the lead-up to the Israeli parliamentary elections on 27 October, with checkpoint closures and movement restrictions tightened.

title: UNHCR Afghanistan: Monthly Protection Update (As of September 2026)
content:
This monthly protection update for Afghanistan provides a comprehensive overview of UNHCR’s different protection programs, aiming to prevent, mitigate and respond to protection risks faced by vulnerable populations in the context of the current humanitarian crisis and in the absence of durable solutions. The data and insights presented are derived from an extensive protection analysis, collected through a variety of robust tools and systems. The activities include protection monitoring, household assessments, voluntary repatriation, returns monitoring, specialized support for persons with specific needs, community engagement, complaints and feedback systems, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), child protection, women protection, and civil documentation. This update aims to highlight key achievements, ongoing challenges, and the critical needs of the affected communities, ensuring a transparent and effective protection response.

PROTECTION MONITORING

UNHCR relies on a broad variety of protection monitoring activities to collect evidence and information on the protection needs and risks of forcibly displaced, returnee and host communities across Afghanistan. These activities include border monitoring, returnee monitoring and community-based protection monitoring (CPBM). The latter includes household assessments, focus group discussions and interviews with key informants. The data collected informs strategic priorities, operational decision-making and advocacy at field, national and global levels shaping the humanitarian and basic human needs response.

title: Yemen Situation: UNHCR Emergency Update - External Update #7 (10 November 2026)
content:
Highlights

▪ Displacement inside Yemen continues to increase, with an estimated 321,000 people newly displaced between 1 August and 7 November, up from 275,245 reported in the previous update. Taiz remains the most affected governorate, accounting for 67% of new displacement, followed by Lahj (20%) and Al Hudaydah (12%). Approximately 75% of newly displaced people are residing in displacement sites, prompting UNHCR to update its contingency planning assumptions.

▪ Movements across the Gulf of Aden continue, although no new arrivals were reported in Djibouti during the reporting period. As of 7 November, 3,836 refugees had arrived in Djibouti, while 365 individuals had arrived in Somalia since 1 September, including recent arrivals through both maritime and overland routes.

▪ Voluntary returns from Yemen to Somalia continue, following the return of 138 Somali refugees on 20 October, the first assisted return movement since the programme was interrupted. An additional 18 Somali refugees are registered for the next assisted spontaneous return planned for 21 November.

title: UNHCR Bangladesh - Operational Update September 2026
content:
KEY UPDATES: SEPTEMBER 2026

FOURTH PRESENCE CONFIRMATION EXER CISE (PCE) O N BHASAN CHAR: The September 2026 Presence Confirmation Exercise found that 26,775 refugees were present on Bhasan Char, reflecting an 8% decrease since December 2025. 94% of those confirmed present expressed an intention to remain, citing safety, better services, shelter and livelihood opportunities. Funding constraints and the absence of a clear national policy framework for Bhasan Char continue to hinder long-term planning and investment. Read the report.

NEW ARRIVALS & BIOMETRIC ENROLLMENT: New arrivals continue to approach UNHCR in Cox’s Bazar camps to be biometrically identified, with 264 individuals enrolled in September, bringing the total to 155,560 people (40,903 families) since January 2025. The Government-approved process enables access to humanitarian assistance for new arrivals, except shelter allocation. However, on 15 September, the Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner (RRRC) requested suspension of enrollment due to concerns over eligibility. UNHCR and the RRRC, who is seeking greater involvement in the process, will hold a technical meeting to refine admissibility criteria.

VIRTUAL COURT H EARING PROJ ECT: To strengthen access to justice, UNHCR and partners launched the virtual court hearing initiative on 1 September. Implemented with partner BLAST, and relevant government counterparts, the project allows refugees and host community victims and witnesses in selected cases to participate in court hearings remotely through secure video links in or near camps. By reducing travel requirements, costs and administrative barriers, the project makes access to justice safer and more efficient; it is expected to increase participation in legal proceedings and reduce withdrawals from cases. Watch the video.

STRATEGIC TRANSFORMATION OF ROHINGYA RESPONSE: As part of ongoing transformation efforts, UNHCR handed over five health facilities in Camps 2 West, 4, 5 and 12 to four Health Sectorendorsed NGOs. The transfers marked an important step in the further rationalization and localization of public health services while maintaining continuity of care. UNHCR continues to provide mental health and psychosocial support in the transferred facilities and manages primary healthcare centres in Camps 3 and 4-Extension.

LIVELIHOODS PRODUCTION: Refugee production centres completed the delivery of 68,060 menstrual hygiene management kits to UNICEF and delivered another 16,110 kits to UNHCR. During September, 893 volunteers, including 764 women, participated in production activities. The centres produced 354,725 sanitary pads, 113,500 items of female underwear, 57,558 kit-carrying bags and 67,805 environmentally friendly bags, linking humanitarian supplies with refugee skills and wage-earning opportunities. To facilitate sustainability, UNHCR’s livelihood partner CNRS is in the process of bringing the camp-based production centres under its social business registration while developing a long-term business plan.

EMERGEN CY PREPAR EDN ESS & RESPONSE: As monsoon rains declined, reported incidents in UNHCR-managed camps fell from 144 in August to 55 in September (62% decrease). Still, the incidents affected 723 people, causing 28 injuries and three fatalities, and damaged or destroyed 76 shelters. Ahead of the post-monsoon cyclone season (October–November), more than 1,700 volunteers and community members participated in cyclone orientation, search-andrescue training, multi-hazard preparedness sessions and emergency drills.

SHELTER & RELOCATIONS: UNHCR completed and handed over 205 Temporary Safer Shelters to families relocating from high-risk areas, while construction of additional shelters continued in Block E of Camp 4-Extension alongside shelter, WASH, site development and energy works. As of 27 September, 413 people (71 households) had relocated from high-risk areas in the camps. Meanwhile, regular shelter assistance reached 3,368 households, while 49 households received emergency support following damage by fire, heavy rain, wind and other incidents. Assistance included bamboo, rope, tarpaulin, wire and pre-cast footings provided following technical assessments and damage verification. UNHCR’s Global Distribution Tool — a biometricenabled digital system to manage distribution of humanitarian assistance — is now in use at all shelter distribution points, improving beneficiary verification, tracking, transparency and accountability.

LPG AND NFI DISTRIBUTIONS: UNHCR and partners continued distributing essential household and clean cooking items across the camps. Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) refills and pressure cookers reached 79,845 households (94% of yearly target), soap and tote bag distributions reached 81% of target households, female hygiene kits 91%, and solar lamps for single-person households 53%.

COMMUNITY-LED INITIATIVES: Nearly 2,000 community consultations involving more than 28,000 participants informed the second phase of Community-Led Initiatives in Cox’s Bazar camps. Planned projects will focus on rehabilitating community infrastructure affected during the monsoon. On Bhasan Char, all ten communityprioritized projects were completed, benefiting 12,587 people (2,641 households) through improvements including roof repairs, drainage, pipe networks, fencing and balcony construction while promoting community ownership and sustainability of the response.

NUTRITION CONCERNS: A September nutrition survey by ACF Canada, funded by UNICEF, WFP and Concern Worldwide, found worsening malnutrition among refugee children in the Cox’s Bazar camps alongside declining diet quality and diversity. Global acute malnutrition reached 14.6% — up from 13.9% in 2025 and 8.6% in 20241 . The survey also found increases in stunting and underweight children, with stunting rising to 42.6% from 41% in 2025 and 40.7% in 2024, and underweight children rising to 36.9% from 33.0% in 2025 and 29.3% in 2024. At the same time, infant and young children’s diets became less diverse and nutritious, with the proportion of young children receiving a minimum acceptable diet falling by half in two years — from 42.6% in 2024 to 21.2% in 2026. The findings underscore the need for sustained nutrition and food-security support amid funding cuts and a shift from blanket to targeted food assistance.

MENTAL HEALTH & PSYCHOSOCIAL SUPPORT (MHPSS): UNHCR strengthened access to evidence-based MHPSS services through a five-day training in Teknaf for 19 community paracounsellors and one psychologist on Integrated ADAPT Therapy, enhancing support for refugees experiencing psychosocial distress. In addition, 16 para-counsellors and one psychologist completed training and supervised practice in Early Adolescent Skills for Emotions (EASE) in August, equipping them to support adolescents aged 10–15 experiencing emotional difficulties, and their caregivers. UNHCR and partners also marked World Suicide Prevention Day (10 September) through activities promoting supportive conversations, and awareness of available assistance and referral pathways.

FUNDING UPDATE: As of 30 September, the UNHCR Bangladesh operation was 46% funded, with USD 92.49 million available against an operating plan of USD 200.6 million. The hyper-prioritized 2026 Joint Response Plan, which appeals for USD 710.5 million to reach up to 1.56 million people, including refugees and Bangladeshi host communities, was 70% funded as of Q3, indicating an overall decrease in available funding compared to 2025.

title: Yemen: Conflict - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms Area) #118, Reporting period: October 2026
content:
The World Food Programme (WFP)-led Emergency Telecommunications Cluster (ETC), now the Telecoms Area of the Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) 1 , was activated in April 2015 in response to the conflict in Yemen. This Situation Report provides a monthly update on LTC Telecoms activities.

Summary Points

• Escalating hostilities further constrained LTC Telecoms in Yemen, with on-site services in Al Turba suspended on 04 October and operations in Al Makha remaining suspended since 09 September. Remote technical support continued where feasible.

• The LTC activated its emergency contingency plan for Taiz, covering coordination, information management, logistics and telecoms support as humanitarian needs and operational requirements continued to evolve.

• In October, LTC Telecoms provided security communications services to 755 humanitarian responders through three operational Security Operations Centres (SOCs) and internet connectivity to 93 humanitarian personnel in Al Mukalla.

title: Quarterly Complaint and Feedback Mechanism Snapshot | Q2 | April–June 2026
content:
Key highlights

• Q2’s surge in tickets was driven by the April rollout of WFP’s Targeting and Prioritization Exercise (TPE), which introduced needs-based food assistance and generated demand for information on food-assistance eligibility and registration updates.

• TPE generated 22,330 tickets, or 16% of the total, through joint WFP–UNHCR Coordinated Help Desks.

• The Helpline stayed open during the Eid Holiday (25–31 May): handling 1,943 tickets and more than 100 urgent protection requests.

• More than 100 partner staff across all 33 camps received training on family reunification processes and eligibility, to identify and support refugees with family members in third countries.

• Help-desk staff received CAIPP refresher training on recording and submitting cases, use of the intake form and navigation of the CAIPP dashboard.

• The overall closure rate rose to 95%, up 13% from Q2. Amid damage from monsoon weather, 98% of urgent shelter cases were closed.

title: South Sudan: Q4 2026 Nutrition Cluster Bulletin
content:
The third quarter of 2026 saw a marked increase in the volume of nutrition services delivered by Nutrition Cluster partners, even as pressure on the treatment supply pipeline re-emerged towards the end of the period. By the end of September 2026, a total of 1,314,866 beneficiaries had been admitted into Community-based Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) programmes during the reporting period. These admissions comprised 299,408 children with Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) enrolled in Outpatient Therapeutic Programmes (OTP), 592,103 children with Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM) treated through Supplementary Feeding Programmes (SFP), 11,426 admissions to Stabilisation Centres (SCs), and 411,929 Pregnant and Breastfeeding Women (PBW) receiving nutritional support.

Despite persistent operational constraints, the response has continued to make steady progress toward the 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP) targets. By the end of September 2026, partners had reached 57% of the annual SAM target, 89% of the MAM target, and 76% of the target for PBW with acute malnutrition (compared with 36% for SAM, 51% for MAM and 41% for PBW at the end of June). Admissions during the third quarter (July–September) totaled 552,847, 39% more than in the second quarter (398,073). The increase was driven by the TSFP child and PBW programmes, where admissions rose by 47% and 73% respectively. In contrast, SAM admissions to OTP decreased by 5% (from 113,534 to 108,212) and SC admissions by 7%: monthly OTP admissions fell from a high of 40,714 in June to 34,022 in September, despite higher screening volumes over the same period. This trend warrants close attention, as the seasonal burden of acute malnutrition is expected to remain high through the final quarter of the year, and correlates with increased stock outs of supplies in some locations. Sustained, predictable funding and an uninterrupted supply of therapeutic and supplementary foods will be essential to prevent programme coverage from declining in the fourth quarter.

title: Somalia : Health Cluster Bulletin - September-October 2026
content:
• The October–December 2026 Deyr rainy season’s El Niño is expected to trigger severe flooding across Somalia, putting an estimated 3.4 million people at risk and threatening to displace up to 804,000.
  • Beyond compounding crisis-level hunger and displacement, the flooding threatens critical health infrastructure and heightens the risk of waterborne disease outbreaks, underscoring the urgent need to strengthen preparedness and pre-position medical supplies.
  • Conflict and healthcare access: Renewed clashes in Baidoa during September raised concerns about civilian safety, damage to health infrastructure, displacement, and disruptions to essential health services.
  • Acute malnutrition: The IPC projected that 1.92 million children aged 6–59 months would require treatment for acute malnutrition between July 2026 and June 2027, including 433,000 with severe acute malnutrition.
  • Communicable disease risks: Cholera/AWD, measles, and diphtheria remain priority public health concerns, highlighting the need for strengthened surveillance, vaccination, case management, and rapid response.
  • Health service disruptions: Humanitarian funding cuts continue to undermine the availability of essential healthcare in Somalia, with further closures of health and nutrition facilities worsening access to vital servic es for vulnerable communities.
  • Maternal, newborn, and child health: National guide lines on Small and Sick Newborn Care, Essential Newborn Care, and Kangaroo Mother Care were launched in September to strengthen the quality of newborn care.

title: Central African Republic: Cash and Voucher Assistance (CVA) - 1 January - 30 June 2026
content:
In the second quarter of 2026, the humanitarian response involving cash transfers (cash and vouchers) in the Central African Republic mobilized 16 actors in 27 subprefectures, totaling 4.5 million USD. These interventions provided assistance to 128,400 people, representing nearly 10% of the 1.3 million people
targeted by the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan (HNRP). Against a backdrop of limited resources and persistent humanitarian needs, the actors focused their efforts on the most vulnerable populations and the highest-priority areas.

Compared to Q2 2025, geographic coverage decreased from 30 to 27 subprefectures (-10%), while the number of beneficiaries fell from 160,800 to 128,400 people (-20%). The amounts transferred also decreased from 5.4 to 4.5 million USD (-16.7%), reducing the actors’ ability to maintain the level of coverage achieved the previous year.

Food security remains the primary sector for the use of cash transfers, with 93,500 beneficiaries in 2026 compared to 76,600 in 2025. This increase reflects the persistence of food insecurity and the priority given to meeting basic needs. Cash transfers account for more than 97% of beneficiaries, largely due to the limited availability of digital financial services in several intervention areas. The fact that the number of sectors using cash transfers has remained stable further confirms the established role of cash as a multisectoral approach to humanitarian response.

Two major developments marked Q2 2026. First, funding for Multi-Purpose Cash Transfers (MPCT) increased from $17,400 to $96,000 (+452%), raising the coverage of their financial needs from 1.8% to 7.9%. Second, the response shifted its focus more toward emergency assistance: 89,900 people (70%) received emergency assistance, compared to 38,500 people (30%) who benefited from resilience-building activities. This trend illustrates the prioritization decisions made in a context of limited resources, with an emphasis on basic needs, while highlighting the importance of maintaining resilience interventions to provide sustainable support to vulnerable populations.

title: Ukraine war situation update | 24 – 30 October 2026
content:
Ukraine Conflict Monitor Update

The longest truce since the start of the war takes place without major incidents in Kherson, while Ukraine destroys several Russian aircraft.

1,681 conflict events

11% decrease compared to last week

165 incidents of violence targeting civilians

19% decrease compared to last week

At least 82 civilians killed by targeted violence

17% decrease compared to last week

983 air- and drone strikes

15% decrease compared to last week

257 shelling events

24% decrease compared to last week

432 armed clashes

7% increase compared to last week

241 Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure

27% decrease compared to last week

Number of events and change compared to last week (per target):

Education: 25 events

Healthcare: 16 events

Energy: 43 events

Residential: 206 events

  • The 27 October to 1 November Oleshky ceasefire marked the longest local ceasefire in the Kherson region since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. However, Russia used the ceasefire to rotate its military units, strengthen its positions, and improve logistics in the area. This suggests that Russia intends to continue attacks in the area, having already resumed strikes on Kherson and Antonivka. The ceasefire was also shadowed by deadly Russian long-range strikes on the cities of Dnipro, Chernihiv, Kremenchuk, and Izium. The events indicate that Russia selectively uses humanitarian grounds to improve its battlefield positions, protect civilians, and gain the United States' support in pressuring Ukraine while continuing its aerial campaign against the rest of the country. Similar humanitarian arrangements might occur in the future; however, they are unlikely to lead to substantial reductions in violence.
  • The Ukrainian military carried out multiple strikes on Russian aircraft during the week as part of a wider effort to undermine Russian air offensive capabilities. On 30 October, a Ukrainian drone attack destroyed a Russian Mi-8 military transport helicopter in Tarasivka in the occupied Luhansk region, while a Neptune missile attack destroyed two Su-34 Russian aircraft at an airbase in the Volgograd region a day earlier. These attacks are a continuation of a limited campaign to destroy Su-34 and Su-35 Russian jets, as well as helicopters earlier this month. Though the campaign will have a limited impact on Russia’s wider bombing campaign in Ukraine, which uses mostly uncrewed systems and ground-launched missile systems, it will reduce Russia’s ability to launch guided aerial bombs at front line regions, such as Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhia.

title: UNICEF South Sudan Humanitarian Situation Report No. 8, 1-30 September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Conflict and insecurity continued to drive displacement, with approximately 446,000 people displaced across South Sudan since the beginning of 2026, including more than 34,000 in Panyijiar and 24,000 in Ulang in September.
  • Food insecurity and acute malnutrition remained critical: In September, 8.99 million people faced acute food insecurity, while global acute malnutrition (GAM) rates among children under 5 exceeded 34 per cent in Ayod, Akobo and Nyirol. Meanwhile, severe drought affecting over 80 per cent of the country threatened agricultural production, livestock and household food security.
  • Cholera transmission declined, but active cases persisted, with 112,148 cases and 1,723 deaths reported by 30 September since the outbreak began in September 2024. Meanwhile, 77 access-related incidents were recorded in September, constraining humanitarian operations and essential service delivery.
  • The 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal remained 47 percent funded, with significant shortfalls in education, WASH and nutrition constraining the response amid rising humanitarian needs.

title: WFP Lao PDR Country Brief, November 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• In October, WFP, in partnership with the Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare, provided 570 mt of food to more than 36,000 people across 48 flood-affected villages in the northern Luang Namtha province. Families received rice, canned fish and vegetable oil to help meet their food needs for 30 days as they recovered from the floods.

• The Cost of Malnutrition study, jointly produced by the National Centre of Nutrition and WFP, indicates that child undernutrition imposes an economic burden equivalent to 5.2 percent of GDP, exceeding Lao PDR's 4.2 percent GDP growth rate and effectively eroding the gains from economic progress.

title: WFP Northern Nigeria - Situation Report #93 (October 2026)
content:
Situation Update

• October harvests are expected to improve food access for households with farmland across northern Nigeria. However, insecurity, repeated displacement and access constraints continue to restrict cultivation and the movement of produce to markets.

• Dry spells and a delayed peak in rainfall have increased agricultural production costs and damaged crop development across the region, further limiting food access and raising the risk of local production shortfalls.

• The latest report indicates that food inflation rose slightly in September 2026 compared with August but remained slightly below September 2025 levels.

• Persistently high food prices continue to erode purchasing power and limit food access despite seasonal improvements in food availability.

• Displaced and vulnerable households in conflict-affected northern Nigeria continue to face barriers to food and livelihoods, keeping humanitarian needs high despite the harvest.

title: Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak: Democratic Republic of the Congo | Kenya | Nigeria Weekly External Situation Report 25, Data as of 7 November 2026
content:
Event description

The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues at a high, sustained level of transmission, with no sign of decline: close to 390 confirmed cases were added during the reporting period and the national seven-day average has stayed between 65 and 67 cases per day. Nord-Kivu now contributes almost as many cases as Ituri and accounts for the entire increase observed over the last 21 days, while contact follow-up fell to its lowest level in weeks at the end of the period. The importation events in Kenya and Nigeria remain contained: no new case has been reported in Kenya since 19 October, six of the seven surviving patients have been discharged and the last contacts will complete monitoring on 11 November, while no secondary case has been identified in Nigeria, where contact monitoring is expected to end on 13 November. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, insecurity in Beni health zone in North Kivu and Bafwasende in Tshopo, health-worker strikes in Bas-Uélé and Tshopo and the continued suspension of response activities in Bafwasende constrain surveillance and response operations.

Democratic Republic of the Congo

As of 7 November 2026, the BVD outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has affected 67 health zones and 247 health areas across eight provinces; no new health zone was affected during the reporting period. Since External Situation Report #24, an additional 388 confirmed cases and 197 confirmed deaths have been reported, bringing the cumulative total to 10 920 confirmed cases, including 5 323 confirmed deaths [crude case fatality ratio (CFR) 48.7%]. Transmission remains highly heterogeneous across affected areas. Ituri continues to account for the largest proportion of cumulative confirmed cases (69.7%), although its relative contribution is declining, while Nord-Kivu (24.7% of cumulative cases; CFR 54.8%) accounted for 46.1% of the cases reported since the previous report, almost as many as Ituri (47.2%). Transmission persists at lower levels in Haut-Uélé (4.9% of new cases), Tshopo and Nord-Ubangi.

National daily incidence rose steadily from May to its highest levels in late July and mid-August, declined through late September and has fluctuated at a high plateau since early October. The seven-day moving average ranged between 65 and 67 confirmed cases per day during the reporting period (64.7 on 7 November, compared with 67.0 on 1 November and a late-October high of 76), still well below the mid-August peak of 94. Provincial trends continue to diverge. Ituri continues its slow decline from the late-July peak (seven-day average of 29 cases per day on 7 November, down from 31 on 1 November and 38 on 19 October), while Nord-Kivu has risen to 31 cases per day (up from 30 on 1 November and 26 on 19 October) and exceeded Ituri on several days of the period. Haut-Uélé remains stable at three to four cases per day, Tshopo reports sporadic cases (last case on 5 November) and Nord-Ubangi reported three further cases in Yakoma and Wapinda. Bas-Uélé, Sud-Kivu and Sud-Ubangi have reported no case in the last 21 days (Figures 1 and 2).

title: Ebola Outbreak, DRC and Region, Situation Report #15 (November 10, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • On May 15, the DRC declared an outbreak of Ebola virus disease (EVD), later confirmed to be caused by the Bundibugyo strain.
  • As November 9, 10,920 confirmed EVD cases and 5,323 confirmed deaths had been reported there.
  • On October 5, a case of imported EVD was confirmed in Kenya, where a patient had traveled from the DRC. There have been nine confirmed cases and two fatalities there.
  • On October 26, a case of EVD was confirmed in Nigeria, where the patient had traveled from Uganda. She was medically evacuated to Switzerland and is recovering.
  • No EVD cases have been confirmed in South Sudan or CAR, but risk of cross-border transmission remains high due to transient populations and porous borders with the DRC.
  • In the DRC, the outbreak remains centered in Ituri province, but cases have also been confirmed in Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, North Kivu, North Ubangi, South Kivu, South Ubangi and Tshopo provinces.
  • Uganda, which released its last confirmed case on July 16, has officially declared its outbreak over.

OUR RESPONSE

  • Across the region, we are providing case management, infection-prevention and control, screening and triage, risk communication and community engagement, training and preparedness planning.
  • We are supporting more than 41 facilities in the screening, identification and treatment of EVD.
  • Our supported sites in the DRC have conducted more than 1.2 million EVD screenings and provided treatment to 3,597 patients, including 1,076 confirmed cases.
  • We have so far trained 3,834 people in the DRC on EVD case management, response and transmission prevention.

With the support of the US Department of State, DG ECHO, and other donors, International Medical Corps teams across the region are actively responding to the outbreak and collaborating closely with ministries of health, key actors and response partners. International Medical Corps has used a hub-and-spoke model since the outbreak was declared to provide case-management support at designated treatment and transit facilities, strengthen IPC in referring health facilities, conduct screening and triage, support risk communication and community engagement in surrounding communities and train health workers on EVD response protocols. We continue to support screening and preparation efforts in Uganda, which has declared its outbreak over, and to prepare South Sudan for a possible outbreak there. Finally, we are participating in research trials for new therapeutics, working closely with a range of academic and health partners.
