title: Nigeria: Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe (BAY) states - Quarter 3 Situation Report, July - September 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Record Nigeria Humanitarian Fund (NHF) allocation helps avert food insecurity in north-east Nigeria, but overall funding shortfalls threaten gains.
  • Coordinated nutrition response expands lifesaving services in the Borno, Adamawa and Yobe (BAY) States with NHF support.
  • Cholera response curbs cases in north-east Nigeria.
  • OCHA Nigeria trains 90 Area-Based Coordinators in Borno State as transition to local humanitarian coordination gathers pace.
  • Non-State Armed Group (NSAG) attacks, displacement and rights violations deepen protection concerns in the BAY states.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Record NHF allocation helps avert food insecurity, but overall funding shortfalls threaten gains

A record allocation from the NHF has helped mitigate acute food insecurity in the BAY States, where conflict, displacement, economic pressures and climate shocks continue to drive humanitarian needs. However, persistent funding shortfalls beyond the NHF's scope and implementation period threaten to reverse recent gains.

In April, the NHF launched its largest-ever allocation of US$121.5 million to respond to immediate needs over six months in Borno and Yobe States as well as parts of north-west and north-central Nigeria. Funded by the United States, the allocation was disbursed at a critical moment, just before the peak of the lean and rainy seasons, with partners already exceeding the allocation target by August.

Food security was prioritized in the NHF allocation, with approximately $49 million - more than 60 per cent of the allocation - going to food interventions. Some 6.4 million people in the BAY states were projected to face acute food insecurity during the June to August lean season, according to the May Cadre Harmonisé update.

Through cash transfers, electronic vouchers and other emergency food support programmes, humanitarian partners helped vulnerable people access food during one of the most challenging periods of the year. In August alone, Food Security Sector partners reached more than 1 million people across the BAY States. Nearly 900,000 people received food assistance, primarily through cash and voucher programmes, while more than 270,000 people benefited from emergency agricultural livelihood support, including inputs (seeds, fertilizer), services and cash assistance aimed at restoring production. The World Food Programme (WFP) alone provided emergency food assistance to more than 740,000 people, reducing severe food consumption gaps and helping families meet immediate needs.

The rapid scale-up demonstrated the value of timely, flexible pooled funding and strong coordination among national and international partners.

Despite this critical work, the Food Security Sector warns that humanitarian needs remain immense. The underlying drivers including insecurity, displacement, restricted access to farmland, disrupted markets, rising food prices and declining purchasing power, persist. Without additional funding, the food security gains achieved through the NHF allocation may prove challenging to maintain.

Coordinated nutrition response expands lifesaving services with support from the NHF

Over the reporting period, humanitarian partners expanded malnutrition prevention and treatment services, helping hundreds of thousands of vulnerable children and mothers access lifesaving nutrition support during the peak malnutrition season.

The scale-up, supported by both NHF funding and bilateral support from other donors, strengthened both prevention and treatment for acute malnutrition in some of the most vulnerable and hard-to-reach communities in Borno and Yobe states.

As malnutrition is driven by multiple interconnected factors, humanitarian partners also scaled up health, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) and protection. UNICEF delivered integrated nutrition and WASH support to 930,000 vulnerable children and caregivers over six months, while other organizations expanded essential services across frontline LGAs.

Although the nutrition situation across the BAY States remained generally stable in July and August, humanitarian partners warned of deterioration risks due to access constraints, commodity shortages and uneven service quality. May to September nutrition projections by the Nutrition Sector identified several high-risk LGAs where sustained treatment and prevention programmes were needed to prevent further deterioration.

Through NHF-funded interventions, nine humanitarian organizations worked alongside Government authorities to expand integrated nutrition services in Borno and Yobe States. These included the Centre for Advocacy, Transparency, and Accountability Initiative, FHI 360, Future Resilience and Development Foundation, INTERSOS, Life at Best Development Initiative, Prosper Global (Mercy Corps), Save the Children International the International Rescue Committee and UNICEF.

In Borno State, more than 79,500 severely malnourished children were treated through outpatient therapeutic programme (OTP) and stabilization centre (SC) services in July and August. Partners also screened nearly 359,000 children for acute malnutrition and provided skilled counselling on maternal, infant and young child nutrition to more than 132,000 pregnant and breastfeeding women. Targeted supplementary feeding programmes continued in several locations.

In Yobe, the State Primary Health Care Board, supported by UNICEF and humanitarian partners, sustained integrated management of acute malnutrition services across all 17 LGAs in the State. Nearly 25,000 severely malnourished children were admitted for lifesaving treatment, while more than 44,000 pregnant and breastfeeding women received counselling and support to improve infant feeding and nutrition practices.

In Adamawa, more than 13,700 severely malnourished children were admitted for treatment through coordinated interventions led by State authorities and humanitarian organizations. Although nutrition conditions in the State remained comparatively stable compared to parts of Borno and Yobe, partners prioritized prevention, surveillance and resilience-building activities.

Despite these achievements, significant challenges remained. Several LGAs in central and northern Borno continued to face elevated levels of acute malnutrition, while access limitations in Abadam, Guzamala and Kukawa LGAs constrained surveillance, response planning and service delivery. In Yobe, severe nutrition concerns persisted in Geidam, Damaturu, Gujba, Gulani, Tarmuwa, Machina and Yusufari LGAs, underscoring the continued need for robust treatment and prevention services.

Operational gaps also affected the quality and continuity of integrated health and nutrition programming. Across multiple locations, shortages of essential medicines, including antimalarial drugs and Amoxicillin, affected treatment services. Facilities also reported shortages of nutrition data tools, registers and reporting materials, while weak supervision and limited operational support in some areas constrained service quality. In Adamawa, critical supplies such as Vitamin A and Albendazole were insufficient ahead of planned health campaigns.

Despite efforts by humanitarian partners, needs continue to exceed available resources. Under the 2026 Nigeria HNRP, the Nutrition Sector requires $94.4 million to meet urgent needs in the BAY States. As of 16 October, $57.6 million had been received.

title: Kenya Population Influx - Moyale/Mandera: DREF Operation (MDRKE075)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

22-10-2026

What happened, where and when?

Armed conflict between the Oromia and Somali communities residing in Ethiopia has resulted from a dispute over administrative control of a contested area between the Oromia Region and the Somali Region of Ethiopia. The conflict has led to insecurity, population displacement, and humanitarian needs among affected communities.

Reports indicate that tensions intensified after authorities from the Somali Region opened an administrative office and raised the regional flag in the disputed area, triggering armed clashes between Oromia-affiliated militia and Somali regional security forces. The death of a 13-year-old girl during the violence reportedly fuelled further unrest.

Clashes intensified from Wednesday night, 21 October 2026, with active exchange of gunshots continuing in Moyale, Ethiopia. As tensions escalated across the border, Kenya began experiencing an influx of people into Moyale Town on the Kenyan side on 22nd October 2026.

The sudden displacement, exposure to violence and insecurity, separation from family and community networks, and uncertainty about safety and return may have significant psychosocial consequences for affected individuals and families. These considerations should be included in ongoing needs assessments and response planning.

As of 25 October, Kenya had received 15,240 people fleeing the conflict in Ethiopia, including elderly persons, women, and children. Of these, 10,950 people are accommodated across six displacement sites: Somare (503 people), Sessi (799), Taqwa (700), Manyatta Burji Madarasa (6,321), St. Mary’s Catholic (317), and Arosa Mixed School (2,310). The remaining 4,290 people are being hosted by local communities in Moyale and surrounding areas. Population movement into these areas remains ongoing, with additional arrivals expected as the situation continues to evolve.

The conflict has resulted in a localized attack on the Oramia community in Mandera town. 176 people have moved to the Mandera Police Station for safety, fearing retaliatory attacks. This indicates a possible population movement situation within Mandera.

Sporadic gunfire continues to be reported on the Ethiopian side of Moyale, disrupting cross-border movement, trade, transport, customs operations and other public services. Continued insecurity raises concerns over further displacement into Kenya should the situation persist.

On 22nd October 2026, the County Government of Marsabit had written to the Kenya Red Cross seeking support in the Humanitarian response.

Population movements into Kenya remain ongoing, with a large number of new arrivals continuing to cross the border. The current figures reflect only those individuals registered by KRCS in the established displacement sites, while others remain unregistered and are sheltering in public places and other community facilities. As a result, the actual number of people on the move will be much higher than the figures currently recorded, with arrivals continuing as the conflict persists.

title: Dominican Republic: Hurricane Melissa - DREF Final Report (MDRDO019)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

23-10-2025

What happened, where and when?

From 21 October 2025 onward, the Dominican Republic experienced heavy rainfall, flooding and landslides as outer bands of Hurricane Melissa impacted the southern and central provinces. The country’s Emergency Operations Center (EOC) declared yellow and green alerts in 22 provinces and the National District, and later red alerts in Barahona, Pedernales, Independencia and Bahoruco, while yellow alerts covered San José de Ocoa, Elías Pina, Dajabón, Azua, San Cristóbal, Peravia, Monte Plata, San Juan and Monte Cristi.

Intense rain-induced flooding and landslides severely disrupted water supply and essential services—dozens of aqueducts were out of operation, and several health facilities experienced outages. Based on preliminary estimates the population exposed to the event is approximately 1.8 million people.

The disruption of safe water access and power outages heightened the risk of waterborne diseases; ongoing soil saturation and forecast for further rainbands maintained an elevated risk of renewed flooding and landslides.

title: Burundi Flood Imminent Crisis 2026 - Imminent DREF Operation (MDRBI028)
content:
Scenario analysis

When and where is the hazard expected to happen?

The seasonal rainfall forecast for September–December 2026, released by the Institut Géographique du Burundi (IGEBU) in late August, indicated an increased likelihood of above-average rainfall across Burundi. This outlook is reinforced by IGEBU’s weekly meteorological bulletin valid from 27 October to 3 November 2026, which forecasts rainfall exceeding 200 mm in parts of the natural regions of Mugamba, Migwa, Kirimiro, Bweru and Buyogoma, and rainfall ranging from 100 to 200 mm across the rest of the country. Above-normal rainfall is expected across all natural regions, with an explicit risk of flooding in low-lying areas.

The regional forecast issued by ICPAC for 27 October–3 November 2026 corroborates this national outlook, indicating that above-normal rainfall is expected in Burundi and neighbouring countries. Taken together, these forecasts identify 27 October to 3 November 2026 as the forecast period of concern, during which persistent and heavy rainfall may increase the likelihood of flooding and related hazards.

The expected rainfall poses a significant risk to low-lying and flood-prone areas, particularly the Imbo natural region, including Bujumbura, where urbanization and limited drainage capacity can contribute to surface flooding during intense or prolonged rainfall. In addition, heavy rainfall over the elevated and sloping areas of the Mirwa natural region may generate substantial surface runoff towards the Imbo plains, increasing river levels and the risk of riverine flooding downstream. The main areas of concern are therefore the forecast high-rainfall zones in Mugamba, Migwa, Kirimiro, Bweru and Buyogoma, as well as low-altitude areas across the country, particularly flood-prone areas of Imbo and Bujumbura.

The anticipated impacts include flooding of homes, roads and public infrastructure; inundation of agricultural land; disruption of transport and access to essential services; and possible displacement of vulnerable households. Saturated soils on steep slopes may also trigger landslides, potentially obstructing watercourses and aggravating downstream flooding.

Furthermore, flooding may contaminate watersources and increase the risk of waterborne diseases, including cholera and diarrhoeal diseases, in the context of the ongoing cholera epidemic. In Bujumbura, intense rainfall may overwhelm urban drainage systems, resulting in localized flooding and disruption to critical infrastructure.

The forecasted period of potential impact is 27 October–3 November 2026, with priority attention required in the high-rainfall areas identified by IGEBU and in low-lying, poorly drained and flood-prone locations, particularly in the Imbo region and Bujumbura.

Continued monitoring of national and regional forecasts is essential to refine the geographical targeting and inform timely preparedness and early action.

title: UNICEF Djibouti Humanitarian Flash Update No. 5 (Refugee influx from Yemen), 2 November 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Since September, 3,836 people have arrived from Yemen, 52 per cent of them children. No new arrivals were reported during the reporting period.
  • Heavy rainfall on 24 October damaged shelters and food supplies in Markazi refugee village, further worsening already precarious living conditions.
  • An acute watery diarrhoea (AWD) outbreak has resulted in 62 cases and three deaths. Inadequate sanitation and overcrowding continue to pose serious public health risks. UNICEF is supporting the Government's AWD response and essential WASH services.
  • A total of 21 separated children have been identified. UNICEF continues to support case management and psychosocial activities, reaching 781 children through child-friendly spaces to date.
  • UNICEF-supported services have identified 115 severe acute malnutrition cases, while only 34 per cent of school-aged refugee children are currently enrolled in school.
  • UNICEF requires US$3 million to support up to 10,000 people over six months, with only 12 per cent of funding secured.

title: UNHCR Regional Bureau for Asia and Pacific: Myanmar Situation Update (Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Myanmar, and Thailand) Aug – Sept 2026
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT

Ongoing conflict, human rights violations, discrimination and natural disasters continued to drive humanitarian needs in Myanmar. By endSeptember, an estimated 4 million people were internally displaced, many with limited access to essential services. Monsoon flooding further compounded the humanitarian situation, affecting more than 600,000 people across the country, including displaced communities. Sagaing, Magway and Mandalay were among the hardest hit, with flooding also reported in Rakhine, Kayin, Kachin and Ayeyarwady.

Funding shortfalls in Bangladesh continued to constrain key services and heighten protection risks in the camps, with critical gaps in protection, shelter and site management. UNHCR phased out of public health and nutrition programming and handed over water, sanitation and health responsibilities in the Ukhiya camps. These changes form part of broader efforts to improve efficiency but have not offset the impact of funding cuts. Despite broader efficiency measures, reduced assistance has increased refugees’ reliance on negative coping mechanisms, including gambling, child labour, child marriage and human trafficking. The protection environment for Myanmar refugees and asylum-seekers in India continued to be shaped by security considerations and administrative measures in border areas. UNHCR engaged with the Government of India, UN agencies and other stakeholders to address the needs of Myanmar arrivals in the north-east.

title: Attacks on Health Care Bi-Monthly News Brief, 16 - 31 October 2026
content:
The impact of violence on health care on patients
Violence against health care has devastating consequences for patients, extending far beyond those directly injured or killed in violence: many are unable to access essential medical care, experience interruptions to ongoing treatment, lose access to medicines and medical supplies, or face delays in emergency care. The damage to health facilities, disruption of services and loss of health workers can have lasting effects, leading to preventable illness, disability and death. For many patients, the consequences persist long after the initial attack.

Patient killings in attacks on health care: the gap between perception and reality
Media coverage can shape perceptions of attacks on health care, particularly when it focuses on incidents involving large numbers of patients killed. Such attacks often attract international attention and prompt investigations because of the horrific nature of the attack. While these incidents are particularly disturbing and important to document, they are not necessarily representative of the wider pattern of violence against health care nor how violence against health care impacts patients. Insecurity Insight's monitoring of attacks on health care recorded 287 attacks on health care in which 1,198 patients were killed between January 2016 and September 2026.1 These incidents accounted for less than 2% of all recorded attacks on health care during a decade of data. Approximately 52% of all patients were killed in just seven attacks. This highlights an important distinction between the visibility of high-fatality attacks characterised by horrendous violence against patients and their frequency within the large scale of violence against health care. Although attacks resulting in large numbers of patient killings receive significant attention, they represent a small proportion of recorded incidents. The vast majority of attacks do not result in patients being killed but they contribute to the destruction of the health system that deprives patients of access to care contributing to the growing burden of excess deaths during conflict.

The following examples illustrate the nature of some of high-fatality patient incidents:

  • 16 March 2026, Kabul, Afghanistan: An airstrike struck Omid Addiction Treatment Hospital, a two-storey, 2,000-bed facility providing treatment and rehabilitation for people with drug dependence. The attack took place at around 21:00, while patients were inside the facility, including in sleeping quarters and communal areas. Three strikes hit different parts of the complex, causing extensive destruction and fires. Families gathered outside the hospital searching for relatives, while survivors described the difficulty of escaping through smoke and debris. Over 200 people were killed and 122 injured, the vast majority among patients.
  • 14 November 2025, North Kivu, DRC: The ADF attacked Byambwe Reference Health Centre overnight, killing over 20 patients and looting medicines and medical equipment. Two health workers were also reportedly abducted. Parts of the facility, including the maternity ward, were set on fire, leaving the health centre inoperable.
  • 28 October 2025, El Fasher, North Darfur, Sudan: The RSF raided Saudi Maternity Hospital, the city's last partially functioning hospital and a critical facility for women and other patients. More than 460 patients and their companions were reportedly killed. Those seeking medical care, including women and children, were among the victims. RSF fighters reportedly entered the wards and killed patients, their companions and medical personnel. Doctors reportedly removed their white coats in an attempt to avoid being identified and targeted. Children as young as eight were among those killed. Six health workers were also forcibly taken away. Find out what people said on social media in the aftermath of the hospital attack here.

These incidents illustrate horrendous violence, but their exceptional scale should not obscure the broader pattern. High-fatality attacks account for a small proportion of recorded incidents, while violence against health care occurs across a much wider range of circumstances that cumulatively undermine the ability to deliver care. Focusing primarily on incidents with large numbers of patient deaths risks overlooking the frequency and cumulative impact of the many other attacks that disrupt health services, endanger patients and undermine access to care and drive up mortality.

title: WFP Kyrgyz Republic Country Brief, November 2026
content:
• 45,021 people assisted in Oct 2026 (59% female)
  • 2,273 mt of food distributed in Oct 2026

KEY HIGHLIGHTS

title: Attacks on Health Care in Sudan, 16-31 October 2026
content:
Data by Insecurity Insight shows that since fighting started between the SAF and RSF in April 2023 and 30 September 2026, 807 attacks on health care took place across Sudan, with over 55% of attacks attributed to the RSF. Health facilities were attacked and damaged at least 232 times while 222 health workers were killed, 144 arrested and 16 kidnapped.

Since January 2026, reported incidents in the Kordofan states accounted for 51% of all incidents, reflecting the intensification of fighting between conflict parties and the threats to health care delivery, health workers and patients. In the first nine months of 2026, 45 incidents affecting health care were reported across the three Kordofan states, exceeding the annual totals recorded in 2025 (35), 2024 (7) and 2023 (24). Of the 45 incidents in 2026, 51% recorded aircraft or drone strikes which damaged health facilities and killed and injured health workers. Most of these incidents were attributed to the RSF, particularly in North Kordofan, and to RSF-allied groups, including the Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North, in South Kordofan. Incidents attributed to the SAF were less frequent and occurred predominantly in West Kordofan. Health facilities were also looted and on at least one occasion, forcibly repurposed, further undermining access to essential health care for civilians. In one such incident in West Kordofan, the RSF reportedly converted a hospital into a field hospital to treat its own members, forcibly evacuating patients in the process, depriving civilians of access to critical medical care at a time when conflict-related needs are acute and health services are already under severe strain.

View the incidents on our interactive map. Download the data. Data is continuously updated and numbers may change if/ when further information is made available. See here for methodology. For data enquiries, please get in touch.

title: Rasuwa Flood Response 2026, Situation Report 12
content: One month after the devastating flash flood, thousands of people remain displaced, and uncertainty remains about the future. The flood response has entered a longer-term relief and early recovery phase, while search and rescue efforts continue in parallel with initiatives to restore access, basic services, and support for displaced and affected families. According to the latest update from the NDRRMA, 1,455 people have lost their lives, 5,285 remain missing, 13,795 have been rescued. To date, authorities have identified and handed over 112 bodies to their families. Currently, 1,085 people are taking shelter in 17 holding centers across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts, including 843 people in 9 centers in Rasuwa, 121 people in 4 centers in Nuwakot, and 121 people in 4 centers in Dhading. Recognizing the need for greater flexibility and dignity among displaced families, the Government of Nepal will provide monthly cash assistance to those who choose not to stay in holding centers. The support will help cover accommodation and livelihood expenses for up to six months, or until alternative housing is arranged. Each family who do not wish to stay in holding centers and until alternative housing arrangement will receive NPR 15,000 per month for families up to four members, with an additional NPR 2,000 per month for every family member beyond four, enabling families to make decisions that best suit their circumstances during recovery.

title: Republic of Haiti: Health Cluster Bulletin #2 (April – May – June 2026)
content:
During the second quarter of 2026, ten major incidents involving armed violence led to the displacement of 50,867 people, a 19% increase compared to the previous quarter. After several months of severe deterioration in the Artibonite and Centre departments, the West department once again became the epicenter of new displacements, accounting for 64% of all movements recorded during the period—primarily due to armed violence in the commune of Cité Soleil.

A decline in suspected diphtheria cases has been observed starting from the 21st epidemiological week. A total of 42 suspected cases have been reported across 15 sites for internally displaced persons (IDPs) in the West Department (Cité Soleil, Delmas, Pétion-Ville, Port-au-Prince) since January 2026.

The cholera outbreak has been steadily declining since its resurgence in October 2022. Following a peak of 3,683 suspected weekly cases in 2023, transmission dropped by nearly 80% in 2024. This downward trend continued into 2025 (with 85 cumulative cases recorded during the same period) and into 2026, with 44 suspected cases reported as of July 18 (a 48% decrease). Transmission levels currently remain low and stable, reflecting successful control efforts. Maintaining surveillance and response capabilities remains crucial to preventing a resurgence, given the active circulation of Vibrio and the persistence of risk factors for transmission.

title: UNFPA Sudan Situation Report (September 2026)
content:
In September, conflict in Blue Nile State intensified and spread to the southern parts of the state, displacing 52,629 people and placing further strain on health, protection and other essential services. Nearly 12,000 displaced people are sheltering in severely overcrowded schools with limited or no access to sanitation, electricity and other basic services.

Insecurity across the three Kordofan States, including drone strikes and fighting around El Obeid, Bara, Dilling, Nuhud and Abu Zabad, continued to drive displacement. According to the Sudan Health Cluster, cholera outbreak also persisted, with 1,501 cases and 92 deaths reported in North Kordofan and 1,299 cases and 115 deaths in South Kordofan as of 30 September. Safety audits and inter-agency assessments in North Darfur, North Kordofan and West Darfur found that gender-based violence (GBV) risks remain severe and continue to intensify.

UNFPA’s 2026 appeal of US$129.2 million is only around 40 per cent funded, leaving a gap of US$78 million, and current response efforts remain insufficient to meet the needs of women and girls. In September, UNFPA and partners delivered more than 145,000 sexual and reproductive health services across 17 states via healthcare facilities and mobile teams. Additionally, UNFPA reached some 93,000 people with essential GBV prevention and response services, including safe spaces, psychosocial support, and dignity kit distributions.

title: Monthly Bulletin for Consumer Price Index and Inflation in Syria - April 2026 [EN/AR]
content:
The April 2026 Consumer Price and Inflation Bulletin in Syria shows that inflationary pressures are no longer driven only by price movements in consumer goods, but have become more clearly linked to the restructuring of public utilities and services, and to attempts to finance the fiscal deficit through pricing and revenue-collection tools that are reflected in the cost of living and production. The Y-o-Y inflation rate reached 27.5 per cent, while the general CPI rose from 918 points (2021 base year) in March 2026 to 950 points in April 2026, recording M-o-M inflation of 3.5 per cent.

The data indicate that M-o-M inflation was concentrated more in services and non-tradable sectors than in food commodities. Education recorded the highest monthly increase at 6.3 per cent, followed by housing, water, electricity and gas at 6.0 per cent, and then household equipment and miscellaneous goods and services at 5.1 per cent each. Although food increased only slightly, by 0.4 per cent, housing and energy remained the main driver of inflation, contributing around 75.7 per cent of M-o-M inflation. This confirms that the main source of pressure in April was the cost of basic services and energy, rather than food alone.

April’s fiscal and monetary policies deepened this trend. The imposition of a tax advance on imports, the continued gap between the official and parallel exchange rates, and the requirement to deliver some remittances in SYP came within the context of the authorities’ efforts to strengthen revenues and control foreign-currency flows. However, these measures transfer part of the cost of fiscal and monetary adjustment to producers, importers and consumers through higher final costs, precautionary pricing, and constraints on operational liquidity.

The bulletin also reveals the continued spatial variation in prices. Housing, water, electricity and fuel recorded the highest coefficient of variation across governorates, followed by education and transport, indicating that local services and public utilities have become among the main sources of price disparity across governorates and monetary spaces. Lattakia recorded the highest M-o-M inflation rate at 6.9 per cent, followed by Aleppo at 5.5 per cent, Homs at 5.4 per cent, and Dara’a at 5.3 per cent.

At the living-conditions level, the abject poverty line for a household reached SYP 3.34 million per month, while the lower poverty line reached SYP 5.26 million, and the upper poverty line reached SYP 7.26 million. The wages of university-educated public-sector employees cover only 33.9 per cent of the abject poverty line and only 15.6 per cent of the upper poverty line, while private-sector wages cover 38.5 per cent of the abject poverty line.

The recent increases in fuel and bread prices are likely to generate a new inflationary wave in the coming months, potentially raising the upper poverty line to more than SYP 7.55 million per month. This indicates that the announced nominal wage increase, even once disbursed, will remain limited in impact unless it is linked to the cost of living and direct social protection policies.

title: Monthly Bulletin for Consumer Price Index and Inflation in Syria - May 2026 [EN/AR]
content:
Executive summary

The results of the Consumer Price and Inflation Bulletin in Syria for May 2026 indicate an acceleration in inflationary pressures, coinciding with the repricing of fuel and the adjustment of the weight of the bread bundle, and the associated increase in transportation, production, and consumption costs. The general Consumer Price Index rose from 716.4 points in May 2025 to 1,002 points in May 2026, recording a Y-o-Y inflation rate of 39.9 per cent. On a monthly basis, the index increased from 945.1 points in April to 1,002 points in May, representing an M-o-M inflation rate of approximately 6 per cent.

Monthly pressures were concentrated in the groups most closely associated with pricing decisions. Prices in the transportation group increased by 17.6 per cent following the adjustment of petroleum product prices on 7 May and the resulting rise in the operating costs of transport services and the transportation of goods. Similarly, reducing the weight of the bread bundle from 1.2 kilograms to 1.05 kilograms, while maintaining its price at SYP 4,000, raised the implicit price per kilogram by approximately 14.3 per cent, from about SYP 3,333 to around SYP 3,810. The decision therefore constituted an effective increase in the price of bread despite the unchanged nominal price of the bundle. The significance of the May shock lies in the fact that it resulted not only from general market developments, but also from direct administrative pricing decisions affecting fuel and bread. Households, particularly poor households dependent on locally earned wages, consequently bore a double burden: higher transportation and energy costs on the one hand, and a higher cost of basic food on the other.

On a Y-o-Y basis, the housing, water, electricity, gas, and other fuels group recorded the highest increase among the main consumption groups, at 58.5 per cent, driven by a 65.7 per cent increase in rents and a 48.9 per cent rise in electricity, gas, and other fuel prices. This reflects the extension of inflationary pressures to essential expenditures that households have limited scope to reduce or forgo, particularly housing, energy, and transportation.

Price levels and living costs also continued to vary across governorates, reflecting differences in energy sources, pricing systems, transportation and supply costs, multiple monetary and administrative spheres, and weak market integration. The abject poverty line for the reference household reached approximately SYP 3.437 million per month, compared with SYP 5.407 million for the lower poverty line and SYP 7.464 million for the upper poverty line. At the governorate level, Damascus recorded the highest abject poverty line, at approximately SYP 4.742 million, while As-Sweida recorded the lowest, at approximately SYP 2.176 million.

title: Monthly Bulletin for Consumer Price Index and Inflation in Syria - June 2026 [EN/AR]
content:
Executive Summary

  • The Consumer Price Index in Syria increased by 0.8 per cent during June 2026 compared to May. This rise was the result of opposite trends. Pressures from rising housing, energy, transportation and education costs are offset by seasonal declines in food prices, especially vegetables. However, this slowdown in the monthly inflation rate compared to the previous month should not be interpreted as a general stability in prices. Annual inflation remained at 40.5 per cent, and the housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuel groups remained the highest inflation group on an annual basis at 59.8 per cent. Therefore, the decline in the monthly inflation rate in June reflects a temporary balance between seasonal declines in food and continuing increases in housing, energy, and transportation, more than it reflects a sustainable improvement in the cost of living.
  • Al-Hasakeh recorded an exceptional trend compared to the rest of the governorates, as its monthly inflation rate reached 24.8 per cent. This increase was mainly linked to the sharp increase in electricity tariffs and the prices of some energy sources, in the context of bringing local pricing systems closer to the tariffs approved in SYP-Governed Areas (SYP-GA). Al-Hasakeh clearly shows the dangers of unifying or approximating pricing systems without gradual implementation or safeguards. The increase in electricity tariffs and free diesel prices, along with the disruption in fuel availability, led to the shock being transmitted to transportation, water, rents, and services. Thus, the governorate has become a revealing case of what can happen when the cost of energy is transferred to consumers and producers more quickly than the ability of local incomes to adapt.
  • Inflation moved during the month under the influence of two opposite factors: The rise in housing, energy and transportation costs pushed the general price level higher, while the decline in vegetable prices by 19.5 per cent contributed to reducing inflation, as a result of the expansion of domestic supply during the production season.
  • In the exchange market, the average price of the dollar in the parallel market increased by about 2.7 per cent during June compared to May, despite the noticeable improvement in the value of the lira during the last week of the month. This late improvement was not enough to change the trend that prevailed in the exchange market during most days of the month.
  • In contrast, wages remained far from keeping pace with the cost of living; The average monthly wage of a university employee in the public sector covered only 44.0 per cent of the family’s abject poverty line. This reflects the continuing wide gap between incomes and prices, and the resulting pressure on families to reduce their consumption or rely on additional sources of income and external transfers.
  • The upper poverty line for a family of five was about SYP 7.47 million per month, which confirms that most wage earners remain unable to secure a basic standard of living. The comparison between incomes and poverty lines also shows that limited inflation during the month does not mean an actual improvement in living conditions, in light of the accumulation of previous increases and the continued weakness of purchasing power.

title: Monthly Bulletin for Consumer Price Index and Inflation in Syria - July 2026 [EN/AR]
content:
Executive Summary

  • Syria’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) declined by 1.9 per cent in July 2026 compared with June, falling from 1010 to 991 points. This decline reflected lower prices in five consumption groups, most notably tobacco, transport, housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels, and food and non-alcoholic beverages, against increases in six groups. The decline did not, however, represent a general improvement in living conditions: the overall price level remained 24.8 per cent higher than in July 2025 and was nearly ten times its level in the 2021 base year.
  • July was marked by a widening gap between official prices and the actual cost of obtaining goods and services. Lower official prices for some petroleum products and the appreciation of the SYP helped reduce the transport and energy indices. However, persistent supply shortages, congestion at fuel stations and high black-market prices limited the extent to which these declines translated into lower transport, production and service costs. Al-Hasakeh provided the clearest example, as shortages of subsidised diesel for public services continued to disrupt generators, bakeries, mills, water stations and local transport.
  • The month also revealed a clear divergence between falling prices for pulses, vegetables and some imported goods, on the one hand, and rising prices for meat, milk and dairy products, on the other. This suggests that food-price deflation was driven mainly by seasonal factors or lower prices for certain imports, rather than by a structural improvement in food security or household purchasing power.
  • The decline in the transport and energy indices did not reflect genuine stability in the fuel market. Repeated adjustments to official prices coincided with persistent supply shortages, congestion at fuel stations and high black-market prices. The effects were particularly severe in Al-Hasakeh, where shortages of subsidised diesel for public services disrupted generators, bakeries, mills, water stations and local transport, limiting the effect of official price reductions on production and service costs.
  • On the monetary front, the Syrian Pound (SYP) appreciated in the parallel market: the average United States Dollar (USD) exchange rate fell from approximately SYP 14001 in June to SYP 13215 in July, while the official rate remained at SYP 12250, narrowing the gap between the two rates to about 7.9 per cent. Nevertheless, the stronger exchange rate did not eliminate price disparities across governorates, particularly in transport, housing and energy, where prices remained closely linked to fuel availability, pricing arrangements and local operating costs.

title: Monthly Bulletin for Consumer Price Index and Inflation in Syria - August 2026 [EN/AR]
content:
Executive Summary

  • Syria’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose by 1.8 per cent in August 2026 compared with July, from 991.5 to 1008.9 points. It approached its June level after July’s decline. Prices rose in nine consumption groups and fell in tobacco and recreation and culture. The general price level remained around 26 per cent above August 2025 and exceeded ten times its level in the 2021 base year, confirming continued pressure on household purchasing power.
  • Food and non-alcoholic beverages; housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels; and transport led the increase, contributing approximately 0.824, 0.521 and 0.319 percentage points respectively. Food and non-alcoholic beverage prices rose by 2.7 per cent, with increases in meat, dairy products, eggs, pulses and vegetables. Transport rose by 4.8 per cent. Inflation was thus concentrated in basic needs on which households find it difficult to cut spending without affecting their diets, mobility and access to services.
  • Rising household needs coincided with a cut in industrial fuel oil prices, while some wheat and cotton producers continued to face payment delays. This shows how economic policy affects groups differently: enterprises may benefit from a cheaper input, while farmers bear the cost of waiting for payment and financing their obligations. Transport development and financial sector modernisation offer future opportunities, but their effects depend on implementation and access to services. Who benefits, and when those benefits reach them, therefore needs to be monitored.
  • The average parallel-market USD exchange rate fell from approximately SYP 13215 in July to SYP 13171 in August, or 0.3 per cent, although it rose by 0.5 per cent between the start and end of August. The remittance rate remained at SYP 12250 per USD. The average USD rate against the Turkish lira (TL) rose by 2.4 per cent. Inflation measured in TL reached 3.5 per cent in Idleb and 2.5 per cent in Aleppo countryside, above the rate in Türkiye. This shows how currency movements and imports interact with supply conditions and local costs in Syria.
  • Spatial price dispersion varied markedly across consumption groups. Housing, water, electricity and fuels had the highest unweighted mean of item-level coefficients of variation at 0.460, followed by education and health at approximately 0.404 and 0.403. Communications recorded around 0.041. These values reflect geographical differences in item prices within each group and confirm differences in the cost of basic needs and services.
  • The household abject poverty line reached approximately SYP 3.46 million per month, the lower line SYP 5.44 million and the upper line SYP 7.51 million. A public sector university graduate’s wage covered only 43.5 per cent of the abject poverty line, compared with 78.5 per cent for a shop worker. A civil society university graduate’s wage slightly exceeded the lower line but remained below the upper line. These findings underline the need to link wage and social protection policies to local living costs, expedite payments to producers, and ensure that easier access to energy, finance and trade improves household incomes and their ability to meet their needs.

title: Monthly Bulletin for Consumer Price Index and Inflation in Syria - September 2026 [EN/AR]
content:
Executive Summary

  • Syria’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose by 8.1 per cent in September 2026 compared with August, from 1008.9 to 1090.4 points. Annual inflation reached approximately 34.1 per cent. Prices increased in all main consumption groups and all fourteen governorates, bringing the general price level to around 10.9 times its level in the 2021 base year. Higher fuel prices drove this acceleration as their effects spread to living, production and service costs.
  • Inflation was concentrated in housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels, which added approximately 5.09 percentage points to the overall rate, followed by transport at around 1.99 percentage points and food and non-alcoholic beverages at around 0.61 percentage points. Together, these three groups accounted for approximately 94.9 per cent of monthly inflation. Transport prices rose by 30 per cent, and housing, water and energy by 11 per cent, including a 28.9 per cent increase in electricity, gas and other fuels. Food prices rose by 2 per cent. These increases affected needs on which households find it difficult to cut spending, as well as inputs essential to production and service provision.
  • Faster price increases coincided with the introduction of new fuel prices on 13 September, adding pressure to living, production and service costs. Comparisons between local prices and international refined product benchmarks require common currencies, reference periods and conversion methods. Such comparisons alone cannot establish import costs or profit margins. Assessing the fiscal and social effects of the decision requires considering suppliers’ revenues alongside the costs of operating public facilities and the burdens on households and enterprises. It also requires disclosure of the components of pricing and the use of any additional resources generated.
  • Quneitra recorded the highest monthly inflation rate among governorates at 11.2 per cent, followed by Ar-Raqqa at 10.2 per cent and Hama at 9.5 per cent. Idleb recorded the lowest rate at 3.4 per cent. The gap between the highest and lowest rates was 7.8 percentage points. Analysis of spatial price dispersion found that housing, water, electricity and fuels had the highest unweighted mean of item-level coefficients of variation, at approximately 0.471, followed by education and health at 0.394 and 0.388, compared with 0.038 for communication. These results show differences in price changes and dispersion across areas. Higher inflation in a governorate does not necessarily mean that it has the highest living costs.
  • The average parallel-market USD exchange rate rose to approximately SYP 13436, up by 2 per cent from August. It also rose by 4.8 per cent between the beginning and end of September. The official rate and the remittance and cash exchange rate remained at SYP 12250 per USD, leaving a gap of around 9.7 per cent between these rates and the average parallel-market rate. The Syrian pound depreciated more rapidly after fuel prices were raised, although establishing a causal relationship requires further analysis. The average USD exchange rate against the Turkish lira (TL) rose by 1.5 per cent. Inflation measured in Turkish lira reached 3.4 per cent in Idleb and 6.3 per cent in Aleppo countryside, compared with 1.84 per cent in Türkiye. This underlines the role of local supply, production, transport and service conditions in explaining price movements alongside changes in the currency’s value.
  • Comparison with August shows that nominal wage increases for the three reference categories did not offset September’s price increases. Using the national CPI as an illustrative benchmark, the real value of a university graduate’s public sector wage fell by approximately 7.4 per cent, a shop worker’s wage by 4.5 per cent and a university graduate’s civil society sector wage by 5.0 per cent. These results distinguish nominal wage increases from gains in purchasing power. Assessing the effects on workers nevertheless requires accounting for the currency in which wages are paid, the cost of needs where they live, deductions, and the regularity of work and wage payments.
  • The household abject poverty line reached approximately SYP 3.71 million per month, the lower line around SYP 5.84 million and the upper line around SYP 8.06 million. A university graduate’s public sector wage covered only 40.6 per cent of the abject poverty line, compared with 75.5 per cent for a shop worker. Even a university graduate’s civil society sector wage, which provided the highest coverage among the three categories, fell slightly short of the lower poverty line and covered 71.9 per cent of the upper line. These results show how little one wage can cover of a household’s needs. Protecting wages and employment, adapting assistance to local living costs and household resources, and ensuring affordable energy and services are therefore central to the response to the price shock.

title: UNHCR Romania Ukraine Refugee Situation Weekly Update #221 - 9 November 2026
content:
Highlights

On 5–6 November, UNHCR, jointly with the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) and the Council of Europe’s Intercultural Cities Programme, organized a two-day training in Bucharest on good practices in migrant and refugee integration for local authorities in Romania and the Republic of Moldova. The event brought together over 25 representatives of local authorities, UN agencies, NGOs and refugee-led organizations to strengthen local capacities and facilitate cross-border exchange on inclusive integration approaches. Sessions covered access to education, employment, housing and healthcare, intercultural inclusion, international protection and coordination among local actors. The initiative contributed to strengthening local partnerships for refugee inclusion.

UNHCR met with Mr. Radu-Adrian Pau, the newly appointed Prefect of Timiș County, who highlighted the importance of the ETC and acknowledged UNHCR’s contribution to supporting the county’s efforts to assist and integrate refugees. In Timișoara, UNHCR briefed H.E. Ms. Anna Hällerman, Ambassador of Sweden to Romania, on the activities and life-saving role of the Emergency Transit Centre (ETC). A meeting with the Timiș County Youth Foundation (FITT) explored opportunities to strengthen engagement with refugee youth. In Arad, discussions with representatives of the local Department for Social Assistance focused on enhancing cooperation to identify the needs of the most vulnerable refugees and facilitate their access to appropriate support and services.

title: Taw Oo District Short Update: Burma Army fighting, shelling, arrest, and looting caused damages and displacement in Daw Hpah Hkoh Township (August 2026)
content:
This Short Update describes events occurring in Daw Hpah Hkoh (Thandaunggyi) Township, Taw Oo (Toungoo) District. On 28 July 2026, fighting happened two times successively between the Burma Army and the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) on a road that led to Thandaunggyi Town. On 8 August 2026, Burma Army soldiers from Thandaunggyi Bayit Naung Tat Myo Town fired a shell into Aa--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract, Daw Hpah Hkoh Township, mildly injuring a 30-year-old woman. She received treatment in P’Shaw Loh village tract. On 9 August 2026, a fighter jet dropped two 300-pound bombs and a howitzer fired more than ten tandem-charge shells into the surrounding P’Shaw Loh village tract. The air strikes and shelling did not kill or injure any villager; however, a Christian church’s bell tower was hit and slightly damaged. Following the air strikes, villagers displaced to other areas. Then once again, on 11 August 2026, Burma Army soldiers intruded into Ab--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract. They arrested villagers, looted a villager’s phone, and later stole villagers’ belongings and properties. They stayed inside villagers’ houses and a school hall. They fired gunshots damaging villagers’ roofs. On the same day, fighting broke out between the Burma Army and armed groups at Ac--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract, causing villagers to displace, and a Burma Army howitzer fired shells into Ae--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract, damaging a villager’s plantation. On 14 August 2026, Burma Army cars brought more soldiers to A Mat #39 army camp. This has increased villagers’ worry that the Burma Army could carry out military activities again.[1]

28 July 2026

On 28 July 2026, in the morning, an unknown battalion of the SAC [State Administration Council,[2] also referred to as the Burma Army[3]] was attacked by a commando army [of the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA)[4]], controlled under Brigade #2. The commando army set up a tripwire on a road next to a garbage dump, located between 6 Miles and Thandaunggyi Town in Taw Oo (Toungoo) District. In the afternoon, SAC soldiers from 13 Miles marched down [to attack the commando army]. Then, fighting happened between the Burma Army and KNLA Battalion #5 soldiers, under the control of Brigade #2, [at a place] located between 7 Miles and Pya army camp.

8 August 2026

On 8 August 2026, in the afternoon, an army camp of the SAC based at Thandaunggyi Bayit Naung Tat Myo Town, Daw Hpah Hkoh (Thandaunggyi) Township, Taw Oo District, fired a shell into Aa--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract,[5] Daw Hpah Hkoh Township. The shell explosion mildly injured a 30-year-old woman named Naw[6] A--- in the lower chest. She received treatment at her house. Now [as of 10 August], having received the treatment, her injury was getting better and there was nothing to worry about [related to the injury].

9 August 2026

On 9 August 2026, at 6 pm, a fighter jet of the SAC dropped two 300-pound bombs successively, outside of Ab--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract. The first bomb was dropped when the aircraft was flying high in the sky, then the second bomb was dropped when it came down closer to the ground. [Because it is the closest air base, villagers believed that] the aircraft came from Taw Oo air base. No villagers were killed nor did they sustain injuries due to the air strikes.

Moreover, [on the same day,] the SAC army camp based in Thandaunggyi Bayit Naung Tat Myo Town used a howitzer and fired more than ten tandem-charge shells into the surrounding areas [both inside and outside] of P’Shaw Loh village tract. One of the shells landed near a Baptist Christian church in Ab--- village. The church’s bell tower was hit and slightly damaged. No villagers were killed nor did they sustain injuries due to the shelling because the church is located far from other villagers’ houses.

Following the incidents, many villagers from Ab--- village displaced themselves [to another place]. Some villagers fled to Toungoo Town and forests, but a few villagers stayed in the village.

11 August 2026

An unknown column of the SAC came to Ab--- village, arrested [an unknown number of] villagers, and seized a villager’s phone. Then they intruded into villagers’ houses, looted villagers’ clothes and rice, and transported the stolen goods in their vehicle and drove off. Some arrested villagers were released on the same day, and some [a couple; exact number unknown] were kept by the Burma Army and forced to navigate for the soldiers.

[Later in the day], on 11 August 2026 at 3 pm, fighting happened between the SAC column and the [KNLA] Battalion #5, under Brigade #2, at the eastern part of Ac--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract. The SAC soldiers from Thandaunggyi Bayit Naung Tat Myo fired shells into Ae--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract, [which villagers believed was] to support the fighting [by attacking villagers, because this can prompt resistance fighters to pull back]. A howitzer shell landed and exploded inside a peanut plantation of a villager and damaged corn stalks, peanut plants, and [a few] rubber trees.

On the same day, following the fighting, the SAC soldiers intruded into Ac--- village, causing villagers to displace. They stayed in villagers’ houses and a school hall [exact duration unknown]. During their stay, they looted villagers’ belonging such as clothes, blankets, a mat, and a pillow. In addition, they also stole villagers’ chickens to cook and eat. They cooked inside the school hall. They also fired gunshots at villagers’ roofs, leaving holes.

14 August 2026

Later, on 14 August 2026, the SAC’s cars transported [more] soldiers to their army camp at A Mat #39, Day Loh village tract, Htaw Ta Htoo (Htantabin) Township, Taw Oo District. Villagers worried that [the Burma Army would] launch military activities again.

This information was provided by a female villager from Ae--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract, and a male villager named Saw[7] B--- from Af--- village, P’Shaw Loh village tract.

Further background reading on the situation on shelling, looting, and displacement in Southeast Burma/Myanmar can be found in the following KHRG reports:

  • Photo Set: Burma Army human rights violations in Southeast Burma (January to June 2026), July 2026.
  • “Taw Oo District Situation Update: Healthcare, education, and military activities in Daw Hpah Hkoh Township (September 2025 to February 2026)”, August 2026.
  • “Taw Oo District Situation Update: Burma Army shelling, arrests, and militarisation; drug issues; and challenges to education, transportation, and livelihood in Daw Hpah Hkoh Township (January to March 2026)”, August 2026.

title: UNICEF Nepal Humanitarian Situation Report No. 8, 2 November 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Children are bearing the brunt of the disaster. More than 32,000 children were affected by the Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi flash floods on 26 August 2026, with many losing loved ones, homes and belongings, and facing heightened risks to their health, education, protection and well-being. Further flash flooding along the Budhi Gandaki River on 11 October affected communities, causing additional damage to infrastructure and access routes.
  • Since the onset of the crisis, UNICEF has worked alongside the Government of Nepal and partners to deliver lifesaving support, reaching more than 50,000 people with safe water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, over 18,000 people with mental health and psychosocial support and 66,000 people with oral cholera vaccination, while providing almost 1,800 children with continued access to learning and reaching over 1,500 children through child-friendly spaces.
  • Winter poses an urgent new threat to affected children and families. With homes, clothing, and essential household items lost, thousands face freezing temperatures. UNICEF has procured 8, 514 sets of warm clothes for children, out of which distribution has been undertaken for 1,234 children. In addition, UNICEF has distributed 1,162 thermal blankets, alongside cash assistance to more than 1,000 households, heated learning spaces, and support for newborns and pregnant women.
  • Recovery must strengthen resilience to future disasters. UNICEF’s response, in line with Government plans, has entered a recovery-focused phase. Rebuilding schools, health facilities, and water systems provides an opportunity to establish safer, more inclusive and climate-resilient services, while investments in preparedness and early warning systems can better protect children before crises strike.

title: Sudan conflict - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms Area) #45 (Reporting period: October 2026)
content:
Summary Points

• LTC Telecoms sustained internet connectivity for approximately 1,700 users across 70 humanitarian locations, supporting humanitarian communications, coordination and response activities across Sudan.

• Five Security Operations Centres (SOCs) remained operational in Port Sudan, Kassala, El Gedaref, Kosti and Damazine, while LTC Telecoms continued providing radio communications support to humanitarian partners.

• LTC Telecoms continued community connectivity services at the Al-Aim Community Centre in Khartoum, where 392 people accessed data connectivity and phone-charging services during October, while joint assessments with WFP in Kosti and El Obeid explored opportunities to expand telecoms services.

title: WFP Madagascar Country Brief, October 2026
content:
770,028 people assisted in September 2026

USD 597,169 cash transferred in September 2026

USD 83.5 million required in the next six months (November 2026 – April 2027)

KEY HIGHLIGHTS

47 Health Cluster Partners (in total, incl.
