title: UNICEF Lebanon Humanitarian Situation Report No. 6, 30 September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Despite the June ceasefire framework, hostilities persisted in southern Lebanon, killing 261 children and injuring 1,058 children since March. Almost 330,000 people, including over 115,000 children, remain displaced, as destroyed homes and unexploded ordnance block returns.
  • The new school year opened with schools damaged or used as shelters, putting children’s safety and learning at risk, while returning families seek access to services in the South.
  • In August and September, UNICEF reached 590,756 children and women through primary healthcare, vaccinated 36,066 children, sustained water supply for over 354,000 people and reached 151,598 people with explosive ordnance risk education.
  • UNICEF helped launch the National Learning Recovery Programme, training around 10,000 teachers.
  • The Lebanon Humanitarian Action for Children appeal was 55 percent funded, with the Social Protection and Palestinian programmes critically under-funded.

SITUATION OVERVIEW AND HUMANITARIAN NEEDS

Despite the ceasefire framework established in June 2026, the humanitarian situation in Lebanon remained fragile throughout August and September. Hostilities persisted across southern Lebanon, with recurrent airstrikes, artillery shelling, demolitions, and land-clearing operations concentrated in Nabatieh, Bent Jbeil, Marjaayoun, and Tyre districts.

According to the Ministry of Public Health (MoPH), cumulative casualties reached 4,386 killed and 12,413 injured by September 26, 2026. Of these, 261 children were killed, and 1,058 were injured. In 2026, MoPH reports that 135 health workers have been killed and 416 injured, with 17 hospitals damaged due to the conflict. According to IOM, as of the end of September 2026, almost 330,000 people remained internally displaced in Lebanon, including over 115,000 children. Over 13,000 displaced people were still living in 154 collective shelters, with under one percent of the remaining IDPs living in 'at-risk shelter conditions' including unfinished buildings, tents, parks, on the streets, or self-settled sites - in Mount Lebanon or the North.5 Many families are unable to return safely due to widespread destruction of homes and public infrastructure, ongoing military operations, contamination by unexploded ordnance and explosive remnants of war, and limited access to essential services and trained personnel. Consequently, secondary displacement persisted, with many families relocating closer to their areas of origin, particularly in Tyre, Nabatieh and Bint Jbeil, overstretching even more water, sanitation, health, education, protection, social welfare and municipal services in areas where humanitarian actors face recurrent access constraints.

While more than 877,000 people have returned to their communities,6 these families and their communities still need humanitarian assistance. Indeed, repeated displacement, worsening socioeconomic conditions, and prolonged disruption of livelihoods continued to erode household coping capacities, placing children and their caregivers at heightened risk of further harm, including negative coping strategies that may result in child labour, child marriage, and access to minimum acceptable diet. However, returns remained uneven, particularly in border villages and heavily damaged communities in the South and Nabatieh. Displacement and uncertain returns continued to heighten protection risks, particularly GBV7 for women and girls, for those living in collective shelters, and those returning to their areas of origin where the availability and adequacy of services is not guaranteed. Child protection needs are expected to remain high with the start of a new school year as some areas remain under the threat of bombardment, some educational facilities continue to serve as collective shelters, and a considerable number of schools have resumed operations despite dire needs for rehabilitation. Explosive remnants of war, alongside other security concerns, housing destruction, and limited basic services constrain sustainable returns.

Humanitarian needs remain significant in hard-to-reach areas in the South of Lebanon, particularly in parts of Bint Jbeil, Marjayoun, Zahrani and Iqlim El Tuffah. Priority concerns include lack of access to services – including health, nutrition, water and schools, psychological distress, family separation, and child labour. In these areas, GBV risks also require continued attention, particularly for displaced women and girls facing barriers to safe and confidential services.

The almost 855,000 Syrian refugees remaining in Lebanon continue to face worsening socioeconomic conditions. Recent assessments indicate deteriorating food security, increasing reliance on negative coping strategies including child labour in hazardous conditions, with more than half of the households remaining below the Survival Minimum Expenditure Basket.8 Rising debt, limited livelihood opportunities, and obstacles to access basic services such as health, water and education are further exacerbating vulnerabilities for both refugees and host communities.

Lebanon hosts approximately 231,000 Palestine refugees across 12 camps and 42 gatherings, including around 209,000 Palestine refugees from Lebanon (PRL) and 22,000 Palestine refugees from Syria (PRS). Around 80 percent of Palestine refugees live below the national poverty line, with limited employment opportunities, and 56 percent are excluded from legal paid employment. Wasting affects 4 percent of Palestinian children and over 9 percent of pregnant and lactating women, with 80 percent of Palestinian children aged 6–23 months not receiving the minimum acceptable diet. Over 41 percent of Palestinian households experience food insecurity, while 90 percent of young children experience child food poverty. Palestinian children face risks including child labour, exploitation, violence and abuse. Palestinian refugee camps face security challenges, violence, and inadequate infrastructure, affecting the safety and well-being of residents, particularly children. Palestine Refugees from Syria face additional challenges related to poverty, residency, civil documentation, movement, and access to employment and education.

title: WFP India Country Brief, November 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW
• India continues to face significant food and nutrition insecurity, despite significant gains in food production and nutrition. Ranked 102 among 123 countries on the 2025 Global Hunger Index, its malnutrition indicators remain above acceptable thresholds: 35percent of children under five are stunted, 19 percent are underweight, and anaemia affects 57percent of women of reproductive age and 67 percent of children aged 6–59 months. The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World, released in July 2026, highlighted significant improvements in the prevalence of undernourishment and the affordability of a healthy diet.
• India runs the world’s largest food‑based safety net, reaching nearly 800 million people every month. Partnering with the Indian Government for over 60 years, WFP is providing technical assistance and capacity strengthening to enhance efficiency, nutrition quality, digital innovation, and climate resilience across the food system.

title: Nigeria: GBV Monthly Dashboard - September 2026
content:
In September 2026, Gender-Based Violence (GBV) response efforts across Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe (BAY) states faced
significant operational challenges, including severe funding cuts, camp closures, and relocations. Borno retained the highest
protection severity in the region, particularly across key affected Local Government Areas (LGAs) such as Dikwa, Gubio, Jere,
Konduga, Magumeri, Mobbar, and Monguno.
The BAY States continued to experience overlapping humanitarian challenges, including severe flooding, attacks on
healthcare facilities by non-state armed groups in Geidam LGA (specifically Gumsa Community) Yobe State, and
displacement across Maiduguri, Jere, Bama, Gwoza, and Monguno. These crises heightened vulnerabilities among IDPs,
women, and adolescent girls, disrupting access to essential services. Flooding and insecurity further increased gender-based
violence risks and worsened living conditions.
Significant service gaps remain, including LGAs lacking case management and GBV reach—such as Gubio in Borno, Demsa
in Adamawa, and Bursari in Yobe. Furthermore, safe shelters and security services are highly inadequate, driven by severe
shortages relative to demand, poor structural quality, and restricted humanitarian access due to insecurity, threatening the
protection of vulnerable women and girls.

title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 8 November 2026
content:
Key Highlights

  • Heavy rains hit the Gaza Strip from the evening of 6 November 2026 through the weekend, causing widespread flooding, the collapse of damaged buildings, damage to shelters, humanitarian facilities and learning spaces, and disruptions to essential services. An infant reportedly drowned and several people were reportedly killed when a sand dune collapsed on their tents.
  • Humanitarian partners mobilized immediately to assess people’s needs, distribute emergency supplies and otherwise support those affected. Nevertheless, humanitarian stocks of tents, tarpaulins, blankets and clothes inside Gaza are virtually exhausted.
  • By 8 November, humanitarian partners received appeals from over 26,000 households whose shelters or other belongings were damaged, with the overall impact believed to be greater. Partners have assessed the needs of 1,877 households, and provided support to 422 households, including with non-food items, at 29 displacement sites.
  • Over 150,000 tents purchased by humanitarian partners and Member States are outside Gaza ready to be dispatched. This includes about 117,000 tents from the Egyptian Relief Committee alone in Al-Arish.
  • Humanitarian funding and Israeli approvals are urgently needed so that enough supplies and machinery can be brought into Gaza, including vacuum trucks, mobile dewatering pumps, engine oil, hoses and heavy machinery.

title: Yemen — Rapid Displacement Tracking Update (1 – 7 November 2026)
content:
IOM Yemen DTM’s Rapid Displacement Tracking (RDT) tool collects data on estimated numbers of households forced to flee on a daily basis from their locations of origin or displacement, allowing for regular reporting of new displacements in terms of estimated numbers, geography, and needs. It also tracks returnees who returned to their location of origin.

From 1 January to 7 November 2026, IOM Yemen DTM tracked 57,317 households (HH) (343,902 Individuals) who experienced displacement at least once.

Between 1 and 7 November 2026, IOM Yemen DTM tracked 2,655 households (15,930 individuals) displaced at least once. The majority of people moved into/within the following governorates and districts:

  • Lahj (1,313 HHs) – Tuban (673 HHs), Al Madaribah Wa Al Aarah (240 HHs), Tur Al Bahah (220 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate originated from Lahj and Ta’iz.
  • Ta’iz (716 HHs) – Ash Shamayatayn (142 HHs), Al Mudhaffar (134 HHs), Al Misrakh (123 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate were internal.
  • Aden (248 HHs) – Al Burayqah (123 HHs), Dar Sad (114 HHs), Kritar - Sirah (11 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate originated from Lahj and Ta’iz.

The majority of people moved from the following governorates and districts:

  • Ta’iz (1,242 HHs) – Al Misrakh (203 HHs), Ash Shamayatayn (176 HHs), Sabir Al Mawadim (168 HHs) districts.
  • Lahj (1,142 HHs) – Tur Al Bahah (504 HHs), Al Madaribah Wa Al Aarah (494 HHs), Al Maqatirah (134 HHs) districts.
  • Al Hodeidah (167 HHs) – Hays (79 HHs), Al Khukhah (72 HHs), Bayt Al Faqih (4 HHs) districts.

IOM identified 372 additional households displaced in the previous reporting period, which covered 25 - 31 October 2026, in the governorates of Aden (272 HHs), Ad Dali (56 HHs), Ma’rib (24 HHs), and Abyan (19 HHs). These figures have been added to the cumulative displacement total recorded since the beginning of the year.

title: Argentina | Economic Crisis - Final Report (MDRAR022)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Description of the crisis

Since 2018, Argentina has been facing a severe economic and social crisis marked by a progressive deterioration in living conditions and a significant increase in humanitarian needs. The crisis has been characterized by a sharp currency devaluation, sustained increases in the prices of essential goods and services, and a substantial loss of household purchasing power. These conditions worsened significantly at the beginning of 2024, when year-on-year inflation exceeded 250 per cent and the costs of food, medicines, transport and basic services rose sharply. As a result, humanitarian needs increased considerably, with many households facing growing difficulties in accessing adequate food, healthcare, hygiene items and other basic necessities. These dynamics disproportionately affected people in situations of greater vulnerability, particularly older people, informal workers, families with children and people experiencing homelessness.

Although some macroeconomic indicators began to improve from mid-2024 onwards, the recovery remained uneven throughout 2025. In the second quarter of 2025, Gross Domestic Product (GDP) recorded year-on-year growth of 6.3 per cent, while accumulated inflation during the first nine months of the year reached 22 per cent and year-on-year inflation stood at around 31.8 per cent. Despite these positive trends, improvements at the macroeconomic level did not translate into sustained improvements in living conditions. Household consumption remained unstable, and the labour market continued to show signs of fragility, with unemployment close to 7.6 per cent and persistently high levels of informal employment.

The deterioration in purchasing power remained one of the defining characteristics of the crisis. By August 2025, the minimum wage (Salario Mínimo, Vital y Móvil) had reached 322,000 Argentine pesos (ARS), while the cost of the total basic basket (Canasta Básica Total) for a household of four exceeded ARS 1,176,000 the following month. Although the minimum wage had increased in nominal terms since the end of 2023, these adjustments failed to keep pace with inflation, resulting in a significant decline in purchasing power. The widening gap between household income and the cost of living continued to limit many families' ability to meet their basic needs and reflected the persistent financial strain experienced by households.

Social indicators also reflected the persistence of structural vulnerabilities. Although official statistics reported a reduction in monetary poverty to 31.6 per cent during the first half of 2025, several analyses highlighted the need to interpret these results with caution due to methodological limitations and the challenges of fully capturing changes in real income and the cost of living. At the same time, household economic fragility remained evident, with high levels of family indebtedness and a growing proportion of household income allocated to debt repayment.

According to official data published by the National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (INDEC), complemented by analyses from the Argentine Red Cross Humanitarian Observatory and specialized secondary sources, the improvements observed in selected macroeconomic indicators had not yet translated into broad-based improvements in household wellbeing. Persistent income disparities, widespread labour informality and continued barriers to accessing essential goods and services continued to disproportionately affect the most vulnerable population groups, reinforcing the need for sustained humanitarian assistance and protection.

title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 5 November 2026
content:
Key Highlights

  • As hundreds of Palestinians begin returning to their homes in two neighbourhoods of Hebron city following a 10-day operation by Israeli forces, humanitarian organizations are supporting local authorities in assessing damage and addressing outstanding needs.
  • Settler violence and access restrictions continue to disrupt the olive harvest, with 377 olive-harvest-related settler attacks recorded since the start of the season in September, already exceeding the total recorded during any previous harvest season; farmers continue to face physical assaults and theft of harvested olives and equipment.
  • Heavy rainfall and flash floods damaged shelters, belongings and livestock fodder of 37 Palestinian households across seven Bedouin communities in the northern Jordan Valley.
  • In the Gaza Strip, strikes continue to cause casualties in populated areas and affect humanitarian operations; attacks have caused reported civilian casualties and hit the vicinities of humanitarian convoys and facilities.
  • The Food Security Sector warns that the daily production and free distribution of meals could reduce by approximately 45 per cent if the current Israeli suspension of the entry of humanitarian and commercial supplies from Egypt continues.
  • As winter approaches, Israeli restrictions on the entry of engine oil and spare parts threaten essential water, sanitation and health services. Shelter conditions remain abysmal, with families’ needs far exceeding the limited resources available to the Shelter Cluster.
  • Maternal and newborn health services are overstretched, with neonatal unit occupancy reaching 151 per cent and special-care baby unit occupancy 199 per cent in September.

title: Heavy Rain and Flooding Incidents Across Gaza, 06-07 November 2026 | Update #1
content:
Overnight rainfall between 06 and 07 November triggered widespread flooding and rain-related incidents across displacement sites in Gaza, affecting thousands of displaced families living in makeshift shelters. As of 09:00 on 08 November, partners had submitted 268 site alerts, of which 264 relate to heavy rain and flooding incidents. Reports were received from 261 unique displacement sites, including 255 sites with Site Management Agency (SMA) support and 6 sites without SMA presence.

Site Management Cluster partners reported incidents and urgent needs through the Zite Manager platform, provided by the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and only captures alerts submitted by participating partners. Reported figures reflect only incidents recorded by partners operating displacement sites and do not capture all rain and flood related impacts across Gaza. The overall scale of damage and humanitarian needs is therefore likely significantly higher than reflected in this update. Based on a joint IOM and Cluster flood-risk assessment and analysis, an estimated 761,000 people (138,000 families) in Gaza displacement sites are likely to be impacted by flooding this winter.

Only 40 per cent of the nearly 1,700 active sites have an SMA presence through the Cluster. Site Management Cluster partners are mobilizing to support site improvement works and community-led flood mitigation activities, such as drainage improvements and slope stabilization, to enable safer, more dignified living conditions. Site Management partners continue to monitor conditions and update reported needs as they prepare a rapid response

title: Desert Locust Bulletin 577 (6 November 2026)
content:
GROUPS FORM IN MAURITANIA

In October, locust populations increased in Mauritania, where solitarious and transiens breeding occurred in the northwest and a few groups of adults and hoppers formed. Solitarious adults were present in the north of the country and in Chad, while no locusts were seen in central Algeria, Western Sahara and Tunisia. No surveys were carried out in Libya, Mali and Niger. In the Central Region, a few isolated adults were seen in southern Egypt, and no locusts were seen in Sudan, Ethiopia, Somalia, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and Oman. During the forecast period, breeding will continue in northwest Mauritania, where more hopper groups and bands will form, and fledging will lead to the formation of more adult groups. A second generation of breeding could start from late November. Breeding will probably occur in northern Mali, Western Sahara and southern Algeria, where hopper groups and bands may form. Solitarious breeding might have occurred, after good summer rains, in northern Mali, Niger and Chad, and southern Algeria, and groups may form. Consequently, locust populations will increase further, and outbreaks could develop in central and northern Mauritania, northern Mali and Niger, Western Sahara and southern Algeria. Surveys should be increased, and control operations will be required in Mauritania, while surveys should be resumed in northern Niger, Chad and southern Algeria. In the Central Region, small-scale breeding is likely to start on the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden coastal plains where recent rainfall occurred, but no significant developments are expected. In the Eastern Region, no locusts were seen in India and Iran, and no significant developments are expected.

title: UNICEF Humanitarian Situation Report No. 3 (BVD Outbreak in DRC: Regional Preparedness and Readiness in Neighboring and At-Risk Countries), Aug-Sept 2026
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, Burundi
content:
Highlights

  • The evolving Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in DRC continues to pose a high risk of regional spread due to cross-border movement, porous borders, and humanitarian vulnerabilities, underscoring the need to sustain preparedness efforts in neighboring countries.
  • At the time of reporting, Kenya has reported nine Ebola cases, while Nigeria confirmed an imported case, which was medically evacuated to Switzerland on 26 October, demonstrating the ongoing risk of cross-border transmission and the importance of robust preparedness systems.
  • Uganda's outbreak was declared over by WHO on 26 August 2026 following 42 days without a confirmed case; however, recent detections in neighboring countries highlight the need for continued vigilance and investment in readiness across the region.
  • UNICEF continues to support governments in IPC/WASH, RCCE, emergency coordination, and preparedness at priority points of entry, including through contact tracing and community surveillance, pre-positioning essential supplies, training health workers, conducting simulation exercises, and strengthening community engagement.
  • Cross-border preparedness remains a key regional priority, with UNICEF facilitating coordination, information sharing, preparedness reviews, and technical support among neighboring countries to strengthen operational readiness and promote a harmonized approach to outbreak prevention and response.
  • UNICEF is appealing for US$150.8 million over six months to support the Ebola response - including US$37.4 million for preparedness and readiness activities in at-risk countries across Eastern, Southern and Western Africa.

HUMANITARIAN CONTEXT

SITUATION OVERVIEW

The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to pose a significant regional threat. First confirmed in Ituri Province on 15 May 2026, the outbreak is unfolding in a complex humanitarian environment marked by insecurity, population displacement, fragile health services, and intense cross- border mobility. As of 30 September 2026, more than 8,224 cases and 3,982 deaths had been reported across seven provinces. Given the risk of international spread, WHO declared the outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC), while Africa CDC designated it a Public Health Emergency of Continental Security (PHECS). In response, UNICEF activated its Level 3 Corporate Emergency Procedures to support a scaled- up regional response.

While Uganda's outbreak was officially declared over by WHO on 26 August 2026, following 42 days without a laboratory- confirmed case, the regional risk remains elevated. Uganda reported a total of 20 cases, including 15 imported from DRC and five linked secondary cases, demonstrating the continued vulnerability of neighboring countries to cross- border transmission.

The outbreak has since spread beyond DRC. At the time of reporting, Kenya confirmed its first imported case of BVD on 5 October 2026 following travel from DRC through Uganda. As of 20 October 2026, Kenya had reported nine confirmed cases, including one death. UNICEF is supporting the Government- led response through RCCE, community- based surveillance, IPC/WASH, frontline preparedness, and essential supply support to strengthen contact tracing, community engagement, and outbreak containment efforts.

Nigeria also reported an imported BVD case on 20 October 2026 in a traveler arriving from Uganda.
The patient was subsequently medically evacuated to Switzerland on 26 October for specialized care, and no additional cases have been reported. However, public health authorities continue monitoring identified contacts and maintaining heightened surveillance and preparedness measures to prevent further transmission.

These developments underscore that, despite successful containment in some countries, the risk of regional spread remains significant. Sustained investments in preparedness, surveillance, rapid response capacity, risk communication, and cross- border coordination remain critical across at- risk countries, particularly those with strong travel and trade links to DRC and affected neighboring states.

title: Kyrgyzstan — Migration Situation Report (January–June 2026)
content: The report provides an overview of migration and mobility in Kyrgyzstan, drawing on the latest available data from national and international sources for the period January - June 2026. It highlights key trends, major national and regional developments shaping migration flows, and their socioeconomic impacts. In addition, it reviews main destination countries for Kyrgyz migrants, recent remittance trends, and evolving mobility patterns.

title: Afghanistan Nutrition Sentinel Site Surveillance Bulletin, 16th Edition - Quarter 3, September 2026
content:
The Community Nutrition Sentinel Site system works across 465 sites in 401 districts to track under‐five malnutrition. It uses simple mid‐ upper‐arm measurements and checks for swelling. The system began in 2023 through close collaboration with partners and local communities.

Trained Community Health Workers collect data every quarter, helping keep information reliable and consistent across places and over time. These workers receive strong practical and classroom training, and 40% of them are women. Selection follows a two‐step random approach: CHWs prepare household listings, then 40 households per site are randomly selected.

title: Multi-country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak Situation Report No. 25 (26 October – 1 November 2026)
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Burundi, Central African Republic
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

The regional Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak remained active during the reporting period, with sustained transmission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and imported cases requiring continued surveillance and response in Kenya and Nigeria. As of 31 October 2026, DRC had reported 10,467 confirmed cases and 5,103 deaths, with transmission reported across 67 health zones in 8 provinces. Ituri remained the epicentre, accounting for approximately 71 per cent of cumulative confirmed cases. Significant gaps remain in early detection, community-based surveillance and response capacity. In Kenya, nine confirmed cases and two deaths had been reported as of 26 October, with seven patients remaining in treatment. Twenty contacts completed the 21-day monitoring period, while 98 remained under monitoring. Disease surveil lance and screening continued at points of entry (PoEs), with support from IOM and other partners, and in health facilities and communities. In Nigeria,active follow-up continued around the one imported case, which remained the country's only confirmed BVD case. As of 31 October, 62 contacts linked to the index case had been identified, categorized and were under follow-up, with no con tact testing positive. Two additional suspected cases reported in Adamawa State during the reporting period were investigated and tested negative

title: Southern Africa Seasonal Monitor: 2026/2027 Agricultural Season (October 1, 2026)
content:
Key Messages

  • As of dekad 1 of October 2026, many areas had not yet recorded an effective rainfall onset. September rainfall over the early-onset areas in the north of the region was uneven: mostly above average in northern DRC, and below average in parts of western and central DRC as well as northern Angola. The onset of effective rainfall typically begins from October and November in many areas.
  • Vegetation and grazing conditions are above-average in southern areas following a wet October 2025 to May 2026 rainfall season and an earlier than typical onset of the 2026-2027 rainfall season in some parts. Contrasting below-average conditions are observed in parts of Namibia, eastern and central Zambia, Malawi, central and northern Mozambique, Tanzania and Madagascar. The forecast warmer and drier than normal October 2026 to May 2027 season is expected to lead to further deterioration of pasture conditions in these areas, reducing grazing availability for livestock.
  • As of the end of September, soil moisture was above average across much of the south and eastern parts of the region, and below average in much of Angola and Madagascar. Water resources are also favorable following a generally average to above-average 2025-2026 rainy season. Major hydropower reservoirs recorded notable increases after the near-record lows in late 2024 that followed the 2023-2024 drought.
  • El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is in a strong El Niño phase, which is expected to peak at very strong intensity and remain strong into early 2027. SARCOF is forecasting below-normal rainfall across much of the central and southern parts of the region, while the northern areas, including northern Angola, much of DRC, Tanzania, northern Zambia, and northern Malawi, are likely to receive normal to above-normal rainfall.
  • Above-normal temperatures are forecast for much of the region from October 2026 to April 2027. Coupled with rainfall deficits, higher temperatures will increase evapotranspiration and crop water demand. This heightens the impact of delayed onset and prolonged dry spells on vegetation and crops, particularly over central and southern areas.
  • Well below-normal tropical cyclone activity is forecast for the 2026-2027 South-West Indian Ocean season, with a significantly reduced risk of landfall over Madagascar, Mozambique, Malawi and Zimbabwe. However, reduced regional activity does not rule out cyclonic activity, and tropical cyclone preparedness remains essential.
  • In light of the forecast below-normal rainfall and above-normal temperatures across much of the region, the potential adverse impacts on crop and livestock production call for the strengthening of anticipatory and response mechanisms as well as the prioritization of monitoring and early warning initiatives to inform timely and targeted interventions and mitigation of adverse impacts.

title: PAHO Regional Situation Report No.15: Measles in the Region of the Americas (6 November 2026)
content:
Summary of the situation

Between epidemiological week (EW) 1 and EW 43 of 2026 (which ended on 31 October 2026), the Region of the Americas reported 57,666 confirmed cases of measles in 17 countries and territories, representing a 4.7-fold increase compared with the same period in 2025.

\Guatemala (34,748), Mexico (13,761), the United States (4,852), Peru (2,862), and Canada (1,126) account for the vast majority (99.5%) of confirmed cases (Map 1). A total of 81 deaths has been reported, including 53 in Guatemala, 23 in Mexico, three in the United States of America, one in Peru and one in Bolivia.

During EW 41 and EW 42 of 2026, the Region of the Americas reported 547 new confirmed cases of measles in six countries and territories, representing a 38% decrease compared with the previous two-week period (EW 39–40; 885 new cases, including 242 retrospectively reported since the last Regional Situation Report). Of the 547 new confirmed cases reported during EW 41–42, the United States accounted for 332, followed by Guatemala 115, Peru with 66, Mexico with 29, Bolivia with four, and Canada with one.

title: World Vision Situation Report #5: Humanitarian Response to Flooding (31 October 2026)
content:
Synopsis:

Prolonged heavy rainfall and flooding have affected communities across Cambodia, disrupting livelihoods and increasing the needs of vulnerable families. As of October 31, 2026, World Vision International in Cambodia had reached 2,635 households, representing 15,560 people, including 5,037 children, with food, safe drinking water, hygiene supplies, water treatment products, and other essential assistance.

Working alongside government authorities, communities, donors, and partners, World Vision is supporting child protection, nutrition, hygiene, and flood safety while helping families recover and strengthen their resilience. The response has been supported by the RISE Consortium and in partnership with the U.S. Department of State, Bureau of Disaster and Humanitarian Response (DHR) through World Vision US, alongside support from World Vision Canada, World Vision Australia, and De Heus.

title: UNHCR Facilitated Return of Syrian Refugees - Lebanon, 31 October 2026
content:
Since January 2025, 711,632 Syrians known to UNHCR have returned to Syria and consequently been inactivated from UNHCR Lebanon records. This includes refugees confirmed to have returned! and those inactivated due to prolonged absence and loss of contact”. Among the 711,632 Syrian returnees, 86% (611,743) returned spontaneously, including 11% (65,500) who returned under duress in late 2024 and remained in Syria; 24% (147,000) identified by the General Security Office (GSO) while crossing through an Official Crossing Point (OCP) without a Repatriation Form; 6% (35,903) identified as returning due to force majeure after 2 March 2026; and 59% (363,340) who were inactivated due to prolonged absence or loss of contact, or whose return was confirmed by UNHCR through interviews with family members. The spontaneous departure figures reflected in the chart indicate the date of inactivation from UNHCR’s database, rather than the date of departure, which explains the high number of inactivations in December 2025 following the completion of the presence verification exercise.

By the end of October 2026, 14% of the 711,632 Syrians who had returned, representing 99,889 individuals, had been assisted by UNHCR: 82,597 under the voluntary repatriation programme and 17,292 under the Return due to Force Majeure (RFM) programme. While facilitated returns dropped from over 6,600 individuals processed in September to 3,000 individuals processed in October, this is attributable to expected seasonal reductions in movements. The RFM programme was implemented between 1 April and 30 June 2026 in response to the escalation of hostilities in Lebanon to provide humanitarian assistance to refugees returning to Syria without a viable alternative for safety. Among those assisted under the RFM programme, 72% returned to their areas of origin in Syria, 19% were women, 59% were children. Almost all (96%) returned in complete families.

title: UNHCR Afghanistan Situation Regional Update September 2026
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT

Afghanistan continued to face a deteriorating protection environment and severe economic challenges amid large-scale returns and deportations from Iran and Pakistan, which are straining already overstretched services. Many returnees face persistent barriers to housing, livelihoods, civil documentation, healthcare and education. The security environment also remained unpredictable, with reported cross-border incidents between Afghanistan and Pakistan in September.

Regional tensions, domestic economic pressures and energy constraints continued to affect the operating environment in Iran. Government-mandated reduced in-person working hours during the reporting period also complicated operational planning, with potential implications for staff movements and assistance delivery.

In Pakistan, escalating cross-border tensions with Afghanistan, including reported airstrikes and clashes, heightened insecurity and affected UN movements. The Government’s implementation of the Illegal Foreigners Repatriation Plan (IFRP) continued to create uncertainty among Afghan communities, despite a decline in arrests and deportations in some areas. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, security measures periodically disrupted inter-provincial travel and UN field access. In Islamabad, Rawalpindi and Punjab, the situation remained relatively calm although Afghan refugees and asylum-seekers faced movement restrictions, economic hardship and barriers to education and healthcare amid fears over arrest and deportation. In Sindh, enforcement actions against undocumented Afghans continued, albeit at lower levels than in August.

Across Central Asia, refugee protection remained challenging, particularly for people seeking access to territory and essential services. In the Kyrgyz Republic, a new resolution established procedures for issuing and managing travel documents for recognized refugees, including administrative deadlines and digital identification requirements, while a decree transferred several migration-related functions to the Ministry of Labour, Social Security and Migration. In Tajikistan, reported forced returns of Afghan nationals, including refugees and asylum-seekers, in the absence of due process, legal assistance or opportunities to appeal, remained a significant protection concern.

title: Sudan Situation: UNHCR Monthly External Update #121 - July 2026
content:
Highlights

▪ Sudan: Fighting intensified in North Kordofan State, with looting and alleged arbitrary killings reported in Bara, Jabrat al-Sheikh, Umm Sayala, Al-Baraka, Um Qurfa, and Kazqil localities, driving fresh displacement. In Blue Nile State, an estimated 1,800 people fled escalating conflict in Geissan for Wad Al Mahi locality, while in Northern State, a drone strike hit electricity infrastructure in Al Dabbah.

▪ Central African Republic (CAR): The Birao Development Hub Plan was officially endorsed by the CAR Prime Minister, marking a key milestone for sustainable development and resilience in refugeehosting areas. The plan opens new investment opportunities to strengthen infrastructure, expand access to essential services, boost livelihoods, and improve local governance, supporting inclusive socioeconomic development for refugees and host communities, fostering social cohesion, and contributing to long-term stability and growth in the region.

▪ Chad: Ongoing clashes around Kulbus and Birak in Darfur, Sudan, continue to displace civilians into Chad, including 3,000 newly arrived asylum seekers during the reporting period. UNHCR, Commission for the Reception and Reintegration of Refugees and Returnees (CNARR), and partners are conducting assessments and pre-registration to strengthen protection and prepare for possible relocation.

▪ Egypt: On 22 July, UNHCR briefed a delegation of the European Parliament Subcommittee on Human Rights on arrivals from Sudan, Egypt’s new asylum framework, registration and documentation challenges, access to national services, and the impact of funding shortfalls on the refugee response.

▪ Ethiopia: Amhara's security situation remained tense and volatile. In Benishangul-Gumuz, conditions around Kurmuk Transit Centre remained unpredictable amid armed clashes, a drone strike resulting in one death and three injuries amongst refugees, and border tensions with Sudan, while Ura and Sherkole sites remained calm and a joint UNHCR- Refugees and Returnees Service (RRS) mission to Kurmuk Town on 29 July concluded safely.

▪ Libya: While demonstrations targeting UNHCR declined, Libya’s online environment remained hostile in July with anti-refugee narratives portraying refugees and asylum-seekers as threats to security, economic stability, and national sovereignty, and humanitarian actors increasingly depicted as foreign interference. UNHCR continued proactive outreach and communication efforts to counter misinformation and reinforce understanding of refugee protection principles.

▪ South Sudan: The Renk County Area-Based Durable Solutions Strategy for Refugees, Returnees and Host Community (2026–2028), was published on 29 July following endorsement by the County Commissioner. The strategy provides a locally led and county-owned framework for advancing durable solutions, centered on six strategic priorities, including implementation of the Renk Transit Centre Exit Plan, land allocation for settlement, strengthened access to basic services, enhanced social cohesion, and increased self-reliance opportunities.

▪ Uganda: Despite Ebola-related movement restrictions, Sudanese asylum-seekers continued to arrive in Uganda as insecurity and humanitarian conditions in Sudan continue to drive people to seek safety and protection outside the country.

title: Mozambique Conflict Monitor Update: November 2026
content:
The last of ISM’s fighters active in Montepuez district since July finally returned to Macomia district around 26 October. Traveling by stolen motorbikes and bicycles, and on foot, they made their way through the Mirate area of Montepuez district around 4 October, before crossing the R698 into Meluco district. By 21 October, they were at the Matandane and Minhanha mining areas in Meluco district. From there, they split into three groups before returning to Macomia district.

ISM’s presence in the Nairoto area of Montepuez from late July to early October was unprecedented. If ISM is to be stopped from establishing a more permanent presence, a significantly improved military response is a priority. Speaking on 27 October, Brigadier-General Sérgio Estrela, the commander of the EUMAMM, identified three key issues holding FADM back. First, a centralized command structure that slows the response time of troops in the field. The issue is particularly acute given that ISM prefers to operate in small, mobile groups. Second, he highlighted the need for better intelligence. Finally, Estrela pointed to logistical and financial obstacles to supporting effective military operations.

Tackling the issues raised will be critical to preventing ISM from establishing a more permanent presence in Nairoto. FADM’s pursuit of ISM through the area in late July and early August demonstrates its capacity. Its failure to follow through points to the wider issues raised by EUMAMM. Directly addressing these issues is beyond the scope of EUMAMM, but will likely feature in diplomatic engagements with countries and groupings, such as the European Union, which support security sector reform in Mozambique.

ISM targets rural communities in Mueda and Muidumbe

Between 21 and 31 October, ISM fighters attacked at least seven locations in an area straddling the Mueda-Muidumbe border, killing at least 19 people. All but one of the victims were civilians going about their daily lives. Among the dead were two cashew nut buyers, who were killed beneath a cashew tree, and some youth brewing the local drink napa to sell. Islamic State media claims for the attacks described the victims as Christians. The only clash with state forces was at Ntuchi village, approximately 10 kilometers from Mueda town.

The killings are alarming for two reasons. First, the attackers were able to move unimpeded for over 10 days in villages close to Mueda town. Mueda is the headquarters of the Local Force and has a significant FADM detachment. ISM’s presence was known locally, but did not trigger an appropriate response from security forces, leaving communities at risk. The attacks further illustrated Estrela’s concerns about intelligence and response times.

Second, the description of the targets as Christian, in what has historically been a Makonde-dominated part of the province, is likely a deliberate attempt to provoke communal tensions in the province. Such tensions have historically helped shape politics in Cabo Delgado, as well as the current conflict. These most recent killings will likely affect relations between people of Makonde and Mwani origins in Mocímboa da Praia town in particular. In August, ISM recently targeted Makonde-dominated neighborhoods in the town, prompting many to leave for Mueda.

ISM remains active in coastal waters, but sustains losses in naval operations

Along the Mocímboa da Praia, Macomia, and Quissanga coast, state forces have been more robust in countering ISM, in both operations at sea and on land that have had some success in disrupting the group’s logistics.

On 17 October, the FADM navy encountered a craft controlled by ISM, killing three, capturing one, and destroying the craft, according to one report. The boat was reportedly commanded by Juma Nguvu, said to be a brother of Suleiman Nguvu, a senior ISM leader. The captured insurgent was informally named as Abdala Assane, said to be close to Hassan Ulanga, ISM’s leader. Assane’s capture may lead to significant intelligence, and the incident is a success for the FADM marines involved.

FADM and the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) were active in coastal areas during the month, though success was mixed. An RDF patrol clashed with ISM near Cogolo village on the Macomia coast, with casualties unknown. On 18 October, the RDF disturbed a group of ISM fighters purchasing supplies at nearby Marijirane, killing at least six ISM fighters and one civilian, according to a local source. Further south, FADM was present in Quissanga district, in the context of a visit to Mahate and Mussemero by Cabo Delgado’s Governor Valige Tauabo on 12 October. The governor’s visit was a positive demonstration of authority in a part of the district through which ISM regularly passes, usually landing by boat at Mussemero after coming from Macomia.

FADM’s behavior was less politic. Two days after the governor’s visit, soldiers beat civilians at Mecuti, on the coast close to Quissanga town. According to a local source, they had refused to leave the neighborhood, having been ordered to do so in previous days. FADM’s presence in Quissanga was not entirely successful. ISM fighters, likely returning from Montepuez, were seen moving through the area again on 21 October, indicating that the area will likely remain a significant route for the insurgents.

title: WFP Zambia Country Brief October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• In September, WFP assisted 59,810 people in Zambia, 58 percent of them female. This included USD 78,595 in cash transfers to 8,721 refugees and asylum seekers in Mantapala Refugee Settlement, covering 70 percent of their minimum food needs, up from 40 percent in previous months.

• WFP provided technical assistance to document Zambia’s school meals journey for the Government’s preparations for the upcoming Global Child Nutrition Forum. Showcasing achievements, lessons learned and the evolution of school feeding into a nationally scaled programme strengthened advocacy and elevated Zambia’s global profile.

• Progress under the Enhanced Smallholder Irrigation and Resilient Nutrition (ESIRN) project included climate-smart agriculture, strengthened livelihoods and improved household resilience. WFP showcased these advances through a donor engagement visit to Serenje District in Central Province.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Zambia's humanitarian context continues to be shaped by recurrent climate shocks, with droughts and floods undermining livelihoods, food security, and household resilience.

• National food security conditions remain stable, with current and projected acute food insecurity affecting less than 5 percent of the population. Government social protection programmes, including Social Cash Transfers, Cash-for-Work and food assistance, continue to support vulnerable households.

• Ongoing and projected El Niño conditions are expected to affect the performance of the 2026/27 agricultural season, with flooding anticipated in northern Zambia and drought conditions forecast in parts of Southern, Western and Eastern Provinces.

• Preparedness measures, including anticipatory action and climate risk financing mechanisms, remain important to mitigate the impact of forecast climate shocks.

• Refugee movements remained stable during the reporting period despite the ongoing conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.

• Zambia continues to face heightened public health risks, including the potential spread of Ebola virus disease and recurrent cholera outbreaks.

• WFP is supporting the Government through an integrated approach that provides life-saving food and nutrition assistance, strengthens livelihoods and food systems, and enhances national capacities for emergency preparedness and shock-responsive social protection, in line with the Zambia Country Strategic Plan (2023–2028).

title: WFP Pakistan Market Monitor Report - October 2026
content:
• Month-on-month, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased by 1.3 percent in September compared to the previous month, reflecting continued upward pressure. The annual inflation increased by 10.26 percent (YoY) compared to September 2025, driven mainly by higher transport, housing energy, and fuels costs. However, it is slightly lower compared to August 2026 CPI of 11.2 percent.
  • Month-on-month food inflation increased by 0.2 percent mainly driven by increased costs of perishable food Items, while annual food inflation reached 8.2 percent compared to September 2025, driven by higher cost of wheat and wheat flour, cooking oil and perishable food items. Meaning households paid 8.2 percent more for the purchase of same food compared to last year - with low-income groups hit the hardest.
  • Prices of wheat and wheat flour increased in September compared to August, with both wheat and wheat flour prices rising by 2.0 percent,signalling growing pressure on key staples. Price of wheat flour was highest in Sindh. Rice Irri-6 price increased modestly while Basmati price decreased on month-on-month comparison.
  • Petrol and diesel prices decreased slightly in November compared to October 2026, however, remained much higher than a year earlier, with Petrol higher by 33 percent and diesel higher by 34 percent, driven by elevated international oil prices and domestic fuel price adjustments.
  • The average ToT was recorded at 10.6 kg of wheat flour which decreased by 2 percent MoM, while on YoY comparison it decreased (worsened) by 15 percent.

title: IOM Nepal Flood Response Situation Report #8 | 5 November 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

Two months after the 26 August flash floods in central Nepal, displacement and damage to homes, infrastructure and essential services continue to drive humanitarian and recovery needs. Access constraints remain a challenge for assistance and impact verification.

Findings from the Rapid Needs Assessment Report identify 8,317 affected households and establishments and 32,872 people across 15 local levels in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Gorkha. Of 4,151 damaged buildings, 72% were completely damaged. Priorities include shelter, household items, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), food, health, Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS), protection and access. Recovery needs include housing, livelihoods, infrastructure, energy, telecommunications, debris management and disaster and climate risk management. The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) provides further details through its Rapid Damage Needs Assessment (RDNA).

IOM continues to support the Government-led response and recovery through site assessments, camp coordination and management, health and protection assistance, non-food items (NFIs) distribution and the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM)

title: UNICEF Cambodia Situation Report No.1 (El Nino 2026-2027 Preparedness), October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • The World Meteorological Organization’s (WMO) September 2026 update indicated a near-100% likelihood that El Niño would persist through February 2027. Its October update highlighted that the event was intensifying and expected to peak around December. [1, 2]
  • Cambodia’s potential El Niño risk window is expected to come late 2026 to mid-2027 (FAO, WFP). The regional outlook indicates an increased likelihood of below-normal rainfall in parts of eastern Mainland Southeast Asia, and above-normal temperatures across much of Southeast Asia including Cambodia. Local impacts will vary. [4]
  • Cambodia’s Ministry of Water Resources and Meteorology (MOWRAM) reported that the country’s rainy season was expected to end around the third week of October 2026, with rainfall gradually decreasing as the country transitioned towards the dry season. The Ministry urged efficient water use and conservation. [3]
  • UNICEF Cambodia’s forecast for 16–29 October indicates below-normal rainfall—up to 20 mm below the 1996–2025 historical average—in parts of Kampong Cham, Kampong Chhnang, Kampong Thom, Kratie, Mondulkiri, and Ratanakiri provinces. Other areas are forecast to receive above-normal rainfall—at least 20 mm above the historical average. Above-normal maximum temperatures are not identified as a concern in this two-week forecast, and no meteorological drought is expected.

title: UNICEF Bangladesh Humanitarian Situation Report No. 76 - 30 September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • UNICEF continued delivering life-saving assistance amid multiple emergencies, including the protracted Rohingya crisis affecting 1.2 million refugees, a nationwide measles outbreak and severe floods and landslides.
  • UNICEF supported the Government’s response to the nationwide measles outbreak, including the Measles-Rubella Catch-up Campaign, targeting 3.4 million children to close immunity gaps and reduce transmission.
  • July floods and landslides claimed 59 lives and affected 1.28 million people, including 519,000 children. UNICEF reached over 126,000 people with emergency WASH assistance and 78,500 children, adolescents and caregivers with mental health and psychosocial support.
  • In Cox's Bazar and Bhasan Char, UNICEF sustained essential services for Rohingya children, reaching 342,400 people with safe water, 232,300 children with education and 120,800 children and women with primary healthcare.
  • Overall, UNICEF reached 613,100 people, including 323,000 children, with multisectoral, integrated life-saving assistance, representing 48 per cent of the annual HAC target.
  • UNICEF's US$108 million humanitarian appeal remained 22 per cent underfunded, with a US$23.9 million gap threatening the continuity of essential services.

title: UNFPA Situation Report: Crisis in Yemen, October 2026
content:
In October, fighting along the west coast and the southern Taiz frontline escalated to levels not observed since 2020. The security situation remains highly volatile, with the crisis continuing to expand. More than 300,000 people have been displaced since August 2026, the vast majority over the past two months. Some 82,000 people were displaced in October alone, most of them from Taiz governorate. More than half of those displaced are women and children.

Women and girls are among the most vulnerable and face serious health and protection risks. UNFPA estimates that 6,400 pregnant women are among those recently displaced. An estimated 600 women are expected to give birth within the next two weeks.

Road closures and insecurity continue to impede access and delivery of humanitarian assistance. Nevertheless, since January 2026, UNFPA has provided life-saving reproductive health, protection services, information and emergency relief to more than 710,000 people. This has been achieved through support to 25 health facilities, 14 safe spaces, three shelters, seven youth spaces, two specialized mental health centres and nine newly activated integrated mobile reproductive health and protection teams.

title: Yemen Emergency Response Situation Report #6 (November 5, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • 319,356 people from 53,226 families have been displaced across Yemen—an increase of approximately 27% from our last situation report.
  • Eighteen of 19 International Medical Corps-supported health facilities remain operational across the west coast, despite continuing access constraints.

OUR FOOTPRINT

  • Across Yemen, International Medical Corps’ programming serves approximately 3.3 million people across north and south Yemen.
  • Our lifesaving multi-sectoral assistance prioritizes active conflict zones and high-risk environments, strengthening community resilience, self-reliance and capacity to withstand recurrent shocks and vulnerabilities in a protracted crisis.

OUR RESPONSE

  • Our mobile medical response has expanded to Abyan and Lahj, where two teams have provided 1,219 medical consultations, screened 444 children and 118 pregnant and lactating women for acute malnutrition, delivered 258 immunization services and conducted 67 antenatal care consultations.
  • Our supported health facilities have provided 23,347 medical consultations to people on the west coast.
  • We have provided 56 metric tons of essential medicines and medical supplies across Aden, Al Dhale’e, Lahj and Taiz and facilitated the transfer of 120 cartons of ready-to-use therapeutic food to Al Mudarabah and Ras Al Arah districts to address critical nutrition needs among displaced children.

title: UNFPA Central African Republic Situation Report - September 2026
content:
In September 2026, the Central African Republic (CAR) faced severe environmental and security crises. Torrential rains and flooding affected 11,325 people across 2,870 households, while armed insecurity and military operations impacted a further 5,205 people and displaced approximately 9,900 residents across Ouham-Fafa and Bowaye. Widespread displacement, destruction of homes, and heightened insecurity have further restricted women’s and girls’ access to essential sexual and reproductive health services and increased the risk of gender-based violence. Gender-based violence accounted for 36 per cent of all protection incidents recorded during the month.

To respond to critical needs across crisis-affected areas, UNFPA and its partners delivered sexual and reproductive health services to 7,660 people during September 2026, including assisted deliveries, emergency caesarean sections, gynaecological consultations, and referrals. Through its gender-based violence response programmes, UNFPA also reached 2,919 people with case management, psychosocial support, and safe referrals. Despite these achievements, significant funding shortfalls continue to constrain UNFPA’s humanitarian response in CAR. In 2026, UNFPA requires USD 13.2 million to deliver life-saving reproductive health and protection services across the country. As of 30 September 2026, USD 10 million remained unfunded.

title: Regional Movement Trends and Patterns LAC - January – June 2026
content:
REGIONAL PANORAMA

The first half of 2026 marked a further shift away from the large-scale northbound transit movements that defined previous years. Human mobility across Latin America and the Caribbean became less concentrated along a small number of transit routes and increasingly reflected a mix of regular migration, return movements, localized cross-border mobility and movements within South America.

Irregular northbound transit continued to fall across several of the region’s principal routes. Northbound movements through the Darién dropped to just 280 during the reporting period, irregular entries recorded in Honduras were 74 per cent lower than in the first half of 2025, and movement monitoring in Guatemala recorded a 62 per cent decline. These reductions point to a continued slowdown in the transit corridors that, until recently, carried large numbers of migrants and refugees towards North America. At the same time, United Sates of America (U.S.) Southwest land-border encounters increased by 26 per cent between the first and second quarters of 2026, indicating a moderate rise after historically low levels at the beginning of the year.

The decline in irregular transit did not mean less mobility overall. Several countries in South America recorded increases in regular cross-border movements, including Colombia, Ecuador and Paraguay. Movement patterns also differed increasingly by nationality. Cuban mobility through Panama and Honduras declined sharply, while asylum applications and migration balances pointed to continued arrivals and settlement in countries such as Brazil and Uruguay. Haitian migration was increasingly facilitated through regular pathways, including family reunification programmes connecting Haiti and Brazil.

Return movements became more visible across the region. Since early 2025 over 271,000 Mexicans were returned from the U.S. returns to Guatemala and Honduras increased by 44 per cent compared with the first half of 2025, removals from the U.S. continued to rise, and southbound movements through Panama remained a notable feature of regional mobility. Forced removals, transfer arrangements, assisted voluntary return programmes and spontaneous returns all contributed to a more complex return landscape, increasing demand for reception, reintegration and protection support in countries of return.

Reasons for movement varied across countries where data were available. In Mexico, protection monitoring found that violence-related factors were the main drivers of departure, with 54% of respondents citing violence, threats, or intimidation. This was particularly common among Hondurans, 68 per cent of whom reported violence, threats, or intimidation as their main reason for leaving, and Haitians, among whom 74 per cent cited general insecurity. In contrast, Venezuelans reported a more balanced mix of protection-related (55%) and economic (43%) reasons for departure in this country6. In Guatemala, most refugees and migrants (76%) identified economic factors as their primary reason for migrating. Intended destinations differed by route, with Venezuela, Colombia, and Peru among the most frequently reported destinations in southbound movements.

Across migration routes, refugees and migrants reported high levels of unmet basic needs, particularly food assistance (98% of refugees and migrants surveyed in Peru and 72% in Guatemala8), as well as water, sanitation and hygiene support. Moreover, and despite lower volumes on several major transit routes, protection concerns remained acute. At least 113 deaths were recorded across the Americas during the reporting period, with drowning, environmental exposure and hazardous transportation among the leading causes. Internal displacement also remained severe, particularly in Haiti, while evidence from Ecuador, Colombia, and Honduras highlighted the growing influence of violence, insecurity and environmental pressures on population movements within countries.

title: Cameroon: North-West and South-West Situation Report No.87, July to September 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • More than 1,600 protection incidents recorded in the North-West and South-West regions.
  • Nearly 900 people displaced in the North-West and South-West regions due to violence and insecurity.
  • More than 4,000 people affected by floods and landslides, with about 500 displaced and five deaths reported.
  • Four improvised explosive devices incidents recorded in the North-West region.
  • A total of 736 children with severe acute malnutrition received life-saving treatment in partner-supported treatment centres.

SITUATION OVERVIEW / HUMANITARIAN ACCESS

During the reporting period July-September 2026, the humanitarian situation in Cameroon’s North-West and South-West (NWSW) regions remained fragile and deteriorated further amid continued clashes between State security forces (SSF) and non-State armed groups (NSAGs). Persistent insecurity, including kidnapping for ransom, arbitrary arrests, the proliferation of illegal checkpoints, extortion, and roadblocks, continued to restrict population movements, hinder access to basic services and livelihoods, and heighten protection risks for affected communities.

The situation remained volatile, with at least 11 improvised explosive devices (IED) incidents recorded during the reporting period, including 10 in the North-West and one in the South-West. While these attacks primarily targeted SSFs and their convoys, civilians remained at significant risk of injury or death from accidental explosions.

Attacks and threats against education intensified ahead of the 2026/2027 school year. NSAGs enforced school-related restrictions, imposed school levies in some areas, and increased intimidation of education personnel, including the abduction of five teachers in Wum (Menchum division, North-West). In September, armed actors also attacked a secondary school in the North-West, disrupting learning activities.

Humanitarian needs remained severe across the two regions, exacerbated by successive lockdowns imposed by NSAGs between 1 and 21 September. The measures restricted movement, disrupted education, livelihoods, and economic activities and limited access to essential services. Lockdown enforcement through threats and sporadic attacks resulted in civilian casualties in both regions and further affected already vulnerable communities.

Continued clashes between parties to the crisis triggered new population displacement and humanitarian needs across the North-West and South-West. In Momo division, an estimated 875 people (175 households) were displaced from Diku to Tikom during the reporting period with many families seeking refuge in nearby bushes. Heavy rainfall that caused flooding and landslides on 5 August affected over 4,157 people, displaced more than 500, caused five reported deaths, including a pregnant woman, and destroyed or damaged 16 houses infrastructure, livestock, and community water systems in Limbe (Fako division), Kumba (Meme division) in the South-West, and in Tinifoimbi Village (Boyo division) in the North-West. While many affected households have returned, those whose shelters were destroyed or damaged remain displaced and in need of assistance. Priority needs include shelter, food assistance, health, WASH, protection, education and livelihood support. In coordination with OCHA and area-based coordination co-chairs, humanitarian partners delivered multipurpose cash assistance, shelter support, psychosocial services, and gender-based violence prevention interventions across affected communities, in addition to the assistance delivered by authorities.

Humanitarian access remained constrained due to insecurity, prolonged lockdown and the presence of illegal checkpoints along key road corridors, including the Bamenda-Widikum axis in Momo division and the Bamenda-Ndop road. These restrictions significantly hindered population movements and limited the transportation of agricultural produce. The operational environment remained highly challenging and required continuous access negotiations amid a fragile, volatile, and rapidly evolving context.

title: Sudan Situation: Sudanese Refugees in Libya (As of August 2026)
content:
Overview

It is estimated that 569,703 Sudanese refugees have arrived in Libya since April 2023. This includes 77,906 refugees who were registered post-conflict, bringing the total number of Sudanese to 93,617. The closure of the border with Sudan and increased border monitoring by Libyan authorities has led refugees to take longer routes, and arrivals via land borders have reached an average of 70 per day from Egypt, Chad, and Niger. Due to the irregular nature of entry, the ad hoc data shared by authorities, and the vast remote land border with Chad, Egypt, and Sudan, combined with movements towards cities along the coast, it remains challenging to provide an accurate number of Sudanese refugees.

title: AAP WG report on consultation with IDP councils 2026 / Звіт з консультації робочої групи з підзвітності постраждалим людям з Радами ВПО 2026 [EN/UK]
content:
OVERVIEW
In August 2026, the Accountability to Affected People Working Group with support of the UNHCR Ukraine conducted a consultation with IDP Councils to gather recommendations for the 2027 humanitarian needs and response planning process. The consultation brought together 22 representatives from different regions of Ukraine.

Based on the discussion, participants broadly agreed on the need to approach displacement as a cycle rather than a single event. Accordingly, they recommended strengthening assistance throughout all stages of displacement, as a significant share of humanitarian support is currently concentrated in frontline areas, while the needs of displaced people in other parts of Ukraine often remain unmet.

Participants noted, for example, that certain types of psychosocial support are available in frontline areas, although not all forms of such support are considered relevant or in demand. At the same time, host communities face shortages of psychological and psychiatric services, while the need and readiness to access such support may increase after evacuation, once people have had an opportunity to recover from their immediate experiences. The social adaptation of children was also identified as a priority, alongside long-term psychological support for both children and adults.

title: Chad: Cholera Outbreak - DREF Final Report (MDRTD026)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

15-09-2025

What happened, where and when?

The cholera outbreak in Chad began with a suspected case notified on 13 July 2025 in Chokoyane Health District (Ouaddaï Province). Vibrio cholerae O1 Ogawa was confirmed by culture on 24 July, and the Ministry of Public Health and Prevention officially declared the outbreak on 25 July. Cross-border transmission from Darfur (Sudan) is considered the most likely source. The Chad Red Cross (CRT) monitored the situation from the declaration onwards.

Initially concentrated in Ouaddaï (Chokoyane, Hadjer Hadid, Adré), the outbreak escalated sharply in early September. Cases rose from 1,891 on 9 September to 2,165 cases and 137 deaths (CFR 6.3%) on 18 September. Community mortality remained high. By midSeptember, the outbreak was active in 8 districts across 3 provinces: five in Ouaddaï (Chokoyane, Hadjer Hadid, Adré, Farchana, Amleyouna), two in Sila (Abdi, Goz Beïda) and one in Guéra (Bitkine). Under the National Response Plan, the Government called on partners for support and prepositioning. CRT was asked to help contain the geographical spread and reduce community-level mortality. The DREF trigger was met on 15 September 2025, and the operation started on 23 September.

During the operation, transmission declined in the initial hotspots. The last cases were notified in Hadjer Hadid on 21 September, Adré on 26 September, Abéché on 29 September, Abdi on 1 October and Chokoyane on 7 October. Weekly new cases fell from about 270 in midSeptember to about 30 from mid-October onwards. However, the outbreak continued to spread westward with population movements. It reached Amdam, Marfa and Abougoudam (Ouaddaï), Tissi (Sila), and from October Hadjer Lamis (Bokoro, Massaguet, Gama, Moyto) and Barh El Gazel (Moussoro). Bitkine (Guéra) became the second-largest focus, with 437 cases.

The last confirmed case was notified on 19 November 2025 in Amdam. As of 7 December, the cumulative total was 2,979 cases and 167 deaths (CFR 5.61%), across 18 districts and 98 health areas in 5 provinces. 95% of patients recovered. The Ministry declared the end of the outbreak on 15 December 2025. In line with its post-epidemic recommendations, CRT, with IFRC support, reoriented its remaining activities towards community-based surveillance, RCCE and hygiene promotion until the end of the operation on 31 March 2026.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 92, as of 3 November 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Ebola preparedness and prevention efforts are ongoing in Bangui and the South-East.
  • Haute-Kotto: 27 children formerly associated with armed groups benefit from socio-economic reintegration support.

GENERAL CONTEXT

Mbomou and Haut-Mbomou Prefectures – South-East

  • No confirmed cases of Ebola virus disease (EVD) have been reported in the Central African Republic (CAR). However, the ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to pose a risk of importation, particularly in the south-east of the country. On 28 October, a coordination meeting held in Bangassou reviewed preparedness measures and identified gaps in surveillance, health facility capacity, prepositioning of supplies, isolation sites, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), as well as risk communication and community engagement. On 31 October, a crisis meeting convened in Ouango brought together local authorities, community leaders and humanitarian partners to assess risks related to cross-border movements from the DRC and strengthen coordination of response measures. Infection prevention and control (IPC) equipment was also delivered to high-risk areas with support from the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF).

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Health

Countrywide

  • To strengthen operational readiness and the resilience of the health system against the risk of an importation EVD, the World Health Organization (WHO) and its partners trained 107 frontline health workers in Bangui from 27 to 31 October, including doctors, nurses, hygienists, rapid response teams, and psychosocial staff. The training covered key areas such as the clinical management of EVD cases, the organization and operation of an Ebola Treatment Centre (ETC), epidemiological and community-based investigation of alerts, as well as psychosocial support and mental health care for affected individuals. The programme concluded with a simulation exercise designed to test coordination and response mechanisms in the event of an Ebola outbreak declaration. These activities are being implemented with support from the CERF.

Heavy rain

Bangui Prefecture

  • On 30 October, the government chaired a strategic meeting bringing together national authorities, United Nations agencies, NGOs and donors to assess the impact of heavy rains that affected several neighborhoods of Bangui and surrounding areas. According to preliminary assessments, more than 5,300 people have been affected by damage to property and continue to face the risk of waterborne diseases with epidemic potential. Discussions focused on priority needs in shelter, non-food items (NFIs), WASH, health, and food assistance, as well as response coordination mechanisms and the limitations of the humanitarian response to the floods. Following the meeting, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) provided essential household items to the Ministry of Humanitarian Action to support assistance to people affected by the floods.
