title: Kenya: Humanitarian situation of displaced people in Moyale, Marsabit County Flash Update No. 2 (5 November)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Intercommunal fighting in the Moyale area of Ethiopia, which began on 18 October, continued to displace people within Ethiopia and drive cross-border movements into Moyale, Marsabit County, Kenya.
  • Regional authorities in Ethiopia reported large-scale internal displacement in Oromia and Somali regions, while violence continued to disrupt markets, transportation, cross-border trade and access to basic services.
  • An estimated 50,000 people crossed into Kenya as of 3 November, with most staying with host communities in Moyale, Marsabit County, Kenya. Women and children constituted the majority of new arrivals.
  • Humanitarian partners in Kenya continued to provide food assistance and scale up health, WASH, protection and shelter interventions. However, humanitarian needs remained acute.
  • The United Nations in Kenya appealed for US$8.9 million to address the most critical life-saving needs over the next three months.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Fighting in the Moyale area of Ethiopia, which began on 18 October and escalated into armed clashes on 22 October, continued to displace people within Ethiopia and drive cross-border movements into Moyale Sub-County, Marsabit County, Kenya. The security situation in Moyale, Ethiopia, remained volatile, with newly arrived refugees and asylum-seekers reporting widespread damage to homes and neighbourhoods. People sheltering near the border faced heightened protection risks, and humanitarian partners were working with local authorities in Kenya to relocate them to safer locations. Stray bullets reportedly injured civilians on the Kenyan side of the border. On 2 November, a woman was reportedly killed by a stray bullet at the Moyale Sub-County offices. Humanitarian access remained constrained in some border areas, including Somare, near the Kenya-Ethiopia border. In response, local authorities deployed additional health personnel and increased police patrols. Schools were identified as temporary accommodation sites following the completion of national examinations.

title: 100,000 risk losing healthcare as key South Sudan border clinic nears closure, warns IOM
content:
Wunthou/Geneva, 5 November 2026 – An estimated 100,000 people risk losing access to essential healthcare in Wunthou, South Sudan according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM) as funding shortages threaten to shut down the only health clinic at Sudan–South Sudan border crossing. The clinic, operated by IOM, provides essential healthcare to refugees, South Sudanese returnees and host communities.

"People are arriving at this border after fleeing violence, often injured, sick or exhausted, this clinic is their first opportunity to receive medical care,” said Vijaya Souri, IOM Chief of Mission in South Sudan. “If it closes, thousands could be left without treatment at the very moment they need it most."

The facility is struggling to cope with rising demand for medical care as more people arrive at the border, many in need of urgent treatment after fleeing violence and enduring dangerous journeys.

Without urgent financial support, the facility risks shutting down by December, leaving thousands without access to emergency treatment, maternal healthcare, vaccinations, primary healthcare, and other life-saving services.

Since the conflict in Sudan began in April 2023, nearly all of the 1.3 million people who have crossed into South Sudan from Sudan have entered through Wunthou, making it a critical entry point for those fleeing the war. Located along the Sudan–South Sudan border, Wunthou also serves as a gateway to the Renk Transit Centre, which continues to accommodate large numbers of South Sudanese returning from Sudan.

Over the course of the conflict, the clinic has provided more than 400,000 medical consultations, administered over 260,000 vaccinations and assisted in the safe delivery of more than 1,000 babies. Health workers have also stabilized 6,022 critically ill and injured patients who were then successfully referred for advanced medical care.

Despite increasingly limited resources, the clinic continues to provide more than 1,000 outpatient consultations every week.

Many people crossing into South Sudan arrive with injuries, untreated illnesses and psychological trauma after experiencing violence, displacement and prolonged periods without medical care. Others suffer from infections linked to unsafe water, poor sanitation, and exposure to harsh conditions during their journeys.

The potential closure also raises wider public health concerns. Beyond treating patients, the clinic plays a critical role in detecting infectious diseases, vaccinating new arrivals, and preventing cross-border outbreaks and spread. Interruptions to these services could increase health risks for displaced populations, the surrounding communities, and threaten global health security.

With Sudan's conflict continuing to force people across borders, pressure on already stretched health services in South Sudan remains high. Sustained funding is urgently needed to keep Wunthou Clinic operational and ensure that people fleeing violence can continue to access essential healthcare.

IOM is seeking USD 131 million through its 2026 South Sudan Crisis Response Plan to provide humanitarian assistance and support to 1.4 million people affected by the crisis.

For More information, please contact IOM Media Center.

title: WHO Weekly Situation Update on Ongoing Health Emergency Events in South Sudan - Week #44, Date: 26 Oct - 1 Nov 2026
content:
PRIORITY ACTIONS

  • Sustain BVD preparedness across the priority counties as DRC reaches 10,467 cases and 5,103 deaths (CFR 48.8%); maintain PoE screening (81,967 events over 31 Oct–2 Nov) and screen air arrivals at Juba International Airport. Investigate the new Juba (Munuki) alert — a Ugandan trader who died on 2 Nov with fever and profuse bleeding after travel to eastern DRC.
  • Operationalize the WHO El Niño health plan (1 Nov–30 Apr): pre-position cholera kits, ORS, RDTs and reagents across five hubs, train 13 RRTs by 31 December, and act on trigger-based early warning for floods, drought and extreme heat. ▸ Sustain cholera response in the four active counties (Fangak, Renk, Rubkona, Mayom), where Fangak cases are rising; drive the 30-day knock-out plan (26 Oct–24 Nov) and push toward the earliest end-of-outbreak declaration (25 November) through 100% RDT testing.
  • Sustain malaria response (44,340 cases, 10 deaths — 58% below 2025); maintain LLIN coverage (96%) and QA microscopy ahead of the Malaria Indicator Survey (Master ToT began 30 Oct).
  • Complete Round 1 Polio NIDs in Ulang (79 of 80 counties reached, 96% coverage) and prepare Round 2 (17–20 Nov); advance the Magwi reactive measles campaign (4–8 Nov) and the new Tonj South conflict response (112 deaths, ~80,000 displaced).

title: UNICEF Syrian Arab Republic Humanitarian Situation Report No.3, 30 September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • During July–September 2026, humanitarian needs remained high amid displacement, returns, sporadic localized insecurity and military operations in southern governorates.
  • More than 5 million people remained internally displaced. While returns continued, the pace slowed during 2026; between July and September, close to 160,000 IDPs and refugees returned, bringing cumulative returns since late 2024 to more than 3.8 million people, including approximately 2 million IDP and 1.8 million refugee returnees.
  • Explosive ordnance continued to pose a serious threat to children. During Q3, 71 child casualties were recorded, including 22 children killed and 49 injured, highlighting continued risks to children and people accessing agricultural and grazing land.
  • In Q3, UNICEF reached 2.6 million people, including 1.7 million children, bringing the cumulative reach to 5.7 million, including 3.6 million children (1.8 million girls).
  • UNICEF's 2026 HAC remained 31 per cent funded, constraining the scale and continuity of essential services.

title: UNICEF Mali Humanitarian Situation Report No. 3, 30 September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Mali’s humanitarian situation remained critical in the third quarter of 2026, driven by insecurity, disease outbreaks, food and nutrition crises, and climate shocks. Coordinated attacks in Gao, Kidal, Mopti and Segou in July, following those of 25 April, further heightened risks. Armed-group blockades, explosive hazards, movement restrictions and administrative constraints continued to impede humanitarian access.
  • Humanitarian needs remain severe, with 5.9 million people, including 3.2 million children, requiring assistance. Nearly1.4 million people need nutrition support, including about 391,000 children with severe wasting, while the Circulating Vaccine-derided Poliovirus type 2cVDPV2 polio outbreak persists with new cases reported in 2026.
  • Since January, despite access and funding constraints, UNICEF support contributed to critical humanitarian results, including health services for 1.3 million people, cVDPV2 vaccination for 1.4 million children, severe acute malnutrition treatment for 146,105 children, psychosocial support for 67,289 children and caregivers, and safe water access for 40,942 people.

title: Somalia Weekly Weather Forecast - Valid From 04 - 10 Nov 2026
content:
Review Summary:

• Moderate falls in the lower Shabelle and Bay, lighter in the north. During 27 October–2 November, Balcad recorded 93.5 mm, Bur Hakaba 92.1 mm, Afgooye 81.1 mm, Awdheegle 69.8 mm and Bardheere 56.5 mm, while most northern stations recorded single falls of less than 50 mm. Satellite estimates (IMERG, 28 October–4 November) indicate 30–42 mm over Badhaadhe, Jamaame, Sablaale, Qoryooley, Jilib and Afmadow districts, where no rain gauges reported.

• By 2 November, 29 stations had already received their full Deyr normal, including Baidoa (405.5 mm, 176% of the Deyr normal), Mataban (333.4 mm, 275%), Galkacyo (253.5 mm, 390%) and Bardheere (278.0 mm, 130%). Burao (21%), Borama (16%) and Qardho (13%) remain far below normal.

• The Shabelle flood-risk peak has passed Belet Weyne. Belet Weyne was above its moderate floodrisk level for four days (26–29 October), peaking at 6.72 m, below the high level. It fell to 4.30 m on 2 November and has risen slightly to 4.76 m today. Bulo Burti peaked at 5.88 m on 30 October and is falling, Jowhar is falling slowly (4.10 m), and the Juba is falling at Dollow and Luuq.

• Radio Ergo callers (22–28 October) reported roads cut by flood water around Belet Weyne, families near the river in Middle Shabelle evacuated without proper shelter, and floods in Baidoa. Satellite images show about 44 km² of flooding in Jowhar district from open river breakages.

title: Conflict Escalation in Yemen - Situation Report #10 (Reporting period: 26 October - 3 November 2026 | Issued: 4 November 2026)
content:
Highlights

• Casualties rose again, led by Lahj. The HEOC register reached 9,730 (7,959 injured, 1,771 deaths) by 30 October, +658 in five days. The period average of ~132 per day is up from ~93 in Sitrep #9. Lahj accounted for 309 casualties (47%).

• Marib recorded the most deaths. Marib reported 36 deaths among 172 casualties (21%). On 30 October alone it reported 117 casualties, including 20 deaths, from Al-Jubah, Harib and the Al-Jawf front.

• West Coast services keep shrinking. In Al-Waziyah, all three partner-supported facilities are non-functional, and October service data from Dhubab could not be collected because of access constraints.

• Displacement has passed 300,000 people (IOM, 1 November), almost all in the past two months. More than 43,000 people have fled Al-Madaribah wa Al-Arah (Lahj) since early October, Aden now hosts more than 56,000, and prices of essential items in Taiz city have risen three- to fivefold.

• New IDP sites are opening without site management. The CCCM October master list records 28 new or reopened sites hosting 21,273 people, none yet covered by a CCCM partner, and 105 sites (74,456 people) in western Taiz districts where the controlling authority changed in October.

• Services reach a fraction of the displaced. WHO funds nine mobile circuits against a plan range of 30–40, and four fixed EMT Type 1 sites against 25–35. Interagency coordination with the Executive Unit for IDPs is needed to establish appropriate gathering points around which services can be planned.

• Cholera continues to decline from its W40 peak (639 in W40, 443 in W43) in the five most-affected governorates; W44 is about 23% incomplete. WHO has prioritised 23 districts (2.25 million people) for an ICG request for single-dose oral cholera vaccine.

• Supplies are still not moving freely. Sana'a airbridge flights on 29 October and 3 November were cancelled, and WHO's second consignment to Taiz city (a 10 MT test shipment with WFP) is awaiting a movement date.

• Only 12% of the plan is funded and the support is short in duration. WHO received US$3.7 million against the US$31 million 90-day plan, leaving US$27.3 million outstanding. A further US$7.3 million is under discussion with ECHO and CERF UF; if all arrive, 65% remains unfunded. This is critical to ensure continuity of the response beyond December 2026.

• Four links in the trauma chain remain unfunded: referral dispatch, a Tier 2 surgical site, ICU surge with fuel for 77 facilities, and rehabilitation after discharge. Without rehabilitation, patients who cannot be safely discharged occupy surgical beds, reducing capacity to admit the next arrivals.

title: Zambia Cholera Readiness and Response 2026: DREF Operational Update (MDRZM027)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

29-09-2026

What happened, where and when?

Zambia has been experiencing the cholera outbreak since 15th August 2025. The first case was detected at Chipwa Health post bordering Tanzania in a region that was experiencing cholera then. Within a few weeks, the disease spread to other parts of Northern Province before sporadic cases were reported on the Copperbelt and Lusaka. While the initial phase was brought under control, through robust intervention such as Risk Communication and Community Engagement, Case Area Targeted intervention, including Oral Cholera Vaccination, a resurgence of cases started being recorded in Lusaka district.

Cholera cases in Lusaka Province have been reported in multiple high-density and peri-urban communities, with Chainda identified as a key hotspot requiring intensified response interventions, including oral cholera vaccination and WASH activities. Transmission in Lusaka is largely linked to densely populated settlements with limited access to safe water and sanitation facilities. In Chilanga District of Lusaka Province, confirmed cases have been concentrated in specific localities, notably the Game–Sangalala area (recording the highest number of cases), Game– Kanchenjela, Linda, and Mt. Makulu, prompting community sensitization and environmental health measures.

On 9 February 2026, the Ministry of Health issued a press release on the cholera situation and other priority public health threats. The outbreak, initially concentrated in Mpulungu District of Northern Province, it began to shift southwards from November 2025, with new outbreaks emerging in Monze District and later in Lusaka Province. This shift reflects the influence of urban mobility, informal settlements, and persistent sanitation challenges. Although several districts have achieved the 28‑day zero‑reporting threshold, the MOH stated Lusaka Province has now become the main centre of transmission, with low‑level but widely dispersed sporadic cases across multiple sub‑districts and health facilities.

As of 25 Feb, the MOH Daily Surveillance Report reported Lusaka District as having the cumulative totals of 271 cases and 4 deaths. In the past few days, there has been a spike in the number of cases reported daily, with 14 new cases in the past 24 hours, reinforcing Lusaka's role as the current driver of national transmission.

According to the Global Cholera Situation Update released on 20 February, Zambia has been classified as “high risk,” with a significant likelihood of rapid transmission acceleration. The country also recorded the highest monthly percentage increase in cholera casesglobally, with a surge of +507.7%.

With continued efforts and support from cooperating partners, the number of cases significantly dropped to the level that the government declared the outbreak over. However, a new case was detected on 13 August 2026 after Vibrio cholerae was laboratoryconfirmed in a patient who had travelled from Chibombo District and was admitted at Apollo Mini Hospital in Lusaka.

Zambia Red Cross Society (ZRCS) concluded its interventions under the MDRZM027 response in August 2026, having supported cholera preparedness and response activities in Lusaka. However, a new cholera outbreak was detected on 13 August 2026, affecting Chiengi, Nsama, Chibombo, and other areas of Lusaka District that were not covered under the initial response. This renewed outbreak necessitated further preparedness and response interventions to address the evolving situation and support affected communities.

Subsequent transmission was identified in several districts: Chongwe, Chibombo, Lusaka, Chilanga, Chiengi and Nsama districts. By 29 September 2026, a total of 304 cholera cases had been reported nationally, including 62 laboratory-confirmed cases, 35 patients receiving treatment, 230 discharges and 11 deaths. Eight of the deaths occurred in the community and three in health facilities, highlighting concerns around delayed care-seeking.

At present, outbreak is affecting Twelve districts across five provinces. In Lusaka Province (537 cases), affected areas include Lusaka, Chilanga and Chongwe districts. Central Province has recorded the second highest cases (221) in Chibombo District four community deaths, with the majority of cases reported from the Mwanjuni Health Facility catchment area around 10 Miles.

The outbreak has also affected Chiengi, Mwansabombwe, Mwense and Nchelenge District in Luapula Province, which has reported 105 cases, including one community death. Nsama and Mpulungu Districts in Northern Province have reported a combined total 42 cases, while Southern Province has reported four cases (Chikankata-2 and Monze-2).

As of 15th October 2026, cumulatively, 966 cases have been recorded with 25 deaths across the Twelve (12) Districts in Five (5) Provinces with a CFR of 1.59 %.

title: Ghana: Registration Report - Anloga District and Keta Municipal (October 2026)
content:
Heavy rainfall experienced across Ghana on 29 June 2026 resulted in widespread flooding across several regions of the country following the overflow of major rivers, streams, and drainage systems. The flood caused loss of life, displacement, and extensive damage to homes, public infrastructure, livelihoods, and essential services, with communities located along riverbanks and low-lying areas experiencing the greatest impacts.

Following a request from the National Disaster Management Organization (NADMO), the International Organization for Migration (IOM) provided technical and financial support for the humanitarian response. In total, 1,694 affected individuals from 448 households were registered, including 263 internally displaced persons (IDPs) across 78 households. The exercise provided detailed information on the specific needs of the affected households to inform government’s decisions in providing aid and supporting the successful resettlement and reintegration of these affected people.

title: Ukraine war situation update | 17 – 23 October 2026
content:
Russia and Ukraine conduct a prisoner exchange, and Ukraine launches an underground attack to counter Russian advances.

Tetiana Gaviuk

Key trends

  • Humanitarian talks led Russia and Ukraine to conduct their first prisoner exchange in two months and agree to a ceasefire in the front line city of Oleshky in the Kherson region, enabling essential supplies to reach civilians who have endured months of siege and the safe evacuation of those who wish to leave the city. Despite this limited progress, major questions over territory and security guarantees remain unresolved. A breakthrough toward a sustained peace deal in expected trilateral talks in November is therefore unlikely.
  • During Operation Veles, Ukrainian forces advanced more than 15 km through gas pipelines to launch an attack behind Russian positions in the Kupiansk direction in the Kharkiv region, killing over 100 Russian soldiers and taking over 30 others prisoner. The underground attack was meant to counter Russian advances and was combined with surface strikes. It partially mirrors previous Russian infiltrations through gas pipelines in Kupiansk and in Russia’s Sudzhanskyi district in 2025. As drone surveillance increases and front line “kill zones” expand, the increased threat of drones, artillery, and mines makes surface movements nearly impossible. Going forward, both Russia and Ukraine will likely rely more on subterranean operations to move supplies, carry out infiltration missions, and launch assaults.

Key events

  1. 17 Oct.

    Kherson — A Russian aerial bomb and drone strike kill three civilians, including an ambulance driver, injure 44 others, and damage a Red Cross building in Kherson city

  2. 22 Oct.

    Kyiv — Russian forces launch 21 ballistic missiles, some with cluster warheads, at Kyiv city, destroying critical and transport infrastructure, killing one civilian, and injuring 22 over two days

  3. 22 Oct.

    Gorodets, Russia — Ukrainian drones hit Russia’s Federal Tax Service data center in Gorodets

Footnotes

title: Bosnia & Herzegovina — Migrant Mobility Situation Report (September 2026)
content: This report provides insights into the profiles, experiences, needs, routes travelled and intentions of migrants transiting through Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH). Data were collected from 1 to 30 September 2026. IOM carried out a route observation exercise in the Republika Srpska, Sarajevo Canton, Posavina Canton, Tuzla Canton, Bosnian-Podrinje Canton and Una Sana Canton to monitor trends in entries and exits as well as transit modalities within BiH. IOM also surveyed 9 migrants in active transit locations such as bus stops or at key entry and exit locations throughout the country as well as 272 migrants in two temporary reception centres (TRCs) in BiH (Blažuj, and Lipa).

title: Yemen - Displacement Caused by Escalation in Western Yemen - Update #17 (4 November 2026)
content:
IOM Yemen DTM continues to record displacement caused by the escalation in western Yemen. On 3 November 2026, IOM Yemen DTM recorded an increase of 10,374 individual IDPs compared to the figure presented in the RDT report distributed on 1 November 2026, bringing displacement between 1 August and 3 November to approximately 308,653 individuals (51,436 households)¹. This brings the cumulative number recorded since the escalation began in June 2026 to 309,709 individuals (51,612 households).

The largest concentration of displaced people was reported in Ta’iz Governorate, hosting 135,648 individuals (44%), followed by Lahj Governorate with 77,052 individuals (25%), and Aden Governorate with 58,884 individuals (19%). Additional displacement was recorded in Abyan with 15,426 individuals (5%); Al Hodeidah with 8,244 individuals (3%)²; Shabwah with 4,854 individuals (2%); Hadramawt with 3,252 individuals (1%); Ma’rib with 2,676 individuals (less than 1%); Al Maharah with 2,226 individuals (less than 1%); and Ad Dali’ with 1,447 individuals (less than 1%).

title: Global Weather Hazards Summary, November 05, 2026 – November 11, 2026
content:
Global Overview: El Niño continues to strengthen. Rainfall deficits are present in parts of equatorial Africa, northwestern Central Asia, across most of Central America, in some areas of Hispaniola, and in much of northern South America.

Africa Weather Hazards

Hot conditions are expected across parts of the Sahel, western Eastern Africa, and Southern Africa; while high flooding risks exist over eastern South Africa.

1) The Sudd wetlands of South Sudan continue to experience inundation.

2) A large part of western Eastern Africa faces dryness due to persisting below-average rainfall over the past 90 days. Southern and southeastern South Sudan and northern Uganda have already experienced deteriorated vegetation conditions, which have resulted in droughts in the region.

3) Central and eastern Liberia and the southern parts of Cote d’Ivoire and Ghana experience dryness due to sustained below-average rainfall and the next weeks’ forecast below-average rainfall.

4) Persistent heavy rainfall continues to pose an elevated risk of flooding across southern part of Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Congo-Brazzaville, and eastern DRC. The forecast heavy rainfall increases the risks of flooding over eastern South Africa and Eswatini during the next week.

5) Hot conditions are expected across a large part of the Sahel, western Eastern Africa, and west-central Southern Africa.

title: Haiti: Nationwide Response - Situation Report No. 3 (as of 30 September 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • 1.49 million people displaced in August, up from 1.47 million in April, as the crisis spreads to rural areas and provincial towns.
  • 335,000 people lack adequate access to health care in Artibonite, where insecurity has forced the closure of 21 health facilities.
  • 253,725 children aged 6 to 59 months are at risk of acute malnutrition by May 2027. The national prevalence of global acute malnutrition rose from 5.1 per cent in 2023 to 7.4 per cent in 2026.
  • Health partners conducted 74,614 medical consultations through 120 mobile clinic deployments.

title: Panama: Earthquake in Azuero & Veraguas - Situation Report No. 08 (as of 4 November 2026, 12:30)
content:
KEY POINTS

  • Almost four weeks after the magnitude 7.5 earthquake of 9 October, around 3,300 people remain in shelters, a quarter fewer than a week earlier, as more families return to their communities.
  • Of the nearly 20,000 homes assessed, more than 4,600 have total damage, and the Government plans to build 2,700 homes for families who lost theirs.
  • Damage to 619 schools and 120 health facilities continues to limit services, as more temporary learning spaces open.
  • A magnitude 5.9 earthquake on 31 October forced authorities to evacuate four hospitals and five health centres as a precaution, but caused no injuries.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Almost four weeks after the magnitude 7.5 earthquake of 9 October, with its epicentre 39 km north-west of Tonosí, the National Civil Protection System (SINAPROC), through the National Emergency Operations Centre (COEN), reports two deaths and 27 injuries. As of 2 November, Damage Assessment and Needs Analysis (EDAN) teams had assessed 19,865 homes and registered 63,767 people. Of those homes, 4,633 have total damage, 11,107 moderate or partial damage and 4,125 minor damage. The people registered include 198 pregnant women and 2,758 people with disabilities. The assessments also report damage to 619 schools and 120 health facilities.

The number of people in shelters continues to fall: 3,356 people (886 families) remain in 113 shelters, down from 4,501 in 141 shelters on 27 October. Almost half are in Veraguas (1,635), followed by Los Santos (1,153) and Herrera (359). In Soná, Río Grande and Mariato, UNICEF, UNHCR and IOM missions found that some families are returning to land near their homes, where they are putting up tents or makeshift structures.

On 31 October, a magnitude 5.9 aftershock forced authorities to evacuate four hospitals, five health centres and the population of Isla de Cañas as a precaution, but caused no injuries. Follow-up inspections found worsening cracks at the hospitals in Aguadulce and Penonomé, in areas with oxygen pipes and electrical lines.

Since the response began, SINAPROC has transported more than 385 tonnes of aid by land and carried out 39 medical air evacuations, and the Agricultural Marketing Institute (IMA) has distributed 81,229 bags of food in 1,548 communities.

The Government has set up an inter-agency commission to build 2,700 homes, and the Ministry of Education (MEDUCA) is demolishing and replacing severely damaged schools. The UN system continues to support the Government-led response in shelter, education, food security, health, protection, water, sanitation and hygiene, logistics and telecommunications.

title: Lao People's Democratic Republic: Flood 2026 - DREF Operational Update (MDRLA012)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

14-08-2026

What happened, where and when?

Since late June 2026, Lao PDR has experienced recurrent flooding, flash floods, waterlogging and landslides associated with the southwest monsoon and Tropical Storm Maysak. The situation worsened throughout July and August as prolonged and repeated heavy rainfall triggered further flooding, particularly in areas already affected by earlier rainfall.

By 18 August, flooding had been reported across eight provinces: Louang-Namtha, Bokeo, Xayabouri, Bolikhamxai, Khammouane, Savannakhet, Sekong and Champasak, with Khammouane and Champasak among the most severely affected. A landslide in Bolikhamxai Province on 16–17 July also resulted in three fatalities.

Further flash floods were reported in Luang Prabang and Oudomxai on 19 August, while weather forecasts warned of continued heavy rainfall and an increased risk of flooding and landslides in northern and central parts of the country during 18–21 August. The repeated weather events prolonged the emergency and increased response needs. Following its assessment of the situation, the (Lao Red Cross) LRC determined on 14 August that additional resources through the IFRC Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) were required to sustain and scale up its response.

title: Zambia Measles Outbreak - DREF Operational Update (MDRZM028)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

08-07-2026

What happened, where and when?

A measles outbreak was confirmed in Shangombo District, Western Province, Zambia, following identification of the index case during Epidemiological Week 19 of 2026 (May 4-10, 2026). The index case was a 6-year-old female from Kapengela Village who presented at Shangombo District Hospital with clinical signs consistent with measles, including fever, maculopapular rash, cough, conjunctivitis, and coryza. Her vaccination history was unknown. A blood specimen collected from the case was tested at the University Teaching Hospital (UTH) Virology Laboratory and confirmed positive for Measles IgM antibodies on 16 May 2026, leading to the formal declaration of the outbreak.

On the 27th of April, 2026 Situlu1 Health Post received a client form Kalungulungu village of Nina district in Angola. The signs of measles started on the 14th April. The patient travelled with three others who also had cough and runny nose. Samples were collected from the index suspected case and the three contacts, transported to the laboratory on the 11th May, 2026.

Prior to confirmation of the outbreak, on 6 May 2026, Shangombo District received an unverified alert of a suspected measles outbreak across the border in Rivungu Municipality, Angola, involving six suspected cases among children aged 2–6 years. The alert was verified through the electronic Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (eIDSR) system, triggering activation of the Public Health Emergency Rapid Response Team (PHERRT) to investigate and coordinate response activities.

Since confirmation of the index case, the outbreak has expanded within Shangombo District, with increasing numbers of suspected and confirmed cases reported which continues to rise even after the vaccination campaign which was conducted between 6th to 11th July 2026. As of 24/08/2026 Shangombo had 1313 cumulative cases, 26 confirmed cases and 13 deaths with a CF rate of 1%.

With the increasing cases in the district, Zambia National Public Health Institute, a specialized Government Institution mandated to lead and coordinate public health security in Zambia made a formal request for support to the National Society on the 8th July 2026 highlighting the gaps.

N’gumbele Health Post has been proposed for inclusion in the ongoing measles response based on the epidemiological and operational situation documented at the facility. The health post recorded 36 measles cases, with cases reported between 3 July and 23 August 2026. Of these, 4 were confirmed cases, 15 were epidemiologically linked, and 17 were clinically compatible, indicating a significant measles burden within the health post catchment area.
The situation is particularly concerning among children, with 14 cases recorded among children aged 0–4 years and 4 cases among those aged 5–9 years. In addition, Nangandu and Masuku have been identified as hotspot villages, highlighting the need for intensified community mobilisation and vaccination messaging in these areas.

The situation at N’gumbele is also associated with important operational challenges, including limited staffing, inconsistent vaccination ivities, difficult access due to flood plains, streams and sandy terrain, and a non-functional cold chain. The facility also serves a population that includes people from across the border, with the assessment noting a porous border and reported cases from Angola. Importantly, N’gumbele which has a population of 3,372 is contributing to the measles case load being managed within Shangombo District. Cases identified at or around N’gumbele are referred to Mambolomoka Health Facility in Shangombo for further management.

Therefore, excluding N’gumbele from the DREF-supported response would leave an important source of cases outside the intervention area while cases continue to be detected and referred into a facility that is within the DREF geographical scope. This creates a gap in the response, as resources would be directed towards managing cases at Mambolomoka without adequately addressing the community and facility-level factors contributing to those cases.
The continued movement and interaction of populations across the Zambia–Angola border further increases the importance of addressing N’gumbele as part of the wider response. Given the porous border and the transboundary population served by the facility, measles transmission can continue across communities even after transmission has been controlled in the immediate DREF-supported areas of Shangombo. As a result, failure to include N’gumbele could contribute to continued transmission, re-introduction of cases and prolonged referral of patients into facilities such as Mambolomoka.

Furthermore, N’gumbele is already recognised within the proposed response adjustments, including the planned deployment and training of additional personnel, demonstrating that the facility has been identified as relevant to the ongoing measles response. Based on the epidemiological linkage, continued referrals to Mambolomoka, the cross-border movement of populations, and the risk of continued transmission and re-introduction of measles into Shangombo District.

title: UNICEF Afghanistan Humanitarian Situation Report No. 9, 1-30 September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Food insecurity and acute malnutrition continued to worsen in Afghanistan, with 15.9 million people facing Crisis or worse levels of food insecurity (IPC Phase 3+), including 3.4 million in Emergency (IPC Phase 4), while child wasting reached its highest recorded levels for the August–October period.
  • UNICEF screened approximately 1.3 million children for wasting, admitting 107,396 children with severe or high-risk moderate wasting for treatment, while providing nutrition counselling to 196,601 caregivers.
  • UNICEF reached 212,103 people with integrated child protection services, including psychosocial support, case management, family tracing and reunification, and gender-based violence prevention and response, prioritizing children and families affected by emergencies, displacement and returns.
  • UNICEF provided 274,043 people with access to safe drinking water and 121,138 people with basic sanitation services, while reaching 175,389 people with hygiene promotion and behaviour change interventions.

title: Malawi: Measles Outbreak Response - DREF Operational Update (MDRMW027)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met
20-07-2026

What happened, where and when?

Malawi is experiencing an escalating measles outbreak, with the Ministry of Health reporting 73 measles alerts through the Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) system during Epidemiological Week 27 (29 June to 5 July 2026). The outbreak follows months of sustained transmission that began with sporadic cases earlier in 2026 and has since developed into localized outbreaks in several districts. Cumulatively, Nsanje has reported 211 confirmed and epidemiologically linked cases since February 2026, Dedza has reported 90 confirmed cases since July 2026, and Balaka has reported 82 laboratory-confirmed cases since January 2026. Epidemiological data further indicate that more than 85% of confirmed cases have occurred among children under 15 years of age, while over 70% of cases were either unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status, demonstrating significant immunity gaps within affected communities. Continued reporting of new laboratory-confirmed cases indicates ongoing transmission and an increasing risk of expansion to neighbouring districts.

The outbreak is most pronounced in the catchment areas of Comfort and Khwisa health facilities in Balaka District, Golomoti and Kaundu in Dedza District, and Osiyana, Ndamera, Nsanje, and Trinity health facilities in Nsanje District. These areas are experiencing a combination of factors that continue to fuel transmission, including low routine immunization coverage, high numbers of unvaccinated children, delayed health-seeking behaviour, weak community surveillance systems, inadequate risk communication, and widespread misinformation regarding vaccination. In Nsanje, cross-border population movement along the Malawi-Mozambique border has intensified the risk of disease spread, while shortages of trained health workers, volunteers, and operational resources have constrained surveillance and response efforts. In Balaka and Dedza, persistent immunity gaps and delayed case detection are contributing to continued transmission within communities.

The outbreak has generated significant public health and humanitarian impacts. Increasing numbers of suspected and confirmed cases have placed additional pressure on district health services through heightened demand for surveillance, laboratory testing, case management, contact tracing, and vaccination outreach activities. Children under five years of age remain particularly vulnerable due to low vaccination uptake, malnutrition, and limited access to health services. In some communities, particularly within parts of Nsanje, religious beliefs and vaccine hesitancy have contributed to delayed treatment-seeking and reduced acceptance of vaccination services, increasing the risk of severe illness and preventable deaths. The continued accumulation of susceptible children and ongoing transmission in Balaka, Dedza, and Nsanje indicate a high likelihood of further spread unless urgent interventions are implemented to strengthen outbreak-response vaccination, community engagement, surveillance, and risk communication activities.

Given the epidemiological trends and operational gaps identified, Balaka, Dedza, and Nsanje represent the highest-priority districts for immediate intervention. These districts continue to experience active transmission driven by substantial immunity gaps, weak community-level disease detection and reporting systems, and challenges in reaching at-risk populations with vaccination and health promotion services. Without rapid scale-up of surveillance, community engagement, social mobilization, and immunization activities, there is a significant risk that transmission will intensify within these districts and spread to surrounding areas, resulting in additional morbidity and mortality among vulnerable children and other susceptible populations.

title: UNICEF Cameroon Humanitarian Situation Report No. 3, July - September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Cameroon’s overlapping crises left 2.9 million people, including 1.5 million children, in need of humanitarian assistance amid conflict, displacement, flooding and disease outbreaks.
  • Over 3,000 cholera cases were reported during this period.1 UNICEF supported two rounds of oral cholera vaccination in seven priority health districts, alongside WASH, case management and community engagement interventions.
  • UNICEF and partners screened 764,134 children for wasting, with 48,315 children with severe wasting admitted for treatment; 36,223 children accessed education, 36,129 children and caregivers received psychosocial support, and 68,329 people accessed safe water.
  • UNICEF’s US$53.8 million appeal remained 86 per cent unfunded, with critical gaps in Child Protection and GBViE (95 per cent), Nutrition (94 per cent), Education (91 per cent) and WASH (76 per cent), constraining the scale and geographic coverage of assistance.

title: UNICEF Venezuela Situation Report No.10 (Earthquake Response), 8 September -19 October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Four months after the 24 June earthquakes, UNICEF is supporting early recovery, adapting services as families relocate while maintaining essential assistance. UNICEF has reached 60,995 people with primary health care, screened 17,810 children for acute malnutrition and provided 21,008 people with safe water. Child protection interventions reached 29,728 people, including 22,999 through community-based mental health and psychosocial support.
  • UNICEF is supporting 52 learning spaces reaching 1,981 children and adolescents, restoring WASH services in schools, health facilities and water systems, and strengthening community-based protection and referrals.
  • UNICEF has mobilized US$33.6 million of the US$65.7 million required for the earthquake response, covering 51 per cent of needs. However, the broader 2026 humanitarian response remains 63 per cent underfunded, underscoring the urgent need for sustained, flexible funding to support recovery while safeguarding assistance for other vulnerable children across Venezuela.

SITUATION OVERVIEW AND HUMANITARIAN NEEDS

Four months after the earthquakes, the response is progressively shifting towards early recovery while maintaining essential humanitarian assistance for families who remain displaced or continue to face significant needs due to housing losses and disruptions to basic services. The continued use of some schools as temporary accommodation is also placing pressure on education infrastructure and affecting the full return of children and adolescents to learning.

Authorities and humanitarian partners are supporting the voluntary transition of affected families from temporary camps to safer and more sustainable accommodation. As of 11 October, 18,055 people remained in 86 transitional camps, while 7,336 people had been relocated and 30 camps had closed .4 Later in October, the Government reported the delivery of 500 transitional housing units in Ciudad Caribia, La Guaira, with an initial 400 families , approximately 1,750 people, moving from temporary camps and tents into the new accommodation.5 These developments reflect the progressive transition from emergency accommodation towards more sustainable housing solutions, although significant temporary accommodation needs remain.

Housing recovery is also advancing, although needs remain substantial. As of 29 September, under the Plan “Venezuela Renace”, authorities reported that 709 homes had been allocated to earthquake-affected families, while construction was under way across 38 worksites for an additional 5,213 housing units.6 Government measures also include the rehabilitation of damaged housing, construction of new units and other mechanisms to support families requiring housing solutions.

The progressive transition of affected families from temporary camps to communities, return areas and more sustainable housing solutions is reshaping protection and service-delivery needs rather than bringing them to an end. As families relocate, protection and service delivery needs are becoming more geographically dispersed, increasing the importance of territorial coordination and effective referral pathways to ensure continuity of child protection, education, WASH, nutrition and other essential services. This transition is particularly important for children and families with ongoing protection cases or specialized needs, as changes in location may affect the continuity of case management, follow-up and access to services unless referral arrangements are adjusted accordingly.

Psychosocial needs also remain significant. Through ongoing community-based interventions, UNICEF and partners continue to identify children, adolescents, caregivers and other affected community members requiring psychosocial support, including cases requiring specialized referral and follow-up. The impacts of bereavement, prolonged displacement, uncertainty regarding housing and livelihoods, relocation and adaptation to new communities can compound existing vulnerabilities. Sustained community-based mental health and psychosocial support, accompanied by specialized referrals where required, remains essential throughout camp closure, relocation, return and housing recovery.

As the response moves further into early recovery, sustained humanitarian support remains essential to ensure that relocation translates into durable recovery rather than new vulnerabilities. Continued assistance will be required to restore access to essential services, accompany affected children and families through relocation and return, and ensure that protection, education, health, nutrition, WASH and psychosocial needs are addressed without interruption, while progressively strengthening community-based systems and resilience.

title: Kenya Flood 2026 - Imminent DREF Operation (MDRKE074)
content:
Scenario analysis

When and where is the hazard expected to happen?

Since the onset of the October-November-December (OND) rainy season, forecasts from the Kenya Meteorological Department have consistently indicated an increased likelihood of above-average rainfall across much of Kenya, with the highest probabilities concentrated in eastern, northeastern, coastal, and several central counties. The monthly outlook highlights enhanced rainfall conditions throughout October and anticipates heavy rainfall events in several parts of the country. The weekly forecast valid 20-26 October similarly indicates widespread rainfall activity across much of the country. These forecasts suggest a continued strengthening of seasonal rainfall towards the end of October. (KMSA Monthly Forecast; KMSA Weekly Forecast 20-26 October).

Sub-seasonal forecast guidance from NOAA GFS further supports this outlook. The Week-1 accumulated rainfall forecast (NOAA GFS Week 1) valid through approximately 2 November indicates widespread moderate to heavy rainfall across central, eastern, northeastern and coastal Kenya, with many areas expected to receive between approximately 60-150 mm of rainfall during the week. The subsequent Week-2 forecast (NOAA GFS Week 2) valid through approximately 9 November continues to show above-normal rainfall across many of the same areas, suggesting persistence of wet conditions beyond the initial rainfall episode. The consecutive weekly forecasts therefore indicate that rainfall is expected to remain elevated into early November rather than being confined to a short-duration event. Taken together, the monthly, weekly and sub-seasonal forecasts point to late October through the first week of November as the period of greatest hydrological concern, with the highest likelihood of peak impacts occurring during the first week of November (1-9 November) when cumulative rainfall from successive wet periods is likely to result in increased soil saturation, elevated river levels, localized flooding, flash flooding and access disruptions, particularly in eastern, northeastern and coastal counties.

The trigger date has been set at 1 November 2026, based on forecast evidence that rainfall is expected to become both more widespread and sustained across Kenya by the beginning of November. While NOAA forecasts indicate localized heavy rainfall developing over parts of western and northern Kenya around 28 October, the NOAA daily accumulated precipitation forecast (NOAA 24h precipitation model) valid 1 November 2026 shows rainfall extending across much of the country, including western, central, eastern and northeastern Kenya.

This outlook is further supported by global forecasting products, which indicate an increased likelihood of heavy rainfall over western, central, northeastern, and southeastern Kenya in the next two weeks. In western Kenya, persistent rainfall since early October, combined with the forecast for continued rainfall, is expected to significantly increase soil moisture levels and lead to widespread soil saturation. Consequently, river and stream levels are likely to rise, increasing the risk of riverine flooding, particularly in flood-prone, low-lying, and poorly drained areas. In contrast, much of northern Kenya has remained relatively dry in recent weeks. Therefore, intense rainfall events are likely to generate substantial surface runoff and increase the risk of flash flooding, especially in arid and semi-arid areas where infiltration rates are low.

Furthermore, heavy rainfall has persisted over southern Ethiopia for more than a week, increasing river levels. This raises concerns about increased river flows into northeastern Kenya through the transboundary Juba-Shebelle river basin, potentially exacerbating flood risks in downstream areas.

In central Kenya, the flood risk is primarily driven by high levels of urbanization. Persistent or intense short-duration rainfall frequently overwhelms drainage systems, resulting in surface flooding and disruption to transportation and critical infrastructure. Given the forecast for heavy rainfall in the coming weeks, urban flood risks are expected to increase significantly across several major population centres.

title: Ethiopia | Landslides and Floods - Final Report (MDRET036)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Description of the crisis

In July 2024, heavy rains, landslides, and flooding in Ethiopia affected more than 500,000 people across 14 zones, displaced over 140,000 people, and claimed approximately 420 lives across seven regions. The Oromia, Sidama, Amhara, Tigray, Gambella, Central Ethiopia, Southwestern Ethiopia, and Southern Ethiopia regions suffered extensive damage, including the loss of more than 8,659 hectares of cropland, the death of 113 livestock, and the destruction of 277 houses.

Gofa, Desnech Woreda, Omorate Town, and multiple zones were identified at high risk of landslide, forcing the relocation of communities to a newer identified area. Since then, ERCS and other humanitarian actors have been actively providing humanitarian support to affected people. ERCS, with support from the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), launched an appeal; Ethiopia Landslides and Floods (MDRET036); initially seeking CHF 6 million. This appeal was later followed by an operational update to expand the scope, geographic coverage, and duration of the intervention from 12 months to 20 months, reflecting the evolving needs on the ground. Ethiopia - Landslides and Floods (MDRET036).

To kick-start the operation, a DREF allocation of CHF 1,000,000 was released. Additional income of CHF 1,253,246 was subsequently received, bringing the total available funding to CHF 2,253,246. Total expenditure amounted to CHF 2,245,195, representing 99.6% utilization of available funding and leaving an unspent balance of CHF 8,051.

The response strategy was designed to address both immediate humanitarian needs and longer-term recovery priorities. Key interventions include the provision of transitional shelter and essential household items, food security and livelihood recovery support through multipurpose cash transfers, distribution of agricultural inputs, and skills development opportunities for youth with start-up capital. In addition, the program integrated Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services, health and psychosocial support, and community-based disaster risk reduction (DRR) initiatives.

Cross-cutting priorities such as Protection, Gender, and Inclusion (PGI) were mainstreamed throughout the response to ensure safe, equitable, and dignified assistance for all population groups, particularly the most vulnerable. Strong emphasis has been placed on community engagement and participation, enabling affected populations to actively contribute to planning and implementation processes, thereby promoting ownership, sustainability, and resilience in recovery efforts.

Overall, the intervention reflects a holistic and integrated approach aimed at supporting communities not only to recover from the immediate impacts of the disaster but also to strengthen their capacity to withstand future shocks. Despite the significant recovery achieved through the operation, affected communities remain vulnerable to recurrent climate-related hazards, particularly landslides, flooding, environmental degradation, and livelihood shocks. Evaluation findings indicate that while access to shelter, water, and livelihoods improved, some households continue to experience limited food self-sufficiency, incomplete livelihood recovery, and ongoing exposure to environmental risks. Continued investment in disaster risk reduction, climate adaptation, livelihood diversification, and community preparedness remains essential to sustain recovery gains and strengthen long-term resilience.

title: DRC: Ebola BVD Outbreak: LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #13 (Reporting period: October 2026)

title: Health Sector Bulletin October 2026
content:
Syria health system key issues, October 2026

• Essential services face a continuity risk. Premature withdrawal of external support could interrupt maternity care, emergency surgery, dialysis, chronic disease treatment, primary health care (PHC) and referrals. The proposed safeguard is an essential-services continuity guarantee, backed by bridge funding, verified replacement capacity and contingency arrangements before support ends.

• Financing and accountability must support sustained operations. Fragmented projects and unconfirmed commitments risk leaving salaries, medicines, maintenance and other recurrent costs unfunded. The proposed response is a transparent, multi-year financing and implementation framework linking public budgets and partner funding, with explicit responsibilities, deadlines, funding sources and reporting. MoH leadership should be supported by the technical stewardship, local institutions and community participation, while preserving necessary humanitarian independence.

• Reconstructed facilities may remain unable to deliver care. Buildings alone cannot ensure services. Staff shortages, unreliable electricity and water, interrupted diagnostics and weak referral transport can leave restored facilities ineffective. Recovery investments should fund complete district service networks, with a suitable workforce and full operating costs, rather than isolated rehabilitation projects.

• Medicine access and household affordability remain central. Patients need uninterrupted access to essential medicines, including insulin, antihypertensives and obstetric medicines. The Outlook calls for reliable procurement, quality assurance and stock monitoring, alongside financial protection. Priorities must also cover maternal and newborn care, noncommunicable diseases, mental health, rehabilitation and malnutrition.

• National integration must address unequal local conditions. Service capacity and access differ across Idleb,
Aleppo, northeast Syria, As-Sweida and rural areas, including within governorates. Displacement and returns add pressure where health services and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) capacity are compromised. Common national standards require locally tailored implementation and safeguards against geographic or political exclusion.

• Outbreak readiness and usable information need strengthening. AWD, measles, hepatitis and other outbreak threats intersect with weak WASH systems, climate shocks and population movement. Priorities include linked surveillance and laboratories, rapid response and catch-up immunization. Existing facility, workforce, utilization and financing data need to support one operational decision system, with confidentiality protections and independent verification.

title: WFP Haiti Country Brief, October 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Haiti’s humanitarian crisis continued to deepen in September amid persistent insecurity, large-scale displacement, economic deterioration and climaterelated shocks. An estimated 5.8 million people faced acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above), including 1.8 million in IPC Phase 4. The number of internally displaced persons exceeded 1.49 million, equivalent to approximately 12 percent of the population – while over 200,000 forced repatriations have been recorded in 2026.

• Insecurity continued to expand beyond Port-auPrince, with intensified clashes between the GSF and armed groups. Attacks, abductions and civilian casualties reported across Artibonite, Centre and other departments disrupted livelihoods, markets and access to basic services. The Central Bank of Haiti projected an eighth consecutive year of economic contraction, with consumer prices rising 17% year-onyear (food contributed 10.6 of the 17 points). Rising prices, limited livelihood opportunities and reduced purchasing power further constrained households’ ability to meet basic needs, placing additional pressure on overwhelmed social services.

• By the end of September only 10% of the adult population (or roughly 717,000 people) had registered to vote (well below the minimum target). The Provisional Electoral Council appointed a new President of the Council, suggesting further uncertainty over long delayed elections set for December 2026, as insecurity, access constraints and logistical challenges continue to affect the electoral process.

title: Situation Update: Middle-East crisis spillover impact on local fuel and food prices, threatening household affordability to nutritious diets in Cambodia (October 2026)
content:
KEY MESSAGES

Fuel and fertilizer prices remained elevated during Q3 2026. Nationwide, diesel prices were up 49% year-on-year (YoY), while urea fertilizer prices in the Tonle Sap provinces increased by 19.4% YoY.

Trade with the Middle East remained volatile due to fluctuations in fuel and LNG imports, highlighting Cambodia's continued exposure to external energy shocks.

The food basket cost remained broadly stable during Q3 2026, although food costs remained higher than a year earlier, especially in rural areas.

Q3 2026 was characterized by easing inflation compared with Q2 levels. However, inflation in September remained 5.3% above 2025 levels, indicating persistent cost pressures on households.

Food purchasing power weakened in Q3 2026 as the wage-to-food ratio declined by 5.1% nationwide and 4.3% at the provincial level, driven by falling non-agricultural wages, while food purchasing power of agricultural labourers remained stable.

BACKGROUND

The ongoing conflict in Middle-East (ME), compounding existing global crises, has intensified regional and global economic uncertainty, with increasing spillover effects on international commodity markets. This has led to disruptions to key trade routes, heightened security risks in major maritime corridors, and increased volatility in global energy markets, driving up transportation and insurance costs. These pressures are being transmitted through global supply chains, affecting the prices and availability of fuel, fertilizer, and selected food commodities, particularly vegetable oil, in Cambodia, an import-dependent country.

To better understand and monitor the potential impacts of the ME crisis on domestic market dynamics, since June 2026, WFP Cambodia has expanded its remote market monitoring from 10 provinces around the Tonle Sap Lake (36 markets), to 24 provinces nationwide (63 markets). Combined with secondary analysis of available prices, income/expenditure, and trade, this approach tracks price fluctuation of food, energy, and fertilizer, with the objective of identifying emerging risks such as price surges, supply constraints, and trade disruptions that may undermine household purchasing power and food security, particularly among vulnerable populations.

title: Somalia | Simplified Early Action Protocol Cholera (EAP №: sEAP2025SO02, Operation №: MDRSO023), 17 October 2026
content:
Activation Overview

On 11 October 2026, the Somali Red Crescent Society (SRCS) activated Trigger 1 (T1) under its Simplified Early Action Protocols (sEAPs) for Acute Watery Diarrhoea (AWD)/Cholera following the confirmation of elevated epidemiological and environmental risks in Puntland and Somaliland. The activation was based on surveillance data indicating a sustained increase in AWD cases, confirmation of cholera transmission, and deteriorating water quality conditions that could accelerate the spread of disease. In Puntland, the Puntland Ministry of Health (MoH) confirmed Vibrio cholerae O1 (Ogawa) in samples collected from Balibusle, Mudug region. A total of 307 AWD cases were reported across 17 locations in Mudug, Bari, Nugaal, and Ras-Asayr regions by epidemiological week 42 of 2026. The majority of cases were concentrated in Balibusle (139 cases) and Rako, Bari (114 cases), while Garowe, one of the priority intervention areas, reported 21 cases. Additional spikes in AWD cases have also been reported in a neighboring location to the selected PAMIs, indicating an expanding risk of transmission across the affected areas. Furthermore, water quality testing conducted by the Puntland Water Development Authority (PWDA) detected E. coli contamination in two of the three main water sources serving Balibusle, highlighting an increased risk of waterborne disease transmission and the potential for further spread of AWD/cholera in the region.

In Somaliland, surveillance data from the Ministry of Health Development (MoHD) reported 842 AWD cases in epidemiological week 41, representing a 5.3 per cent increase from the previous week and continuing an upward trend observed since epidemiological week 38. Since the beginning of 2026, a cumulative 35,439 acute diarrhoea cases have been reported. The highest caseloads have been recorded in Awdal, Togdheer, Maroodi Jeex, Sahil, Sanaag, and Sool regions. Additional spikes in AWD cases have also been reported in a neighboring location to the selected PAMIs, indicating an expanding risk of transmission across the affected areas. In parallel, the SRCS community-based surveillance system, through the Nyss platform, reported an increase in AWD alerts from affected communities, providing additional evidence of escalating public health risks.

title: PER: Pluvial/Flash Flood - 11-2026 - Flood Fenómeno El Niño #2 (2026-11-03)
content:
Description

According to Complementary Report No. 15400, updated on 3 November 2026 at 06:57, the department of Tumbes has reported 324 people severely impacted and 625 people affected, along with 2 destroyed homes, 110 uninhabitable homes, and 225 affected homes. The report also indicates impacts on 10 educational institutions, one health facility, and 2 km of local roads. The province of Zarumilla accounts for the vast majority of displaced people (320) and uninhabitable homes (109), with the district of Aguas Verdes being the most severely affected, reporting 316 displaced people, 108 uninhabitable homes, and three affected educational institutions. In contrast, the province of Tumbes concentrates most of the affected population (265 people) and the reported impacts on education, health, and road infrastructure. It should be noted that the Damage and Needs Assessment (EDAN) remains ongoing at the local government level; therefore, the reported figures are preliminary and subject to revision as additional information becomes available

Through Supreme Decree No. 149-2026-PCM, the Government of Peru declared a 60-day State of Emergency in selected districts across 24 departments and the Constitutional Province of Callao, including Tumbes. During the emergency period, regional and local authorities will implement immediate risk reduction, response, and rehabilitation measures. The decree establishes that response activities will be financed through the institutional budgets of the respective government entities, without requiring additional allocations from the National Treasury.

The event has been linked to anomalous weather conditions associated with the Coastal El Niño phenomenon. According to specialists from the National Meteorology and Hydrology Service of Peru (SENAMHI), rainfall accumulations exceeding 100 mm have been recorded in areas where seasonal precipitation is typically limited to only 2 to 3 mm, highlighting the exceptional nature of the event.

Response operations are ongoing. The Ministry of Housing, Construction and Sanitation conducted a drone overflight over the Puerto Perú sector in Aguas Verdes to assess damage and activated the El Beso Early Warning and Response System (SARE), operating two pumps that evacuated approximately 84 m³ of accumulated water resulting from the rise of the Tumbes River. In the district of Tumbes, operational teams and two hydrojet units were deployed to remove standing water and restore drainage system functionality.

The Ministry of Education has temporarily shifted educational services from in-person to virtual modalities in affected areas as a preventive measure. In addition, personnel from the Rapid Disaster Intervention Company of the Armored Infantry Battalion No. 211 were deployed to the Urcus sector in the district of Corrales to support drainage and canal-cleaning activities in coordination with local authorities.

Looking ahead, SENAMHI forecasts the continuation of heavy to extremely heavy rainfall between 4 and 6 November, particularly in Tumbes, while moderate to heavy rainfall is expected in the inland coastal areas of Piura.

title: El Niño Update: Busuma and Musenyi Refugee Sites in Burundi (October 2026)
content:
1. Executive Summary

Busuma. Between 17 and 21 October 2026, torrential rains, strong winds and lightning affected all sectors of the refugee response. The validated assessment of 18 October recorded 510 tents affected, including 425 destroyed and 85 washed away, leaving approximately 2,000 people in need of relocation. Around 120 households had been relocated preventively before the complete collapse of a communal shelter. A subsequent report of more than 200 shelters completely destroyed should not be added to the 510-tent ﬁgure until deduplication is completed. One lightning-related death was recorded and ten people received medical care. The rains also affected drainage, WASH facilities, the Global/WHO Clinic, internal roads and learning spaces serving nearly 800 children.

Musenyi. The assessment conducted on 22 October 2026 focused primarily on shelters and contingency preparedness. Eight households completely lost their tents. Five semi-durable houses were damaged, three of which have already been repaired, while two still require rooﬁng sheets. Partial damage to the roof of communal shelter No. 6 affects four households. Ten spaces can accommodate 22 family tents for priority households, subject to validation of the beneﬁciary list. This capacity does not correspond to 22 conﬁrmed disaster-affected households. Termite-damaged poles, deteriorated tarpaulins and stagnant water require preventive measures.

Operational priorities. In Busuma, immediate interventions include safe relocation, stabilization of gullies and unstable infrastructure, desludging of latrines, water quality control, continuity of health care and education, and targeted assistance to households with conﬁrmed losses. In Musenyi, validated priorities include tent installation after beneﬁciary validation, provision of rooﬁng sheets to the two households concerned, rehabilitation of communal shelter No. 6, maintenance of communal shelters, drainage of stagnant-water areas, and preservation of the Rub Hall and contingency spaces.

Methodological limitation. Figures must remain disaggregated by site, sector and damage category. No overall total of affected households or shelters should be published before lists are consolidated and deduplicated. For Musenyi, needs outside shelter and drainage remain to be conﬁrmed through targeted sectoral assessments.

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response – Situation Report #32 (1 to 31 October 2026)
content:
The thirty-second Situation Report provides an update on the response of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) to the earthquakes that affected Venezuela on 24 June 2026. During the reporting period, IOM continued providing multisectoral support to affected populations through interventions in Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM), health, protection, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and early recovery, with a particular focus on housing solutions and support for voluntary relocation processes.

Highlights

IOM supported relocation processes and housing solutions across the four planned camps. During the reporting period, progress was made in formalizing voluntary departures to Ciudad Caribia, including the signing of exit agreements, household profiling and monitoring of protection risks associated with relocation. In César Nieves, the mass relocation process formally began and 61 people remained accommodated at the end of the reporting period.

IOM strengthened early recovery efforts through progress on the housing repair pilot project in César Nieves and Mare Abajo (Atanasio Girardot - Barrio Vargas), including community assemblies, technical validations, housing mapping, establishment of community committees and coordination with authorities to implement repairs to earthquake-affected homes.

IOM expanded access to essential services through mobile health clinics and MHPSS, protection and WASH activities in planned camps and affected communities. It also promoted violence prevention activities for women and girls, child protection and Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA), strengthening the integrated response throughout recovery and relocation processes.

IOM Activities

Since the onset of the response, IOM has provided 102,487 services and assistance, reaching 60,189 unique individuals across earthquake-affected states. During October, the organization continued supporting the management and co-management of planned camps, strengthening coordination mechanisms with national, state, and municipal authorities, as well as humanitarian actors operating in the areas of intervention.

In the health sector, IOM teams and partners maintained primary healthcare services, sexual and reproductive health care, mental health, pediatrics, and other specialized services through fixed facilities and mobile outreach activities. In parallel, epidemiological surveillance, health promotion activities, and follow-up support for individuals with specific needs were conducted.

Protection interventions included case management, legal counselling, support to vulnerable individuals, psychological support activities, documentation assistance, violence prevention, and strengthening community-based protection mechanisms. In addition, the mainstreaming of Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) continued across response operations.

In the WASH sector, IOM supported hygiene promotion activities, distribution of supplies, service monitoring, water supply interventions, and infrastructure improvements in camps and affected communities. Complementary early recovery activities focused on the assessment and rehabilitation of housing, community spaces, and prioritized infrastructure to facilitate the progressive return to safer living conditions.

IOM Planned Response

During the next reporting period, IOM will continue supporting voluntary relocation processes and the implementation of housing solutions for earthquake-affected families, while maintaining protection risk monitoring, updating information on displaced populations, and coordinating with relevant authorities to promote sustainable solutions.

In addition, the organization will continue providing integrated health, mental health and psychological support, protection, and WASH services, alongside early recovery interventions aimed at strengthening community resilience, improving living conditions for affected populations, and consolidating progress toward long-term recovery.

title: WFP Burkina Faso Country Brief, October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• In September, WFP distributed 1,476 mt of food assistance, reaching 10,000 refugees and 127,777 vulnerable people, while 28,000 people were assisted through e-vouchers in Titao.

• WFP provided nutrition support to 44,352 children and 16,217 pregnant and breastfeeding women and girls, while expanding community outreach through 79 new GASPA groups.

• WFP finalized school feeding plans for 175,000learners in 616 schools ahead of the 2026-2027 school year.

• UNHAS operated 136 flights to 25 destinations, including Koro and Mopti in Mali, transporting 858 passengers and supporting three medical evacuations.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Burkina Faso continues to face a complex crisis driven by insecurity, climate shocks, and structural vulnerabilities. Dependence on rainfed agriculture increases exposure to climate variability, while insecurity remains the main driver of humanitarian needs, with around 2 million internally displaced people limiting access to land, markets, and basic services.

• Results from the April 2026 food security analysis estimated 1.66 million people would face crisis-level food insecurity (IPC Phase 3+) during the June–August 2026 lean season, including 223,000 in emergency conditions. Although this represents an improvement from 2025 (2.3 million people), food insecurity remains concentrated in conflict-affected northern and eastern regions.

• These disparities underscore the need for targeted interventions that combine emergency assistance with resilience-building efforts.

• WFP’s 2026 operational plan aims to support around 350,000 beneficiaries per month, requiring approximately 5,775 mt of food commodities monthly between June and December.

• However, available resources remain insufficient, with significant funding gaps already experienced in August, putting the continuity and predictability of assistance at risk.

content:
• Needs remain severe: About 2.7 million Kenyans in the arid and semi-arid lands (ASALS) and 351,000 refugees face Crisis or worse (IPC Phase 3 and above) food insecurity. About 1 million children and women and girls need treatment for acute malnutrition.
