title: UNHCR Türkiye Monthly Operational Update (September 2026)
content:
The challenges refugees face may vary from person to person. While some issues can be addressed through immediate action, most require systematic follow-up. Over the years, UNHCR has developed a protection response structure to provide responsive and remedial support to individuals at heightened risk.

UNHCR receives referrals through its counselling line, corporate email address, partners and other relevant actors in the field. After receiving the case, an assigned caseworker supports each refugee, provides a safe environment for communication, and builds a healing relationship based on trust.

The caseworker informs the refugee of all available options and helps them identify and reach solutions by leveraging their strengths and working with service providers. The caseworker assesses each case to identify needs and potential solutions/responses, and refers to relevant services including those provided by public institutions, local authorities and NGOs.

title: PER: Pluvial/Flash Flood - 11-2026 - Flood Fenómeno El Niño (2026-11-03)
content:
Description

According to COEN-INDECI Preliminary Report No. 1106, as of 07:50 on 2 November, intense rainfall caused material damage in the districts of Matapalo, Aguas Verdes, and Zarumilla in Zarumilla Province, as well as in the districts of Tumbes, Corrales, Pampas de Hospital, and San Jacinto in Tumbes Province. The heaviest precipitation primarily affected localities such as San Jacinto and Matapalo, located near the Ecuadorian border, where water accumulation generated the most critical conditions.

In the city of Tumbes, the heavy rainfall significantly disrupted normal nighttime activities. The city’s main square (Plaza de Armas), which typically attracts large numbers of residents during the evening, remained largely deserted as many families returned early to their homes to seek shelter from the rains.

The same report indicates that the Damage and Needs Assessment (EDAN) is still being conducted by local authorities. As a result, no fatalities, injuries, or health impacts have been reported to date.

One of the most affected localities is Puerto Perú settlement, located in the district of Aguas Verdes, where flooding has had significant impacts on both the population and housing. This event occurred in the context of intense rainfall and water accumulation in vulnerable urban areas.

As part of the response efforts, the Peruvian Army has deployed personnel from the Rapid Disaster Response Company (CIRD) to the most affected locations. In addition, the Regional Government of Tumbes is coordinating the deployment of water pumps and specialized equipment to flooded areas. At the national level, the Ministry of Health (MINSA) has announced the installation of a field hospital to address potential emergencies resulting from the heavy rains. The facility is expected to have a capacity of between 80 and 120 beds and will provide care for patients affected by dengue, leptospirosis, and other emergency-related health conditions. Similarly, the response capacity of the Regional Hospital II-2 JAMO will be strengthened.

Furthermore, according to the National Meteorology and Hydrology Service of Peru (SENAMHI), the Tumbes River reached the red alert threshold after recording a flow rate of 1,021.33 m³/s at 05:00 on 2 November, exceeding the established red alert threshold of 1,000 m³/s. However, by 08:00 the river flow had decreased to 910.43 m³/s, returning to the orange alert level.

Finally, according to SENAMHI Report No. 306-2026-SENAMHI/DMA/SPM, moderate to extremely heavy rainfall is forecast for Tumbes and the inland coastal areas of Piura, while light to moderate rainfall is expected along the coastal regions of Lambayeque and La Libertad. In addition, the Short-Term Weather Advisory indicates that red-level rainfall conditions may persist in several provinces of the Piura and Tumbes departments until 3 November. According to the report, accumulated rainfall across the coastal region is expected to range between 0.1 mm and 80 mm within a 24-hour period, with a high probability of occurrence exceeding 60 per cent.

title: North Macedonia Flood 2026 - DREF Final Report (MDRMK011)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

29-01-2026

What happened, where and when?

During January 2026, North Macedonia was affected by a prolonged cyclonic weather system that brought persistent and intense rainfall across several parts of the country. According to the National Hydro meteorological Service (UHMR), rainfall exceeding 30 l/m² was recorded in the central and eastern parts of the country, accompanied by unstable weather conditions and thunderstorms. The combination of heavy precipitation, saturated ground and snowmelt contributed to the overflow of several rivers and resulted in localized and widespread flooding, particularly in the municipalities of Kičevo and Ohrid.

The flooding affected residential areas, houses, basements, yards, business premises, public spaces and road infrastructure, causing significant disruption to daily life and local mobility. Several neighborhoods and low-lying areas were inundated, while damage to roads and access routes further restricted movement and access to essential services. The impact was particularly significant for households in vulnerable situations, including low-income families, older people, people with disabilities, families with young children and people living in flood-prone or substandard housing. Affected households reported damage to homes and loss of essential household items, while some experienced temporary displacement and increased economic hardship. Small businesses and livelihoods were also affected, reducing the coping capacity of vulnerable households.

Heavy rainfall continued between 2 and 11 January, resulting in sustained high river levels and further flooding in Kičevo and Ohrid, including a flash flood in the Kičevo area. As damage and needs assessments progressed, additional households were identified as having sustained losses to housing, household belongings and livelihoods. The scale and duration of the emergency resulted in humanitarian needs exceeding the initial local response capacity.

On 16 January 2026, local crisis management authorities in Kičevo and Ohrid requested the Red Cross of the Republic of North Macedonia to continue and scale up humanitarian assistance to affected communities. Based on the identified needs and in coordination with the relevant authorities, the Red Cross of the Republic of North Macedonia initiated a DREF operation to support the most affected and vulnerable households with emergency humanitarian assistance.

A second period of severe weather occurred between 14 and 16 February 2026, when prolonged and intense rainfall caused the rapid rise and overflow of several rivers, including the Zajashka and Slupčanka rivers. Flooding affected several municipalities, with the most significant impact again reported in Kičevo, as well as in parts of Tetovo, Gostivar, Saraj and surrounding settlements.

In Kičevo, the overflow of the Zajashka River affected residential neighborhoods, streets, basements, yards, business premises, agricultural land and local road infrastructure. Landslides and damaged roads further restricted access and disrupted transport. Vulnerable households were particularly affected, with many experiencing damage to their homes, loss of essential belongings and temporary displacement. More than 270 people were evacuated in Kičevo.

Throughout the emergency, the Red Cross branches, in coordination with municipal authorities, emergency services and the Crisis Management Centre, supported affected communities through evacuation assistance, distribution of humanitarian relief items, provision of drinking water and other immediate response activities. In Kičevo, the Red Cross branch provided assistance to approximately 200 households, including food and hygiene parcels, blankets, sleeping bags and drinking water.

The successive flooding events in January and February, combined with the prolonged rainfall and exposure of vulnerable households, increased humanitarian needs and placed additional pressure on affected communities. The DREF operation therefore focused on addressing the immediate humanitarian needs of the most vulnerable affected households and supporting the Red Cross response capacity during the emergency and early recovery period.

title: Dominican Republic: Population Movement 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRDO022)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

12-10-2026

What happened, where and when?

The Dominican Republic continues to experience sustained humanitarian needs associated with cross-border population movements linked to the continuing crisis in Haiti. In Dajabón, these needs are evident among Haitian people undergoing migration processing and return procedures, particularly children, pregnant women and people requiring health assistance, family contact or protection referrals. Movement volumes fluctuate, while needs for timely care, drinking water, food and personal hygiene assistance persist.

Dajabón branch records show 15,697 admissions to the migrant interdiction centre during July–September 2026, compared with 12,550 during the same period in 2025, an increase of 25.1 per cent. Recorded admissions of children increased from 628 to 3,229, raising their proportion from 5.0 to 20.6 per cent. Adult women’s admissions increased from 2,657 to 6,202. These changes have implications for ageappropriate assistance, health services, family contact and safe referrals. The figures represent admissions rather than verified unique individuals or people assessed as requiring assistance.

While the Dominican Red Cross continues to provide humanitarian assistance at the Dajabón migrant interdiction centre, service provision depends on a team of no more than five volunteers whose availability varies because of employment commitments. Limited personnel availability and operational resources prevent a regular service schedule. Fluctuating admissions, the increased proportion of children recorded in 2026 and continuing health, protection and family contact needs place demands on this limited capacity. Additional support is needed to improve the continuity and organisation of existing services and strengthen the branch’s ability to adapt to changes in demand.

Movements have fluctuated considerably. In 2026, the centre recorded 9,745 admissions in January–March, 24,492 in April–June and 15,697 in July–September. During the third quarter, admissions declined from 7,265 in July to 3,597 in September. The situation therefore reflects variable demand and a changing population profile rather than a continuous increase. Available records do not establish a consistent seasonal pattern.

The branch’s reporting documents dehydration, hypertension, injuries, a pregnant woman requiring hospital referral and unaccompanied children requiring assistance. Current services include pre-hospital care, drinking water, food rations, Restoring Family Links and hygiene assistance when supplies are available. However, services depend on a team of no more than five volunteers with variable availability and no regular operating schedule. Access to the centre is restricted from 18:00 until the following day. The National Society also reports reduced physical presence of several humanitarian organisations in Dajabón; current service coverage and referral arrangements require further verification.

The initial operational focus is Dajabón, in the north-western Dominican Republic, particularly the migrant interdiction centre and the proposed nearby Humanitarian Service Point. A multisectoral assessment will cover selected locations in Monte Cristi, Dajabón, Elías Piña, Independencia and Pedernales to establish needs, existing services and operational priorities. All activities will take place within Dominican territory, and assessment coverage does not imply equivalent needs or planned service points in every location.

The situation was ongoing throughout the January–September 2026 reporting period. Following the IFRC Regional Director’s September visit to Dajabón and subsequent exchanges, the National Society decided at a meeting on 12 October 2026 to proceed with a DREF request, informed by the comparison of branch records and available response capacity. This date marks the institutional decision to seek additional support in a slow-onset context. The proposed operation will strengthen existing branch services, support establishment and equipping of a Humanitarian Service Point subject to authorization, and undertake a multisectoral assessment to guide current assistance and inform a separately resourced longer-term strategy.

title: Yemen — Rapid Displacement Tracking Update (25 – 31 October 2026)
content:
IOM Yemen DTM’s Rapid Displacement Tracking (RDT) tool collects data on estimated numbers of households forced to flee on a daily basis from their locations of origin or displacement, allowing for regular reporting of new displacements in terms of estimated numbers, geography, and needs. It also tracks returnees who returned to their location of origin.

From 1 January to 31 October 2026, IOM Yemen DTM tracked 53,226 households (HH) (319,356 Individuals) who experienced displacement at least once.

Between 25 and 31 October 2026, IOM Yemen DTM tracked 2294 households (13764 individuals) displaced at least once. The majority of people moved into/within the following governorates and districts:

  • Ta’iz (1183 HHs) – Al Mudhaffar (306 HHs), Ash Shamayatayn (229 HHs), Al Misrakh (201 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate were internal.
  • Lahj (683 HHs) – Al Madaribah Wa Al Aarah (277 HHs), Tuban (182 HHs), Al Maqatirah (134 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate originated from Lahj and Ta’iz.
  • Shabwah (159 HHs) – Ataq (132 HHs), Mayfaah (7 HHs), Bayhan (5 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate originated from Ta’iz and Al Hodeidah.

The majority of people moved from the following governorates and districts:

  • Ta’iz (1624 HHs) – Al Misrakh (450 HHs), Jabal Habashi (355 HHs), Ash Shamayatayn (212 HHs) districts.
  • Lahj (460 HHs) – Al Madaribah Wa Al Aarah (443 HHs), Tur Al Bahah (7 HHs), Al Qubaytah (5 HHs) districts.
  • Al Hodeidah (103 HHs) – Hays (41 HHs), Al Khukhah (37 HHs), Ad Durayhimi (5 HHs) districts.

IOM identified 653 additional households displaced in the previous reporting period, which covered 18 - 24 October 2026, in the governorates of Aden (466 HHs), Al Maharah (69 HHs), Abyan (40 HHs), Lahj (30 HHs), Ma’rib (28 HHs) Hadramawt (11 HHs), and Ad Dali (9 HHs). These figures have been added to the cumulative displacement total recorded since the beginning of the year.

title: UNICEF Nigeria Humanitarian Flash Update No. 1 (Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease), 30 October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • As of 30 October 2026, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) reports one laboratory-confirmed case of Ebola disease (Bundibugyo species) in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), confirmed on 20 October. No deaths have been reported; the patient was evacuated on 26 October to Switzerland A suspected case reported by Rivers State on 23 October tested negative.
  • Sixty-two contacts, including healthcare workers, domestic staff, the patient’s spouse and a Bolt driver, have been identified, categorized and are under follow-up; none has tested positive. The national Incident Management System has been activated at the highest level.
  • UNICEF’s proposed support will align with the government-led response, focusing on risk communication and community engagement (RCCE), community-based surveillance, WASH and infection prevention and control (IPC), essential supplies, and community alert and referral linkages. The scope will depend on identified needs and agreement with NCDC and FCT authorities.

Situation overview

As of 30 October 2026, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) Ebola Disease Situation Report reports one laboratory-confirmed case of Ebola disease (Bundibugyo species) in Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nigeria, with no deaths. The patient, a 42-year-old woman, returned from Uganda via Addis Ababa on 3 October 2026 and became symptomatic on 7 October, with fever, diarrhoea, generalized body aches and sore throat; no bleeding was reported. She went to a private health facility on 10 October and was admitted to a second private facility on 11 October. NCDC was notified on 19 October, and the NCDC National Reference Laboratory confirmed the case on 20 October; phylogenetic sequencing has been concluded with the African Centre of Excellence for Genomics of Infectious Diseases (ACEGID). She was medically evacuated out of Nigeria on 26 October to Switzerland. Sixty-two contacts, including healthcare workers, domestic staff, her spouse and a Bolt driver, have been identified and categorized; none has tested positive to date.

A further suspected case reported by Rivers State on 23 October tested negative.

The Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare and NCDC have activated the national Incident Management System at the highest level, coordinated by the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, and finalized an Incident Action Plan. Response measures include contact tracing with daily follow-up by exposure category, revised case definitions (version 3, 22 October), preparation of the University of Abuja Teaching Hospital as an isolation and treatment centre, IPC needs assessments across states and facilities, prepositioning of PPE and laboratory supplies, public advisories and social listening, and enhanced surveillance at points of entry. The nine days between first presentation (10 October) and notification (19 October) raise concern about exposure among healthcare workers, other patients and caregivers at both facilities. Immediate priorities are to complete follow-up of all contacts, close facility IPC gaps, establish referral pathways for suspected cases and strengthen readiness in high-risk states. Clear public communication and community engagement, including countering rumours and stigma, will support early reporting of suspected cases.

title: Yemen Joint Monitoring Report: Bimonthly Update on Food and Nutrition Security Crisis Risks (September 2026, No. 17)
content:
KEY MESSAGES

  • In September 2026, the Joint Monitoring Report (JMR) recorded 114 critical and 357 heightened risk alerts, compared with 23 critical and 453 heightened alerts in July. The key change in September was the sharp increase in critical alerts, rather than the overall number of alerts, driven by conflict (65 critical and 45 heightened) and displacement (38 critical and one heightened), as well as drought (11 critical and eight heightened). The proxy food imports indicator remained above the risk threshold in all governorates except Socotra (303 heightened alerts).
  • Conflict-induced displacement has surged. The IOM Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM)recorded 258,751 people displaced by the escalation between August 1 and October 20. Ta’iz hosts 48%, followed by Lahj (25%) and Aden (15%), and more than 3,700 people have crossed the sea to Djibouti. Many families have been displaced for the second, third, or fourth time, adding to around 3.1 million people already displaced in areas under the control of the Government of Yemen (GoY).
  • Food security is deteriorating rapidly in GoY-controlled areas. By mid-September, 74% of households in GoY-controlled areas could not meet their minimum food needs, including 41% facing severe food deprivation, an all-time high, with deterioration being most acute in areas where conflict, displacement, rising prices, and pre-existing food insecurity converge. Fighting has cut humanitarian access to parts of Ta’iz and Al Hodeidah, and WFP and its partners have lost access to more than 600,000 people in need of assistance in Ta’iz in IPC 4 areas. The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) projects Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes in Al Hodeidah, Hajjah, and Ta’iz through January 2027. Since the encirclement of Ta’iz city intensified on 30 September, more than one million people have been cut off from basic supplies, including food. WFP has had to reallocate food planned for pre-existing IPC 4 distributions to the emergency response, creating gaps in later distribution cycles.
  • Food price pressures increased in September in both areas of control. The minimum food basket (MFB) rose by around 7% month-on-month in areas under the control of Ansar Allah (AA), reaching its highest level in the past year (around USD 91, higher than the GoY value), and by around 2% in GoY-controlled areas, where it has risen steadily since the regional conflict escalation, making it around 7% higher than a year earlier. Field reports point to sharper increases in conflict-affected areas, with vegetable oil 35% more expensive year-on-year in GoY-controlled areas and wheat flour prices in Ta’iz city up by 15% since the escalation. Food remains available in accessible markets, and the main driver of food insecurity is collapsing purchasing power.
  • Fuel supply has contracted sharply, and fuel prices are rising across Yemen. Recorded fuel imports fell by 73% year-on-year in September, with no petrol or diesel reaching northern ports. In September, official diesel and petrol prices in AA-controlled areas rose by around 21% and 11%, respectively, while in GoY-controlled areas, fuel prices were around 50% higher than a year earlier and gas prices rose by around 22% year-on-year. Exchange rates remained stable in both areas (around YER 1,570/ USD 1 in GoY and YER 531/USD 1 in AA areas), limiting currency-driven price pressures, but higher fuel costs are likely to push up transport, milling, water, and food prices.
  • The conflict in Yemen is increasingly entangled with the wider regional war. With the Strait of Hormuz largely closed since the start of the US–Israel war with Iran in February 2026, Saudi oil exports have shifted toward the Red Sea, raising the strategic value of the Bab Al Mandab Strait. AA attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and airports have intensified, including strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport that killed at least 14 people. The simultaneous disruption of the Hormuz and Bab Al Mandab chokepoints is likely to keep freight, insurance, and fuel costs high for Yemen’s food and fuel imports.
  • A very strong El Niño adds import-driven and livelihoods-related risks. El Niño reached very strong levels in September 2026. FEWS NET identifies Yemen as one of the countries most exposed to its indirect impacts through international imports, as Australia supplied more than a third of Yemen’s wheat imports from 2024–2025 and its 2026–2027 wheat crop is forecast to fall by 14–17%. Wheat flour is Yemen’s primary staple food, and its price increase has significant implications for poorer households. However, the rainfall outlook for Yemen for September 2026-February 2027 is near normal and global grain supplies remain relatively strong, so El Niño is expected to compound existing pressures rather than drive food insecurity on its own.
  • Overall, food security risks have increased sharply and are expected to continue worsening over the coming months as active frontline fighting, mass displacement, loss of humanitarian access and funding, rising prices, and regional maritime insecurity interact in a context where more than half of the population was already projected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse levels of food insecurity. Based on these developments, the JMR Risk Team recommends triggering the Food Security Crisis Preparedness Plan for Yemen.

title: Lebanon: Inter-Agency Response Update - (31 October 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Protracted displacement and limited returns: The number of internally displaced people back in their areas of origin increased by 13 per cent since September, to 964,689, while around 304,500 people remain displaced outside their areas of origin.
  • Explosive ordnance contamination and access restrictions: Landmines, explosive remnants of war and continued military activities continue to threaten civilian safety and restrict access to agricultural lands, particularly during the olive harvest season, undermining livelihoods and recovery.
  • Education resumes amid damaged infrastructure and continued use of schools as collective shelters. The academic year commenced in mid-September although approximately 57 public educational facilities remain in use as collective shelters and despite extensive damage to schools across South and Nabatieh governorates.
  • Shelter consolidation underway. Humanitarian partners are prioritizing safe, voluntary and dignified relocation for IDPs still in shelters scheduled to close, with targeted assistance for vulnerable displaced households inside and outside shelters amid funding and access constraints.

title: Situation report 03: Cyclone Arnab, with Cyclone Murasu outlook (03 November 2026)
content:
OVERVIEW

Very Severe Cyclonic Storm Arnab crossed the Andhra Pradesh–Yanam coast near Narsapur on 28 October with winds of 125–135 km/h, then moved over south Odisha, bringing 546 mm of rain in 24 hours at Patrapur, Ganjam. Floods and landslides followed in Ganjam, Gajapati and Kandhamal, marooning about 70 villages in Ganjam. From 30 October to 1 November, LOCAL member Youth for Social Development (YSD) assessed 53 of the worst-hit villages across nine blocks. Purushottampur holds more than half the affected households; Mohana's hill villages have the highest rate of house damage. In Andhra Pradesh, the Godavari delta remains the worst hit.

GOVERNMENT RESPONSES

  • Odisha: 313 rescue teams from NDRF, ODRAF and Fire Services are deployed [2], and 2,328 marooned people in Ganjam have been identified for airlift [8]. Navy Sea King and ALH sorties delivered about 1,800 kg of food and drinking water to Sara Bhimpur, Ganjam, on 31 October and 1 November [9]. At Gidipabali, 177 personnel are searching for 10 people still missing after a landslide; the operation runs to 3 November [10]. Ex gratia is ₹4 lakh per death.
  • Andhra Pradesh: 290 relief centres sheltered 84,396 people, with ₹5 lakh ex gratia per death. Power has been restored in 4,881 of 5,404 affected villages. An Inter-Ministerial Central Team toured Konaseema, West Godavari, Kakinada and East Godavari from 31 October to 2 November; the state put preliminary losses at ₹4,526 crore on 2 November, after assessing ₹4,764 crore on 31 October.

title: Lebanon: What's New? LRP Update October 2026
content: The first edition of the Inter-Agency Response Update provides an overview of the evolving humanitarian situation, response efforts, and coordination priorities under the 2026 Lebanon Response Plan (LRP) Addendum. It highlights continued displacement, with over 304,500 people remaining outside their areas of origin, alongside persistent protection risks, damaged infrastructure and restricted humanitarian access, particularly in south Lebanon. The update also outlines ongoing efforts to support displaced households inside and outside collective shelters, facilitate safe and dignified returns, maintain essential services and strengthen winter preparedness. It further examines operational challenges and coordination efforts to address emerging needs amid funding and access constraints.

title: Afghanistan Seasonal Monitor: Above-average precipitation and above-normal temperatures are expected early in the 2026-27 wet season
content:
Key Messages

  • The CHIRPS-GEFS short-term forecast indicates cumulative precipitation across most of the country will remain near average (within +/- 10 mm) through November 10, 2026. Exceptions include isolated areas in the northeast and east, where precipitation deficits of 10–25 mm below average are possible, and isolated locations in the southeast along the Pakistan border, where precipitation surpluses of 10–25 mm above average are forecast (Figure 1).
  • The Copernicus Climate Change Services (C3S) cumulative precipitation forecast during November 2026 – January 2027 indicates increased likelihood of above-average precipitation in most areas (Figure 2).
  • The very strongEl Niño event is expected to continuethrough January–March 2027.
  • The Copernicus Climate Change Services (C3S) temperature forecast indicates increased likelihood of above-average mean daily temperatures through the end of January 2027 (Figure 3).
  • Above-average precipitation may promote stronger early-season snowpack development and greater basin-level snow water volumes than those observed during previous years. However, the forecasted above-average daytime temperatures could offset some of these gains by pushing the rain-snow line to higher elevations.
  • Currently, land preparation activities are underway in areas of winter wheat cultivation. Sowing is expected to begin and gradually intensify in these areas as precipitation and soil moisture conditions become increasingly favorable.
  • Farmers are likely to complete winter wheat sowing by December 2026 if sufficient precipitation is received by the end of the year. Wheat sowings are expected to exceed average levels, supported in part by a 10–12% decline in improved-seed prices that has enhanced farmers’ access to quality seed.
  • Countrywide, groundwater levels will likely remain below average throughout the 2026/27 season despite localized gains due to the forecasted average to above-average precipitation in the coming months.
