title: Nepal: Rasuwa Flood Situation Report No. 12 (As of 30 October 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • The Interagency Accountability to Affected People (AAP) Working Group has been activated, led by UNICEF, to institutionalize community engagement and accountability, supporting local authorities to establish help desks and feedback mechanisms that enable affected populations to influence response priorities and recovery programming.
  • To support market recovery in areas affected by disrupted transport links, WFP piloted a helicopter-supported market access initiative connecting producers in Gre, Rasuwa, with buyers in Nuwakot and Kathmandu. The pilot transported more than 8 metric tons of potatoes and cabbages, enabling approximately 140 farmers to access markets and reducing the risk of produce losses while helping restore local market linkages.
  • A new Cash Advisor has been deployed to support the Cash Coordination Working Group (CCWG), strengthening technical capacity for multipurpose cash assistance, shelter-related cash programming, and the coordination of recovery-focused cash interventions.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Nepal continues to face the cumulative impacts of successive flood events, with affected communities experiencing ongoing recovery challenges due to damage to homes, livelihoods, and critical infrastructure. Following the devastating floods in Rasuwa and surrounding areas on 26 August, flash flooding along the Budhi Gandaki River on 11 October affected parts of Gorkha and Dhading districts, causing further damage to infrastructure and disrupting road connectivity and access to affected communities.

However, WFP market monitoring indicates that markets in flood-affected areas of Rasuwa, Dhading and Nuwakot are recovering, with 81 per cent of surveyed traders reporting functional markets in October, up from 55 per cent in September. Food availability was reported as sufficient in 78 per cent of interviews, and staple food prices remained largely stable, suggesting that market conditions are generally supportive of marketbased assistance and cash-based interventions. However, recovery remains uneven, particularly in Rasuwa, where localized supply constraints, higher transport costs and elevated food basket costs continue to affect market performance.

title: WFP Namibia Country Brief October 2026
content:
In October, WFP supported the Government of Namibia to distribute 4,893 mt of rice to 383,084 households across all 14 regions. EU-supported integrated ECD interventions in Kunene contributed to a 74 percent increase in enrolment and participation at Otuvero ECD Centre. WFP also advanced home-grown school feeding and sustainable village initiatives, with infrastructure at five schools confirmed ready for handover and community management, alongside verification of sustainable village sites and market opportunities. WFP and the Office of the Prime Minister also finalized a national targeting methodology and standard operating procedure to improve transparent, equitable and evidence-based humanitarian assistance.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Namibia is home to approximately 3 million people living across 824,292 km², making it one of the least densely populated countries in the world. The country's vast geography presents persistent challenges for service delivery, market access and emergency response operations.

• Namibia's operating environment remains increasingly complex following its reclassification by the World Bank from an upper-middle-income to a lower-middle-income country. Looking ahead, forecasts indicate a developing El Niño event that could result in below-average rainfall across Southern Africa during the 2026/27 season. Reduced rainfall may adversely affect agricultural production, constrain regional cereal supplies and heighten food security risks. Given Namibia's dependence on food imports, these pressures could contribute to higher food prices and increased vulnerability among households still recovering from the impacts of the 2023/24 drought.

• Through its 2025–2029 Country Strategic Plan, WFP continues to provide technical support to the Government of Namibia across four strategic priorities: strengthening emergency preparedness, anticipatory action and response systems; enhancing social protection systems to better reach vulnerable populations; strengthening food systems and improving smallholder farmer livelihoods; and providing ondemand services to Government and partners.

title: Sudan: Humanitarian Health and Nutrition Bulletin: Blue Nile Under Strain: Displacement, Malaria and Attacks on Civilians Drive an Acute Health Emergency
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• Fighting in eastern Wad Al Mahi and Roseires localities in early October displaced about 6,800 people in four days (3–6 Oct). Families have been displaced twice in six weeks, with most now concentrated in and around Roseires town and Azaza [6,19].
• Civilians, displacement sites and health care are under attack: a strike near the Abu Shendi site killed at least 31 people, most of them women and children (9 Oct), and a strike put Um Darfa hospital out of service (11 Oct) [3].
• SAPA's comprehensive mobile clinic has recorded 3,185 consultations. More than 99% of patients with a recorded status were IDPs, 63% were female and 48% were children under 15.
• Malaria dominates at the peak of the transmission season (57% of consultations). The respiratory share has more than tripled (11% to 35%) and diarrheal disease has risen from 1% to 8%, mostly among children under five, consistent with crowding, cold nights and unsafe water.
• Of 39 children aged 6–59 months screened by MUAC, 11 (28%) had acute malnutrition, although screening was not systematic. FEWS NET projects Emergency (IPC Phase 4) in Kurmuk and Geissan through January 2027 [9].
• Each escalation was followed within days by new arrivals and more patients. After Al-Kadalo IDPs reached Azaza on 22 October, SAPA consultations rose 47% in four days (Section 2).
• According to the field team, SAPA is the only health provider currently operating in Azaza. Its priority needs are malaria commodities and nets, WASH at Azaza, nutrition supplies, MHPSS, and the protection of health care.

title: Moyale Emergency: Inter-agency situation report #4
content:
Overview

The security situation in and around Moyale remains volatile following armed clashes that erupted on 22 October. The use of heavy weaponry has been reported, with clashes continuing on a daily basis. New arrivals are reporting that homes, buildings and neighbourhoods have been damaged and destroyed. Initial estimates from sources in Ethiopia estimated some 80,000 people may be internally displaced in Ethiopia.

There are reports that the armed forces have regular pauses to allow for humanitarian passage for civilians to leave. Displacement is ongoing within Ethiopia and across the border into Kenya. The Kenyan Defense Forces are securing the border. Based on the latest estimates from local authorities, the number of new arrivals has now reached approximately 50,000 individuals, underscoring the scale of the crisis and the rapidly growing pressure on local infrastructure, public services, and host communities. Most new arrivals are reported to be women and children, alongside older people and persons with disabilities who may face heightened risks.

title: LTC Palestine - Gaza Strip Conflict Factsheet: October 2026
content:
Operation overview

Armed conflict between Palestinian militant groups and Israeli military forces began on 07 October 2023. The conflict has resulted in a severe humanitarian crisis and significant disruption to communications networks, impeding humanitarian operations. The WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC Telecoms) was activated on 31 October 2023 to meet the urgent need to support access to reliable, shared communications services for humanitarian organizations operating in Gaza.

Communication needs in Gaza

The 10 October 2025 ceasefire enabled partners to gradually resume operations and scale up aid in previously inaccessible areas. However, extensive damage to Gaza’s telecommunications infrastructure and continued restrictions on telecommunications equipment continue to severely constrain services supporting humanitarian operations.

LTC Telecoms response

Coordination and information management (IM) — LTC Telecoms is working with local and regional partners to align needs and facilitate the approval and entry of telecommunications equipment into Gaza, strengthening Security Communications Systems (SCS) and shared connectivity in key Gaza response areas. IM efforts deliver situation reports and dashboards to inform coordination, decisions, and advocacy across audiences.

Telecommunications equipment— Since 07 October 2023, COGAT has approved and delivered 20 satellite phones, 30 VHF radios, 98 tracking devices, and four solar kits to Gaza. LTC Telecoms continues to work with partners to support approval processes for pending telecommunications equipment requests.

Internet connectivity and user support — Gaza’s connectivity has sharply declined due to infrastructure damage, equipment gaps, access constraints and import restrictions, continuing to affect the continuity and expansion of connectivity services across Gaza. LTC Telecoms operates a help desk in Deir Al Balah, with expansion planned.

Security communications — LTC Telecoms supports 24/7 UNDSS-managed SOCs in Gaza and Jerusalem and VHF radio communications across five Gaza operational locations. In 2026, LTC Telecoms and UNDSS trained 172 UN personnel, including SOC operators, and five WFP staff on VHF radio programming to strengthen emergency readiness in Gaza and Jerusalem.

title: Ukraine Situation: Moldova - Operational Update (September 2026)
content: As of September 2026, 146,667 refugees from Ukraine were present in the Republic of Moldova. Although large-scale arrivals have stabilized, new arrivals and protection needs persist. Since 2022, the Regional Refugee Response Plan (RRP) has coordinated assistance and protection among the Government, UN agencies and civil society. As the RRP ends in December 2026, the response is shifting towards greater government leadership and refugee inclusion in national services, while providing targeted assistance for the most vulnerable refugees. Progress has been made in developing government-led roadmaps to advance refugee inclusion. The education roadmap, approved in 2025 and planned to be extended beyond 2026, supports efforts to simplify enrolment procedures, expand learning support and monitor refugee children’s access to education. The Health Nexus Strategy and the roadmap on labour market integration and social protection have been finalized and are awaiting formal approval. These frameworks help identify barriers to accessing national services, set out practical actions, clarify institutional responsibilities and outline resource needs for implementation. Implementing these plans will require sustained government leadership and technical and financial support from UN agencies, civil society and development partners.

title: Sudan Nutrition Sector Bulletin, January – September 2026
content: The Sudan Nutrition Sector Bulletin for January–September 2026 gives an overview of the nutrition situation and the humanitarian nutrition response across Sudan. Drawing on data and updates from sector partners, it reviews the current situation and the achievements of the treatment and prevention programmes against the People in Need and targets. It also covers findings from the SMART surveys conducted in 2026, multi-sectoral convergence with the Food Security, Health and WASH sectors, coordination highlights, and response priorities for the rest of the year. The bulletin also covers the availability of core nutrition supplies at national, state and facility level, the main challenges facing the response, and the sector’s funding status. It is intended to support partners, donors and other stakeholders with evidence for advocacy, resource mobilisation and programme planning.

title: WFP Chad Country Brief, October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• WFP provided life-saving food assistance to 163,748 acutely food-insecure people, primarily Sudanese refugees, through cash-based transfers and in-kind distributions.

• Compared with previous monthly caseloads, September emergency food assistance coverage was significantly lower due to funding shortfalls, which required WFP to skip the monthly distribution cycle except in Adré and for new arrivals.

• Based on forecasts of below-average rainfall and persistent dry conditions threatening the harvest, WFP continues to implement its first drought anticipatory action in Chad. In September, WFP provided cash assistance to 53,874 people, bringing the total number of unique people reached with anticipatory support to 170,000 since the action was triggered in July 2026.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Chad remains one of the world’s poorest countries and continues to face a complex humanitarian crisis marked by displacement, insecurity, and food insecurity. As of October 2026, Chad hosted nearly 1.58 million refugees, making it the secondlargest refugee-hosting country in Africa after Uganda. Sudanese refugees account for 89 percent of the total and are primarily concentrated in the eastern provinces. In the Lake Chad Basin, escalating violence continues to exacerbate humanitarian needs and drive further displacement. These challenges are compounded by persistent food insecurity: according to the May 2026 Cadre Harmonisé analysis, nearly 3.2 million people experienced acute food insecurity during the June-August 2026 lean season. The 2026 agricultural season has faced significant agroclimatic stress due to delayed rains and persistent rainfall deficits. Deteriorating vegetation has delayed crop development, reduced pasture regeneration and strained water resources, affecting both agriculture and pastoralism.

title: Palestine - Conflict LTC Situation Report (Telecoms Area) #74 (Reporting Period: October 2026)
content:
The World Food Programme (WFP)-led Emergency Telecommunications Cluster (ETC), now the telecoms area of the Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1, was activated on 31 October 2023 in response to the crisis in Gaza. This Situation Report provides a monthly update on LTC Telecoms activities.

Summary Points

• Telecoms services across Gaza remained severely constrained, with approximately 75 percent of infrastructure reported damaged or destroyed since October 2023. Equipment shortages and access restrictions continued to limit network reliability, maintenance and recovery efforts.

• LTC Telecoms continued to coordinate with humanitarian partners on telecoms planning, equipment-entry requests and connectivity services. Import restrictions persisted, including the denial of a request to facilitate the entry of six satellite phones for UNDSS.

• LTC Telecoms strengthened inter-agency security communications through continued UN VHF radio standardization and Basic Security Communications Systems (SCS) training for 31 humanitarian personnel from UN agencies and international NGOs.

Humanitarian Overview

Humanitarian conditions across Gaza remained critical during the reporting period, amid continued military activity, displacement, widespread damage to civilian infrastructure and severe constraints on access to essential services. Civilians continued to face heightened protection risks, particularly in areas near the “Yellow Line,” while humanitarian organizations operated amid insecurity and access restrictions.

Many displaced people remained in deteriorated tents and makeshift structures ahead of the cold and rainy season. Approximately 950,000 displaced people were assessed as living at sites exposed to medium or high flood risk, including more than 400,000 at high risk. Shortages of shelter materials and machinery, limited access to suitable land and a lack of viable relocation options continued to constrain preparedness.

Humanitarian operations remained constrained by insecurity, access restrictions, shortages of essential supplies and funding gaps. Food Security Sector partners expected to reach fewer than one million of Gaza’s estimated 2.1 million people with monthly food assistance from October onwards, while funding shortages also threatened the continuity of essential WASH services. Restrictions on the entry of critical supplies and equipment continued to affect health and WASH operations.

title: Panama: Earthquake LTC Situation Report (Telecoms Area) #1 (Reporting period: 9 – 31 October 2026)
content:
This situation report provides an update on the telecommunications situation and response activities following the earthquake that struck Panama on 9 October 2026. The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) has activated a six-month Limited Emergency Operation (LEO) in support of the Government-led response. Although the Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 is not officially activated for this response, LTC Telecoms is supporting interagency coordination and information sharing.

Summary Points

• Following the magnitude 7.6 earthquake on 9 October, WFP activated a six-month Limited Emergency Operation (LEO) to support the Government-led response. LTC Telecoms is providing coordination, technical assessment and information sharing.

• The LTC Telecoms Coordinator deployed to Panama on 21 October and conducted field assessments across Veraguas, Los Santos and Coclé provinces. As priorities shift towards recovery, telecoms support is increasingly focused on connectivity at Emergency Operations Centres (EOCs) and other priority government facilities.

• WFP Panama established Starlink connectivity at the temporary hospital in Tonosí on 12 October and is supporting connectivity enhancements at EOCs in Penonomé and Aguadulce, while assessing requirements linked to an additional 24 prefabricated field offices across 12 locations requested by the Government.

title: WFP Panama External Situation Report on Earthquake Emergency, 29 October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• Within the nationally led response and following a request from the Government of Panama, WFP continues to provide logistics infrastructure, emergency connectivity, technical assistance and common services to national institutions and humanitarian partners.

• Four Mobile Storage Units (MSUs) and nine prefabricated facilities have been deployed across affected areas, strengthening temporary storage, health and operational capacity, while additional prefabricated facilities are under consideration.

• WFP has completed market assessments across affected areas of Los Santos and Veraguas to inform potential assistance modalities, including the feasibility of cashbased assistance.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Nearly three weeks after the magnitude 7.7 earthquake that struck Panama, assessments continue, with the greatest impacts recorded across Los Santos, Herrera, Veraguas and Coclé.

• Two fatalities and 27 injuries have been reported, while assessments have registered 52,874 people affected and 4,501 people remaining in 141 temporary shelters.

• Damage to 619 schools, 120 health facilities, 66 road sections and 22 bridges continue to disrupt services and limit access to some communities, especially in rural areas.

• Rain and weather conditions along continuing over 1,000 aftershocks and seismics activity are hampering recovery efforts.

• Following the national state of emergency declared on 10 October, the Government continues leading the response through a High-level Inter-Institutional Committee, including various Ministries and the National Civil Protection System (SINAPROC, for its Spanish acronym) through its Emergency Operations Centre (COE, for its Spanish acronym).

title: UNHCR Romania Ukraine Refugee Situation Weekly Update #220 - 2 November 2026
content:
Highlight

At the end of October, UNHCR Romania issued a call for applications for its first Humanitarian Datathon, “Counted In: Advancing Inclusive National Statistics for Forcibly Displaced Persons”, in collaboration with the ReMAP Network, UNHCR partner the Centre for Comparative Migration Studies (CSCM), the University of Bucharest and the West University of Timișoara. A datathon is a collaborative research sprint that brings together students, researchers, data scientists and practitioners to analyse data and generate innovative insights around a specific theme. This datathon will focus on statistical inclusion, with participants contributing to the development and testing of a tool to measure the inclusion of forcibly displaced persons in national statistics. The initiative builds on UNHCR’s Statistical Inclusion Navigator (IncNAV), with Romania serving as a case study. The event will take place in two phases: an online research phase, featuring mentoring sessions and panel discussions, from 23 November to 9 December, followed by a two-day in-person event in Timișoara on 10–11 December, where participants will present their findings to a jury.

title: Lebanon: Middle East Escalation, LTC Situation Report (Telecoms) #11: October 2026
content:
This situation report provides an update on telecoms activities delivered by the Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC)1 in support of the humanitarian response in Lebanon. The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP)-led LTC was activated on 16 March 2026.

Summary Points

• LTC Telecoms supported the establishment of communications services at the Humanitarian Notification Operations Coordination Centre (HNOCC) in Beirut, including VHF radio, satellite communications, redundant internet connectivity and backup power arrangements.

• LTC Telecoms consolidated Starlink requirements from humanitarian organizations and submitted them to the Ministry of Telecommunications (MoT) on 23 October. On 27 October, the team successfully established internet connectivity during an initial test of an authorized WFP Starlink kit [see photo].

• LTC Telecoms continued coordination with humanitarian partners and government counterparts on telecoms preparedness and contributed technical inputs to 2027 humanitarian response planning.

Humanitarian Overview

The security situation in Lebanon remained volatile during October, particularly in South Lebanon and Nabatieh governorates, where continued military activity, infrastructure damage and access restrictions affected humanitarian operations. Insecurity, damaged housing, disrupted essential services and protection risks continued to affect displaced and returning communities.

The humanitarian response continued through a government-led, OCHA-coordinated multi-sector approach, with priorities increasingly shifting towards early recovery.

title: Philippines Cebu Earthquake 2025 - DREF Final Report (MDRPH057)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

30-09-2025

What happened, where and when?

On 30 September 2025, at precisely 9:59, a strong 6.9-magnitude earthquake struck off the coast of Bogo City, marking it as the strongest recorded earthquake in Cebu province to date. The epicentre was located near Bogo City in northern Cebu, with an estimated shallow depth of about five kilometres, where intense ground shaking led to the collapse of buildings, destruction of roads, and power outages. Neighbouring municipalities, including Daanbantayan, Medellin, San Remigio, and even parts of Cebu City also felt the severe impact of the earthquake. The event’s aftermath affected two regions, Central Visayas (Region VII) and Eastern Visayas (Region VIII), with Northern Cebu in Region VII bearing the brunt of the impact and damages.

According to the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS), the quake was tectonic and was caused by an offshore fault that had remained dormant for over 400 years, which has now been identified as the Bogo Bay Fault. PHIVOLCS issued a tsunami advisory for coastal communities exposed to the risks of abnormal sea level disturbances following the main shock, but this was later lifted after monitoring confirmed that no significant tsunami threat remained. Within the first 48 hours of the event, PHIVOLCS recorded over 7,000 aftershocks. Although aftershocks continue to occur at the time of reporting period, seismic activities recorded are registering lower magnitudes below 3.0 and often remain unfelt by the affected communities in Bogo and neighboring areas.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 316: Week 4 - October 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Market Overview

During the 4th week of October, national average prices showed generally modest week-on-week movements, while several commodities remained elevated compared with last year and their three-year averages. Rice and cooking oil prices continued to face supply-side pressures amid disruptions to regional trade routes and slower imports. In contrast, pulses remained relatively affordable, supported by increased domestic availability, local production and imports from Central Asia, while restricted export opportunities and weak demand contributed to lower prices. Fuel and fertilizer costs remained elevated, adding pressure to agricultural production, transportation and household purchasing power. Meanwhile, limited demand for improved seeds and animal feed, alongside increased local availability, contributed to lower prices for these inputs.

Food Categories:

National average food prices recorded limited week-on-week movements, although notable annual and longer-term price disparities persisted across commodities.

• Wheat and wheat flour prices increased marginally during the week and show a significant increase year-on-year with wheat grain prices up by 12%, high-price wheat flour up by 7% and low-price up by 11%.

• Rice prices also show a marginal increase from last week (Palawi) and a significant increase from last year, with Palawi rice 19% higher and Sholae rice 32% higher than last year. Moreover, both varieties remained 20% above their three-year averages.

• Weekly movements in cooking oil, pulses, sugar, salt and bread remained limited. However, cooking oil and sugar prices remain 14% and 11% higher than last year, while pulses and bread show declines.

• Vegetables prices show a slight weekly increase with tomato prices up by 9.8%, potato 2.7% and onion by 2.6%. However, year-on-year comparison show notably higher prices of potato while tomato and onion show declines.

Non-Food Categories:

Terms of Trade (ToT): Purchasing power remained constraint for both labour-dependent households and pastoralists, as declining income and higher prices limit their access to food.

• Unskilled Labour ToT: The nominal unskilled labour ToT marginally declined to 9.7 kg of low-price wheat flour, representing a 15% decline from last year and 13% below the three-year average. The continued deterioration indicates sustained pressure on labour income relative to food prices.

• Labour Availability and Wages: Unskilled labour availability remained at 2.0 days per week, 13% below last year and 20% below the three-year average. Unskilled labour wages also declined by 5% year-on-year, contributing to a 26% decline in the real unskilled labour ToT compared with last year and 31% below the three-year average.

• Pastoralist ToT: A pastoralist could exchange a one-year-old female sheep for 257 kg of low-price wheat flour, 13% below last year's level and 8% below the three-year average, indicating continued pressure on the purchasing power of livestock-dependent households.

• Fertilizers and agricultural input prices show marginal weekly changes. However, year-on-year show mix movements; DAP and urea remained 9% and 22% higher than last year, respectively. Meanwhile, improved seed and animal feed prices remained below last year, by 9% and 6%, respectively.

title: Afghanistan Complex Emergency - DREF Operational Update (MDRAF020)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

04-03-2026

What happened, where and when?

From 26 February through the first week of March 2026, airstrikes and border clashes between Afghanistan and Pakistan affected ten provinces: Kabul, Kandahar, Khost, Kunar, Laghman, Nangarhar, Nuristan, Parwan, Paktia, and Paktika. The escalation followed several days of rising tensions, during which airstrikes in Nangarhar and Paktika caused civilian casualties, and cross-border exchanges of fire were reported between armed forces on both sides.

Hostilities remained largely concentrated along the border areas, but airstrikes continued to threaten civilian populations across a wide geographic zone. UNAMA recorded at least 185 civilian casualties with 56 people killed and 129 injured. It is estimated that 16,370 families are newly displaced following these hostilities, in addition to the 7,000 families that remain displaced since the August 2025 eastern region earthquake. OCHA reports significant damage to civilian infrastructure, leading to suspension or closure of essential health services, including a 20-bed emergency hospital in Nangarhar, 20 health facilities across the eastern, southeastern, and southern border provinces, and 8 nutrition service delivery sites across Khost, Kunar, and Nangarhar provinces.

On 4 March, a Special Movement Strategic Platform meeting was convened by the ICRC, ARCS, and IFRC, and the presented needs resulting from the escalation triggered the formal request for Movement support. The DREF operation was launched following the scale of humanitarian impact and the need for an immediate response.

In April, hostilities continued but at a lower frequency and intensity as compared to March. Periodic mortar shelling and airstrikes have damaged schools and health facilities in the eastern region, particularly in Kunar, Nangarhar and Kandahar provinces. The cross-border tensions and sporadic limited hostilities continue to date focusing mainly on the border regions.

title: Afghanistan | Earthquake - Operation Update #5 (MDRAF019)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Description of the crisis

On 31 August 2025, a 6.0-magnitude earthquake struck southeastern Afghanistan near Jalalabad, approximately 30 km from Momand Dara (Nangarhar) and Nurgal (Kunar). The earthquake caused significant shaking across Kunar and Nangarhar, with effects also felt in Laghman and Nuristan. There were considerable aftershocks, including a 5.6- magnitude on September 5 and a 4.9-magnitude on September 23, that exacerbated the damage and complicated response efforts.

The southeastern Afghanistan earthquake caused severe destruction, killing over 2,150 people, injuring more than 3,600, affecting nearly half a million people, and left more than 221,000 people in urgent need of humanitarian assistance. Thousands of houses were destroyed, and over 3,000 families were displaced in Kunar and Nangarhar. Key infrastructure – including health facilities, schools, water networks, and electricity and telecommunication lines – were also damaged.

Then, on 3 November 2025, a second major earthquake of 6.3 magnitude hit northern Afghanistan near the Balkh–Samangan border at a depth of 28 km. The tremor was widely felt across northern and central Afghanistan and as far as Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. Casualties reported up to 26 killed and over 1,172 injured, and about 3,027 houses were damaged or destroyed. This second major earthquake hit already vulnerable communities, damaging 22 health facilities and rendering 91 schools and 18 water sources unusable, further disrupting daily life and increasing public health risks.

Despite the significant life-saving humanitarian assistance provided in the past months, there remains limited access to clean water, insufficient health services and facilities, and many struggle to live with limited livelihood opportunities. There were also widespread losses of food stocks, crops, livestock and tools, exacerbating food insecurity, disrupting agricultural cycles, and impacting markets. People affected by the earthquake already have preexisting vulnerabilities and are forced into further negative coping strategies.

A year after the southeastern earthquake and the launch of the Appeal, thousands of families continue to be displaced, and are still living in temporary shelters in displacement sites. These temporary shelters are not adequate for the approaching winter season nor with the El Nino likely to bring above-average rainfall, especially for the northern regions. These displacement settlements have continued to expand with the influx of returnees, resulting in people living in overcrowded spaces with overstretched services. The overall humanitarian situation remains very difficult, and recovery interventions are much needed for shelter, healthcare, food assistance, and protection. The operation has transitioned to early recovery with a continued provision of basic services such as health. Recovery activities continue to address persisting needs in shelter, livelihood support, health, and water and sanitation.

title: Zambia | Drought: Early Action Protocol Activation (EAP No: EAP2023CR02, Operation No.: MDRZM025), 14 October 2026
content:
EARLY ACTION PROTOCOL ACTIVATION

Activation Overview The Zambia Red Cross Society has activated its Early Action Protocol for Drought

1.0 Background

Following the approval of the Drought Early Action Protocol (EAP), the Zambia Red Cross Society (ZRCS) successfully implemented readiness activities across 16 of the 19 identified high-priority drought-prone districts in Zambia. These interventions aimed to strengthen institutional and community preparedness, enhance operational readiness, and facilitate the timely implementation of anticipatory actions ahead of forecast drought impacts. The activities were undertaken across three provinces, covering the following districts:

  • Eastern Province: Mambwe, Lundazi and Chasefu.
  • Southern Province: Sinazongwe, Gwembe, Kalomo, Kazungula, Monze, Zimba and Mazabuka.
  • Western Province: Mulobezi, Senanga, Mwandi, Sikongo, Sesheke and Sioma.

These readiness interventions contributed to strengthening ZRCS's capacity to operationalise the approved EAP and support timely, coordinated and risk-informed anticipatory action in drought-vulnerable communities.

2.0 Situation Overview and Anticipated Hazard Impacts

Zambia faces an elevated risk of meteorological and agricultural drought during the 2026/2027 rainfall season, associated with anticipated very strong El Niño conditions and unfavourable regional climate drivers. The Zambia Meteorological Department (ZMD) Seasonal Rainfall Forecast, issued on 11 September 2026, projects below-normal rainfall across Southern, Western, Lusaka and much of Central Province, extending into parts of Eastern and North- estern Provinces. Delayed rainfall onset and prolonged dry spells are anticipated, particularly between December 2026 and February 2027, coinciding with critical crop development and flowering stages.

These conditions are expected to adversely affect agricultural production, pasture availability, livestock productivity, water resources and household livelihoods. The anticipated drought coincides with deteriorating food security conditions, with the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) projecting an increase in the population experiencing Crisis-level acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3) from approximately 698,000 people during April– eptember 2026 to 1.25 million people during October 2026–March 2027. Districts classified in IPC Phase 3 are projected to increase from 4 to 28. Drought impacts are expected to emerge from November–December 2026 and intensify between December 2026 and February 2027, increasing the risk of crop failure, livestock stress, reduced household income and negative coping mechanisms.

3.0 Seasonal Forecast, Trigger Monitoring and Activation Justification

The decision to activate the Zambia Drought Early Action Protocol is informed by two converging forecasts; ECMWF and the ZMD 2026/2027 Seasonal Rainfall Forecast. The ZMD seasonal forecast anticipates very strong El Niño conditions, accompanied by a positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) and negative Subtropical Indian Ocean Dipole (SIOD). These climate drivers are expected to suppress rainfall across much of southern and central Zambia, increasing the likelihood of agricultural drought.

The forecast indicates below-normal rainfall during October–December 2026 (OND) across Southern, Lusaka, much of Central and southern Western Provinces. During November 2026–January 2027 (NDJ), rainfall deficits are projected to extend across Western, Southern, Lusaka, much of Central and parts of Eastern and North-Western Provinces. The December 2026–February 2027 (DJF) outlook indicates continued rainfall deficits across substantial parts of the country, accompanied by prolonged dry spells during critical crop development stages. The convergence of these forecast signals provides a strong technical basis for timely anticipatory action to minimise drought-related livelihood losses and humanitarian impacts.

The approved EAP establishes an October activation threshold of at least 45% probability of below-normal precipitation under the ECMWF SEAS5 seasonal forecasting system. The ECMWF October forecast indicates a 50-60% probability of below average rainfall over Zambia during November 2026–January 2027 (NDJ) season.

4.0 Geographical Coverage and Implementation Duration

Geographical prioritization will be informed by forecast drought exposure, projected food insecurity, historical vulnerability and operational feasibility. Southern and Western Provinces are important priority areas exhibiting significant food security vulnerabilities due to anticipated rainfall deficits, prolonged dry spells and dependence on rain- ed agricultural livelihoods. Final intervention districts and communities will be selected within the approved EAP geographical coverage using district-level risk and vulnerability assessments and following consultations from the National Anticipatory Actions Technical Working Group. The EAP provides an early action lead time of approximately three months and an implementation period of three months. Subject to authorization, interventions are anticipated to commence in October 2026 and continue for approximately three months, prioritizing delivery ahead of the expected peak drought impacts between December 2026 and February 2027.

5.0 Early Action Targeting

The Zambia Drought Early Action Protocol (EAP) overall targets 3,755 vulnerable households (22,530 people) through anticipatory interventions addressing food security, livelihoods, water access and drought preparedness. Targeting prioritises drought-exposed households with limited coping capacities, including rain-fed smallholder farmers, livestock- ependent households, female- and child-headed households, older persons, persons with disabilities and food- nsecure households. Beneficiary selection and verification will employ community-based targeting, vulnerability assessments and local government structures, integrating Protection, Gender and Inclusion (PGI), Community Engagement and Accountability (CEA), and safeguarding principles.

Following operational and budgetary adjustments, implementation coverage has been reduced from five to two districts, with sectoral targets revised as follows:

  • Livelihoods: Agricultural input support remains same 800 households (4,800 people).
  • Multipurpose Cash Assistance: Coverage reduced from 3,755 to 2,500 households (15,000 people).
  • WASH: Borehole rehabilitation8 (20) coverage maintained at 3,755 households (22,530 people), alongside WASH kit assistance for 500 households. A total of 20 boreholes will be rehabilitated.

These adjustments prioritise available resources towards the most vulnerable populations while maintaining pre-agreed anticipatory actions.

6.0 Planned Early Actions and Expected Outcomes

Subject to activation authorization, ZRCS will implement predefined early actions comprising drought early warning dissemination, distribution of drought-tolerant agricultural inputs, rehabilitation of community boreholes, provision of essential WASH supplies and unconditional cash assistance to eligible vulnerable households to receive ZMW 1,855. These interventions will strengthen household preparedness, protect agricultural production and livelihood assets, sustain access to safe water, preserve essential food consumption and reduce negative coping mechanisms. Implementation will be coordinated with IFRC and other humanitarian partners and relevant government technical departments through the district disaster risk management structures.

Overall, the proposed activation seeks to reduce anticipated drought-related losses, strengthen household coping capacities and mitigate humanitarian impacts through timely, forecast-informed anticipatory action, while ensuring that formal activation and financing decisions comply with the established EAP governance framework.

title: UNICEF Panama Humanitarian Situation Report No. 6 (Earthquake), 24-30 October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Monitoring visits conducted by UNICEF, UNHCR, and IOM in Soná, Río Grande, and Mariato indicate a gradual transition from the emergency response phase to early recovery. In several communities, families have begun returning to land near their homes or relocating within their communities of origin, reducing the population residing in some temporary displacement sites. In this context, the continuous monitoring of the situation and UNICEF’s targeted support remain essential to prevent setbacks and ensure that the needs of children are addressed in a timely manner.
  • Despite these advances, temporary shelter needs persist for families whose homes were destroyed or whose land remains uninhabitable. In several communities, the construction of improvised shelters using locally available materials was observed while assessment processes, debris removal, and recovery efforts continue to advance.
  • Field assessments continue to identify significant gaps in water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH), including limited access to safe drinking water, an insufficient number of adequate sanitation facilities, and risks associated with wastewater management and vector-borne threats, particularly in coastal communities and temporary settlements.
  • Educational infrastructure continues to be one of the primary concerns. In communities in Río Grande, severe damage and the complete collapse of educational facilities serving multiple communities were verified, affecting the continuity of learning for children and adolescents.
  • In coordination with the Ministry of Education, UNICEF initiated the support and installation of three child-friendly protection and education-in-emergencies spaces in Veraguas Province, expanding access for children and adolescents to recreational, learning, and psychosocial support activities.
  • Monitoring missions continue to reveal psychosocial support needs among children, adolescents, and caregivers, associated with the loss of housing, uncertainty regarding recovery, and the prolonged impact of the emergency.

title: UNICEF State of Palestine Humanitarian Situation Update (Hebron), 30 October 2026
content:
ESCALATION IN HEBRON DISPLACES MORE THAN 480 FAMILIES, INCLUDING OVER
1,800 CHILDREN, AND DISRUPTS ACCESS TO ESSENTIAL SERVICES

Highlights

  • The update covers the humanitarian impact of the escalation in Hebron that began on 23 October 2026, including large-scale displacement, movement restrictions and disruptions to essential services. As of 29 October, Hebron Municipality reported 483 displaced families (4,304 people, including 1,845 children), with more than 300 families lacking access to safe shelter.
  • The report highlights the effects on children and families, including disruptions to education affecting more than 251,000 students across 691 schools in Hebron Governorate, priority humanitarian needs, and risks associated with prolonged displacement, restricted access and the approaching colder season.
  • It also outlines UNICEF’s emergency response through the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM). Between 26 and 29 October, UNICEF partners distributed 889 kits (hygiene, baby, dignity and recreational kits) reaching 249 households (1,403 people, including 716 children), while additional supplies have been mobilized to support further response and preparedness efforts.
  • The update includes UNICEF’s advocacy messages on the protection of children, humanitarian access, education, shelter, water and sanitation services, and the rights of children deprived of liberty.
  • It further presents the funding requirements of UNICEF’s 2026 HAC appeal, which remains 54 per cent unfunded, with a funding gap of USD 400.9 million.

title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 29 October 2026
content:
Key Highlights

  • Families along the “Yellow Line” in Gaza are facing reported arson attacks and recurrent shootings as Israeli forces place additional yellow cement blocks nearby; despite shortages in humanitarian supplies, those displaced as a result of such pressures are receiving rapid support through available stocks.
  • Acute respiratory infections represent 60 per cent of all medical consultations reported by the Health Cluster between 18 and 25 October, followed by skin diseases (21 per cent) and acute watery diarrhea (18 per cent).
  • Amid multiple reports of strikes affecting humanitarian operations, UNOPS reported three security incidents over three consecutive days affecting its convoys and premises.
  • In the West Bank, humanitarian partners are supporting local authorities in responding to the needs of approximately 3,000 Palestinians reportedly displaced during an ongoing operation by Israeli forces in Hebron city, following a shooting attack by two Palestinians who killed two Israeli soldiers. Displacement figures remain under verification.
  • October has already recorded the highest monthly number of settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage since documentation began in 2006, with a total of 397 incidents reported between 1 and 26 October.
  • Between 20 and 26 October, 62 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage were documented across 49 West Bank communities, including 38 olive-harvest-related attacks.
  • In Khirbet Ras al Ahmar, Tubas governorate, 24 Palestinian herding families comprising 94 people, including 40 children, were displaced amid increasing access restrictions and settler attacks.

Gaza Strip

The reporting period is 19-25 October 2026 unless otherwise specified.

Multiple Israeli airstrikes, shelling, shooting and naval fire were recorded, reportedly causing civilian casualties and further destruction. Israeli incursions and demolitions were also reported near the “Yellow Line.” Humanitarian partners continue to operate amid ongoing insecurity. Since 19 October, a UN site in Deir al Balah has come under fire. There have also been three separate shooting incidents near three UN schools. On 26 October UNOPS reported three incidents over three consecutive days affecting their convoys and premises. These were close proximity explosions; drivers detained at checkpoints, and multiple small arms rounds striking one of the UNOPS guesthouses.

Families in areas along the so-called “Yellow Line” continue to face reported arson attacks, recurrent shooting and the placement of new yellow cement blocks by Israeli forces, which signal that the area is unsafe. In recent days, new blocks have been observed in Ash Shuja’iyyeh and parts of Deir al Balah. On 25 October, tents sheltering displaced households were set on fire in the Ash Shuja’iyyeh area of Gaza city. The UN and partners visited the site on 26 October to assess needs, identifying 9 families affected by the incident, who received emergency assistance and were willing to relocate. This incident followed another fire reportedly instigated by armed Palestinians reportedly linked to Israeli forces a few days earlier, triggering the new displacement of 137 households. Humanitarian partners mobilized support for the affected families, including new tents, tarpaulins, blankets, and hygiene kits. Approximately 130 households remain at the site, living in difficult conditions.

According to the Ministry of Health in Gaza, which operates under the de-facto authorities, 33 Palestinians were reported killed and 188 injured between 20 and 26 October, bringing the total number of casualties since the ceasefire agreement to 1,559 fatalities and 5,608 injuries. Another 42 fatalities were retroactively added to the total number after their identification details were approved by MoH.

The Logistics Cluster reports that, between 19 and 25 October, out of 651 UN and partner trucks carrying humanitarian supplies manifested for entry into Gaza, 586 were successfully offloaded on the Israeli side of Kerem Shalom, of which 291 came from Ashdod, 187 from Egypt and 54 from Jordan. Compared with the previous week, the number of humanitarian trucks manifested for entry decreased by 16 per cent, but the percentage of offloaded trucks remained stable.

The private sector collected 343 commercial truckloads into the Gaza Strip between 19 and 25 October, based on data from the Gaza Chamber of Commerce shared with the Cash Working Group. This represents a 9 per cent increase compared with the previous week (12-18 October), during which a halt in commercial imports was reported in connection with a high fee said to be charged by the de facto authorities, with conflicting narratives over whether that fee was voluntary or imposed.

Of the total, the Chamber of Commerce indicates that 129 carried food supplies, 73 solid fuel, 68 shelter materials, 38 hygiene items, 25 cooking gas, 2 medicines and medical supplies, and one stationery. Seven trucks – or 2 per cent of the total – carried non-essential items, representing a significant drop compared with the 25-35 per cent recorded in the past week (12-18 October).

The reported halt in commercial entries seems to have had a direct impact on bakeries resuming daily production and prices, with the cost of flour and fresh products increasing by over 70 per cent compared to the week (12-18 October), based on information from the Gaza Market Monitoring Committee (GMMC). The Food Security Sector reports that some partners were forced to adjust the cooked meal menu, scale down or pause free bread and fresh produce distribution due to shortages of fruit, vegetables and wheat flour and high prices.

Flood risk mitigation efforts ahead of winter

As the winter approaches, conditions remain dire across the Strip. On 19 October, OCHA and humanitarian partners assessed six displacement sites in the An Nasser neighbourhood of the Khan Younis governorate, none of which has an active organization providing site management presence. Five sites that cumulatively host 750 households are situated in Al Joura, a low-lying area approximately 30 metres below the surrounding ground level. A sixth site, Al Ilm, hosts 250 households, with shelters located both along the cliff edge and in the low-lying area. The team examined flood and erosion risks, explored possible site-improvement measures, and documented priority humanitarian needs requiring partner follow-up. Families reported lacking enough shelter materials, sanitation, water access, food assistance, health care and cash-based support. The team has mobilized support accordingly.

The Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) Cluster conducted a rapid field assessment of the Abu Rashid stormwater basin and pumping station near the “Yellow Line” in Jabalya, North Gaza; the assessment revealed the basin is incapacitated due to lack of power and access being unsafe. Without an emergency rehabilitation and stabilization intervention, the stormwater lagoon is at risk of flooding during the winter, directly affecting nearby displacement sites at risk of flooding. A further detailed assessment is taking place to explore possible mitigation options.

In the Mawasi area of Khan Younis, the WASH Cluster also implemented mitigation works at a displacement site located within a stormwater basin to reduce the risk of flooding.

Meanwhile, the UN Development Programme (UNDP) reports that its teams are using recycled crushed concrete to raise and level shelter sites ahead of winter.

Communicable diseases

Communicable diseases accounted for 18 per cent of all medical consultations conducted by Health Cluster partners during the reporting period, with acute respiratory infections representing 60 per cent of reported diseases, followed by skin diseases (21 per cent) and acute watery diarrhea (18 per cent). An increase in probable viral and bacterial meningitis cases has also been observed since September, primarily in Gaza governorate. Case investigations, line-listing, cerebrospinal fluid follow-up, and laboratory confirmation activities are ongoing, while access to laboratory supplies remains critical for effective outbreak response.

Humanitarian response activities at a glance – Gaza Strip

19–26 October 2026 (unless otherwise specified)

Food Security: As of 26 October, 16 of 17 commercial bakeries supported through a “fuel-only” production model were operational, while 21 subsidized bakeries continued producing approximately 80,000 two-kilogram bread bundles daily. As of 22 October, partners prepared 586,000 meals daily through 90 kitchens and delivered them to 1,368 locations across the Gaza Strip. During the ongoing October distribution cycle, approximately 422,000 people (116,000 households) received food parcels and wheat flour through 28 distribution points, providing around 50 per cent of minimum caloric requirements. Partners also completed one round of fodder distributions to approximately 2,250 livestock holders and launched a second round targeting 2,250 herders and 730 working-animal owners.

Shelter and Site Management: Shelter Cluster partners reached 8,590 households with shelter and non-food item assistance, distributing 734 tents, 1,891 winter clothing kits, 44 bedding kits, 960 blankets, 1,858 toolkits, 2,190 sealing-off kits, 1,256 sheets of transparent plastic and 123 refugee housing units (RHUs).

Health: WHO started cascade training on polio, disease surveillance and adverse events following immunization across four governorates, targeting approximately 300 medical doctors from international and local NGOs. Partners equipped facilities with infection prevention and control supplies , including alcohol-based hand rub, chlorine, personal protective equipment and environmental cleaning materials. Between 21 and 27 October, 69 patients, including 12 children, were medically evacuated through the Rafah crossing alongside 93 caregivers. Since the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025, WHO has supported the evacuation of 3,547 patients, along with 5,855 caregivers, through the Rafah and Kerem Shalom crossings, including 2,746 patients and 4,065 companions evacuated via Rafah since its reopening on 2 February 2026.

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene: Partners continued preparing for the cold and rainy season winterization preparedness activities in displacement sites, including through road improvement and flood-mitigation works. They distributed 260 water tanks, 6,500 jerry cans, 7,000 tarpaulins, 9,500 bars of soap and 5,000 kilograms of laundry soap.

Protection: Protection partners reached 13,454 people with direct protection services, including mental health and psychosocial support, psychological first aid, case management, legal assistance, explosive ordnance risk education, disability inclusion support and community accountability activities. An additional 1,803 people received protection-sensitive and intersectoral assistance, including food vouchers, hygiene items, menstrual hygiene management kits, sexual and reproductive health services and assistive devices. Protection monitoring activities included six focus group discussions and 73 key informant interviews, reaching 732 people across 13 neighbourhoods. Partners also supported 230 returnees with psychological first aid, emergency assistance and referral services. Child protection partners reached 4,122 children and 2,564 caregivers with mental health and psychosocial support services, including individual and group counselling, psychological first aid, trauma recovery interventions and parenting support. Partners provided case management services to 138 newly identified at-risk children, facilitated 86 referrals for specialized services, and continued support for 58 children in alternative care. Awareness-raising and community engagement activities reached 1,216 children and 1,064 caregivers. Emergency assistance included the distribution of 10,000 winter clothing kits and 600 stationery kits, while 147 vulnerable children received cash assistance.

Joint Distributions | Emergency Response: Joint Distribution Consortium processed appeals for help following 14 reported incidents affecting 525 households across Gaza. The appeals included seven in Gaza affecting 372 households, five in Khan Younis affecting 59 households, and two in Deir al Balah affecting 94 households. The reported incidents included nine airstrike incidents affecting 517 households, four accidental fire incidents affecting seven households, and one displacement incident affecting one household. Based on rapid assessments, 84 households were classified as high-need, 324 as medium-need, and 117 as low-need. Assistance was prioritized according to the type of incident, level of damage, and assessed household needs.

title: UNHCR Flash Update #1 – Blue Nile State
content:
Situation Overview and Humanitarian Needs

▪ Security conditions in Blue Nile State have steadily deteriorated since end-August 2026, triggering displacement from Geisan and Al-Kurmuk localities to Ed Damazin, Al-Roseires and Wad Al-Mahi localities. This newest displacement is increasing pressure in these areas which were already hosting a sizeable number of Sudanese returnees and refugees from South Sudan and Ethiopia. In October, a drone strike on the Abu Shandi displacement camp in the Blue Nile region killed over 30 civilians, predominantly women and children, and left dozens injured, compounding a dire humanitarian crisis.

▪ Approximately 99,300 people were displaced from Geisan, Al-Kurmuk and Baw localities in Blue Nile State between January and August 2026 according to IOM's Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM). Displacement occurred both within affected localities and towards Ed Damazin, Wad Al-Mahi and AlRoseires. Most newly displaced people sheltered in informal gathering sites (58 per cent) or with host families. UNHCR field reports indicated further displacement following recent insecurity in Wad AlMahi and Geisan, with most newly displaced people seeking safety in Alazaza, Al-Roseires locality.

▪ Separately, Sudan’s Commission of Refugees (COR) and UNHCR recorded the arrival of 166 individuals (48 households) from Ethiopia at Camp 6 in Wad Al-Mahi locality between July and September 2026.

▪ Humanitarian needs in areas hosting newly displaced households were already high prior to the latest displacement, and with new displacement, the situation has been exacerbated. Unfortunately, due to insecurity, access to displacement sites has become increasingly constrained which has affected the ability of partners to undertake comprehensive needs assessment, monitoring or deliver assistance or protection services.

▪ Nevertheless, inadequate shelter, limited access to water and sanitation services, insufficient site management arrangements, and overcrowding have been reported in several displacement sites, all increasing protection risks particularly among the most vulnerable. Newly displaced households have reported urgent needs for shelter, basic relief items, food assistance, health care services, safe water, and sanitation support. Specialised protection services are also limited, with few service providers, particularly to undertake case management, make referrals and provide information or protection counselling.

title: Somalia Monthly Humanitarian Update October 2026
content:
• At least 175,000 people have so far been affected by El Nino-linked heavy rains and flash floods in several regions; shelters, latrines and water points have been damaged or flooded.
  • From October to December, at least 3.4 million people are projected to face flood risks, with Hiraan, Middle Juba and Lower Juba regions most exposed.
  • Partners activated a floods anticipatory action plan backed by US$7 million from the Central Emergency Response Fund and $2 million from Somalia Humanitarian Fund.
  • Renewed conflict and insecurity in Bay region, South West State, is causing new displacement and further complicating humanitarian operations.
  • Somalia renewed its commitment to ending polio through expanded vaccination campaigns, innovative delivery approaches, and strengthened public health capacity.
  • This month’s update also includes human interest stories on an inclusive school supporting children with disabilities in in Gaalkacyo and a displaced father in Baidoa supporting his community through hygiene promotion.

Thousands affected as heavy rains reported in several areas

Heavy rains were reported in several regions across Somalia in October, affecting more than 175,000 people. Gaalkacyo, Abudwaq, and Baidoa are the most affected areas, respectively. Area Based Coordination (ABC) teams reported 1,515 shelters or houses destroyed and 4,498 damaged over the course of the month due flash flooding. Also damaged or flooded were 2,110 latrines or flooded, 137 water points, 72 schools, while 55 health facilities were affected. Projections show that heavier rains and flooding are expected over the coming weeks. During the last week of October, the Shabelle river level rose significantly, approaching moderate flood-risk thresholds in Belet Weyne district in Hiraan region region. Water levels also rose in Bulo Burto. However, levels on the Juba river remained low.

The FAO - Somalia Water and Land Information Management (SWALIM) programme forecasted heavy rainfall over the upper Shabelle catchment in Ethiopia in late October, with river levels in Belet Weyne and Bulo Burto expected to continue rising. Partners are concerned that further rainfall and rising river levels could trigger displacement, disrupt road access and constrain the movement of humanitarian and commercial supplies, particularly along key corridors serving Jowhar, Bulo Burto and Jalalaqsi.

Flood risk analysis shows that up to 3.4 million people could be affected by flooding between October and December, especially in Hiraan, Middle Juba and Lower Juba regions. IOM and the Danish Refugee Council estimate that more than 874,000 people may be displaced from their homes, with flooding accounting for 92 per cent of the projected displacement. Belet Weyne and Gaalkacyo are among the areas facing the greatest threat, with about 229,000 and 82,000 people, respectively, at risk of displacement.

title: Pakistan Weekly Market Monitor (week ending 29 October 2026)
content:
• Staple food (wheat flour, edible oils, and pulses) prices remained 23 percent above pre-Middle East conflict levels, as of 29 October, reflecting a combination of domestic market factors and higher fuel and import costs.
  • Wheat flour prices recorded a marginal decrease (-0.8%) during the week, while overall remained 30 percent above pre-conflict levels.
  • The cost of basic food basket for a six-member household stood at PKR 18,669 per month (USD 66.7) equivalent to PKR 4,667 per week (USD 16.7) nationwide, excluding lower cost items such as vegetables or spices.
  • Petrol and diesel prices remain 46% and 45% above pre-conflict levels. A marginal decline was noted in the price of petrol (-0.4%) and a slight increase in the price of diesel (+2.5%) this week.
  • Food prices remain elevated despite adequate commodity supplies and stable market availability.
  • Middle East conflict regional disruptions to key shipping routes continue to exert upward pressure on fuel and domestic inflation.

title: Ukraine Health Cluster Bulletin #9 (September 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• September 2026 was the worst month of September for civilians since the full-scale escalation began in 2022, according to the UN HRMMU. At least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured, an 85 per cent increase compared to September 2025. Attacks continue to damage homes, schools, health facilities, transport, supply chains, and other civilian infrastructure, leaving civilians exposed to danger at any time of day.

• Long-range weapons remained the leading cause of civilian casualties, accounting for 53 per cent of the total. The growing use of advanced drone technology is stretching air defences and contributing to mass casualty incidents in multiple regions. In Kyiv, civilian casualties were recorded on 22 out of the month’s 30 days, a frequency not seen in the capital in any other month since the full-scale escalation. Kherson, Sumy, Zaporizhzhia, Donetska, and Dnipropetrovska were also heavily affected. Health Cluster partners continue to support the post-strike response, providing 1,335 consultations and 216 medical transfers, and prepositioning medical supplies to receiving health facilities to cover 3,674 people since the beginning of the year.

• Attacks on humanitarian and pharmaceutical warehouses and on manufacturers are disrupting medical supply chains and the delivery of essential medicines to frontline facilities and communities, as well as mobile team operations. Some 6 out of 13 partners surveyed reported having no emergency stock available to deploy in case of immediate need. Two frontline interagency convoys delivering assistance were missing the 700 requested Over-The-Counter (OTC) medicine kits due to medicine shortages.

• Displacement remained elevated as hostilities persisted, and frontline shifted, particularly in Donetska oblast. According to the Ukraine Protection Cluster, 16,898 people were registered in September at transit centers where partners operate. Compared with the previous month, Donetska oblast evacuee arrivals rose by nearly 30 per cent, from 7,274 to 9,415, mainly from Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. In September, some 17 partners provided 4,669 medical consultations at transit centers, and two health partners provided assistive technologies.

title: South Sudan Humanitarian Update (as of 30 October 2026)
content:
Highlights

• More than 5,100 refugees and returnees from the Democratic Republic of the Congo need urgent humanitarian support.

• A national simulation exercise identifies gaps in Ebola preparedness.

• Insecurity and displacement deepen needs in Jonglei and Upper Nile states.

• Drone strikes reportedly kill dozens of people, deepening humanitarian needs in Abyei Administrative Area.

• Conflict, rainfall deficits and economic pressures worsen food insecurity.

• Insecurity and bureaucratic constraints continue to impede humanitarian access.

title: Dengue Epidemiological Situation in the Region of the Americas - Epidemiological Week 40, 2026
content: In the epidemiological week (EW) 40 of 2026, a total of 1,845,488 suspected cases of dengue were reported, resulting in a cumulative incidence of 283 cases por 100,000 population. This represents a decrease of 54% compared to the same period in 2025 and 61% compared to the average of the last 5 years. Figure 1 shows the trend of suspected dengue cases as of EW 40.

title: DRC — Internal Displacement Overview (July 2026)
content:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) faces a complex internal displacement situation driven by armed conflict, insecurity and natural hazards. In the eastern provinces, prolonged conflict and insecurity remain the primary drivers of large-scale displacement, while other regions of the country are also affected by conflict, insecurity and disasters, including floods and landslides. The humanitarian situation is further complicated by public health emergencies, including the Ebola virus disease outbreak declared in May 2026. Understanding displacement dynamics across the DRC is essential to inform immediate humanitarian assistance and longer-term programming.

This Internal Displacement Overview – July 2026 presents updated country-level estimates of internally displaced persons (IDPs) and returnees, drawing on three assessments conducted by IOM's Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) between January and July 2026. Mobility Tracking (MT) assessments were conducted in the four eastern provinces of Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu and Tanganyika between 27 May and 10 July 2026, and in 16 health zones across Kinshasa, Kwango, Kwilu and Maï-Ndombe between 25 January and 21 February 2026. Additional data were collected through MT Light between 16 May and 19 June 2026, covering 368 health zones across 22 provinces. Together, these assessments cover 499 of the country's 519 health zones across all 26 provinces, providing a nationwide overview of internal displacement and returns.

title: Earthquake in Panama | Humanitarian update - Reference period: (9–15 October 2026)
content:
On October 9, 2026, a magnitude 7.5 earthquake primarily affected the provinces of Herrera, Los Santos, Veraguas, and Coclé. More than 22,400 people were affected, and damage to homes, schools, and health facilities limited access to essential services. Women and girls face specific needs and risks, including a lack of safe shelter, gender-based violence, psychosocial impacts, and increased caregiving responsibilities.

Urgent and flexible funding is needed to support the humanitarian response and early recovery over the next three to six months. Assistance will prioritize women and girls, including older women, caregivers, and women with disabilities, and will promote a gender-responsive, human rights-based, and inclusive response.

title: Global Price Watch September 2026 Prices (October 30, 2026)
content:
Key Messages

  • In West Africa, staple food prices showed mixed trends but broadly remained below the five-year average. New harvests drove seasonal price declines in coastal countries and Niger, while seasonal price increases were recorded in parts of Burkina Faso, Mali, and Chad. Prices rose in Nigeria due to delayed harvests and high transportation costs. Cameroon recorded modest cereal price increases in northern markets due to a surge in exports to Chad, while the Central African Republic (CAR) continued to experience elevated maize and rice prices (Page 3).
  • In East Africa staple food price trends diverged in September. Prices rose sharply in Sudan, Uganda, and Burundi amid tightening supplies, elevated demand, and high fuel and transport costs. Recent harvests supported seasonal price declines in Somalia, South Sudan, and Tanzania, while maize prices remained broadly stable in Kenya. Cereal prices remained significantly above average in several conflict-affected markets, particularly Sudan, South Sudan, and Ethiopia (Page 4).
  • In Southern Africa, maize prices increased across most markets in September. Prices were higher in South Africa, Zambia, and Malawi, while remaining broadly stable in Tanzania, Mozambique, and Zimbabwe. Prices trended downward in Lesotho, supported by favorable imports from South Africa. Staple food prices increased in parts of DRC and Madagascar due to lean season conditions and tightening supplies. Maize prices remained below last year's levels in Zambia, Mozambique, and Lesotho, but were above September 2025 levels in South Africa and Malawi (Page 5).
  • In Central America, staple grain prices were stable or increased, as the delayed and staggered primera harvest continued to constrain seasonal supply increases amidst negative expectations for the postrera harvest. In Haiti, yellow maize prices were stable but above average due to reduced spring production and lower stocks. In Venezuela, monthly inflation remained below 10 percent, and food prices declined. In Colombia, cereal prices remained stable due to ample import supply, while potato and cassava persisted above average due to production declines (Page 6).
  • In the Middle East and Europe, staple food prices were stable or increased across both regions. In Syria, staple prices increased alongside rising diesel prices and currency depreciation. In Yemen, wheat flour, rice, and sunflower oil prices were stable, but shipping disruptions kept prices above average. In Lebanon, wheat flour prices increased while rice and lentils were stable. Wheat flour prices increased in both Gaza and the West Bank, with the increase in the former due to reduced humanitarian inflows. In Ukraine, bread, wheat flour, and buckwheat prices increased, due partly to logistics disruptions and high energy costs (Page 7).
  • In Asia, staple food prices were mixed, reflecting seasonal harvests, elevated fuel costs, and localized supply disruptions. Prices remained broadly stable in Afghanistan and Sri Lanka, while Pakistan's wheat flour prices declined modestly following several months of increases. In Burma, rice and palm oil prices increased sharply amid flooding, conflict, and import constraints, while Nepal experienced localized price increases driven by festival demand and monsoon-related transport disruptions (Page 13).
  • International markets tightened in September, reflecting increased upside risk from global supply chain shocks. Maize prices increased 8.2 percent, driven by Black Sea trade disruptions and adverse weather. Wheat prices generally increased for the same reasons. Rice prices increased, driven by India’s weak monsoon, with Thai quotes 33.2 percent above September 2025. Brent averaged 116.8 USD/bbl, driven by scarce diesel and attacks on Gulf pipeline infrastructure. Fertilizer prices were mixed, with urea up 4.5 percent and potash down 5.0 percent. No grain faces a global shortfall, but importers face higher fuel and freight costs (Page 2).

title: Cyclone Arnab: Andhra Pradesh, Yanam (Puducherry) and Odisha (Date: 30 October 2026, Time: 08:00 IST)

title: Multi-Country Ebola Bundibugyo Outbreak Update n°24
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Nigeria
content:
According to the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as of 24 October 2026, the country had reported 9,964 confirmed cases of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD), including 4,841 deaths, representing an increase of 412 cases and 239 deaths since 18 October. Since the beginning of the outbreak, 66 health zones across 8 provinces have reported at least one confirmed case. Ituri remains the epicentre, accounting for 72 per cent of cumulative cases, while transmission continues to be concentrated in Ituri and North Kivu. On 24 October, 88 new confirmed cases were reported (44 in Ituri, 39 in North Kivu and 5 in Haut-Uélé), compared with 97 on 18 October. A total of 38 deaths were reported, including 26 community deaths. Contact follow-up improved from 76.9 per cent on 18 October to 87.1 per cent on 24 October, although it remains below the 95 per cent target, with 4,855 contacts not seen. Laboratory surveillance indicated ongoing transmission, with 512 samples tested on 24 October and a positivity rate of 17.2 per cent. The outbreak continues to place significant pressure on frontline response capacities, with 269 frontline workers affected since the start of the outbreak, including 180 in Ituri and 45 in North Kivu.

The regional situation evolved further during the reporting period. In Nigeria, authorities confirmed the country's first imported BVD case in Abuja on 20 October, making it the fifth country to report a case since the outbreak was declared in DRC. By 24 October, 53 contacts had been identified and were under follow-up, while a suspected case reported in Rivers State subsequently tested negative. In Kenya, the number of confirmed cases increased from seven to nine, including one death. All secondary cases remain epidemiologically linked to the imported index case, and no transmission outside the identified cluster has been reported.

Key highlights include:

  • The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has reported 9,964 confirmed cases and 4,841 deaths. Transmission remains concentrated in eastern DRC, with 88 new confirmed cases reported on 24 October, primarily in Ituri and North Kivu.
  • Nigeria confirmed its first imported BVD case on 20 October, with 53 contacts identified and under follow-up.
  • In Kenya, confirmed cases increased to nine, all linked to the imported index case, with no evidence of wider community transmission beyond the identified cluster.
  • IOM has supported more than 51.8 million health screenings at points of entry and points of control across affected and at-risk countries since the beginning of the response.
  • Nearly 48.2 million people have been reached through risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) activities.
  • Preparedness and response activities continue across DRC, Uganda, Burundi, Rwanda, South Sudan, Kenya and Nigeria, while preparedness efforts are ongoing in Angola, CAR, Cameroon, Ethiopia, the Republic of the Congo, Tanzania and Zambia.
  • Population Mobility Mapping (PMM), flow monitoring and surveillance activities continue to guide risk-based interventions along high-risk mobility corridors, border areas and mobility-affected settings.

For more information, please consult the report HERE.

title: Heavy Rains and Flooding in the Grand Sud and the West - Flash Update No. 2 (as of 29 October 2026)
content:

  • Eight deaths have been recorded: three in the West, three in Nippes, one in the South and one in Grand’Anse.
