title: WFP Palestine Emergency Response External Situation Report #99, 29 October 2026 (Reporting period: 1-15 October 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• Funding shortages have required WFP to reduce food assistance in Gaza by around one-third, with monthly support falling from 1.6 million to 1.1 million people, leaving some 500,000 vulnerable people without critical assistance as winter approaches. The provision of hot meals has also reduced from 250,000 to 150,000 meals per day, with people now receiving meals on alternate days.

• Funding cuts risk reversing fragile food-security gains, with 1.4 million people, or 67 percent of Gaza’s population, still facing acute food insecurity.

• Urgent funding, increased humanitarian and commercial flows, and the opening and sustained operation of more crossings and routes are critical to restore and scale up lifesaving assistance across Gaza.

SITUATION UPDATE

• Airstrikes, shelling and gunfire continued across Gaza, while incursions, demolitions and further advancement of the “Yellow Line” of military control raised protection concerns and risks of further displacement. Humanitarian movements continued to face logistical and coordination constraints affecting the timely entry of assistance.
• Winter-related risks are mounting, with an estimated 950,000 displaced people living in sites at medium-to-high risk of flooding, including more than 400,000 at high risk. Available supplies could partially cover only 18 percent of the 294,250 families requiring winter shelter assistance, while shortages continue to affect essential health and water services.
• Malnutrition remains a serious concern, with around 3,000 children aged 6–59 months admitted for treatment each month. In September alone, more than 2,800 children were admitted for treatment, including over 360 children with severe acute malnutrition, underscoring persistent nutritional vulnerability despite recent modest improvements in some nutrition indicators.
• In the West Bank, violence, movement restrictions and damage to productive assets continued to affect Palestinian livelihoods and access to agricultural land. Risks are particularly pronounced during the olive harvest, with some 200 harvest-related settler attacks documented between 1 September and mid-October, alongside increasing constraints on farmers’ ability to access and cultivate their land.

title: Situation Update No. 6: Escalation of hostilities and displacement across Yemen Update No. 6 | As of 25 October 2026 | Reporting period: 1 August – 25 October 2026 | Countrywide
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • Displacement continues to grow, with more than 281,000 people displaced. Most have fled fighting in Ta’iz and along the West Coast, and a new surge from Lahj in mid-October shows that the crisis is spreading rather than stabilizing.
  • People in and around Ta’iz City face growing hardship. With access to several city districts severely restricted, health facilities face shortages of fuel, water and medicines, some supplies for the city are still awaiting delivery, and fewer displaced families are able to leave the governorate.
  • Civilians continue to bear the brunt of the fighting. As of 27 October, OHCHR had documented 263 civilian casualties, including 67 people killed. Children account for 97 of the casualties and about half of those killed.
  • 207,480 IDPs (29,640 households) have been reached with first-line RRM assistance, and most have received their kits; almost 9,000 registered families are still waiting as supply pipelines, clearances and insecurity slow delivery.
  • Second-line assistance lags far behind needs. Emergency cash has reached most verified families and food assistance just over half of verified households, but shelter and WASH support has reached only a minority of households in need, and nutrition treatment a small share of those targeted, leaving families in crowded sites exposed as cholera spreads.
  • Protection risks are rising. Partners report more family separation, explosive ordnance risks, eviction threats and a growing risk of gender-based violence, while five safe spaces for women and girls have closed.
  • Partners continue to deliver in hard-to-reach areas. A small number of national and international partners keep health, water, shelter, cash and mine action services running in the West Coast.
  • Access getting more constrained. Taiz continues to be encircled with limited access for humanitarian and commercial supplies. Humanitarian movements are being restricted at checkpoints despite approved permits, and damaged roads are slowing supplies between Ta’iz and the south.
  • Much of the displacement in areas under the de facto authorities goes unrecorded. Unverified estimates point to thousands of newly displaced families in Ta’iz, Ibb, Al Bayda and Dhamar.

title: Cuba: Arboviral outbreak - DREF Final Report (MDRCU012)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

15-10-2025

What happened, where and when?

In the eastern provinces of Granma, Santiago de Cuba, and Guantánamo, a sharp rise in suspected and confirmed cases was reported from late September 2025 onward. Epidemiological projections at the time indicated that transmission was expected to continue increasing in these provinces during the following weeks.

On 6 October 2025, during a high-level meeting held in Matanzas and chaired by the President of the Republic, MINSAP identified Matanzas as the epicenter of the national outbreak. The Minister of Public Health attributed the situation to a combination of environmental, climatic, and structural factors, including persistent rainfall, high temperatures, inadequate waste management, and challenges in water supply, which had created favorable conditions for mosquito proliferation (salud.msp.gob.cu, 10 October 2025).

On 15 October 2025, the Ministry of Public Health (MINSAP) issued an official update confirming the simultaneous circulation of dengue, oropouche, and chikungunya viruses throughout the country and reported the first dengue-related fatalities.

To strengthen the response, MINSAP deployed a medical contingent composed of physicians, nurses, epidemiologists, and technicians, led by the Minister of Public Health, to the municipalities of Cárdenas and Colón, with support from brigades from Havana and other provinces. These teams implemented intensified fumigation campaigns, environmental sanitation measures, larval and adult mosquito control, and active epidemiological surveillance. Hospitals managed patients presenting warning signs or severe symptoms, while authorities promoted community participation through the elimination of breeding sites and the implementation of local focal-control measures.

The co-circulation of multiple arboviruses significantly increased the public health burden. Hospitals in the most affected provinces experienced sustained pressure owing to growing numbers of admissions, leading authorities to decentralize care to municipal facilities for patients without warning signs. Pregnant women, children, older adults, and persons with disabilities were prioritized for medical follow-up because of their increased risk of complications. Reports of recurrent febrile syndromes and multiple infections within short periods suggested overlapping transmission cycles.

The outbreak occurred in a context of heightened national vulnerability. Less than a year earlier, Hurricanes Oscar (Category 1, Guantánamo) and Rafael (Category 3, Artemisa) had caused extensive damage to infrastructure, power systems, and essential services. The cumulative effects of these events had weakened key public health and vector-control capacities while increasing community vulnerability.

Within this context, the Cuban Red Cross (CRC), in its auxiliary role to public authorities, supported the government-led response from 4 October 2025 onward through health promotion activities, vector-control interventions, and community-based self-focal actions aimed at eliminating mosquito breeding sites. However, limited access to essential materials and supplies constrained the organization's ability to expand and sustain the response at the required scale.

In the weeks following the official declaration of the outbreak, the epidemiological situation evolved rapidly from an initial concentration in Matanzas and the eastern provinces to a nationwide epidemic.

The impact of Hurricane Melissa further exacerbated the outbreak. Intense rainfall, localized flooding, and damage to housing, water supply systems, and road infrastructure created favorable conditions for the proliferation of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes in the provinces prioritized under the DREF operation. Simultaneously, damage to bridges and secondary roads hindered access to certain communities, causing temporary disruptions to fumigation and focal-control activities that MINSAP had been implementing since the onset of the outbreak.

Hurricane Melissa acted as an epidemiological amplifier during the most critical phase of the outbreak. Increased breeding opportunities resulting from heavy rainfall and flooding, combined with reduced operational access caused by infrastructure damage, contributed to higher transmission rates in the most affected eastern provinces. These conditions also increased demand for clinical case management services.

This "double impact", characterized by heightened entomological risk and reduced operational access, contributed to increased transmission and incidence rates in the eastern provinces and generated an immediate rise in demand for healthcare services.

According to MINSAP, by epidemiological week (EW) 48, the arboviral endemic channel remained within the epidemic zone, and incidence continued to increase in both the eastern provinces and Matanzas. During EW 48, 5,717 new chikungunya cases were reported, bringing the cumulative total for 2025 to 38,938 cases. Dengue transmission remained active across 14 provinces, 43 municipalities, and 51 health areas. Although only three deaths had been reported up to November, MINSAP confirmed a total of 33 arboviral disease-related deaths by the end of EW 48, predominantly among individuals under 18 years of age. Severe cases, including severe dengue requiring hospitalization, continued to be reported and required specialized clinical management.

The rapid deterioration of the epidemiological situation, reflected in the increase in confirmed deaths and severe cases, shifted the operational focus from vector control alone toward ensuring timely and effective clinical case management.

title: Dominican Republic: Floods - DREF Operational Update (MDRDO021)
content:
Description of the Event
Date of event

12-04-2026

What happened, where and when?

From 7 April 2026, a trough system affected the Dominican Republic, generating intense rainfall and prolonged atmospheric instability across the country. At the height of the emergency, the National Emergency Operations Centre (Centro de Operaciones de Emergencias – COE) placed 28 provinces under alert: 4 under red alert, 17 under yellow alert and 7 under green alert, due to the risk of urban and flash flooding (COE Situation Reports, update of 16 April 2026).

The emergency reached a critical point on 12 April 2026, with ten fatalities reported. In response, the Government declared a State of Emergency through Decree No. 234-26 for the provinces of Santo Domingo, Puerto Plata, Espaillat, Valverde and Santiago, as well as the National District. This measure enabled the scaling up of response efforts in the most affected areas (Government of the Dominican Republic, Decree No. 234-26).

The intensity and duration of the rainfall, combined with saturated soils and the wide geographic spread of the impacts, resulted in a complex, multi-sectoral emergency. According to COE Situation Report No. 3, updated on 16 April 2026, more than 28 communities were cut off, five bridges sustained structural damage and approximately 30,500 people were evacuated to collective centres or hosted by relatives and friends.

The most affected areas included Santo Domingo, San Cristóbal, Puerto Plata, Espaillat, María Trinidad Sánchez, Valverde and the National District. Puerto Plata was the most severely affected province, particularly the municipality of Montellano, where the overflow of the Camú River affected 3,424 households. The flooding also forced the temporary closure of the municipal hospital, disrupting access to health services for approximately 20,753 people at the time (COE, 2026; local authority reports).

Many of the affected areas had also experienced recent hydrometeorological events and had not fully recovered when the April 2026 flooding occurred. This compounded existing vulnerabilities and reduced the capacity of households and communities to cope with the additional shock.

title: Conflict Escalation in Yemen - Situation Report #9 (Reporting period: 20 – 25 October 2026 | Issued: 28 October 2026)
content:
Highlights

• Daily casualties are falling, but deaths are not. The HEOC register reached 9,072 (7,395 injured, 1,677 deaths) by 25 October, +559 in six days. Daily totals declined from 153 on 20 October to 27 on 24 October before rising again to 56 on 25 October. The period average of ~93 per day is about half that of Sitrep #8 (168/day).

• Marib is the most lethal front. Marib recorded 45 deaths among 143 casualties (31%), more than Taiz (34 of 237) and Lahj (21 of 158). On 22 and 23 October, deaths in Marib outnumbered injuries.

• Report of Health care came under fire again in Taiz. On 20 October HEOC reported Al-Arous Hospital (Sabir Al-Mawadim) was hit by mortar fragments, and an ambulance was destroyed by a projectile, killing its driver and paramedic.

• Shabwah's toll is being revised upwards. The Shabwah Health Office now reports 69 deaths and 166 injured from the 19 October missile strike on Al-Alam Camp near Ataq, against 205 casualties (47 deaths) in the HEOC register. Twenty-one critical patients were transferred to Mukalla.

• Displacement reached 276,301 people (46,044 HH) by 24 October (IOM DTM). New arrivals have slowed sharply since mid-October, but Taiz still hosts 46% of IDPs. Marib's primary care network is significantly weakened: 6 MMTs remain of 31 in 2025.

• Cholera continues to decline from its W40 peak in the five most-affected governorates (639 in W40, 447 in W42), but 3 confirmed cases and 1 death in Marib point to spread beyond the southern belt. WHO has prioritised 29 districts for an ICG request for oral cholera vaccine.

• WHO delivered 56 trauma and emergency kits to Taiz city on 24 October (46 TESK, 10 IEHK) with medicines and MCH supplies, about 30 MT in total, to three hospitals and one health centre.

title: Bolivia Pluvial/Flash Flood 2025 - DREF Final Report (MDRBO020)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event
13-12-2025

What happened, where and when?

On 17 November 2025, hydrological monitoring in El Torno Municipality recorded a river level of 3.15 metres, classified as an “Extraordinary Rise”, indicating an increased risk of flooding in the department of Santa Cruz, in eastern Bolivia.

On 13 December 2025, intense and prolonged rainfall caused the Piraí River and its tributaries to overflow, triggering severe flash floods across several municipalities, including El Torno, Porongo, Colpa Bélgica, Warnes and Montero. The floods swept away homes, damaged roads and bridges, and isolated rural communities. On 14 December, after the emergency exceeded the technical, operational and financial response capacity of the Autonomous Departmental Government of Santa Cruz, a Departmental Disaster was declared through Departmental Decree No. 512. Municipal emergency declarations were also issued in El Torno, Porongo and Warnes, enabling the mobilization of rescue operations, humanitarian assistance and temporary shelters.

The emergency remained active during the following months as rainfall persisted and access conditions continued to deteriorate. On 28 March 2026, intense overnight rainfall caused renewed flooding in El Torno. The new inundations affected areas where soils were already critically saturated, according to the National Meteorology and Hydrology Service (SENAMHI), further damaging access routes and temporarily isolating rural communities.

title: Myanmar Health Cluster Bulletin September-October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Almost 690K people have been reached with life-saving health services in 227 townships in Myanmar between 1 July and 30 September 2026. An additional 126K people were reached in townships that are excluded from the 2026 HNRP.
  • In spite of ongoing rains, cholera/Acute Watery Diarrhoea (AWD) cases show a decreasing trend. Continued monitoring is needed to avoid resurgence of cases. 1.4M doses of Oral Cholera Vaccines (OCV) were administered in downtown townships in Yangon, while the OCV campaign in Sittwe township is severely hampered by intensified fighting, with 74% of the 300K doses of OCV administered.
  • Widespread flooding and landslides in Ayeyarwady, Tanintharyi, and Yangon caused displacement and damage, increasing the risk of landmine incidents due to moving Explosive Ordnances (EO).
  • Floods also resulting in increase in malaria and dengue cases, especially in endemic areas in Karenni, Tanintharyi, Kachin, Chin and Sagaing. Partners continue to report severe shortages in supplies, especially bednets - Between 1 January and 30 October 2026, 118 attacks on health care were reported by Insecurity Insight, compared to 62 verified incidents by WHO’s Surveillance System for Attacks on Health Care (SSA). The majority of attacks are recorded from Sagaing, followed by Rakhine.

title: UNHCR Mozambique Operational Update - January-June 2026
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT

Since 2017, around 1.3 million people have been displaced internally due to the ongoing conflict in northern Mozambique where non-state armed groups (NSAGs) carry out repeated attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure. The fourth quarter of 2025 saw a sharp deterioration in the security situation in northern Mozambique, with an expansion of violence into Nampula province. NSAG attacks in Memba district marked a significant shift in the conflict’s dynamics, with more than 100,000 people displaced in two weeks in November alone. Since July 2025, an estimated 300,000 people have been newly displaced amid escalating insecurity in Northern Mozambique, with civilians continuing to face violences killings, abductions, looting and the destruction of homes and infrastructure. The rapid influx of displaced families has overwhelmed local capacities and heightened protection risks.

Mozambique remains one of the world’s most climate vulnerable countries, with around 148,000 people displaced due to climate-related events. Over a million people were affected during the 2024-2025 cyclone season, where many of the hardest-hit areas were already hosting large numbers of IDPs uprooted by conflict. The climate crisis continues to strain local capacities and deepen protection risks for displacement-affected communities.

Mozambique also continues to host approximately 24,000 refugees and asylum seekers primarily from Central and Eastern African countries, many of whom have lived in protracted displacement for over a decade.

KEY RESULTS (JANUARY-JUNE 2026)

  • 8,637 persons obtained identity documents, enabling access to services and enhancing freedom of movement.
  • 39,699 protection kits distributed including cash-based interventions.
  • 107,768 persons were supported and empowered to prevent and respond to gender-based violence.
  • 15,804 individuals were provided with legal assistance.
  • 5,000 persons with disability supported.
  • 2,319 individuals were supported through feedback and response mechanisms to voice their needs, concerns and feedback.

title: DTM Sudan Focused Flash Alert: Blue Nile State (Update 004) | Publication Date: 29 October 2026
content:
Between 11 January and 15 October 2026, an estimated 119,782 individuals (23,598 households) were displaced from locations across Blue Nile state.

  • A total of 119,782 IDPs marks a 21 per cent increase compared to the previous update, up from 99,277 IDPs recorded on 23 August 2026.
  • Individuals were displaced from locations across Geisan (40,090 IDPs), Al Kurmuk (31,165 IDPs), Baw (27,192 IDPs), and Wad Al Mahi (21,335 IDPs) localities.
  • Individuals were displaced to seven localities in Blue Nile, including locations across Ed Damazine (45,815 IDPs), Ar Rusayris (36,950 IDPs), Baw (12,687 IDPs), Wad Al Mahi (11,685 IDPs), Geisan (10,275 IDPs), Al Kurmuk (1,385 IDPs), and At Tadamon (985 IDPs).
  • While the overall IDP population in Blue Nile primarily stayed with host families (55%), newly displaced households were more likely to reside at informal gathering sites (56%) or in schools and other public buildings (20%).
  • Approximately 56 per cent of IDPs were female, compared to 44 per cent male. Nearly half (45%) were children, under the age of 18.

For further information on displacement across Sudan, see DTM Sudan Displacement and Return Snapshot (10). DTM reports on all events triggering displacement within Sudan via Early Warning Flash Alerts.

title: Yemen - Displacement Caused by Escalation in Western Yemen - Update #16 (28 October 2026)
content:
IOM Yemen DTM continues to record displacement caused by the escalation in western Yemen. On 27 October 2026, IOM Yemen DTM recorded an increase of 12,522 individual IDPs compared to the figure presented in the RDT report distributed on 26 October 2026, bringing displacement between 1 August and 27 October to approximately 286,711 individuals (47,779 households). This brings the cumulative number recorded since the escalation began in June 2026 to 287,767 individuals (47,955 households).

The largest concentration of displaced people was reported in Ta’iz Governorate, hosting 128,484 individuals (45%), followed by Lahj Governorate with 71,100 individuals (25%), and Aden Governorate with 53,016 individuals (18%). Additional displacement was recorded in Abyan with 15,102 individuals (5%); Al Hodeidah with 8,244 individuals (3%); Shabwah with 3,420 individuals (1%); Hadramawt with 2,820 individuals (1%); Ma’rib with 2,280 individuals (less than 1%); Al Maharah with 1,968 individuals (less than 1%); and Ad Dali’ with 1,333 individuals (less than 1%)

title: Crisis in Palestine: UNFPA Situation Report (April-September 2026)
content:
A year of ceasefire, yet little relief for women and girls. Unsafe shelter, deprivation and daily uncertainty continue to erode their health, safety and dignity.

Pregnancy grows more precarious as miscarriages surge. Worsening maternal health signals the mounting toll of hunger, hardship and overstretched services.

Rising gender-based violence restricts safe options for women and girls. Violence, coercion and exploitation increasingly dictate women’s and girls’ struggle to meet basic needs.

A generation’s future is on hold. Prolonged trauma and shrinking opportunities to learn, earn and participate threaten young people’s well-being and aspirations.

West Bank communities face compounding violence and escalating isolation. Violence and restrictions uproot families and cut them off from healthcare, protection, education and livelihoods.

UNFPA continues to scale up its response: From April to September 2026, UNFPA has expanded life-saving support across Gaza and the West Bank, reaching over 727,000 women, girls and youth with services and essential supplies.

title: PAHO Regional Situation Report No.14: Measles in the Region of the Americas (22 October 2026)
content:
Summary of the Situation

Between epidemiological week (EW) 1 and EW 41 of 2026 (which ended on 17 October 2026), the Region of the Americas reported 56,753 confirmed cases of measles in 17 countries and territories, representing a 4.8-fold increase compared with the same period in 2025. Guatemala (34,535), Mexico (13,691), the United States (4,410), Peru (2,698), and Canada (1,124) account for the vast majority (99.5%) of confirmed cases (Map 1). A total of 81 deaths has been reported, including 53 in Guatemala, 23 in Mexico, three in the United States of America, one in Peru and one in Bolivia (1).

During EW 39 and EW 40 of 2026, the Region of the Americas reported 643 new confirmed cases of measles in six countries and territories, representing a 32% decrease compared with the previous two-week period (EW 37–38; 946 new cases, including 259 retrospectively reported since the last Regional Situation Report) (Figure 1). Of the 643 new confirmed cases reported during EW 39–40, the United States accounted for 320, followed by Guatemala 211, Peru with 68, Mexico with 39, Canada with three, and Bolivia with two2.

Despite declining transmission in some countries of the Americas, with Rt estimates below 1 (Table 3), persistent low-level transmission may continue through sporadic and hard-to-detect chains of infection. This "drop-by-drop" transmission pattern can sustain virus circulation for more than 12 months, delaying outbreak closure and increasing the risk of re-establishment of endemic transmission, which could ultimately jeopardize a country's measles-free status.

title: Cyclone Arnab: Andhra Pradesh, Yanam (Puducherry) and Odisha (Date: 29 October 2026, Time: 08:00 IST)
content:
SITUATION UPDATE

A. Situation Overview (28–29 October 2026)

Very Severe Cyclonic Storm Arnab crossed the Andhra Pradesh coast near Narasapuram (West Godavari). The landfall process began at about 01:30 IST on 28 October, with sustained winds of 125–135 km/h gusting to 150 km/h. IMD forecast a storm surge of 1.5–2.5 m over low-lying Kakinada and Yanam. North coastal AP and south Odisha were hit hardest by rain. The system is moving NNW inland and weakening.

title: Situation Report: Severe Cyclonic Storm Arnab (29 October 2026)
content:
CURRENT SITUATION

  • Severe Cyclonic Storm Arnab completed landfall southwest of Yanam, Andhra Pradesh, on the morning of 28 October. The system has weakened to a severe cyclonic storm and is forecast to further weaken into a depression by 29 October as it moves inland over southern Odisha and Chhattisgarh.
  • Five deaths have been reported in Andhra Pradesh in cyclone-related incidents.
  • Government Preliminary assessments indicated that around 180 houses had been damaged, while more than 220 trees had fallen across roads, disrupting transport and movement in several areas.
  • LOCAL member reports indicate waterlogging, fallen trees and disrupted sanitation in Gopalpur and Rangeilunda blocks, with approximately 10–15 houses reportedly damaged.
  • In Baxipalli ODRP, 42 households were reportedly affected by flooding, six roofs were lost and 12 people were rescued.
  • Flooding has also been reported in ODRP Colony, Podampeta.
  • In Andhra Pradesh, approximately 89,000 people were being evacuated to 101 relief camps as of 27 October. Kakinada district reported more than 10,000 people accommodated in around 495 shelters;5 while 10,176 households across 37 villages in Visakhapatnam district were identified as being at risk;
  • In Odisha, 47,830 people were reported evacuated across eight districts; The largest planned evacuation numbers were in Nabarangpur (11,200), Gajapati (11,000) and Malkangiri (9,850).
  • Red warnings for extremely heavy rainfall were issued for Gajapati and Ganjam districts in Odisha.
  • The IMD bulletin also indicated flash-flood risk across 35 districts—15 in Andhra Pradesh, 11 in Odisha and nine in Chhattisgarh.
  • Fisherfolk were advised to remain ashore until 29 October
  • Fallen trees have reportedly blocked roads in Anakapalli, Visakhapatnam, Kakinada and Konaseema districts.14,15 The Uppada coastal road has also reportedly been washed away

title: Tanzania: Floods in Morogoro DREF Final Operation (MDRTZ043)
content:
What happened, where and when?

Between 28 and 31 December 2025, heavy rainfall in Kilosa District, Morogoro Region, combined with runo from the adjoining Dodoma highlands, caused severe river overows and widespread ooding across Tindiga, Magole, and Dumila wards. The oods directly aected 1,009 households (5,045 people), with 382 households (1,910 people) displaced after their homes were destroyed or rendered uninhabitable, particularly in low-lying areas along the Mkondoa River in Tindiga ward. In addition, 301 households in Magole and Dumila wards had roofs blown o by strong winds, leaving their houses weakened and unsafe. The disaster damaged housing, washed away crops and food stocks, killed livestock, and disrupted livelihoods. Public infrastructure, including roads, water supply systems, sanitation facilities, and community services, was also aected, limiting access to safe water, adequate sanitation, health services, and education. However, road access was restored within a few weeks through government rehabilitation eorts, and access to basic services such as health and education improved.

The evacuation of families to temporary camps increased pressure on basic services, heightened protection risks, and increased the risk of waterborne and vector-borne disease outbreaks. To date, the 382 displaced households remain in temporary camps while awaiting allocation of relocation plots promised by the government.

As of 30 April 2026, displaced households continued to face WASH-related challenges, including limited access to safe water and sanitation facilities, which increased the risk of waterborne diseases. Remaining humanitarian needs included hygiene kits, referrals for medical services, school materials for children, mental health and psychosocial support services, and shelter construction materials.

title: El Niño Preparedness & Response Situation Update - Issued by IMPAACT Program, Issue No. 1 (October 2026)
content:
Key Messages

  • El Niño is firmly established and is expected to strengthen further.
  • The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) forecasts show near 100% likelihood that El Niño will persist through February 2027.
  • El Niño conditions are currently present in the Pacific Ocean, and the latest forecasts indicate a high likelihood that the event could intensify into a very strong El Niño.
  • The recently released GHACOF-74 (74th Greater Horn of Africa Climate Outlook Forum) regional outlook indicates that the October–December 2026 season has a very high probability (up to 90%) of receiving above- average rainfall.
  • The positive phase of the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) is already established, with wetter-than-normal conditions and above-normal rainfall forecast across much of the region during the OND 2026 season.
  • IMPAACT has activated Anticipatory Actions for flood in Ethiopia and Somalia in October 2026, based on locally agreed triggers and thresholds, with continued monitoring of evolving risks and trigger conditions in Djibouti to inform potential activation. Additionally, SCAALA will use the GHACOF74 forecasts to inform readiness interventions in Ethiopia and Somalia where the program is currently functional.
  • SCALAA and IMPAACT will focus on and continue to support the financing of both preparedness and readiness measures, as well as anticipatory action/early action measures, alongside strengthened community-level risk communication and Early Warning Systems (EWS), to enable timely action before forecast hazards escalate into humanitarian crises in Somalia and Ethiopia.
  • IMPAACT will strengthen multi-hazard early warning, harmonize triggers and thresholds, facilitate timely information and risk sharing, identify cross-border hotspots, and enhance cross-border coordination to support timely and coordinated preparedness and action building on lessons drawn from IMPAACT and other initiatives.
  • IMPAACT and SCAALA will strengthen Anticipatory Action Technical Working Group (AATWG) coordination from regional, National to community levels and support the harmonization of contingency plans, linking climate and risk information with practical, trigger-based Early Action.
  • IMPAACT will strengthen coordination with key technical and operational partners, including FAO, WFP, IFRC, national and sub-national disaster risk management authorities, other humanitarian partners, and donors including DG ECHO, to enhance preparedness, complementarity, and coordinated action to anticipate and mitigate the potential impacts of El Niño.
  • Significant gaps and priority needs remain in El Niño preparedness and response across the Greater Horn of Africa region.
  • IMPAACT will contribute to addressing priority gaps across its three program focus countries, Ethiopia, Somalia, and Djibouti, with particular emphasis on strengthening the financing and pre-positioning of Anticipatory Action (AA), and translating climate and risk forecasts into timely, targeted, and trigger-based action.

title: Cook Islands Dengue Outbreak - DREF Final Report MDRCK003
content:
What happened, where and when?

A dengue fever outbreak was ocially declared in the Cook Islands on 22 May 2025. Transmission spread across Rarotonga and the outer islands of Aitutaki, Atiu, Mauke and Mangaia, aecting both urban and remote communities. At the peak of the outbreak, the rapid increase in cases placed considerable pressure on the national health system and required a coordinated multi-sectoral response.

Since the declaration of the outbreak, the Cook Islands recorded a cumulative total of 1,251 dengue cases, with 1,250 people making a full recovery and one dengue-related death. During the height of the outbreak, a high proportion of cases were reported among children, which increased public health concerns and reinforced the need for community-based prevention measures.

The outbreak placed signicant strain on surveillance, case management, public awareness and vector-control activities. Outer-island communities faced additional challenges because of geographic isolation, limited access to health services, reduced health workforce capacity and logistical constraints in transporting personnel and essential supplies.

The Government of the Cook Islands activated a national taskforce led by Ministry of Health (MoH). Public awareness campaigns, community outreach and environmental clean-up initiatives were implemented to promote dengue prevention and early care-seeking behaviours. As dengue case numbers escalated, the Ministry of Health (MoH) formally requested the Cook Islands Red Cross Society (CIRCS), in its auxiliary role to the public authorities, to support the dengue outbreak response. This formal request, received on 2 February 2026, served as the trigger date for the DREF operation.

title: Viet Nam Monsoon Flood 2025 - DREF Final Report (MDRVN025)
content:
What happened, where and when?

From the second half of 2025, multiple tropical storms and typhoons battered the northern and north-central provinces of Viet Nam, resulting in widespread and prolonged oods, ash oods and landslides that impacted over 20 provinces, with extensive damage to infrastructure, housing and livelihoods. While the initial storms in July and August aected an estimated 100,000 people, mainly in Nghệ An, Điện Biên and Sơn La provinces, further storms and subsequent oods increased the number of people aected to approximately 800,000 by October 2025, including in additional provinces such as Lào Cai, Phú Thọ, Tuyên Quang, Lạng Sơn, Quảng Ninh, Thanh Hóa, Hà Tĩnh and Thừa Thiên-Huế. The successive typhoons (Wipha, Ragana, Kajiki, Bualoi and Matmo) between July and October 2025 aected some of the same areas within a short period.

As of early 2026, the aected provinces had transitioned into the early recovery phase, with ongoing humanitarian needs in previously aected areas. Access had largely been restored, although some remote and mountainous locations remained intermittently inaccessible due to landslides. Recovery eorts in housing, livelihoods and infrastructure continued, and despite the absence of a nationwide emergency declaration, communities remained vulnerable to localised ooding and landslides during the upcoming rainy season.

By the end of the IFRC-DREF operation in July 2026, most aected communities had moved beyond the immediate emergency phase, with households progressively restoring their living conditions and livelihoods. Over the course of the operation, recovery conditions progressively improved as emergency assistance, government-led recovery measures and community eorts supported the restoration of housing, livelihoods, basic services and local infrastructure. However, some households, particularly those in remote and mountainous areas and those with signicant housing or livelihood losses, continued to face recovery challenges and remained vulnerable to further ooding and landslides

title: PHL: Population Movement - 10-2026 - PHL: Returning Filipinos from Sabah (2026-10-29)
content:
Sources for data marked as Other

(1) City Government of Zamboanga: ZC Braces for Arrival of 10K deportees from Malaysia; (2) Philstar: Zamboanga braces for arrival of 10,000 deportees from Malaysia; (3) Malaymail: Malaysia, Philippines discuss swift repatriation of 5,000 undocumented migrants detained in Sabah depots

Description

Malaysian and Philippine officials have been discussing a repatriation of thousands of undocumented Philippine immigrants who have been held in detention centers in Sabah, Malaysia. It was recently decided to start the repatriation of some 10,000 Filipinos, to be conducted in weekly batches of around 800 people. These Returning Filipino Nationals (RFs) will be received by the City of Zamboanga, which has already requested support from the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) to ensure efficient management of the repatriation.

According to the City Government of Zamboanga, the first group of 800 people is expected to arrive on 30th of October, with the subsequent groups arriving every 7 days. Zamboanga City Administrator has tasked the City Engineer’s Office to help in the transport of deportees from the seaport to the Processing Center and the City Social Welfare and Development Office (CSWDO) to assist in the profiling of the returnees. The CDRRMO and City Health Office will likewise assist in the conduct of medical check-ups and deployment of ambulances and emergency medical teams.

The DSWD has already reached out to the Philippine Red Cross, among other NGOs, with a request of support to ensure safe and dignified treatment of the RFs while the repatriation is ongoing and the people are staying in temporary processing centers. The requested support includes temporary shelters or tents, non-food items, and camp coordination and management support; from PRC, the request specifically lists water bladders, water tanks, hygiene kits, and portable latrines. It should be noted that the situation is still developing and the needs can be updated as everything becomes clearer.

title: Nepal Flash Floods Emergency Response - Situation Report 9 | World Vision | 28 October 2026
content:
Communities affected by the Nepal Flash Floods continue to face significant challenges as they recover from the loss of homes, livelihoods, water systems, and essential infrastructure. Families remain in need of safe water, protection support, livelihood opportunities, and assistance to rebuild their lives.

In response, World Vision International Nepal, together with local partners and government stakeholders, has reached more than 41,700 people with emergency relief, clean water support, child protection services, health assistance, and cash-based recovery programmes.

As the response transitions from emergency relief to long-term recovery, World Vision will continue supporting affected communities through the restoration of water systems, rehabilitation of community infrastructure, livelihood recovery, education support, and resilience-building initiatives to help families recover with dignity and build a stronger future.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 91, as of 27 October 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Women living with obstetric fistula receive medical treatment in Haute-Kotto.
  • High cross-border population mobility between the DRC and south-eastern CAR continues to pose a significant risk of Ebola virus disease (EVD) cross-border transmission.
  • More than 1,500 people undertake preventive displacement in Ouham-Pendé.

GENERAL CONTEXT

Haute-Kotto Prefecture – Central Region

  • On 21 October, a staff member from a humanitarian organization was threatened by armed elements. Community members and staff from a United Nations agency were also subjected to similar threats. One day earlier, another NGO staff member received verbal threats from an armed individual while carrying out child protection activities. These incidents highlight an operating environment marked by increasing risks for humanitarian actors and the populations they assist.

Ouham-Pendé Prefecture – Western Region

  • Approximately 1,500 people pre-emptively fled Bilsem village on 21 October due to security concerns. Displaced households sought refuge in the bush, at temporary farming sites, or in nearby localities, including Gaïboula, located 5 km from Bocaranga. The population movement followed community tensions arising from a dispute between a herder and a farmer. The following day, local authorities intervened to ease tensions and strengthen security measures. Following improvements in the security situation, the displaced people returned to their areas of origin.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Health

Countrywide

  • As of the reporting, no Ebola cases have been recorded in the Central African Republic (CAR). According to a regional analysis by REACH, the Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to expand across the northeastern provinces, with 9,637 confirmed cases and 4,602 deaths reported as of 18 October 2026. The outbreak has recently spread to the health zones of Dungu, Alimbongo, Ango and Wapinda, the latter two, located in close proximity to the CAR border. Population mobility data indicate that population movements and economic exchanges along major road and river corridors could facilitate cross-border transmission, particularly between Nord-Ubangi and the Central African prefectures of Basse-Kotto and Haut-Mbomou. The localities of Yakoma, Gbadolite (DRC, bordering south-eastern CAR) and Zemio have been identified as particularly exposed to risks associated with cross-border movements. Furthermore, the presence of more than 264,000 Central African refugees and asylum seekers in the DRC, mainly in Nord-Ubangi, Sud-Ubangi and Bas-Uele provinces, could increase cross-border movements between the two countries and heighten the risk of virus importation. In this context, enhanced epidemiological surveillance at points of entry, early detection of suspected cases, and preparedness of health facilities in border areas remain critical to mitigating the risk of disease spread in the Central African Republic. In August, the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) allocated US$3 million to strengthen prevention efforts in high-risk areas, reinforce surveillance and isolation capacities, support community engagement, and improve access to water.

Protection

Haut-Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

  • On the margins of the high-level visit to Zemio on 21 October by the Prime Minister of the Central African Republic, accompanied by several government ministers, the Humanitarian Coordinator and representatives of United Nations agencies, UNFPA distributed dignity kits to 50 survivors of gender-based violence (GBV). The kits included bags, cloth wraps, towels, sanitary pads, toothpaste, toothbrushes, laundry and bathing soap, underwear and body cream.

title: NRC Somalia: Monthly Programme Update (September 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Conflict, drought, food insecurity and flood risks intensified, with over 774,923 people displaced since January and 14,832 newly displaced in Baidoa.

title: DOM: Population Movement - 10-2026 - Dominican Republic - Haiti Border (2026-10-28)
content:
Description

The Dominican Red Cross reports ongoing humanitarian needs associated with population movements towards Haiti through the Dominican border area. Available operational evidence is concentrated in Dajabón, where the branch assists people passing through the migrant interdiction centre. The situation is characterised by fluctuating movements and continuing needs for pre-hospital assistance, drinking water, food, personal hygiene, family contact and protection referrals.

Dajabón branch records show 15,697 admissions during July–September 2026, compared with 12,550 during the same period in 2025, an increase of 25.1 per cent. Recorded admissions of children increased from 628 to 3,229, raising their share from 5.0 to 20.6 per cent. These figures represent admissions, potentially including repeat entries, rather than verified unique individuals or people assessed as requiring assistance. Movements fluctuated within the quarter, with admissions declining from 7,265 in July to 3,597 in September.

Branch reports document dehydration, hypertension, injuries, pregnancy-related concerns requiring hospital referral and cases involving unaccompanied children. Children separated from caregivers, pregnant and breastfeeding women, older people, people with disabilities and those with chronic conditions may require adapted assistance and timely referrals. Language barriers and loss of family contact can further restrict access to support. The extent of unmet needs has not yet been systematically quantified.

Current branch activities include pre-hospital assistance, drinking water and food rations supported by National Society headquarters, Restoring Family Links through telephone calls and phone charging, and hygiene assistance when supplies are available. Services depend on no more than five volunteers whose availability varies because of employment commitments, preventing a regular operating schedule. Access to the centre is restricted from 18:00 until the following day.

The National Society also reports reduced physical presence of several humanitarian organisations in Dajabón. The implications for current service coverage and referral capacity require verification, including whether assistance remains available remotely or through partners.

Following the IFRC Regional Director’s September visit to Dajabón and subsequent discussions, the National Society decided on 12 October 2026 to request DREF support. The proposed operation focuses on strengthening existing branch services, establishing and equipping a Humanitarian Service Point subject to authorisation, and conducting a multisectoral assessment in selected locations in Monte Cristi, Dajabón, Elías Piña, Independencia and Pedernales. All proposed activities will take place within Dominican territory.

The assessment will clarify needs, existing services and operational priorities, while providing a baseline for a separately planned and financed longer-term humanitarian strategy. The DREF application remains under review; proposed activities and population targets do not represent assistance already delivered.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: No

NS Requests International Assistance: No

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by National Society

General

  • Water & Sanitation
  • Food aid
  • RFL
  • First Aid
  • Relief/Supply distribution

Summary

The Dominican Red Cross Dajabón branch provides humanitarian assistance at the migrant interdiction centre through a team of up to five volunteers. Their availability varies because of employment commitments, and services do not follow a regular operating schedule. Ongoing activities include first aid and pre-hospital assistance, referrals to public health facilities, drinking water and food rations supported by National Society headquarters, and personal hygiene kit distributions when supplies are available. Monthly branch records report 3,409 hygiene kits distributed during July–September 2026; this figure represents items distributed rather than verified unique recipients. Restoring Family Links services include telephone calls and phone charging to help people maintain or restore contact with relatives. Volunteers also facilitate referrals to competent protection services, including CONANI, particularly for unaccompanied and separated children. National Society headquarters and IFRC have reviewed branch reporting and discussed operational needs to inform the DREF application. The proposed multisectoral assessment, additional staffing, surge deployment and establishment of a Humanitarian Service Point remain planned activities. A consolidated number of unique people assisted across existing services is not available.

Actions taken by Federation

General

Other

Summary

The IFRC Latin Caribbean Country Cluster Delegation, based in Santo Domingo, is supporting the Dominican Red Cross through review of Dajabón branch records, comparison of 2025 and 2026 data, analysis of operational capacity and preparation of the DREF application and budget. Following the Regional Director’s September visit to Dajabón, IFRC has accompanied discussions with National Society headquarters to define priorities, strengthen coordination and develop a focused operational strategy. The proposal has been revised in response to regional and Geneva feedback, prioritising existing branch services, a proposed Humanitarian Service Point and a multisectoral border assessment. The DREF application remains under review. The assessment surge deployment and additional operational support have not yet been implemented.

Actions taken by RCRC

General

Other

Summary

Consultations have been held with ICRC representatives covering the Dominican Republic from Venezuela and with the ICRC delegation in Haiti to share the proposed DREF approach. ICRC requested involvement in reviewing the proposal, particularly regarding Restoring Family Links and engagement with migration authorities. The Italian Red Cross maintains a presence in the country and has previous maternal and child health experience in Elías Piña. CRD also collaborates with the French and German Red Cross. No specific operational contributions from these Participating National Societies have been confirmed for the proposed operation.

Actions taken by others

The General Directorate of Migration (DGM) manages migration processing at the Dajabón interdiction centre. CONANI is a key counterpart for referrals involving children, particularly unaccompanied and separated children. Public health facilities receive people requiring medical assessment and treatment. Coordination mechanisms involving relevant authorities provide a basis for discussing access, services and referral arrangements. In September 2025, UNICEF reported providing safe spaces at migration processing centres in Dajabón, Elías Piña and Santiago for children, adolescents, pregnant women and breastfeeding women. Management was assigned to DGM in coordination with CONANI. Their current functionality, staffing and service coverage require verification. UNHCR reporting for January–June 2026 documents coordination with DGM, UNICEF, OBMICA, CONANI, UNFPA and local organisations on protection referrals, documentation verification, family tracing and service mapping in Elías Piña and the southern border area. These activities demonstrate existing coordination arrangements but do not establish current coverage in Dajabón. Dajabón branch records from 2025 also document contributions from IOM and Save the Children to food and hygiene assistance. More recently, the National Society reported that UNHCR, IOM, World Vision and Save the Children no longer maintain a physical presence in Dajabón. The timing and implications of these changes, including any assistance continuing remotely or through partners, have not yet been fully verified.

title: Zimbabwe Hailstorm Response DREF 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRZW030)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

05-10-2026

What happened, where and when?

On 5 October 2026, a severe hailstorm accompanied by heavy rainfall and strong winds struck Masvingo Urban, causing extensive damage to residential properties, public infrastructure, schools, health facilities, businesses and household livelihoods. Department of Civil Protection and ZRCS conducted a physical assessment on 6 October 2026 identified widespread damage across the city, particularly to residential roofs and windows. Preliminary findings indicate that approximately 8,500 houses had their roofs blown off or damaged, while more than 90% of an estimated 17,000 houses assessed had shattered windowpanes. The president declared the hailstorm a state of disaster within affected areas.

The disaster has affected an estimated 67,500 people across approximately 13,500 households, according to preliminary assessment findings (Department of Civil Protection, 2026). Many affected families are living in damaged homes that offer limited protection from adverse weather conditions, increasing their need for emergency shelter and essential household assistance. Although no displacement was reported at the time of the initial assessment, temporary accommodation and evacuation arrangements have been established for households whose homes are unsafe or require urgent intervention.

The storm has also disrupted essential services and critical infrastructure. Extensive damage to electricity infrastructure has resulted in widespread power outages, affecting municipal water pumping, drainage and sewerage systems. These disruptions have heightened concerns regarding access to safe water, adequate sanitation and the risk of waterborne diseases. Damage has also been reported at key health facilities, including Masvingo Provincial Hospital, Runyararo Maternity Clinic and Northwest Clinic, as well as several schools and other public institutions, compromising access to essential health and education services.

Household livelihoods have also been affected, with reported damage to gardens, fruit trees, poultry and small businesses, further undermining income sources and household food security. The widespread destruction has created high demand for roofing materials, which are reportedly in short supply, potentially delaying repairs and prolonging exposure to unsafe living conditions. Affected households require urgent assistance, including emergency shelter materials, essential non-food items, blankets, safe water, sanitation and hygiene support, food assistance, education support and psychosocial services.

In response to the scale of the disaster, the Government of Zimbabwe has declared a State of Disaster, and Civil Protection Committees and other relevant government structures have been activated to coordinate the response. The Zimbabwe Red Cross Society (ZRCS) is supporting response efforts through needs assessments, household registration, emergency shelter and non-food assistance, community engagement, health and hygiene promotion, and coordination with government authorities and humanitarian partners.

Given the scale of the damage, disruption to essential services and the immediate needs of affected households, a coordinated and targeted humanitarian response is required to address urgent shelter and basic household needs, reduce public health risks, protect vulnerable groups and support early recovery. This concept note therefore seeks to provide a framework for a timely, needs-based and accountable response that complements government-led efforts and prioritises the most affected and vulnerable households in Masvingo Urban.

title: Colombia | Earthquake - Operation Update #2 (MDRCO036)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Description of the crisis

On 10 August 2026, at 07:34 local time, a 7.4 Mw earthquake struck western Colombia. The epicentre was located in the municipality of San José del Palmar, Chocó Department, at a depth of 103 km. The earthquake was felt across much of Colombia, as well as in Ecuador, Panama and Venezuela. According to the Colombian Geological Survey (SGC), it was the strongest earthquake recorded in Colombia in the 21st century.

Subsequent seismic activity continues to be monitored by the SGC, which has identified two distinct patterns in Chocó Department. As of 29 September, 333 aftershocks associated with the main earthquake had been recorded, mainly concentrated in San José del Palmar, El Litoral del San Juan and Sipí, at depths ranging from 70 to 105 km. According to the SGC, this activity has progressively decreased in frequency and magnitude. In parallel, a separate seismic swarm remains active in the vicinity of Istmina, Medio San Juan, Sipí and El Litoral del San Juan, at depths ranging from 30 to 70 km.

According to Situation Report No. 84 issued by the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) on 21 September 2026, the earthquake has affected 500 municipalities across 16 departments. Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, Chocó, Quindío and Caldas account for 94 per-cent of all affected families nationwide. The report indicates that 778,281 people (326,648 families) have been affected, with 335 deaths, 4,516 people injured and 105 people reported missing. The UNGRD also reports 36,478 houses destroyed and 206,931 damaged, as well as 758 buildings collapsed and 6,047 damaged. Damage has also been reported to 4,431 educational facilities, 402 health facilities and 6,094 community facilities, as well as 182 water supply systems, 531 roads, 133 bridges (119 vehicular and 14 pedestrian) and five airports. Direct physical damage to infrastructure is estimated at COP 42.1 trillion (approximately USD 13.2 billion), equivalent to around 2.3 per cent of Colombia's Gross Domestic Product (GDP), with damage concentrated mainly in Risaralda, Valle del Cauca, Chocó, Caldas and Quindío.

The Single Registry of Disaster-Affected People (Registro Único de Damnificados – RUD) provides complementary figures, recording 778,279 people (364,670 families), as well as 104,037 uninhabitable houses, of which 19,143 are reported as destroyed, and a further 119,752 damaged houses. Differences between the two sources reflect their respective data collection and consolidation methodologies. While UNGRD figures are compiled from reports submitted by territorial authorities, the RUD records households formally registered as disaster-affected and serves as the basis for accessing national government assistance. RUD figures remain subject to eligibility verification, data cross-checking and data cleaning processes. They may therefore include duplicate records and are subject to revision in subsequent updates.

Search and rescue operations have concluded. A total of 1,849 rescuers were deployed, including 16 accredited Colombian Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) teams comprising 779 rescuers; four international teams from the United States, Ecuador and Israel, comprising 138 personnel; and 34 additional support teams comprising 932 personnel. These operations resulted in the rescue of 356 people and the recovery of 259 bodies. International teams completed their missions and returned to their respective countries between 19 and 23 August.

The emergency is unfolding in a context of concurrent seismic, hydrometeorological and climate-related hazards. This evolving situation requires the continued provision of assistance to people with immediate humanitarian needs, while progressively integrating disaster risk reduction and resilience considerations into early recovery interventions.

The El Niño phenomenon represents an additional factor influencing the evolution of the emergency. According to an official communication issued by the Institute of Hydrology, Meteorology and Environmental Studies (IDEAM) on 8 October 2026, the conditions required to officially declare an El Niño event in Colombia had been met for five consecutive overlapping three-month periods. IDEAM also indicated a probability exceeding 80 per cent that the event would reach strong to very strong intensity during the first quarter of 2027, and a 75 per cent probability that it would rank among the strongest events observed since 1950. IDEAM further confirmed that Colombia's second rainy season would continue during October and November 2026, particularly affecting the Andean, Pacific and Caribbean regions, although rainfall levels were expected to remain below normal due to the influence of El Niño. Wildfires have already been reported in areas affected by the earthquake and prioritized for the response.

This situation may have differentiated impacts across earthquake-affected areas. Reduced rainfall and higher temperatures could increase the risk of water shortages and wildfires in some locations, while parts of the Pacific region may remain exposed to episodes of heavy rainfall and landslides. In this context, information published in September 2026 identified Valle del Cauca, one of the departments prioritized by the operation, among the areas under a red alert for wildfires issued by IDEAM. This highlights the coexistence of hazards that could further exacerbate the vulnerabilities of affected communities. Consequently, recovery and rehabilitation activities will need to consider multiple risk scenarios and the potential additional impacts on water systems, livelihoods, shelter, infrastructure and essential services. This requires a multi-hazard approach, with operational planning and implementation adapted to evolving conditions and risks at the local level.

The institutional context of the response has also evolved since the onset of the emergency. Through Decree 1261 of 2026, the National Government declared a State of Economic, Social and Ecological Emergency in response to the severe public calamity caused by the earthquake, with the aim of facilitating the adoption of extraordinary measures to address its impacts.
