title: UNICEF Ukraine Humanitarian Situation Report 62, 1 January to 30 September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • The third quarter of 2026 brought the heaviest civilian toll in Ukraine since the opening weeks of the full-scale invasion. The number of child casualties verified in 2026 (809) has now surpassed the total verified child casualties for all of 2025 (744), highlighting the alarming impact of the escalation of the war on children in recent months.
  • Winter 2026-2027 is expected to be the most dangerous winter for children in Ukraine since the start of the full-scale war. UNICEF has accelerated winter preparations, providing US$45 million to the Ministry of Social Policy and Family Unity’s Humanitarian and Resilience Account to cover 104,000 households with a one-time winter cash transfer. District heating systems have been strengthened for 3.2 million people, and 22 health facilities have newly-installed energy back-up systems, benefiting 200,000 people. Further urgent support to water and heating systems, health facilities, schools and families will be rolled out by the end of the year.
  • Recent tests results show that one-third of 15-year-old students are 1.5 years behind in science and math, and half are two years behind in reading. So far this year, 124,928 students have participated in UNICEF-supported catch-up classes.
  • UNICEF and partners have reached 375,137 people with mental health and psychosocial support this year, including 219,023 children. In an August UNICEF survey, nearly half of people (46 per cent) reported emotional exhaustion almost every day.

title: UNICEF Sudan Humanitarian Situation Report No. 46, 1 to 31 August 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Despite nearly 5 million returns reducing Sudan’s overall IDP population, escalating conflict in Blue Nile, Darfur and Kordofan displaced more than 58,000 people in August alone.
  • UNICEF supported health interventions reached 751,400 people with cholera outbreak response and 769,900 people following a diphtheria vaccination campaign in high-risk localities. UNICEF supported the treatment of 51,506 children with Severe Acute Malnutrition and provided IYCF counselling to 183,264 caregivers. UNICEF also enabled 271,000 people to access safe water and reached 44,400 people with critical WASH supplies.
  • With UNICEF support, 14,600 children accessed education opportunities, and 57,200 received learning materials. UNICEF also reached 112,700 people with critical Mental Health and Psychosocial Support services and provided Gender-Based Violence services to 84,000 people.
  • As of 31 August 2026, UNICEF had mobilized US$352.2 million against US$962.9 million HAC appeal (63 per cent funding gap). Increased flexible funding is urgently required, particularly for critically underfunded child protection programme.

title: Haiti: Heavy rains and flooding in the Grand Sud – Flash Update No. 1 (as of 28 October 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • 4 people died, 3 in Nippes and 1 in the South-East, and 2 fishermen are missing in Abricots (Grand’Anse).
  • 1,920 families affected in Nippes, where 1,767 houses are flooded and 48 small houses destroyed.
  • 630 houses flooded in Grand’Anse, where 4 houses were washed away in Gommiers.
  • 3 critical facilities flooded in Grand’Anse: the Corail community hospital, the Fond’Icaques national school and the Chambellan public market.
  • 200 houses flooded in Les Cayes (South), where several sections of the Ravine du Sud dykes collapsed.
  • The Directorate General of Civil Protection (DGPC) has placed the entire Grand Sud on orange alert.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Since 24 October 2026, heavy rains have affected the South, Nippes and Grand’Anse departments. Several rivers have overflowed their banks, flooding many communes. According to situation reports from the Departmental Committee for Risk and Disaster Management (CDGRD) of Grand’Anse and the Departmental Directorates of Civil Protection (DDPC) of Nippes and the South, and to a 26 October report from the organization Entraide Médicale Internationale (EMI), three people died in Nippes and one in the South-East, and two fishermen are missing in Abricots (Grand’Anse).

Nippes department is the hardest hit, with 1,767 houses flooded, 48 small houses destroyed and 1,920 affected families. In Grand’Anse, 630 houses were flooded, as were the Corail community hospital, a school and a public market. In the South, several hundred houses were flooded, including about 200 in Les Cayes, where several sections of the Ravine du Sud dykes collapsed.

Agricultural and livestock losses are reported in a region already affected by drought. Several dirt roads were damaged, making access to some communes difficult. Population displacement has been reported. Families have found refuge with relatives in Grand’Anse, in schools in the South and Nippes, and in a church in Baradères.

Departmental civil protection structures have partially activated emergency operations centres. They monitor the situation and conduct awareness-raising activities with communities. At this stage, the information collected remains preliminary; additional multisectoral data is expected as field assessments are consolidated.

title: Yemen Situation: UNHCR Emergency Update - External Update #6 (28 October 2026)
content:
Highlights

▪ Displacement from Yemen continues to rise, with newly displaced populations reaching 275,245 people between 1 August and 24 October, exceeding initial planning assumptions. Taiz remains the most affected governorate, accounting for 72% of new departures and hosting 49% of those newly displaced. Revised planning scenarios are being prepared as the number of people displaced has exceeded initial planning assumptions.

▪ Movements across the Gulf of Aden continue, with arrivals reaching 4,151, including 3,836 to Djibouti and 315 to Somalia as of 25 October.

▪ On 20 October, the first return flight from Yemen to Somalia took place since the assisted voluntary programme was halted due to the escalation of hostilities. Some 138 Somali refugees departed from Aden to Mogadishu.

title: UNFPA Bangladesh Situation Report | Protracted Humanitarian Crisis in Bangladesh, 1 July - 30 September 2026
content:
Monsoon floods and landslides affected 43,000 refugees, with 15 fatalities and the displacement of 9,707 people. The disasters also damaged health and gender-based violence facilities and disrupted essential services. UNFPA maintained comprehensive sexual and reproductive health services, deploying mobile medical teams and providing emergency transport for high-risk pregnant women and obstetric emergencies. Gender-based violence caseworkers and volunteers delivered psychosocial first aid and referrals, while women-friendly spaces and youth centres provided temporary shelter. UNFPA also provided 2,753 dignity kits to affected women and girls.

New arrivals of refugees from Myanmar continued to enter Bangladesh, adding further pressure on already overstretched services. Meanwhile, security conditions in the refugee camps deteriorated, with increasing reports of gender-related killings, gang rape, intimate partner violence, and child marriage.

Between July and September, UNFPA-supported facilities delivered 65,879 sexual and reproductive health services, while 153,721 people accessed gender-based violence prevention, risk mitigation, and response services. Additionally, 127 UNFPA-supported adolescent and youth centres and community learning facilities recorded nearly 140,000 visits for life skills development, emotional support, and referrals.

title: UNHCR Ethiopia | PMS Report Ethiopia Tigray Region | Northwestern Zone (Shire Indaselassie town) | March 2026
content:
OVERVIEW

UNHCR, in partnership with OSSHD, conducted a Protection Monitoring and Solutions (PMS) Assessment to evaluate the situation of internally displaced populations (IDPs) residing in IDP sites and IDPs living within host community. The assessment also examined the availability, accessibility and quality of services provided to IDPs with the view to identifying protections and informing intervention and response efforts.

The PMS assessment was conducted from 18 to 20 March 2026 in Shire Indaselassie town, Northwestern Zone of the Tigray Regional State.

title: UNHCR Guatemala Operational Update, January - June 2026
content:
CONTEXT

Guatemala, a multiethnic and multilingual nation, plays a strategic role in regional mobility. In recent years, it has become an increasingly important destination for asylums-eekers. Its geographic position places Guatemala at the centre of complex displacement dynamics, generating significant challenges and critical opportunities for national institutions and humanitarian actors.

Throughout 2026, Guatemala recorded a rise in asylum applications, particularly from nationals of Honduras, El Salvador, Venezuela, and Nicaragua, while hosting 8,663 refugees and asylum-seekers. Return movements also increased, with more than 31,780 Guatemalan returnees arriving from the United States and Mexico by June, a 47.1% increase compared to the same period in 2025. Many returnees brought valuable skills but faced significant reintegration challenges, increasing the risk of redisplacement amid violence, poverty, inequality, and limited access to basic services.

Despite these challenges, Guatemala continues to advance inclusive development, disaster preparedness, and regional solidarity, with UNHCR supporting protection space, local integration and reintegration, and technical expertise on displacement and statelessness. UNHCR maintains its presence through a national office in Guatemala City and a field presence in Esquipulas, Chiquimula.

title: Global Weather Hazards Summary, October 29, 2026 – November 4, 2026
content:
Global Overview: El Niño continues to strengthen. High risk of flooding in parts of equatorial Africa, Central America, Hispaniola, and Colombia.

Africa Weather Hazards

Abnormal heat is forecast in the eastern Sahel; High risks of flooding with ongoing heavy rain in the horn of Africa.

1) Inundation in the Sudd wetlands of South Sudan persists.
2) Large 90-day rainfall deficits led to abnormal dryness across southern Sudan, South Sudan, Uganda and western Kenya. Additionally, deteriorated vegetation conditions, driven by drought, have been observed over South Sudan, and northern Uganda. Abnormal dryness over Ethiopia and Sudan have been removed due to end of season.
3) Central/eastern Liberia, southern Cote D’Ivoire, and southern Ghana are under Abnormal Dryness because of sustained below-average rainfall over the past 30 and 90 days.
4) Recent heavy rainfall has caused flooding in eastern Ethiopia and parts of Somalia. Water in rivers and streams may take a while longer yet to recede.
5) Recent rains plus forecasted heavy rainfall elevates flood risk in southern Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Congo, and east-central DRC. Forecasted heavy rains may also cause flooding in southeastern Madagascar.
6) Abnormal heat is forecast in northern Cameroon, southern Chad, northern/eastern CAR, southwestern Sudan, western South Sudan, and along the western Ethiopia border as above-average temperatures are expected to persist for 3 or more consecutive days in this region during the next week.

title: Kenya: Humanitarian situation of displaced people in Moyale, Marsabit County Flash Update No. 1 (28 October 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • About 50,000 people have crossed into Moyale town in Kenya due to renewed intercommunal fighting in neighbouring Ethiopia, as of 28 October.
  • Humanitarian needs are increasing rapidly, with food, water, sanitation and hygiene, healthcare, and protection services being the most urgent needs.
  • Humanitarian partners, the Kenya Red Cross Society and authorities are scaling up humanitarian response.
  • A rapid joint multisectoral assessment is under way to inform inter-agency response planning.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Renewed intercommunal fighting in Moyale, Ethiopia, which reportedly started on 18 October, has triggered significant displacement across the border into Moyale town in Marsabit County, Kenya. As of 28 October, about 50,000 people had crossed into Kenya, according to authorities and partners, with women and children accounting for a significant proportion of arrivals. Some are staying in six temporary camps - Oriental Mission Church (OMC), Arosa Mixed, Sessi, Taqwa, Somare and St Mary’s), and others are reportedly staying with host communities. In Mandera, about 200 people are sheltering at the police station. These figures are preliminary, as partners and authorities are still conducting assessments, and numbers are expected to rise as movements continue. Plans are under way for a rapid joint multisectoral assessment of the wider reported caseload, including people hosted by relatives and community members, to identify additional unmet needs.

The influx is straining temporary accommodation, host households and essential services, creating urgent needs for food, safe water, sanitation, shelter, essential household items, health care and protection. Marsabit is one of Kenya’s 23 Arid and Semi-Arid Lands (ASAL) counties and was already facing food insecurity before the influx, which compounds pressure on local resources. Continued fighting could trigger further cross-border movements. Intercommunal tensions in the Moyale border area have repeatedly driven people across the border into Kenya. In 2012, violence displaced an estimated 20,000 people into Kenya, and in 2018, fighting reportedly forced some 20,000 people to seek refuge there. Each of these episodes generated urgent humanitarian needs.

title: Democratic Republic of the Congo: DIEM-Impact qualitative study of Ebola, conflict and agricultural livelihoods in Ituri, North Kivu and South Kivu (September 2026)
content:
Filippo Fossi and Patrick Minyangu

Synopsis (short abstract) The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), through Data in Emergencies (DIEM), conducted a qualitative study of the impact of Ebola disease and conflict on agricultural livelihoods in Ituri, North Kivu and South Kivu provinces in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. This rapid assessment used a cross-sectional, mixed-methods design based on semi-structured key informant interviews conducted in August 2026 across the three provinces. The assessment is the first stage in a larger study that will integrate quantitative household survey data in the coming months.

title: UNICEF State of Palestine Humanitarian Situation Update and Humanitarian Response (West Bank), 16 October 2026
content:
NO SAFE ROUTE TO CHILDHOOD: HOMES, SCHOOLS AND WATER ARE NO LONGER SAFE FOR CHILDREN IN THE WEST BANK, INCLUDING EAST JERUSALEM

Highlights

  • Across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, demolitions, settler violence and related access restrictions have displaced an average of 17 people, including eight children, per day in 2026 so far, double the daily average recorded over the preceding three years.
  • From 1 January to 30 September 2026, 91 Palestinians, including 24 children, were reported killed by Israeli forces or settlers, and more than 2,100 Palestinians, including 275 children, were injured by Israeli forces or settlers across the West Bank. From 7 October 2023 to 9 September 2026, at least 1,216 Palestinians, including 263 children, were killed, while at least 13,300 Palestinians, including 2,186 children, were injured.
  • Settler attacks have become a leading cause of injuries to Palestinians in the West Bank, accounting for 55 per cent of all recorded injuries to Palestinians in 2026.
  • Education is increasingly at risk: 84 schools in Area C and East Jerusalem remain under pending demolition or stop-work orders, threatening continued access to education for thousands of children.2
  • Violence and economic hardship in the West Bank affect more than 800,000 people who require healthcare, as well as water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) support.
  • Around 140,000 children across the West Bank, including in refugee camps, face barriers to accessing education.

title: WHO Weekly Situation Update on Ongoing Health Emergency Events in South Sudan - Week #42, Date: 12 – 18 Oct 2026
content:
PRIORITY ACTIONS ▸

▸Sustain BVD preparedness across the 15 priority counties as DRC reaches 9,637 cases; maintain PoE screening (181,662 over 15–21 Oct), RCCE and cross-border coordination as Kenya manages a 9-case cluster and Nigeria confirms an imported case.

▸ Respond to the Hepatitis E outbreak in Chuil/Nyirol, Jonglei (67 cases, 4 deaths; CFR 33% in pregnant women) with WASH and chlorination at the IDP site, protection of pregnant women, and laboratory confirmation.

▸ Sustain the Sudan-crisis nutrition response at Renk (1,692 children screened; 159 SAM, 18 MAM; 173 PLW) and the acute-malnutrition and displacement response in Warrap and Jonglei.

▸ Sustain malaria response (50,828 cases, 16 deaths — 57% below 2025); maintain ITN coverage and QA microscopy ahead of the Malaria Indicator Survey.

▸ Sustain the Round 1 Polio NIDs campaign (69 counties · 60% of 3.9M under-fives) after two new cVDPV1 detections in Urror and Rubkona, and investigate the new measles outbreak in Malakal.

title: WHO Weekly Situation Update on Ongoing Health Emergency Events in South Sudan - Week #43, Date: 19 – 25 Oct 2026
content:
PRIORITY ACTIONS

▸ Sustain BVD preparedness across the 15 priority counties as DRC reaches 9,964 cases and 4,851 deaths; maintain PoE screening (54,602 over 25–26 Oct) and screen air arrivals at Juba International Airport as Kenya releases contacts and Nigeria medevacs its imported case.

▸ Operationalize the WHO El Niño health plan (1 Nov–30 Apr): pre-position cholera kits, ORS, RDTs and reagents across five hubs, train 13 RRTs by 31 December, and act on trigger-based early warning for floods, drought and extreme heat.

▸ Sustain cholera response in the four active counties (Mayom, Rubkona, Fangak, Renk); push toward the earliest end-of-outbreak declaration (18 November) through 100% RDT testing.

▸ Sustain malaria response (47,072 cases, 8 deaths — 58.6% below 2025); maintain LLIN coverage (96%) and QA microscopy ahead of the Malaria Indicator Survey.

▸ Complete the Round 1 Polio NIDs campaign in the five remaining counties (75 of 80 reached, 79% coverage), and advance the Magwi and Malakal measles outbreak responses.

title: Kenya Humanitarian Update, October 2026 | Save the Children Kenya
content: The October 2026 Humanitarian Update highlights escalating humanitarian needs in Kenya, including the displacement of approximately 15,240 people following cross-border conflict in Ethiopia and the continued refugee response for 871,568 refugees and asylum seekers, over half of whom are children. Kenya has also reported nine Ebola Virus Disease cases, including two fatalities, while an estimated 2.0–2.49 million people are projected to face acute food insecurity by March 2027. Above-average rainfall may increase flooding and disease risks in arid and semi-arid counties. Save the Children continues to support affected communities through child protection, mental health and psychosocial support, emergency health interventions, and inclusive education for refugee children.

title: UNHCR Lebanon- Operational Update (September 2026)
content:
Context

Lebanon continues to face significant humanitarian, recovery and reconstruction needs amid a complex political and security environment. Addressing the UN General Assembly on 25 September, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam called for continued humanitarian funding, particularly for displaced people, alongside support for early recovery, reconstruction and development. The Lebanon Response Plan 2026 Addendum provides a framework for coordinated support that addresses immediate humanitarian needs while strengthening resilience, restoring essential services and laying the foundations for longer-term recovery in vulnerable communities across the country.

Security conditions remained volatile, particularly in southern Lebanon. Continued military activity, airstrikes and demolition operations affected civilian infrastructure, agricultural land and access to services. In South Lebanon and Nabatieh governorates, extensive housing damage and fear of renewed displacement continued to shape families’ decisions about returning. Households continued to move back and forth between locations, while psychological distress and disrupted education remained prominent concerns.

Lebanon remains among the countries most affected by forced displacement globally, hosting one of the largest refugee populations per capita. As of end September, 329,686 people remained internally displaced, while 877,203 had returned to their district of origin. Despite continued returns, damaged housing, insecurity, unexploded ordnance, disrupted services, and limited livelihood opportunities continued to hinder recovery and households’ ability to meet basic needs. Families remaining in displacement faced difficulties accessing adequate shelter, while host communities remained under considerable pressure.

title: Ukraine war situation update | 10 – 16 October 2026
content:
Ukraine Conflict Monitor Update

Russian strikes on civilian vessels threaten navigation in the Black Sea, while Ukraine finishes Operation Vivaldi.

1,969 conflict events

5% increase compared to last week

197 incidents of violence targeting civilians

At least 116 civilians killed by targeted violence

1,134 air- and drone strikes

4% increase compared to last week

346 shelling events

3% increase compared to last week

469 armed clashes

2% increase compared to last week

283 Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure

29% increase compared to last week

Number of events and change compared to last week (per target):

Education: 25 events

Healthcare: 13 events

Energy: 59 events

Residential: 234 events

  • For the second week in a row, Russian forces struck civilian vessels in the Black Sea under the purported goal of disrupting supplies to Ukraine. Russia struck five grain and cargo vessels in the Exclusive Economic Zones of Bulgaria and Romania and two chemical tankers in Romania’s territorial waters near the Sulina mouth of the Danube River. Since the start of October, Russian strikes along the Western Black Sea coast have led to 12 reported fatalities of sailors, while 18 sailors are still missing. These figures far exceed the total over the previous quarter. While littoral states, such as Bulgaria, Romania, and Turkey, are scrambling to set up a NATO air defence mission against drone strikes, Russian strikes are expected to worsen Black Sea navigation security over the coming months, increase insurance costs for vessel operators, and affect global food prices by blocking Ukrainian wheat and grain exports.
  • In the final part of its Operation Vivaldi, Ukraine’s Third Army Corps reported regaining another 101 km² in the direction of Lyman in Donetsk, retaking 16 settlements in total. Although preparations were initiated in early 2026, the local operation was announced in September to counter Russian efforts to encircle and attack the so-called “fortress belt” cities of Slovyansk and Kramatorsk, the two largest cities still under Ukrainian control in the Donetsk region. Local Ukrainian counteroffensives, such as Operation Vivaldi and the Oleksandrivka direction operations, suggest that Ukrainian forces can still thwart Russia’s attempts to threaten key towns and take territory, despite troop and munition replenishment issues.

title: Yemen, MENA | Population Movement - Emergency Appeal Operational Strategy (MDRYE018)
content:
DESCRIPTION OF THE EVENT

Hostilities in Yemen in July 2026 intensified further in late August and early September, triggering large-scale population movements and increased humanitarian needs across affected governorates. Families have fled affected areas toward neighbouring governorates, and cross-border movements to Djibouti have added a regional dimension to the crisis.

According to IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), 251,125 people, representing 41,853 households, were displaced between 1 August and 17 October 2026. Broader IOM tracking recorded 271,020 displaced people, representing 45,170 households, between 1 January and 17 October 2026. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates in Sana’a has also reported approximately 80,000 displaced households. However, these Ministry figures have not been independently verified and differ in geographic coverage and methodology from IOM data. They should therefore be presented separately. The IOM figures represent recorded displacement movements during specific reporting periods, not Yemen’s total internally displaced population.

This escalation compounds an already protracted humanitarian crisis. The IFRC Emergency Appeal identifies 22.3 million people requiring humanitarian assistance nationwide, with approximately 5.2 million people already internally displaced before the latest escalation. Years of escalation, economic deterioration, food insecurity, recurrent disease outbreaks and weakened public services have reduced households’ capacity to withstand further shocks.

Fighting and insecurity are disrupting access to healthcare, education, markets and essential supplies. Displaced families arriving with limited possessions require shelter, household items, food, safe water and healthcare, while host communities face increasing pressure on services and resources. Repeated displacement also further erodes livelihoods and increases protection risks. This volatile situation then creates the potential for further movement and underscores the need for sustained humanitarian access and a flexible response.

Severity of humanitarian conditions

Impact on accessibility, availability, quality, use and awareness of goods and services

Displaced families face overlapping barriers to shelter, food, safe water, sanitation, education and healthcare. Insecurity and road closures disrupt markets, supply routes and humanitarian assistance, while lost livelihoods, depleted assets and rising prices reduce households’ purchasing power. Isolated communities face particularly severe constraints as commercial supplies and essential services become increasingly difficult to sustain.

An Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) analysis released in May projected that approximately 5.4 million people in Government-controlled areas would face IPC Phase 3 or above during October–December 2026. However, this geographically limited projection predates the latest escalation and does not capture its full consequences.

Shelter and sanitation conditions remain critical as well and IOM assessments in displacement sites on 5 October identified inadequate safe shelter as the most significant vulnerability. Some households were sleeping outdoors, while women and girls highlighted shortages of appropriate latrines, compromising privacy, dignity and safety. On 14 October, the World Food Programme (WFP) reported that 800,000 people were beyond its reach.

Health and education disruptions also further restrict essential support. UNICEF has reported interrupted healthcare and schooling as well as damage to infrastructure serving children and families. Displacement also increases the need for accessible information on available assistance, functioning facilities and referral options.

Impact on physical and mental well-being

Violence, inadequate shelter and interrupted healthcare increase risks of injury, untreated illness and preventable deaths, and since the onset of this latest escalation, ICRC has highlighted that rising casualties and displacement are straining Yemen’s already-weakened health system. Demand for emergency care in turn reduces capacity for other services, while displaced people struggle to access medicines, vaccination, maternal healthcare and treatment for chronic disease.

Cholera in particular presents an immediate public health concern. UN News reported on 13 October that Yemen had recorded 8,034 suspected cholera cases and 27 deaths in 2026, with one-quarter of suspected cases occurring in the preceding four weeks. Disrupted services, overcrowded shelters and inadequate access to safe water increase the risk of cholera transmission. Poor sanitation and hygiene conditions in informal settlements then further heighten outbreak risks, while delayed treatment increases the danger of severe dehydration and death.

Food insecurity further compounds these risks against a backdrop of severe pre-existing nutritional vulnerabilities, with WFP reporting 2.2 million acutely malnourished children under five nationwide. Continued isolation and interrupted assistance threaten further deterioration, particularly among young children and pregnant and lactating women. Fear, bereavement, separation and repeated displacement also increase psychological distress and psychosocial support needs.

Risks and vulnerabilities

Repeated displacement is further exhausting households' coping capacities. A rapid assessment conducted by IOM across three displacement sites found that approximately 45 per cent of assessed households had experienced previous displacement. Associated asset losses and unstable livelihoods further undermine their ability to cope, increasing the risk of harmful coping strategies, including child labour. These findings reflect the households assessed in the three sites and should not be generalized to the wider displaced population.

Female-headed households, separated children, older people, persons with disabilities and people requiring regular treatment face overlapping barriers to safe movement and assistance in this context as well. Women and girls face additional protection concerns too where shelter and sanitation are inadequate, while people with limited mobility or resources may be unable to leave isolated areas or reach services.

Internal displacement and cross-border movements thus create distinct but intersecting needs. WFP’s 16 October reporting described families travelling for days without adequate food or water, as well as inordinate pressure on reception arrangements in Djibouti. These conditions compound the vulnerabilities of displaced populations while placing additional strain on host communities, shared services and already limited resources.

Assistance should therefore prioritize vulnerability across groups, combining accessible services, protection referrals, reliable information and community feedback. The evidence indicates worsening hunger and disease risks but does not establish a confirmed famine classification.

title: Lebanon Complex Emergency, Operation update #5 (MDRLB017)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Description of the crisis

Lebanon entered 2026 facing a protracted and multidimensional crisis shaped by the cumulative effects of the financial and economic collapse that began in 2019, the consequences of successive rounds of hostilities since October 2023, large-scale population displacement, weakened public services and infrastructure, and persistent institutional and financial constraints. While the country had begun to show signs of economic stabilization and recovery during 2025, the renewed escalation of hostilities on 2 March 2026 abruptly reversed this trajectory and generated a new large-scale humanitarian emergency. The World Bank estimates that the renewed conflict derailed Lebanon’s fragile recovery and projects the economy to contract by 6.4 per cent in 2026, further constraining household purchasing power, livelihoods, public finances and the capacity of already overstretched institutions and services to respond to humanitarian needs.

The renewed escalation of hostilities on 2 March 2026 triggered large-scale displacement across Lebanon, with more than 1.2 million people forced to flee their homes at the height of the crisis. Many displaced families sought refuge in collective shelters, including public schools and other facilities, while others stayed with host families or in temporary accommodation. By 13 April, approximately 140,914 people were accommodated in 684 collective shelters. As the intensity of hostilities gradually decreased, displacement patterns shifted, with increasing numbers of families returning to their areas of origin and a progressive reduction in collective shelter occupancy. By 24 June, the number of people residing in collective shelters had decreased to 80,611 across 584 sites, while 523,249 people had returned to their communities. This trend continued over the following months, alongside the gradual closure and consolidation of collective shelters, particularly those established in public schools ahead of the new academic year. As of 29 September, IOM recorded 329,686 internally displaced persons, including 14,277 people in 154 collective sites, while 877,203 people had returned to their areas of origin.

Despite the substantial return movements, conditions in many affected areas remained challenging. Extensive damage to residential buildings and essential infrastructure left many households unable to return to their homes, while others returned to partially damaged properties or areas where basic services remained disrupted. Continued airstrikes and security incidents, particularly in southern Lebanon, alongside explosive ordnance risks and limited livelihood opportunities, further constrained safe and sustainable returns. Consequently, significant shelter and early recovery needs persisted among displaced and returning populations, despite the overall reduction in displacement figures. According to the Ministry of Public Health, as of 10 September 2026, 4,383 people had been killed and 12,406 injured since the renewed escalation began on 2 March.

The crisis has unfolded alongside broader and increasingly complex population movements. Lebanon continues to host a large refugee population, while movements between Lebanon and Syria have increased amid changing conditions in both countries and wider regional instability. The 2026 Lebanon Response Plan estimates that approximately 1.12 million displaced Syrians are living in Lebanon. Return movements to Syria have taken place alongside continued arrivals and internal movements, creating a complex protection environment involving Lebanese communities, refugees, migrants, internally displaced people and returnees.

The renewed conflict has also exacerbated Lebanon’s existing food security and socioeconomic crisis. The April 2026 IPC update estimated that approximately 1.24 million people, or 24 per cent of the analysed population, would face Crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) between April and August 2026, compared with 874,000 people between November 2025 and March 2026. By 30 September, UNICEF reported that four in five surveyed households were struggling to afford basic necessities, demonstrating the extent to which renewed conflict has compounded years of socioeconomic deterioration and depleted household coping capacities.

Public services and infrastructure have also sustained significant impacts. Health facilities and ambulances have been affected by attacks, while insecurity and damage have disrupted access to health care. By June 2026, the Ministry of Public Health reported that 17 hospitals had been damaged, including three that were forced to close. Since the renewed escalation began, 133 healthcare workers had been killed and 402 injured, while 172 attacks on emergency medical service vehicles and stations had been recorded. The education sector has similarly been affected and that among 1,089 education facilities assessed, 436 were damaged and 37 destroyed. Damage and disruption to water, sanitation, electricity, housing and other essential infrastructure have further constrained access to basic services in affected and return areas.

By the end of September 2026, the situation had evolved from the peak phase of mass displacement towards a complex combination of continued humanitarian response, population return and early recovery. However, the security situation remained volatile, with ongoing attacks and airstrikes, particularly in southern Lebanon, continuing to result in casualties, damage and disruption and affecting conditions for safe and sustainable return. Significant displacement, damaged infrastructure, socioeconomic deterioration and continued hostilities therefore mean that Lebanon remains in a fragile humanitarian situation.

title: Burundi BVD Ebola preparedness - DREF Operational Update (MDRBI026), 27 October 2026
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

21-05-2026

What happened, where and when?

On 15 May 2026, the Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) officially declared an outbreak of Ebola Virus Disease (BVD) caused by the Bundibugyo strain in Ituri Province, in the northeastern part of the country. On the same day, the Republic of Uganda also declared an outbreak of the same Ebola strain, with the epicenter located in Ituri. In response to the evolving situation and the cross-border implications of the outbreak, the World Health Organization (WHO) subsequently recognized the event as a major public health concern due to its spread in border areas and the high risk of regional transmission.

The Bundibugyo strain currently has no approved vaccine, increasing concerns among health authorities and humanitarian partners. Ebola Virus Disease is a severe and often fatal illness transmitted through direct contact with infected bodily fluids, contaminated materials, or infected animals. The disease can cause large outbreaks with significant mortality if not rapidly contained.

As of the date the emergency plan of action was written (May 2026), the epidemiological situation is still critical.
As of 20 October 2026, no confirmed cases of Ebola virus disease have been reported in Burundi, according to the information provided. On 16 October 2026, the Ministry of Public Health refuted reports of a suspected case at Prince Régent Charles Hospital in Bujumbura. The individual tested negative for Ebola and other viral haemorrhagic fevers.

However, the regional epidemiological situation remains a concern. The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), the epicentre of the ongoing outbreak involving the Bundibugyo virus, continues to report cases and deaths. According to the figures cited in the available information, the World Health Organization (WHO) reported 8,728 confirmed cases and 4,205 deaths as of 6 October 2026. The risk of cross-border transmission is heightened by reported cases in neighbouring countries. In Kenya, an imported case linked to the DRC was confirmed in early October, and the patient died on 5 October. Contact tracing and follow-up measures were initiated, with subsequent reports indicating additional positive cases among individuals identified through contact investigations. In Uganda, authorities reported that no active cases remained following the discharge of the last patient on 16 July 2026.

Burundi is considered a high-risk country due to its geographical proximity to the affected areas and its strong social and economic links with both the DRC and Uganda. Particular concern exists along major travel and trade corridors connecting Burundi to affected areas, including the Bujumbura–Goma, Bujumbura–Kivu, Bujumbura-Nairobi, and Bujumbura–Entebbe routes, through both land and air transport. The provinces bordering the DRC, as well as major entry points and urban centers receiving travelers, are considered areas at heightened risk of disease importation.

Recognizing the threat posed by the outbreak, the Government of Burundi, in collaboration with health partners including the Burundi Red Cross Society and the IFRC, finalized and validated a National Ebola Preparedness and Response Plan on 22 May 2026. Preparedness efforts remain ongoing as the outbreak continues to evolve in neighboring countries and the risk of importation into Burundi remains high.

title: Congo BVD Preparedness 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRCG031)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

09-10-2026

What happened, where and when?

On 15 May 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) officially declared an outbreak of Ebola virus disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, initially detected in Ituri Province. The spread of the outbreak to other provinces, particularly South Ubangi, has heightened concerns about the risk of the disease being introduced into neighbouring countries. On 10 September 2026, the first confirmed case was reported in Bulu Health Zone, South Ubangi. As of 6 October 2026, two confirmed cases, including one death, had been recorded in the province. This evolving epidemiological situation poses a risk to the Republic of the Congo, given its geographical proximity to affected areas in the DRC and the intensity of cross-border population movements.

Likouala Department requires particular attention due to regular exchanges between communities in the two countries, commercial activities, and population movements, particularly along river routes. The localities of Bétou, Dongou and Impfondo, as well as the main entry and transit points, are priority areas to be assessed with the health authorities to determine preparedness needs.

In response to this risk, on 9 October 2026, the Ministry of Health and Population held a meeting to announce the publication of the National Preparedness Plan for Bundibugyo Virus Disease. This milestone strengthened the national preparedness framework and mobilized institutional, technical and humanitarian stakeholders around the priorities established to anticipate the possible introduction of the disease into the country. It also highlights the need to ensure that partners’ interventions are aligned with national guidance and to strengthen the operational capacities of stakeholders expected to contribute to preparedness efforts.

In this context, the Congo Red Cross (CRC), in coordination with the Ministry of Health and Population and other relevant partners, needs to strengthen its preparedness capacities to contribute effectively to national efforts. Its network of staff and volunteers is a key asset for risk communication and community engagement, community-based surveillance, the early identification and reporting of alerts, and the promotion of infection prevention and control (IPC) measures, including Safe and Dignified Burials (SDB).

Preparedness must also include strengthening teams’ capacities in Safe and Dignified Burials, in accordance with national protocols, respect for the dignity of deceased persons and their families, and applicable safety requirements. Training teams, clarifying roles and responsibilities, and coordinating with health authorities are essential to ensure appropriate mobilization when needed.

The proposed DREF operation therefore aims to strengthen CRC’s preparedness capacities, particularly in Likouala Department, to support national efforts before any potential introduction of the disease. Activities will be implemented in a complementary manner with those of the health authorities and other partners, in line with the priorities of the National Preparedness Plan and the needs identified. In the event of a suspected introduction of the disease, alerts will be referred to the relevant health focal points through established national mechanisms. Alert verification and case confirmation will remain the responsibility of the health authorities. Any operational mobilization of CRC, including for Safe and Dignified Burial activities, will be coordinated with the relevant authorities and conducted in accordance with applicable national protocols.

title: UNRWA Situation Report #237 on the Humanitarian Crisis in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem [EN/AR]
content:
Highlights

The Gaza Strip

  • On 12 October, UNRWA opened a new health facility in Jabalia and began receiving patients. As UNRWA’s northernmost health facility in the Gaza Strip, the clinic expands access to health services for underserved communities. Together with the Saftawi Health Centre, the two facilities provide new anchor points for delivering health services to thousands of Palestine Refugees in the area.
  • UNRWA recorded several significant armed incidents affecting its facilities and schools-turned-shelters. At least six displaced people, including a child, were injured and one person was killed while sheltering inside UNRWA facilities, mostly as a result of stray bullets. Operations at several facilities across Rafah, Khan Younis and the Middle Area were also temporarily suspended, either due to insecurity or following evacuation orders issued by Israeli forces.
  • UNRWA’s winterisation response is underway, with winter emergency teams activated across all areas to clean manholes, gullies, and drainage networks, identify high-risk locations, inspect available equipment, and put preventive measures in place, including sandbags in flood-prone areas. Winterisation preparedness, however, remains seriously constrained by limited operational capacity: many pumps to address flooding are not functioning due to lack of engine oil and spare parts, and heavy machinery cannot enter Gaza.

The occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem

  • Marking three years since the attacks of 7 October 2023, movement and access re-strictions were tightened across the occupied West Bank.
  • The olive harvest season officially commenced on 15 October, accompanied by settler violence and access restrictions impacting Palestinian farmers in several areas of the occupied West Bank. During the reporting period, one Palestinian was reportedly killed in an incident related to settler violence.

Key Points

The Gaza Strip

Fatalities and injuries

  • Between 7 October 2023 and 9 October 2026, according to the Ministry of Health, as reported by the Health Cluster, 74,370 Palestinians were killed in the Gaza Strip and another 175,371 were injured. This includes 1,481 fatalities and 5,410 injuries between the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025 and 9 October 2026.
  • UNRWA has recorded 394 colleagues killed in the Gaza Strip since the start of the war (311 UNRWA personnel and 83 persons who were supporting UNRWA[2], as of 20 October.

Health crisis

  • Hypothermia remains a serious risk, particularly for newborns and infants, with deaths reported in previous winters since the war began. UNRWA health and nutrition teams are strengthening counselling for women and caregivers on breastfeeding, skin-to-skin care and other simple measures to keep children warm. Infant warming units are being distributed across UNRWA health facilities to address emergency cases. However, supply restrictions have prevented the entry of additional warmers for community distribution, while use of existing units depends on unreliable electricity supplies.
  • In September, six UNRWA health centres also experienced temporary disruptions due to overloaded generators having to be switched off until new lubricant oil can be found. This highlights the growing operational impact of the shortage of fuel, lubricant oil, and spare parts on the delivery of healthcare.

Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) needs

  • According to the WASH Cluster’s Light Touch Monitoring Survey, completed in September, 84 per cent of the population are experiencing frequent, unpredictable disruptions in access to safe, clean, and reliable water for daily drinking, cooking, and hygiene. Water insecurity thus remains a significant concern, despite signs of improvement (91 per cent of the population reported water insecurity in the previous round).
  • Access to basic hygiene supplies also remained severely constrained, with 89 per cent of households reporting insufficient access to essential hygiene items.

Displacement, site management

  • UNRWA continues to monitor the movement of displaced persons and displacement sites. A total of 113 UNRWA collective emergency shelters host 65,000 internally displaced persons.

Shelter needs

  • According to the Shelter Cluster’s classification, based on surveys conducted between 14 and 28 June, an estimated 1.98 million people, representing 94 per cent of the population of the Gaza Strip, require shelter and non-food item assistance (NFI). The assessment also suggests that 58 per cent of the population is facing critical or catastrophic shelter needs, meaning severe deficiencies in shelter conditions or lack of access to essential services and NFIs that expose them to serious health, safety, and dignity risks.

Operational implications and humanitarian response

  • Around 10,500 Palestinian UNRWA personnel continue to provide services and assistance to people in the Gaza Strip. In the occupied West Bank, UNRWA also plays a central role with more than 4,000 of the Agency’s Palestinian personnel providing education, health, and other services to Palestine Refugees.
  • All UNRWA international staff are prevented from entering the Occupied Palestinian Territory - the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem. This follows the implementation of laws passed by the Israeli parliament on 28 October 2024[3] that purport to prohibit UNRWA’s operations in areas that Israel considers its sovereign territory, including occupied East Jerusalem, and seek to bar any contact between Israeli officials and UNRWA. Israeli authorities have not granted the Agency’s international staff visas or permits to enter the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including the Gaza Strip, since the end of January 2025.
  • Since March 2025, the Israeli authorities have been blocking UNRWA from directly bringing humanitarian personnel and aid into the Gaza Strip. Despite the huge needs on the ground, UNRWA was therefore unable to distribute the aid it had pre-positioned outside Gaza, which included enough food parcels, flour, and shelter supplies for hundreds of thousands of people.

The occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem

  • According to OCHA, between 7 October 2023 and 9 October 2026, 1,143 Palestinians – at least 250 of them children – were killed in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem. Ninety-six of them have been killed since the beginning of 2026.
  • Marking three years since the attacks of 7 October 2023, movement and access re-strictions were tightened across the occupied West Bank.
  • Settler violence and harassment continued to account for a significant percentage of recorded protection incidents, with 395 incidents and at least 115 related injuries reported from 7-20 October alone. In addition to widespread reports of obstruction and attacks targeting the olive harvest, sustained pressure on Palestinian communities is contributing to an increasingly coercive environment and heightened protection concerns.
  • A Palestinian from Burqa was reportedly killed in the context of settler violence on 7 October. Other Palestinians sustained injuries during the incident. The incident underscores the high levels of settler violence currently affecting Palestinian communities, particularly during the olive harvest season.
  • On 10 October, a Palestinian from Beit Ula was shot and killed by Israeli forces using live ammunition in Hebron City.
  • Israeli forces have continued to keep all entrances to Madama village closed since 11 October.
  • The olive harvest season officially commenced on 15 October, accompanied by settler violence and access restrictions impacting Palestinian farmers in several areas of the West Bank. On 16 October, in Abu Falah, a foreign journalist was among the injured. On 17 October, in At-Tayba, a European diplomatic delegation came under attack during a visit to observe the olive harvest.

title: WFP Colombia Earthquake Emergency Situation Report, 20 October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• More than 778,000 people remain affected by the earthquake across 16 departments. As of 18 October, WFP had reached 47,078 people. Available resources will allow to extend assistance to 109,178 people based on government registries, food security evidence and market analysis.

• The earthquake response is unfolding amid overlapping humanitarian pressures, including deteriorating security conditions, elevated wildfire risk, El Niño and other weather-related emergencies. Access restrictions, displacement and confinement are compounding needs in conflict-affected areas, while dry conditions and belowaverage rainfall are placing additional pressure on rural livelihoods, water availability and food security.

• WFP is mobilizing complementary resources across programmes to preserve response continuity and expand coverage.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• More than 50 days after the 10 August earthquake, 778,282 people remained affected across 16 departments. The earthquake has added to Colombia’s already complex humanitarian context, where conflict, displacement, access restrictions and climate-related shocks continue to affect vulnerable populations. With 104,048 homes uninhabitable and 6,903 people living in temporary settlements, critical gaps persist in food security, shelter, WASH and protection, particularly in remote and conflict-affected areas.

• The earthquake has further intensified Colombia’s pre-existing humanitarian challenges, compounding needs and constraining relief operations in priority areas where communities face overlapping impacts from conflict, displacement and disaster-related losses. Between 1 January and 6 October, around 2,000 violent events affected 974,245 people nationwide. Humanitarian access restrictions affected 678,620 people, while attacks against civilians, displacement, armed actions and explosive devices affected more than 92,000 people.

• Weather-related risks remained elevated amid persistent dry conditions and below-average rainfall, adding pressure to communities and response capacities already affected by the earthquake. Wildfire risk was particularly high: as of 6 October, the National Hydrology and Meteorology Institute (IDEAM) reported alerts in 32 municipalities, including red alerts in Tolima, Cundinamarca and Huila, while UNGRD recorded 416 wildfire events across 18 departments during September, affecting more than 26,500 hectares. These conditions also increase the risk of water shortages, livelihood losses and other climate-related impacts.

title: Updated: Rapid Protection Assessment Report - El Obeid
content:
The report provides an overview of the evolving protection situation in El Obeid, highlighting the deteriorating protection environment, increasing displacement-related vulnerabilities, and persistent gaps in access to essential services and humanitarian assistance.

Key findings highlight:

  • Heightened protection risks, including insecurity, gender-based violence, child protection concerns, psychosocial distress, and barriers to civil documentation.
  • Critical gaps in basic services, particularly water, sanitation, food assistance, and adequate shelter, which further exacerbate protection risks.
  • Significant disparities across displacement sites, including limited humanitarian presence, weak registration systems, and inadequate identification and referral mechanisms for persons with specific needs.
  • Increasing pressure on host communities, whose coping capacities continue to deteriorate amid prolonged displacement and limited resources.

The September follow-up mission reaffirmed the findings of the May assessment and underscored the urgent need for strengthened protection monitoring, coordinated multisectoral interventions, improved referral pathways, and targeted assistance to the most vulnerable populations.

We hope the findings and recommendations will inform ongoing humanitarian response planning, operational prioritization, advocacy, and resource mobilization efforts to address critical protection needs in El Obeid.

We encourage partners and relevant stakeholders to review the report and consider its recommendations in their respective response planning and interventions.

title: WFP Ghana Country Brief, September 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Ghana continues to face persistent regional and socioeconomic disparities, with northern and rural communities disproportionately affected by poverty, food insecurity and climate-related shocks.

• As a food-deficit country, Ghana remains vulnerable to erratic rainfall, rising temperatures, global commodity price fluctuations and other economic pressures that affect agricultural production, livelihoods and access to nutritious diets.

• According to the Cadre Harmonisé analysis, an estimated 1.5 million people (IPC Phase 3-5) are projected to face crisis-level food insecurity between June and August 2026. While severe food insecurity has declined slightly, overlapping vulnerabilities linked to poverty, unemployment, climate and economic shocks continue to affect households, particularly in rural areas. Women remain disproportionately impacted, with female-headed households facing higher levels of food insecurity and limited access to livelihood opportunities.

title: Monthly Report on the Implementation of Epidemic Intelligence in the Americas - Health Emergency Information and Risk Assessment Unit (HIM) - September 2026
content:
I. Regional Epidemic Intelligence Activity

A. Detection of early warning flags and signals At the regional level, the Health Emergency Information and Risk Assessment Unit (HIM) of the PAHO Health Emergencies Department (PHE) operates through the continuous epidemic intelligence phases, scanning multiple sources to identify Early warning flags1 (information indicating a potential acute public health risk) in the Americas Region.

Early warning flags are triaged to identify if these are signals2 requiring verification in close coordination with Member States3. Once verified, a signal may be classified as an event. PAHO conducts risk assessments and continuously monitors these events, including epidemiological and geospatial analysis, while facilitating information exchange with Member States and partners and producing actionable intelligence and technical support to guide timely public health decisions and response across the Americas.

title: UNHCR Haiti Factsheet, July - September 2026
content:

  • On World Humanitarian Day, UNHCR participated in a community discussion organized by its partner, ODELPA, focused on the challenges facing humanitarian actors amid insecurity and growing needs in Haiti.
  • In August, UNHCR delivered a training session as part of the Haiti Summer University, organized by the Haitian Institute for Human Rights. The session targeted students engaged in the human rights field and focused on international protection, refugee rights, and asylum procedures.
  • On 21 September, UNHCR participated in the Citizen Forum for Peace, organized by the Office de la Protection du Citoyen (OPC) and the UN Country Team, to mark the International Day of Peace, discuss social cohesion and civic participation.
  • UNHCR and its partners conducted protection monitoring missions to Belladère, Ouanaminthe, Cap-Haïtien, and Kenscoff to assess displacement trends and protection risks. The missions supported birth registration for vulnerable groups and, through ICDH coordination with the National Archives, facilitated access to birth certificate extracts.
  • In the framework of CERF-funded activities, UNHCR strengthened the capacity of partners ICDH, OCNH, ANH, ODELPA, AVSI, and REACH/ACTED to enhance coordination and protection standards, strengthening referral pathways and access to lifesaving services for people with international protection needs.

title: Gender-Based Violence Situation Brief: Quarters 2 & 3, 2026 (April – September 2026)
content: Women and girls in Somalia continue to face heightened risks of gender-based violence (GBV) amid conflict, climate shocks, displacement and severe funding shortages. title: UNICEF Democratic Republic of the Congo Humanitarian Situation Report No. 4 – Ebola Outbreak (Bundibugyo Virus), 30 September
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Children continued to bear a disproportionate share of the outbreak. As of 30 September, children accounted for approximately 27 per cent of confirmed cases but nearly 38 per cent of deaths, with children under five representing almost two-thirds of child deaths.
  • In response to the outbreak’s geographic expansion, UNICEF scaled up its multisectoral operations from 60 to 63 health zones, maintaining a presence in all 16 hotspots.
  • Community-based surveillance was strengthened through the deployment of 3,469 additional community mobilizers. Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) activities expanded to 55 affected health zones, mobilizing 11,513 frontline and community actors, extending collaboration from 108 to 114 radio stations, and launching intensified digital engagement and rumour management.
  • Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) interventions transitioned from initial deployment to implementation at scale. UNICEF delivered more than 590,000 litres of safe water, expanded support to health facilities and schools, strengthened decontamination capacity, and deployed assistance to newly affected areas.
  • With the start of the school year, 167,343 children and adolescents accessed safe and adapted learning opportunities, while 158,188 unique children received school or IPC/WASH kits.
  • UNICEF requires US$ 113.5 million for its revised six-month response plan. As of 30 September, US$ 41 million had been mobilized, leaving a US$ 72.5 million funding gap. Timely, flexible funding is urgently required to sustain outbreak control, protect children and maintain essential health including mental health and psychosocial support, nutrition, education, IPC/WASH and protection services in communities already affected by conflict, displacement and cholera.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL SITUATION UPDATE

Between 1 and 30 September 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported 2,050 additional confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) cases and 979 deaths. As of 30 September, cumulative confirmed cases had reached 8,300, including 4,018 deaths, corresponding to a case fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.4 per cent. The outbreak continued to expand geographically, with confirmed cases reported for the first time in Sud-Ubangi Province, bringing the number of affected provinces to seven (Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, Bas-Uélé and South-Ubangi).

During September, an additional three health zones reported confirmed cases, increasing the total to 63 affected health zones, representing 37.7 per cent of the country's 167 health zones. 16 health zones across North Kivu, Ituri and Haut-Uélé provinces were identified as Ebola hotspots, highlighting the scale of transmission and the need for increased prevention, surveillance and response measures. UNICEF maintained an operational presence across all 16 hotspot health zones, delivering services in support of the Ebola response.

The outbreak is now the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC and the second largest globally. Ituri province remains the epicentre, accounting for 75.8 per cent of all confirmed cases 6,293 cases and 2,902 deaths, followed by North Kivu 1,601 cases and 950 deaths and Haut-Uélé 346 cases and 144 deaths. Transmission also continued in Tshopo, Bas-Uélé, South Kivu and South-Ubangi. Women and girls represent approximately 53.4 per cent of reported confirmed cases.

Children aged 17 years and below account for approximately 27.4 per cent of confirmed cases and 37.6 per cent of reported deaths, indicating a disproportionate mortality burden among children. Children under five bear the greatest burden, representing approximately 63.8 per cent of deaths among children aged 17 years and below.

During September, 16 health workers were identified among confirmed cases reported during the month, underscoring ongoing risks to frontline responders.

title: Shabelle River: Climate Update and Riverine Flood Risk Advisory (Digniin) - Deyr 2026 Flood Advisory No. 4 (26 October 2026)
content:
Observed Rainfall

Rain returned to the Shabelle catchment from 23 October. Satellite estimates show about 19 mm on average over the catchment above Belet Weyne during 19–26 October, nearly all of it in the past three days. Since the start of the month (1–24 October), 200–500 mm has fallen over Hiraan, Galgaduud and the Gode–Kelafo area, more than six times normal in places.

River Levels

Belet Weyne reached the moderate flood risk level (6.50 m) this morning at 6.56 m, after rising every day for a week. Deefow, near the Ethiopian border, is still rising (6.90 m, about 4 m since 13 October). Bulo Burti is rising slowly (5.36 m), and Jowhar, below moderate flood risk level since 20 October, is steady at 4.28 m. Satellite radar (Copernicus, images to 24 October) shows possible flooding over about 55 km² in Jowhar district, consistent with open river breakages.

title: Juba River: Climate Update and Riverine Flood Risk Advisory (Digniin) - Deyr 2026 Flood Advisory No. 4 (26 October 2026)
content:
Observed Rainfall

Rain returned to the upper Juba River catchment from 23 October. Satellite estimates show about 36 mm on average over the catchment above Dollow and 30 mm above Luuq during 19–26 October, nearly all of it in the past three days. Since the start of the month (1–24 October), most of Gedo, Bay and Bakool has received 200–500 mm, far above normal, while the Ethiopian headwaters and the Kenyan part of the catchment received less and were below normal in places.

River Levels

After falling slowly over the past week, the level at Dollow rose by 0.12 m overnight to 2.88 m today, 1.62 m below the moderate flood risk level (4.50 m), and Luuq is at 2.78 m, 2.72 m below its moderate flood risk level (5.50 m).

title: UNICEF Panama Humanitarian Situation Report No. 5 (Earthquake), 16-23 October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Two weeks after the 9 October earthquake, humanitarian needs remain significant in the provinces of Los Santos, Veraguas, Coclé and Herrera. Although response actions have addressed the most immediate needs of affected populations, thousands of people continue to face challenges related to temporary displacement, loss or damage of housing, disruptions to basic services, and impacts on educational infrastructure.

  • According to the latest official assessments, 12.365 homes were assessed and 40.880 people registered through the Damage Assessment and Needs Analysis (EDAN). Damage to housing remains one of the main impacts of the earthquake, affecting 2,896 families, of whom 908 have reported the total loss of their homes. In addition, 160 shelters continue to provide temporary accommodation to 5.779 displaced people. The provinces of Los Santos, Veraguas, Coclé and Herrera account for the majority of reported impacts.

  • During the reporting period, UNICEF maintained its support to the Government-led response through coordination, monitoring and assistance actions in water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), education, and child protection. Monitoring missions conducted in the Azuero Peninsula showed that, although the emergency has evolved into an early recovery phase, significant humanitarian gaps persist, particularly for displaced families, children and persons with disabilities.

  • UNICEF expanded its response through the distribution of 133 mosquito nets funded by DG ECHO, support to water and sanitation interventions implemented together with its implementing partner at the temporary site of La Pericada, and the coordination of actions aimed at educational recovery and psychosocial support for children and adolescents affected by the earthquake.

  • Despite progress in the emergency response, significant humanitarian needs remain among displaced families, children and adolescents affected by educational disruption, and communities with limited access to adequate water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services. Likewise, psychosocial support and protection needs remain for the most vulnerable populations affected by the emergency.

content:

1. Description

Flooding continued to affect communities across Cambodia in October following heavy rainfall in September and early October. According to figures reported by the Asian Disaster Reduction Center, citing a DCA/WFP update, as of 5 October, flooding had affected 109,985 families across 10 provinces. A total of 9,027 families had been evacuated, 88,811 houses and 313 schools had been affected, and more than 209,867 hectares of agricultural land had been impacted.

According to the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, as of 16 October, flooding had affected 240,583 hectares of agricultural crops across 14 provinces, of which 107,353 hectares were damaged, including 98,662 hectares of rice crops. Although floodwaters had receded in some areas, affected households continued to face agricultural losses, food insecurity and reduced livelihood opportunities.

Request For Assistance

No

Summary

IFRC CCD Bangkok and the Asia Pacific Regional Office (APRO) continue to monitor the evolving situation and remained ready to support CRC, as required, in responding to the needs of flood-affected communities.

According to information shared by CRC, the organisation distributed flood relief assistance to 4,231 families across 12 provinces: Banteay Meanchey, Battambang, Kampong Chhnang, Kampong Cham, Kandal, Kratie, Pailin, Pursat, Preah Sihanouk, Siem Reap, Stung Treng and Takeo. The Government continued to coordinate flood response activities, monitor impacts and provide emergency assistance through provincial authorities and the Cambodia Food Reserve System. title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 22 October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • In the West Bank, 148 Palestinians were injured by Israeli forces or settlers between 13 and 19 October, including 69 in olive-harvest-related settler attacks.
  • Since 1 September, 272 olive-harvest-related settler attacks have been documented, exceeding the totals recorded during the entire 2024 and 2025 harvest seasons.
  • Israeli settlers set fire to a mosque in Jerusalem governorate, bringing to 14 the number of mosques vandalized by settlers since the beginning of 2026 in the West Bank.
  • According to WHO, 146 attacks on health care were recorded in the West Bank between January and September 2026, resulting in four fatalities and 43 injuries, alongside 131 instances of obstruction to health-care delivery.
  • In Gaza, as of 22 October, eight children had been reported killed and 20 injured in just six days. These are among hundreds of children who have been reported killed since the announcement of the October 2025 ceasefire.
  • According to the Gaza Market Monitoring Committee, the price of food items soared. Potatoes reportedly rose by 72 per cent, and the food basket increased by 20 per cent on average.
  • Due to funding shortages, Food Security Sector partners are only being able to reach less than one million people out of an estimated 2.1 million in Gaza with monthly food aid from October 2026 onwards. Meanwhile, 60 per cent of funds required by the Shelter Cluster to help people prepare for the cold and rainy season remains unmet and 11 partners might have to cease the delivery of drinking water by truck.
  • Across the Strip, trauma, surgical and rehabilitation supplies, as well as specialized medicines for noncommunicable diseases remain scarce due to ongoing aid entry restrictions. Oncology diagnostics and imaging are severely compromised.

West Bank

The reporting Period is 13–19 October 2026 unless otherwise specified.

The humanitarian situation in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, remained severe amid operations by Israeli forces, settler violence, demolitions, damage to homes and productive assets, and restrictions on access to land and essential services. No Palestinian fatalities were recorded during the reporting period, while 148 Palestinians, including six children, were injured: 92 by Israeli forces and 56 by settlers. Of those injured, 74 (50 per cent) were in the context of settler attacks, including 69 during olive-harvest-related incidents. On 13 October, during an eight-hour operation in Ramallah city, Israeli forces injured 59 Palestinians, including two children, mainly through tear gas inhalation, and raided and closed the offices of a Palestinian human rights organization.

Settler violence remained at high levels, with 83 attacks recorded across 48 communities during the reporting period, resulting in casualties or damage to homes, a mosque, at least 151 olive trees and other property. Since the beginning of 2026, 2,159 settler attacks resulting in Palestinian casualties, property damage or both have been documented across more than 300 communities, averaging 7.4 attacks per day, compared with five per day in 2025. On 14 October, Israeli settlers set fire to a mosque in Mikhmas village, northeast of Jerusalem, causing extensive damage to its interior. They also smashed windows, sprayed anti-Palestinian slogans on the mosque's walls and set fire to a nearby vehicle. Since the beginning of 2026, settlers have vandalized 14 mosques across Palestinian villages in Nablus, Tulkarm, Ramallah and Jerusalem governorates. On 17 October, in Ma'in (Hebron), nine Palestinians, including a woman, were injured during an incident involving Israeli settlers and forces, in which settlers reportedly stole 139 sheep from four animal pens and damaged residential and livelihood assets belonging to four families.

During the reporting period, Israeli authorities demolished or forced Palestinians to demolish 21 Palestinian-owned structures, displacing 37 people. Of those displaced, 32 were affected by demolitions carried out for lack of Israeli-issued building permits, which are impossible for Palestinians to obtain. Another five were displaced during an operation by Israeli forces; on 16 October, Israeli forces fired tear gas canisters into a residential apartment in Area B of Kafr Malik village (Ramallah), causing a fire that rendered it uninhabitable. On 13 October, three Palestinian refugee households comprising 16 people, including 10 children, were displaced in At Tur, East Jerusalem, after a residential building was partially self- demolished by its owners and the remaining demolition was carried out by Israeli authorities, citing the lack of an Israeli-issued building permit. Since the beginning of 2026, approximately 1,790 Palestinians have been displaced by demolitions for lack of Israeli-issued building permits across the West Bank, including 668 (37 per cent) in East Jerusalem.

On 22 October, the Acting Special Coordinator, Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator, Ramiz Alakbarov, visited Jenin governorate with diplomatic representatives from 13 Member States to hear directly from Palestinian communities affected by settler violence, access restrictions and prolonged displacement. In Arraba, olive farmers described how recurrent settler attacks and Israeli-imposed access restrictions are undermining their livelihoods, while humanitarian partners briefed the delegation on protective accompaniment and legal assistance. In Qabatiya, the delegation met Palestinians displaced from Jenin Camp since early 2025 who remain unable to return to their homes. Alakbarov called for the protection of Palestinian farmers, accountability for attacks against them, increased humanitarian funding and measures to enable the safe and dignified return of displaced residents.

title: Yemen — Rapid Displacement Tracking Update (18 – 24 October 2026)
content:
IOM Yemen DTM’s Rapid Displacement Tracking (RDT) tool collects data on estimated numbers of households forced to flee on a daily basis from their locations of origin or displacement, allowing for regular reporting of new displacements in terms of estimated numbers, geography, and needs. It also tracks returnees who returned to their location of origin.

From 1 January to 24 October 2026, IOM Yemen DTM tracked 49,388 households (HH) (296,328 Individuals) who experienced displacement at least once.

Between 18 and 24 October 2026, IOM Yemen DTM tracked 2269 households (13614 individuals) displaced at least once. The majority of people moved into/within the following governorates and districts:

• Lahj-(900 HHs) – Al Madaribah Wa Al Aarah (534 HHs), Tuban (179 HHs), Al Maqatirah (92 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate were internal.
• Taiz-(600 HHs) – Al Mudhaffar (162 HHs), Mashrah Wa Hadnan (143 HHs), Ash Shamayatayn (132 HHs) districts. All displacements in the governorate were internal.
• Aden-(553 HHs) – Al Burayqah (409 HHs), Dar Sad (93 HHs), At Tawahi (22 HHs) districts. Most displacements in the governorate originated from Lahj.

The majority of people moved from the following governorates and districts:

title: Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar October 2026
content:
Earlier this month, a Rohingya man shared with me how five of his children were killed in Rakhine State. A woman spoke of her husband’s abduction nine years ago and the anguish of not knowing what has happened to him. They were amongst more than 200 Rohingya that I met during my recent visit to Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh – all of whom carried the trauma of losing their loved ones, homes and land. Most of those I met had arrived in Bangladesh within the past two years. Since early 2024, more than 154,000 Rohingya have crossed the border from Rakhine State, fleeing the conflict between the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army.

Understandably, many Rohingya are closely following the case before the International Court of Justice (ICJ) concerning Myanmar’s alleged failure to comply with its obligations to prevent and punish genocide against the Rohingya in 2016 and 2017. Many expressed hope that the Court’s decision, expected in the coming months, would help pave the way for their return home. But a legal decision alone cannot make that return possible. Until the violence in Rakhine State ends, Rohingya cannot return safely. Nor are the Rohingya the only community at risk: civilians from all ethnic groups in Rakhine State face the threat of attack. Just a few weeks ago, an airstrike near a market in Kyauktaw killed more than 50 people and injured dozens more, including many women and children.

title: WFP Sudan Country Brief - October 2026
content:
• In September, WFP assisted 3.1 million people, including 880,000 people in areas classified as at Risk of Famine (RoF).

  • Due to lack of funding, the number of people reached in September declined significantly from the 4.1 million people reached in August.

  • WFP provided 9,600 mt of in-kind general food assistance (GFA), reaching 1.2 million people.

  • GFA cash-based transfers (CBT) reached 1.4 million people with USD 8.8 million in assistance. However, the exchange rate depreciated sharply. The rate reached its lowest at SDG 7,500 per US dollar, compared to SDG 5,600 in July and SDG 6,150 in August, reducing households purchasing power and creating pressure to renegotiate retailer prices, which in turn delayed implementation in some locations.

title: UNHCR Romania Ukraine Refugee Situation Update - 26 October 2026
content:
Highlight

Working closely with government authorities, communities and partners, World Vision continues to respond to urgent needs.
