title: UNICEF Kenya Humanitarian Flash Update No. 1 (Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease), 20 October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • As of 20 October 2026, Kenya reported nine confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease cases, including one death. The additional eight cases are identified as close contacts and health workers linked to the first case, having tested positive while in quarantine and are receiving care
  • Of the eight confirmed cases, three are healthcare workers, one is a cleaner, and the remaining four are household/family contacts of the index case.
  • Of 135 contacts listed, 134 are in quarantine. Follow-up was reported for all quarantined contacts; tracing continues for the 1 untraced contacts.
  • UNICEF is supporting the Government-led response, building on risk communication, community engagement and frontline preparedness activities. A six-month US$9,469,500 million response package is proposed to strengthen RCCE, surveillance, IPC/WASH, PPE and logistics.

Situation Overview

Kenya confirmed its first imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease on 5 October 2026 following travel from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) through Uganda. The patient died on 5 October. A second confirmed case, a 39-year-old close contact, developed symptoms on 13 October while in quarantine and subsequently tested positive. As of 19 October, the Ministry of Health reported eight confirmed cases and one death.

Contact tracing and surveillance remain central to interrupting further transmission. The national situation report records 130 listed contacts, including 128 (98.5%) in quarantine and 2 not in quarantine. This is above the global contact tracing benchmark of 85% required to break the chain of transmission of the disease. Intensive efforts are ongoing to trace and quarantine the two remaining contacts. Kenya has activated national and Nairobi County public health emergency operations centres, incident management arrangements and county readiness measures. Screening is taking place at 26 points of entry. Risk communication efforts are addressing public questions about transmission, symptoms, quarantine and reported cases.

title: WFP Somalia Country Brief October 2026
content:
• An estimated 5.4 million people are projected to face crisis levels of hunger or worse (IPC 3+) between October and December 2026, including nearly 1.5 million people in emergency levels of hunger (IPC 4).

title: Sudan Crisis: Cross-Regional Population Movement Emergency Appeal No. MDRS1001 - Revised Operational Strategy #2
content:
OPERATIONAL STRATEGY REVISION

More than three years after the outbreak of conflict in Sudan, the regional humanitarian consequences of the crisis remain severe and continue to evolve. While conflict, displacement, food insecurity, disease outbreaks and protection risks persist across the region, population movements have become increasingly dynamic, with ongoing refugee arrivals occurring alongside growing numbers of refugees and displaced people returning to Sudan and other countries of origin. As of October 2026, more than 5 million returnees to Sudan have been reported. Neighbouring countries are currently hosting 4,6 million refugees, asylum-seekers and returnees, placing sustained pressure on already stretched services, infrastructure and resources and limiting host communities’ capacities to absorb these impacts. Humanitarian needs therefore remain significant across the displacement continuum, requiring continued support for refugees, returnees, people on the move and vulnerable host populations.

This revision accompanies the extension of the Regional Emergency Appeal and reflects the evolving phase of the crisis rather than a fundamental change in direction. The core strategic priorities of the operation remain relevant with a continued focus on the provision of integrated life-saving and protection-focused assistance, migration support services at points of entry and humanitarian service points, community health interventions, and National Society strengthening. However, the revised strategy places greater emphasis on supporting increasingly diverse movement patterns, including return movements, while expanding support to host communities and investing in activities that strengthen resilience and recovery where conditions permit. This will include building on current investments made on community infrastructure, basic services and community systems, while supporting communities and National Societies to better understand evolving vulnerabilities, capacities and priorities as a basis for informing longer-term recovery and sustainable solutions approaches. The revision also recognizes the importance of ensuring that the capacities, community structures and operational systems established through the response continue to generate sustainable benefits beyond the immediate emergency context.

The revised Operational Strategy is designed to remain flexible and responsive to a highly uncertain context. Should conflict dynamics, displacement trends, or humanitarian needs deteriorate further, the IFRC Network will retain the ability to rapidly scale up life-saving assistance, protection services, and migration support across affected countries. At the same time, ongoing analysis of humanitarian trends, operational capacity, funding prospects, and country-specific contexts will inform future decisions on transition pathways. During the extension period, the IFRC and National Societies will undertake regular reviews of transition readiness to determine where activities may progressively be integrated into longer-term planning frameworks, while ensuring that essential humanitarian support remains in place where needs continue to be acute. This includes sustaining community-based MHPSS capacities and referral pathways established through the response, particularly where psychosocial needs persist beyond the immediate emergency phase.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 315: Week 3 - October 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Market Overview

During the 3rd week of October, national average prices showed generally modest week-on-week movements, while several commodities remained elevated compared with last year and their three-year averages. Rice and cooking oil prices continued to face supply-side pressures amid disruptions to regional trade routes and slower imports. In contrast, pulses remained relatively affordable, supported by increased domestic availability, local production and imports from Central Asia, while restricted export opportunities and weak demand contributed to lower prices. Fuel and fertilizer costs remained elevated, adding pressure to agricultural production, transportation and household purchasing power. Meanwhile, limited demand for improved seeds and animal feed, alongside increased local availability, contributed to lower prices for these inputs.

Food Categories:

National average food prices recorded limited week-on-week movements, although notable annual and longer-term price disparities persisted across commodities.

• Wheat and wheat flour prices increased marginally during the week and show a significant increase year-on-year with wheat grain prices up by 12%, high-price wheat flour up by 7% and low-price up by 11%.

• Rice prices also show a marginal increase from last week and a significant increase from last year, with Palawi rice 18% higher and Sholae rice 32% higher than last year. Moreover, both varieties remained substantially above their three-year averages, by 19% and 21%, respectively.

• Weekly movements in cooking oil, pulses, sugar, salt and bread remained limited. However, cooking oil and sugar prices remain 13% and 9% higher than last year, while pulses and bread show declines.

• Vegetables prices continue to fluctuate modestly during the week. However, compared to last year, potato remained 22% above last year. In contrast, tomato and onion prices were 51% and 7% lower, respectively.

Non-Food Categories:

Terms of Trade (ToT): Purchasing power remained constraint for both labour-dependent households and pastoralists, as declining income and higher prices limit their access to food.

• Unskilled Labour ToT: The nominal unskilled labour ToT stood at 9.8 kg of low-price wheat flour, representing a 14% decline from last year and 12% below the three-year average. The continued deterioration indicates sustained pressure on labour income relative to food prices.

• Labour Availability and Wages: Unskilled labour availability remained at 2.0 days per week, 12% below last year and 20% below the three-year average. Unskilled labour wages also declined by 5% year-on-year, contributing to a 25% decline in the real unskilled labour ToT compared with last year and 30% below the three-year average.

• Pastoralist ToT: A pastoralist could exchange a one-year-old female sheep for 257 kg of low-price wheat flour, 13% below last year's level and 8% below the three-year average, indicating continued pressure on the purchasing power of livestock-dependent households.

• Fertilizers and agricultural input prices show marginal weekly changes. However, year-on-year show mix movements; DAP and urea remained 8% and 23% higher than last year, respectively. Meanwhile, improved seed and animal feed prices remained below last year, by 9% and 6%, respectively.

title: IOM Hurricane Melissa Situation Report #19
content:
Jamaica: IOM Hurricane Melissa Response Situation Report No. 19 (Reporting Period: November 2025 – September 2026)

Nearly one year after Hurricane Melissa impacted Jamaica, IOM continues to support recovery and resilience-building efforts in the country’s most affected communities. This 19th Situation Report outlines progress across shelter rehabilitation, emergency shelter upgrades, non-food item (NFI) assistance, livelihoods support, and psychosocial services delivered in partnership with the Government of Jamaica, local authorities, implementing partners, and affected communities.

Key achievements include shelter repair support reaching 3,989 households, including both light and heavy repairs, alongside Build Back Safer initiatives that have reached approximately 21,000 households through awareness-raising and technical guidance. IOM has also advanced improvements to community centres identified as potential emergency shelters, strengthening preparedness and protection capacities ahead of future hurricane seasons.

During the reporting period, IOM finalized its NFI distribution activities, providing essential household items to vulnerable hurricane-affected families and bringing total beneficiaries of NFI assistance to more than 31,200 individuals. Debris removal and Cash-for-Work interventions have concluded, benefiting 5,928 people while helping restore access to critical infrastructure and supporting local economic recovery. Psychological First Aid activities also concluded after reaching more than 1,000 individuals and training 104 community focal points and volunteers.

Looking ahead, IOM will continue expanding shelter repair assistance, complete upgrades to remaining community shelters, strengthen joint initiatives with UN partners, and undertake post-intervention monitoring to assess impact and inform future preparedness and recovery efforts. The report highlights the importance of sustained partnerships and investment in resilience to help communities better withstand future disasters.

title: Congo Likouala Flood 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRCG030)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

09-10-2026

What happened, where and when?

Between 9 and 10 October 2026, heavy rainfall caused flooding in several localities of the Likouala Department, in the Republic of the Congo. Rainfall continued on 10 October, particularly between midnight and noon in the district of Impfondo and its surrounding areas, worsening the flooding and damage in several neighbourhoods and villages.

The event affected four districts in Likouala: Épéna, Impfondo, Bétou and Dongou. According to preliminary data reported by the Congolese Red Cross, the floods affected a total of 28,135 people across the four districts, including 17,980 people in Épéna and Impfondo combined. In Épéna, most of the villages reported in the initial information were reportedly affected, while in Impfondo, several neighbourhoods and villages were impacted by heavy rainfall and overflowing water. The reported consequences include the destruction of or damage to houses, damage to roads, losses of crops and food stocks, and the destruction of fishing equipment. Several families were forced to leave their homes and seek temporary shelter with relatives or neighbours. The floods also disrupted the livelihoods of affected populations and raised concerns regarding access to safe drinking water and health risks associated with water contamination.

In response to this situation, the Ministry of Social Affairs and Humanitarian Action (MASAH) convened a humanitarian coordination meeting on 9 October 2026 to review the impact of the floods and prepare a joint rapid multisectoral assessment mission. The authorities requested support from humanitarian partners to contribute to the response. The data currently available remain preliminary and will need to be updated and validated through the multisectoral assessment to confirm the extent of needs, identify the most vulnerable households and adjust the intervention targeting, if necessary.

The available figures remain preliminary and require further verification to confirm the extent of the damage and the exact number of people affected.

title: WFP Colombia Country Brief, August 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• From January to July 2026, WFP assisted approximately 423,427 people across Colombia, providing life-saving food assistance and cashbased transfers to populations affected by conflict, climate shocks and mixed migration.

• On 10 August, a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck central-western Colombia, affecting an estimated 466,606 people across 15 departments. Preliminary assessments indicate disruptions to livelihoods, local markets and essential services, increasing food security risks among vulnerable households and generating additional humanitarian needs related to shelter, early recovery and food assistance.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Despite being an upper-middle-income country, Colombia continues to face a complex humanitarian and food security crisis. WFP's joint food security assessment in the 15 most vulnerable departments found that 37 percent of households, equivalent to approximately 7 million people, experience moderate or severe food insecurity. Nationally, food insecurity remains at around 25 percent, with Atlántico, Sucre, and La Guajira reporting the highest prevalence of severe food insecurity.

• The humanitarian situation is further compounded by persistent violence, forced displacement, the presence of non-state armed groups, mixed migration flows, natural hazards, and economic shocks. From January to July 2026, an estimated 814,000 people were affected by violence, while more than 990,000 people were impacted by weather-related events across the country. According to the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP), 6.9 million people require humanitarian assistance in Colombia, including 6.6 million in need of food security and nutrition support. Colombia's decades-long armed conflict has resulted in 10.3 million registered victims, approximately 90 percent of whom are internally displaced persons. In 2025 alone, violence affected more than 1.6 million people and added approximately 150,000 new victims to the official registry.

• This already challenging context was further aggravated by the 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck Colombia on 10 August 2026, affecting an estimated 466,606 people across 15 departments and approximately 145 municipalities. Preliminary assessments indicate humanitarian needs related to shelter, food security, livelihoods and early recovery, while disruptions to local economies, markets and informal livelihoods have reduced household incomes and increased vulnerability among affected populations. WFP's rapid food security impact analysis identified Chocó, Valle del Cauca and Risaralda as the departments with the highest concentrations of highly vulnerable earthquake-affected populations, followed by Quindío and Caldas, highlighting the potential for increased food insecurity among households with limited capacity to withstand additional shocks.

• Colombia also hosts one of the largest migrant populations in Latin America, with approximately 2.8 million migrants residing in the country. By the end of June 2026, 51,938 migrants had entered and transited Colombia irregularly, representing a 38 percent decrease compared to the same period in 2025.

• WFP has operated in Colombia since 1969. Through its Country Strategic Plan, WFP supports national priorities on food security, humanitarian response, early recovery, and peacebuilding, contributing to SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals).

title: WFP Colombia Country Brief, September 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

The earthquake caused significant damage to infrastructure and housing, with more than 242,000 homes affected and 521 roads damaged or destroyed, limiting access to affected communities and the delivery of humanitarian assistance.

By the end of August, 306 municipalities remained under fire-risk alerts, while high temperatures and reduced rainfall continued to pressure water resources, agriculture, and energy generation. Up to 2.9 million people could be affected, exacerbating food insecurity and humanitarian needs.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Despite being an upper-middle-income country, Colombia continues to face a complex humanitarian and food security crisis. WFP's joint food security assessment in the 15 most vulnerable departments found that 37 percent of households, equivalent to approximately 7 million people, experience moderate or severe food insecurity. Nationally, food insecurity remains at around 25 percent, with Atlántico, Sucre, and La Guajira reporting the highest prevalence of severe food insecurity.

• The humanitarian situation is further compounded by persistent violence, forced displacement, the presence of non-state armed groups, mixed migration flows, natural-related emergencies, and economic shocks. From January to August 2026, an estimated 856,000 people were affected by violence, while more than 1.5 million people were impacted by weatherrelated events across the country.

• This already challenging context was further aggravated by the 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck Colombia on 10 August 2026, affecting more than 778,274 people across 15 departments and approximately 145 municipalities. Humanitarian needs continue especially those related to shelter, food security, livelihoods and early recovery, while disruptions to local economies, markets and informal livelihoods have reduced household incomes and increased vulnerability among affected populations. WFP's rapid food security impact analysis identified Chocó, Valle del Cauca and Risaralda as the departments with the highest concentrations of highly vulnerable earthquakeaffected populations, followed by Quindío and Caldas, highlighting the potential for increased food insecurity among households with limited capacity to withstand additional shocks.

• Prior to the August earthquake, the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) had identified 6.9 million people with humanitarian needs in Colombia, driven by armed conflict, displacement, food insecurity, climate-related shocks and mixed migration flows. After the earthquake, the Humanitarian Country Team issued an Addendum to the HRP, estimating that an additional 1.2 million people had humanitarian needs as a result of the emergency, increasing the total number of people in need to 8.1 million. • Colombia also hosts one of the largest migrant populations in Latin America, with approximately 2.85 million migrants residing in the country. By the end of August 2026, 69,072 migrants had entered and transited Colombia irregularly, representing a 39 percent decrease compared to the same period in 2025.

title: Escalation in the Middle East and beyond — Mobility Report - 22 october 2026
content:
17 June 2026, the United States of America and the Islamic Republic of Iran reached an agreement on a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) concerning the cessation of hostilities. The escalation in the Middle East and beyond had triggered a humanitarian crisis affecting multiple regions in an already fragile context. A resurgence of hostilities in recent weeks is placing pressure on humanitarian access and threatens civilian and essential services. Mobility dynamics across the region and beyond due to renewed escalation remains uncertain. The situation continues to be highly fragile, requiring sustained monitoring and operational preparedness.1 In the Islamic Republic of Iran, the humanitarian situation continues to be shaped by recurring escalations.
Disruption to basic services and infrastructure persist while restrictions on maritime and air transports have affected movement and humanitarian access.2 Overall, population movements remain localized, temporary, and economically driven, with no signs of mass displacement.
In Yemen, displacement increased significantly following the escalation of conflict along the West Coast in early September 2026. Between 07 June and 19 October 2026, IOM Yemen DTM recorded approximately 258,679 displaced individuals, the majority of whom were hosted in Ta’iz and Lahj governorates. Many families are experiencing repeated movements and seeking refuge in already overstretched displacement sites and host communities. In addition as of 17 October, 3,836 Yemeni nationals arrived in Djibouti, reportedly fleeing the deteriorating security situation.3 In Lebanon, displacement nationwide remains significant despite continuing returns. As of 29 September 2026, 329,228 people remain internally displaced across 618 cadasters, a 3 per cent decrease compared to the previous reporting period (as of 15 September 2026). Returns have continued, with 877,203 returned IDPs reported as of 29 September 2026, marking a 1 per cent increase from the previous round (as of 15 September 2026).4 Meanwhile, cross-border flows into the Syrian Arab Republic are continuing, with a total of 916,973 movements recorded as of 19 October 2026. Sources include DTM Syria, in coordination with border authorities, the Iraq Border Point Commission, and Pakistani authorities. Increases and decreases noted below are week to week chan

title: WFP Panama: External Situation Report on Earthquake Emergency (21 October 2026)
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• At the request of the Government of Panama, WFP started responding within 24 hours of the earthquake. WFP is currently supporting the national response, in coordination with UN agencies and the humanitarian community, through logistics infrastructure, emergency connectivity, technical assistance and common services for national institutions and humanitarian partners.

• To date, WFP has deployed four Mobile Storage Units (MSUs) to affected areas, alongside additional logistics, power and connectivity equipment, helping strengthen temporary health capacity, humanitarian storage, shelter, and response operations.

• WFP developed a six-month emergency response framework to sustain logistics and telecommunications services and potentially complement Government food assistance. Further assessments and Government requests will inform the scale, targeting and appropriate response modality.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• A powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck Panama on 9 October, with the strongest impacts reported across Los Santos, Herrera, Veraguas, and Coclé provinces.

• The Government declared a national state of emergency on 10 October and established a High-level Inter-Institutional Committee to coordinate the response, including various Ministries and the National Civil Protection System (SINAPROC, for its Spanish acronym) through its Emergency Operations Centre (COE, for its Spanish acronym).

• Assessments are still ongoing, with one fatality and 27 injuries reported to date. At least 35,065 people have been affected, and 5,628 remain in 126 shelters, mainly in Veraguas and Los Santos. Over 4,000 houses, 619 schools, and 120 health facilities have been impacted. Rain, landslides and swollen rivers continue to constrain access to isolated communities and compound water and sanitation gaps.

• WFP visited the areas most affected by the earthquake as part of an initial inter-agency assessment. The mission found that markets are gradually recovering, although functionality remains more limited in smaller rural communities and hard-to-reach areas, requiring further assessments.

title: UNHCR Tunisia Monthly Operational Update (September 2026)
content:
7,515 refugees and asylum-seek-ers* are registered with UNHCR, most from countries affected by armed conflict and widespread vio-lence.

Among them are people with critical protection needs, including victims of torture, gender-based violence survivors, and unaccompanied chil-dren.

UNHCR provides essential assis-tance to persons under its mandate and supports third-country solu-tions, including resettlement and voluntary return

title: Pakistan Weekly Market Monitor (22 October 2026)
content:
• Staple food (wheat flour, edible oils, and pulses) prices remained 24 percent above pre-Middle East conflict levels, as of 22 October, reflecting a combination of domestic market factors and higher fuel and import costs.
  • Wheat flour prices recorded a slight increase (1.0%) during the week, while overall remained 31 percent above pre-conflict levels.
  • The cost of basic food basket for a six-member household stood at PKR 18,719 per month (USD 67) equivalent to PKR 4,680 per week (USD 16.6) nationwide, excluding lower cost items such as vegetables or spices.
  • Petrol and diesel prices remain 47% and 41% above pre-conflict levels despite a slight decline in prices of petrol (-3.6%) and diesel (-1.7%) this week.
  • Regional energy market volatility and disruptions to key shipping routes continue to exert upward pressure on domestic inflation.
  • Food prices remain elevated despite adequate commodity supplies and stable market availability.

title: Multi-Country Ebola Bundibugyo Outbreak Update n°23
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Burundi, Kenya
content:
According to the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as of 18 October 2026, the country had reported 9,552 confirmed cases of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD), including 4,602 confirmed deaths, resulting in a case fatality rate of 48.2 per cent. Since the beginning of the outbreak, 66 health zones across 8 provinces have reported at least 1 confirmed case. Ituri remains the epicentre, accounting for 72.9 per cent of cumulative confirmed cases. During the reporting period, transmission remained concentrated in Ituri and North Kivu. On 18 October, 97 new confirmed cases were reported (48 in North Kivu, 42 in Ituri and 7 in Haut-Uélé), compared with 88 on 11 October. A total of 41 deaths were reported, including 30 community deaths, while 20 patients recovered. The national contact follow-up rate stood at 76.9 per cent, down from 81 per cent on 10 October, highlighting continued gaps in contact follow-up in active transmission hotspots. Laboratory testing remained substantial, with 500 samples analyzed on 18 October with a positivity rate of 19.4 per cent, compared with 20.8 per cent on 11 October. The outbreak continues to place considerable pressure on frontline response capacities. Since the beginning of the outbreak, 269 frontline workers have been affected, including 180 in Ituri and 45 in North Kivu. Continued infections among frontline personnel reinforce the importance of sustained infection prevention and control (IPC) measures, availability of appropriate protective equipment and operational readiness across affected areas

In Kenya, four additional BVD cases were confirmed on 17 October, bringing the national cumulative total to seven confirmed cases, including the deceased index case. The additional cases comprised one close relative of the index case and three health-care workers who had provided care to the index case. Importantly, all four cases were already in quarantine when detected. As of 17 October, 128 of 130 listed contacts (98.5%) had been traced and were in quarantine, and the Ministry of Health reported no evidence of community transmission.

Key highlights include:

  • The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has reported 9,552 confirmed cases and 4,602 deaths. Transmission remains concentrated in eastern DRC, with 97 new confirmed cases reported on 18 October, primarily in North Kivu and Ituri
  • In Kenya, four additional cases were confirmed among known contacts already in quarantine, bringing the cumulative total to seven confirmed cases. Authorities report no evidence of community transmission at this stage.
  • IOM has supported more than 48.2 million health screenings at points of entry and control across affected and at-risk countries since the beginning of the response
  • Nearly 45 million people through risk communication and community engagement activities.
  • Preparedness and response activities continue across DRC, Uganda, Burundi, Rwanda, South Sudan, and Kenya, while preparedness efforts are ongoing in several neighboring countries to strengthen surveillance, community engagement, operational readiness, and cross-border coordination.
  • Population mobility assessments and flow monitoring continue to guide risk-based interventions along high-risk mobility corridors, border areas, and other mobility-affected settings.

For more information, please consult the report HERE

title: UNICEF Yemen Humanitarian Situation Update No.1 (Escalation of Conflict in Yemen), 11 October 2026
content:
Rising Displacement, Cholera and Acute Malnutrition Amid Taiz Escalation

Highlights

  • Escalating hostilities around Taiz and disruption of the main southern supply route are restricting civilian movement and deliveries of essential supplies.
  • IOM recorded over 200K people displaced (estimated 110,000 children) from 3 September to 10 October. New displacement rose by 26 per cent in the week ending 6 October.
  • During the period from 4 to 10 October 2026, the largest concentration of displaced people was reported in Taiz Governorate, hosting 19,950 people (70 per cent)
  • In Taiz, 98 health facilities are partially functional or non-functional. In Lahj, 85 schools have closed because of fighting.
  • UNICEF requires US$13.7 million to expand and sustain the response

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Hostilities around Taiz have intensified, disrupting the Taiz–Aden Road. Infrastructure damage and contested access have effectively cut the city’s main southern supply route, restricting humanitarian and commercial deliveries. Fighting continues around Taiz and along the corridors, increasing risks for families seeking safety and disrupting access to essential services.

In Aden, drone activity and anti-aircraft fire raise concerns for civilian safety and humanitarian operations. On 7 October, the Ministry of Transport reported missile and drone attacks at Aden International Airport, prompting the diversion of an incoming civilian flight and evacuation of passengers and staff. Further disruption could affect civilian travel and humanitarian access.

title: Conflict Escalation in Yemen - Situation Report #8 (Reporting period: 12 – 19 October 2026 | Issued: 20 October 2026)
content:
Highlights

  • Casualties continue to rise on four fronts and a new one has opened in Shabwah. The HEOC register reached 8,513 (6,939 injured, 1,574 deaths) by 19 October, +1,340 in eight days. Daily totals eased to 102–142 between 15 and 18 October, then jumped to 428 on 19 October, the highest single-day report this month, driven by Shabwah (Jardan, 205 casualties, 47 deaths) and Lahj (140).
  • Lethality is up. Deaths made up 21.8% of casualties this period (cumulative 18.5%). Marib accounted for 77 deaths in five days and Shabwah for 51 in two.
  • Taiz city remains the most critical gap. The main Haygat Al-Abd road is cut; 42 facilities in the city report severe shortages of medicines, fuel, oxygen, blood and reagents. The Joint Medical Emergency Committee estimates US$624,900 to keep five public hospitals running for three months (fuel and staff incentives).
  • Displacement keeps growing: IOM DTM counts 256,591 people (42,764 HH) as of 19 October, up from 201,217 on 7 October. RRM has reached 24,164 HH; in Taiz 629 HH were on alert on 19–20 October and none could be assisted.
  • Cholera is trending down but not over. Suspected cases in the five most-affected governorates fell from 639 (W40) to 562 (W41); W42 is incomplete. Part of the drop may reflect reduced care-seeking in conflict areas. MoPHP has asked WHO to support 10 DTCs for three months; supplies reached 8 priority DTCs on 15–18 October.
  • WHO delivered 168 trauma and emergency kits (US$121,198) to five hospitals in Abyan, Aden, Lahj and Marib on 13 October, completed cholera supply deliveries to 8 priority DTCs in Aden, Abyan and Al-Dhale'e on 15–18 October, and began emergency dispatches of TESK, IEHK and medicines to Ataq on 20 October in response to the Shabwah escalation.

title: Doo Tha Htoo District Short Update: Burma Army shelling killed a five-year-old, injured 12 villagers, including two children, and caused destruction in Kyeh Htoh Township (August 2026)
content:
This Short Update describes events occurring in Kyeh Htoh (Kyaikto) Township, Doo Tha Htoo (Thaton) District, in August 2026. On 19 August 2026, at around 11:40 am, Burma Army Artillery Unit #310, under Light Infantry Division (LID) #44, based in Theinzayet Town, Kyeh Htoh Township, fired two 120 mm mortar rounds into Karen National Union (KNU)-controlled areas in Kyeh Htoh Township. One of the mortar shells landed and exploded near a football pitch in Hd--- village, Zi Pyaung (P’Loh Hkee) village tract, Kyeh Htoh Township, sending shrapnel into the football pitch while students, teachers, parents, and villagers were attending a friendly football match between schools. The shrapnel killed a five-year-old kindergarten student, named Saw V---, and injured 12 villagers, including two children. There was no fighting or armed resistance in the area at the time. The injured villagers were transported to Zc--- station hospital in Rk--- Town, administered by the Burma Army, approximately a 30-minute drive from Hd--- village. Following the attack, villagers lived in fear and anxiety, with some stopping work and travel and others continuing to do so cautiously because they had no choice. Students also became too afraid to attend school, resulting in the temporary closure of schools in Zi Pyaung village tract.[1]

On 19 August 2026, at around 11:40 am, Burma Army[2] Artillery Unit #310, based in Theinzayet Town, Kyeh Htoh (Kyaikto) Township, Doo Tha Htoo (Thaton) District, and under the control of Light Infantry Division (LID)[3] #44, based in Kyeh Htoh Township, fired two 120 mm mortar rounds into a KNU [Karen National Union][4]-controlled area [also in Kyeh Htoh Township]. One of the mortar shells landed and exploded in Hd--- village, Zi Pyaung (P’Loh Hkee) village tract,[5] Kyeh Htoh Township, while another mortar shell landed and exploded in Gn--- village, Mok Kha Maunk (Moh Hk’Maw) village tract, Kyeh Htoh Township. [Due to the security situation, KHRG was unable to document any effects of the mortar shell in Gn--- village.] There was no armed resistance force or fighting happening in the area at the time when [Burma Army] Artillery Unit #310 fired the mortar shells indiscriminately. When the Burma Army was firing mortar shells, students, teachers, parents, and other villagers from Js---, Kr---, Ng---, Sj---, and Hd--- villages, [all located in Zi Pyaung village tract,] were holding a friendly football match between schools at a football pitch in Hd--- village [and shrapnel from the explosion hit people on the football field].

One of the Burma Army’s mortar shells landed and exploded on the roof of the house of U[6] S--- and Daw[7] P--- located near the football pitch in Hd--- village. The house was destroyed.

Shrapnel from the explosion hit a 5-year-old kindergarten student named Saw[8] V---, the son of U J---, on his head and he died on the spot. In addition, 12 villagers, all from Hd--- village, were injured by shrapnel. [Saw V--- and all 12 injured villagers were on the football field when they were hit by the shrapnel.] These villagers are:

  • Saw L--- (18 years old), son of U O--- and Daw Q---, was injured on his legs and right palm. He was severely injured.
  • Maung[9] R--- (17 years old), son of U W--- and Daw H---, was injured on his left elbow. He was severely injured.
  • Saw Y--- (18 years old), son of U Z--- and Daw K---, was injured on his back. He was not severely injured.
  • Ma[10] M--- (32 years old), daughter of U S--- and Daw P---, was injured on her back and right thigh. She was severely injured.
  • Maung C--- (18 years old), son of U T--- and Daw I---, was injured on his chest. He was not severely injured.
  • U J--- (37 years old), son of U S--- and Daw P---, was injured on his left hand. He was severely injured.
  • Naw[11] N--- (34 years old), daughter of U X--- and Daw A---, was injured on her left hand. She was severely injured.
  • Maung B--- (19 years old), son of U D--- and Daw E---, was injured on both of his hands. He was severely injured.
  • Saw Aa--- (26 years old), son of U Ak--- and Daw Ag---, was injured on the left side of his torso. He was not severely injured.
  • Saw Ac--- (30 years old), son of U Ae--- (mother’s name unknown), was injured on his thighs. He was not severely injured.
  • Maung Ai--- (11 years old), son of U Aj--- and Daw Al---, was slightly injured on his head. He was not severely injured.
  • Daw P--- (55 years old), daughter of U Ao--- and Daw Ap---, was slightly injured on her head. She was not severely injured.

Shortly after the incident, injured villagers were transported to [Zc---] station hospital, located in Rk--- Town, Kyeh Htoh Township, and administered by the Burma Army. Some of the injured villagers were transported by car from Hd--- monastery, located in Hd--- village, while others were transported from the village in other villagers’ cars. It takes around 30 minutes by car from Hd--- village to the station hospital. The injured villagers still needed to pay treatments fees, but they did not know how much they needed to pay. To help cover the costs of the deceased villager’s funeral, villagers went house to house in Hd--- village collecting donations. A private donor (name unknown) living abroad donated 3,000,000 kyats (1,428.57 USD[12]) and U Ar--- from Pq--- village, Pyin Ka Ton Kone village tract, Kyeh Htoh Township, donated 1,000,000 kyats (476.19 USD) to the family [of the deceased child].

After the incident, even though the villagers did not move to a safer place, they could no longer travel and work peacefully, and their lives were full of fear and anxiety. Some villagers stopped working and travelling altogether, while others continued to work and travel cautiously because they had no choice. Students in the village also no longer dared to go to school, so the schools [in Zin Pyaung village tract] closed temporarily for two weeks. However, due to an air strike in the township [that occurred while the schools were initially closed], schools in Js---, Kr---, Ng---, Sj---, and Hd--- villages remained closed [as of October 2026].

Further background reading on the situation on attacks on villagers in Southeast Burma/Myanmar can be found in the following KHRG reports:

  • ကဘီယူၤဟဲလံ Aircraft coming! : Impacts of air strikes on local communities and villagers’ protection strategies in Southeast Burma since the 2021 coup., November 2024.
  • “Kler Lwee Htoo District Incident Report: A Burma Army landmine injured two displaced villagers in Moo Township (March 2026)”, September 2026.
  • “Doo Tha Htoo District Short Update: Burma Army shelling, air strikes, and arbitrary arrests harmed local villagers in Kyeh Htoh Township (March to December 2025)”, September 2026.
  • “Mergui-Tavoy District Short Update: Burma Army air strike killed a villager in Ler Muh Lah Township (August 2026)”, September 2026.

title: WFP DRC Country Brief September 2026
content:
In August, WFP assisted 1.55 million people in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, distributing 12,179 mt of food and USD 10 million in cash assistance. Beyond sustaining large-scale emergency operations in conflict-affected eastern provinces, WFP played a central role in the Ebola response, providing food assistance to affected households and supporting outbreak logistics. WFP also expanded nutrition services for vulnerable women and children and strengthened community resilience through livelihoods, agricultural production and market access initiatives.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• The humanitarian situation in eastern DRC remains worrying, with North Kivu, South Kivu, Tanganyika, Haut-Uélé and Ituri facing persistent insecurity and ongoing violence.

• Clashes involving armed groups in North and South Kivu triggered significant population movements towards safer areas. In North Kivu, fighting involving the M23 and other armed groups in Walikale, Masisi and Kibabi caused new displacement and further constrained humanitarian access. In South Kivu, clashes along the Kaziba–Ciburhi axis and in Uvira and Fizi territories forced many families to flee to neighbouring communities.

• The displacements have significantly increased humanitarian needs, particularly for food assistance, shelter, healthcare, water, and protection services, while placing additional pressure on host communities and already overstretched basic services.

• The 17th Ebola outbreak in the DRC declared in May continues to spread, worsening an already fragile humanitarian situation. As of 29 September, there were 8,224 confirmed cases, 3,982 deaths, and 2,121 recoveries across 63 health zones in seven provinces.

• In DRC, Ebola-affected areas overlap with regions where nearly 2.6 million people are classified in IPC Phase 3 or above. Movement restrictions and loss of livelihoods could disrupt markets, reduce household income and limit access to food, further worsening acute food insecurity.

title: WFP Rwanda Country Brief, October 2026
content:
In September, WFP assisted 185,528 people across Rwanda, distributing 300 mt of food and USD 521,734 in cash-based assistance. Refugee response remained the core operation, reaching 117,261 refugees, asylum seekers and returnees, though rations remained at 50 percent due to funding constrains. WFP also completed comprehensive socio-economic profiling in all refugee camps to inform future targeting and graduation pathways. At the same time, WFP strengthened national preparedness for floods, drought and Ebola risks, while advancing school feeding initiatives and promoting climate-smart livelihoods to enhance community resilience.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• In September 2026, the average cost of the food basket increased by 3 percent compared with August 2026 and by 7 percent compared with September 2025. Although recent harvests supported domestic food availability, these gains did not translate into sustained price relief, as food inflation and elevated fuel and transport costs continued to place pressure on markets. The rising cost of the basket further constrained refugee households’ purchasing power, particularly given the persistent gap between assistance levels and the cost of meeting minimum food needs.

• With above-average rainfall anticipated during the September–December season because of El Niño, WFP and Government partners intensified contingency planning for floods and landslides. Priorities included defining emergency transfer values and inkind baskets, strengthening early-warning and telecommunications readiness, and testing coordination arrangements through simulation exercises. Rwanda is expected to be highly affected by both drought and floods.

• While Rwanda remains without confirmed Ebola cases, WFP continues to support Government-led readiness through logistics, storage, and coordination support.

title: WFP Malawi Country Brief, October 2026
content:
In September, WFP assisted 409,294 people in Malawi, distributing 136 mt of food and USD 2.4 million in cash assistance. WFP continued supporting over 64,000 refugees and asylum seekers in Dzaleka Refugee Camp while strengthening protection systems ahead of a transition to targeted assistance. WFP also provided home-grown school meals to 161,233 learners in 173 schools and supported a nationwide review of the School Health and Nutrition Policy. To strengthen resilience and food systems, WFP launched a contract farming pilot linking 100 smallholder farmers to buyers and mobilized USD 1.85 million for anticipatory action in drought-prone districts.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Malawi is a small, landlocked country in SubSaharan Africa with a population growing rapidly by 3 percent per year. With most livelihoods dependent on rainfed agriculture, communities are highly vulnerable to the effects of drought and cyclone-induced floods.

• Malawi also faces weak economic growth (GDP growth around 1.8 percent in 2024; International Monetary Fund, 2025), high risk of overall debt distress, low primary school completion (44 percent; Malawi Ministry of Education, Science and Technology, 2025), a high prevalence of stunting (37.6 percent; UNICEF, 2024) and high HIV prevalence (6.2 percent; World Bank, 2025). Together, these factors constrain household income-earning opportunities, weaken resilience to shocks and increase vulnerability to food insecurity, malnutrition and other humanitarian needs, driving continued demand for social protection and humanitarian assistance.

• Recurrent climate shocks, including Tropical Storms Ana and Gombe in 2022, Tropical Cyclone Freddy in 2023, the 2024/25 El Niñoinduced drought, and Tropical Cyclone Jude and Tropical Storm Chido in 2025 have impacted harvest and livelihoods.

• According to Famine Early Warning System Network (FEWSNET), Malawi remains highly vulnerable to climate shocks affecting food security across southern Africa and is projected to be among the countries most severely affected by the forecasted El Niño event.

title: WFP Ethiopia Country Brief, October 2026
content:
In September, WFP assisted 2.1 million people across Ethiopia, delivering 14,212 mt of food and USD 4.5 million in cash assistance. WFP sustained large-scale support despite insecurity and access challenges, reaching 762,335 refugees and expanding nutrition services to 601,100 women and children. WFP also advanced refugee inclusion through digital payment solutions and financial services, while scaling up school feeding to improve access to education and nutrition. In anticipation of worsening drought conditions, WFP positioned to expand assistance in Afar, Amhara and Tigray, where food insecurity and humanitarian needs continue to deepen.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• With nearly 140 million people, Ethiopia is Africa’s second most populous country. Ethiopia has made significant progress in infrastructure, energy development and economic reform.

• Despite this progress, food inflation, climate shocks, insecurity, and displacement continue to heighten food security concerns. Supply routes have been disrupted by hostilities, delaying food assistance in some regions.

• El Nino-related rainfall deficits have contributed to uneven Kiremt rainfall, with relatively favourable conditions supporting crop development in western areas while adversely affecting agricultural production, pasture conditions and water availability in parts of Tigray, Amhara, Afar and eastern Oromia. The Meher harvest is expected to improve food availability in surplus areas, though drought-affected households are likely to face reduced harvests, earlier stock depletion and continued market dependence.

• In southern and southeastern Ethiopia, abovenormal October–December rainfall may improve pasture and water availability, but also increases the risks of flooding, displacement, infrastructure damage and disease outbreaks.

• Ethiopia hosts over 1.13 million refugees and asylum-seekers, including new arrivals from Sudan and South Sudan.

• Humanitarian needs are expected to remain elevated into early 2027, while funding shortfalls continue to constrain the response.

title: WFP Nepal External Situation Report, 22 October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• WFP scaled up cash assistance, reaching 22,428 flood-affected people in Dhading, Nuwakot and Rasuwa.

• The Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster received and stored 2,058 m³ of humanitarian cargo and dispatched 714 mt of partner relief items through logistics hubs in Kathmandu and Nuwakot.

• An additional 1,000 m2 of storage capacity is now available in Dhunche, Rasuwa.

Situation Overview

• Nepal continues to grapple with the impacts of successive floods and landslides, with affected communities facing prolonged recovery needs and damage to homes, livelihoods and critical infrastructure. The devastating 26 August floods in Rasuwa and surrounding areas were followed by flash flooding along the Budhi Gandaki River on 11 October, affecting Gorkha and Dhading and further disrupting infrastructure and access.

• The Joint UN assessment in Gorkha district, following the Budhi Gandaki flood, indicates that immediate humanitarian needs are largely covered through ongoing government relief efforts, with functional markets and adequate food availability; however, medium-term recovery challenges persist for some displaced households due to unresolved land tenure and compensation issues linked to the Budhigandaki Hydropower Project.

WFP Response

• WFP is supporting the Government-led response with the Ministry of Home Affairs and the National Disaster Risk Reduction & Management Authority (NDRRMA) through emergency food assistance, common logistics, field monitoring and assessments.

• WFP distributed 127 mt of food assistance to 15,700 people in the first round, followed by 36 mt food commodities to 4,312 people and 0.52 mt fortified biscuits for 624 students in the second round.

• On 25 September, WFP launched multi-purpose cash assistance, providing flood-affected households NPR 45,000 to cover six weeks of essential food and non-food needs.

• As of 20 October, WFP processed the first cashassistance tranche for 5,216 flood-affected households (20,298 people) across 11 local governments in Dhading, Nuwakot and Rasuwa.

title: Syrian Arab Republic - Emergency Mobility Tracking and Cross Border Monitoring Situation Update - Round 24 (19 October 2026)
content:
Cross-border arrivals from Lebanon continued at a relatively steady pace during the reporting period, with no major departure from the gradual movement pattern observed since the 17 April 2026 ceasefire. Between 2 March and 19 October, DTM recorded 132,574 arrivals across 1,191 communities spanning all 14 governorates of Syria. Syrian nationals accounted for the vast majority of recorded arrivals, while Lebanese nationals represented less than 1 per cent.

Monitoring at four assessed Syrian-Lebanese border crossings recorded approximately 916,973 movements into Syria over the same period, of which 98 per cent involved Syrian nationals and 2 per cent Lebanese nationals. A further 4,780 Lebanese nationals were recorded transiting through Syria towards Jordan, underscoring the country's continued role in facilitating onward movement alongside arrivals into Syria.

Movement patterns continued to vary according to access conditions at individual Points of Entry (PoEs). Arida remains closed following the suspension of operations on 6 August for technical works on the Lebanese side. At the operating PoEs, KIs reported ongoing needs relating to transportation, basic assistance and access to services at and beyond the crossings.

DTM continues to monitor cross-border movements and changes in access conditions, with current findings indicating that movement patterns have remained relatively gradual and stable.

title: UNICEF Ghana Humanitarian Flash Update No. 1 (Yellow Fever Outbreak), 1 - 18 October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • The Ministry of Health in Ghana officially declared a yellow fever outbreak in affected districts of the Upper West Region on 9 October 2026.
  • As of 12 October 2026, the Upper West Region reported 121 suspected cases of yellow fever across 7 of its 11 districts. 19 of the suspected cases were positive for yellow fever with 3 confirmed. All 3 confirmed cases died.
  • Three districts (Wa West, Sissala West and Sissala East) account for 86 cases (71 per cent of all suspected cases).
  • The affected districts are located within a border corridor characterized by high population mobility, including refugee and livestock-raising communities, which may increase the risk of cross-border transmission and complicate surveillance and response efforts.
  • Nearly 50 per cent of suspected cases (60 cases) are in children under 15 years including 16 children under 5 years and 44 children aged 5-14 years.
  • The Government started a reactive vaccination campaign on 14 October 2026 in the 3 districts with PCR-confirmed cases (Wa West, Sissala East and Sissala West), targeting 244,870 eligible persons aged 9 months to 60 years.

Situation Overview

On 31 August 2026, the Upper West Regional Health Directorate was notified of three patients with symptoms of acute haemorrhagic fever. National, regional and district response teams, with support from WHO, conducted active case searches, health-facility record reviews, risk assessments and entomological investigations. Samples were sent to Ghana’s National Public Health and Reference Laboratory, with selected samples referred to a regional laboratory in Dakar, Senegal, for confirmatory testing.

As of 12 October 2026, the Upper West Region had reported 121 suspected yellow fever cases across 7 of the region’s 11 districts. Wa West, Sissala West and Sissala East remain the most affected districts, accounting for 86 of the 121 suspected cases. Children under 15 account for nearly half of suspected cases. Nineteen cases tested positive for yellow fever (IgM-positive). Three cases were further confirmed through advanced laboratory testing in Dakar; all three persons died.

Recorded deaths among investigated cases include 8 institutional deaths and 5 community deaths; not all have been established as yellow fever deaths. Sustained surveillance, timely referral, safe burials and community engagement remain critical.

Following approval from the International Coordinating Group (ICG), the Government undertook a reactive vaccination in Wa West, Sissala East and Sissala West, targeting 244,870 eligible people aged 9 months to 60 years, with a mop-up beginning on 19 October 2026.

UNICEF deployed staff members to monitor the reactive campaign in the three districts. UNICEF also facilitated the procurement of approximately 190,000 vaccine doses to support the reactive vaccination campaign. This campaign is expected to be the primary intervention to interrupt transmission and prevent further spread.
Additionally, UNICEF has been supporting RCCE activities across all seven affected districts. To date, 432 frontline workers and community volunteers have been trained in surveillance, referral, immunization and RCCE; 81 community volunteers, religious and traditional leaders, teachers and media representatives are supporting community engagement activities; 7 radio stations are disseminating lifesaving information; and 250,000 people have been reached through RCCE interventions.

The outbreak is affecting a border region with communities that move with their livestock, as well as refugee and host populations that may face barriers to timely information, vaccination and health services. Misinformation, delayed reporting and resource constraints may further hinder the response. Reactive vaccination, early detection and referral, strengthened surveillance, mosquito-bite prevention and sustained community engagement remain critical to controlling the outbreak.

title: Occupied Palestinian Territory Emergency Response Activity Update #60, 1 - 30 September 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

Nearly one year after the ceasefire took effect, humanitarian needs across Gaza remain severe. Israeli authorities have confined the population to 35 per cent of Gaza; early recovery remains well below the required scale and essential services and infrastructure remain severely damaged. Winterization is particularly urgent, as shelter needs remain immense and essential supplies and services remain severely constrained.

Throughout September 2026, Israeli restrictions on the entry of essential supplies and equipment, together with critical funding shortfalls, continued to endanger civilians and deepen needs as winter approaches. The collapse of a war-damaged residential building in Gaza city on 16 September, reportedly killing 21 people including 12 children, was a stark illustration of the dangers facing the thousands of people sheltering in thousands of damaged structures assessed as unsafe. IOM’s flood risk assessment also points to the scale of what is coming, with close to a million people living on site exposed to flooding as the rainy season begins.

Briefing the Security Council on 28 September, the UN Acting Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, Ramiz Alakbarov, stressed that essential systems and services must be restored without further delay and that winterization efforts must be urgently scaled up and facilitated. He reported that humanitarian access remained severely constrained, with only one crossing open for the passage of goods, and that severe shortages of clean water, medical care, fuel and shelter persisted. The latest report by the Office of the United Nations Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process (UNSCO) calls for the minimum conditions needed to move from humanitarian response to early recovery at scale — with the starting point being Palestinian leadership and ownership.

title: UNICEF Djibouti Humanitarian Flash Update No. 4 (Refugee influx from Yemen), 19 October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • As of 17 October 2026, 3,836 refugees had arrived in Djibouti from Yemen (Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, UNHCR). Children make up 51,8 per cent of the total refugee population (1,987 children). Children under five make up 15,9 per cent of the total population.
  • The Acute Watery Diarrhoea (AWD) remains a serious threat to children. As of 17 October, 56 cases and 3 deaths have been reported and children under 15 account for 71 per cent of cases. While new cases have slowed since the peak of 5 October, the first case in the host community was reported on 14 October and overcrowding and sanitation gaps keep the risk of further spread high. The Ministry of Health leads the response, and UNICEF supports case management, supplies, infection prevention and control (IPC), water treatment and risk communication.
  • Sanitation is the most critical gap. As of 19 October, 43 emergency latrines serve the site, or about 89 people per latrine. The Sphere standard is a maximum of 20 people per latrine. Phase 1 of the site extension alone requires 84 latrines, 84 bathing facilities and 21 water points.
  • Child protection needs are growing. As of 19 October, 13 separated children who arrived with extended family members had been identified through registration and by UNICEF-supported community volunteers. As of 18 October, the UNICEF-supported child-friendly space had reached 540 children (69 per cent girls). As of 13 October, 381 refugee children were enrolled in school.
  • UNICEF requires 3 million United States dollars (USD) to respond to the needs of children and families over six months. As of 19 October, the appeal is 12 per cent funded.

title: Yemen Emergency Response Situation Report #5 (October 22, 2026)

title: WFP Central African Republic Country Brief, October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• More than 2 million people continued to face acute food insecurity, while insecurity, displacement and refugee inflows linked to the Sudan crisis continued to drive humanitarian needs, particularly in northeastern CAR.

• WFP provided food, cash-based assistance, school feeding and resilience support to approximately 117,400 people during September 2026, including refugees, internally displaced persons, returnees and vulnerable host communities.

• WFP advanced preparations for a new round of assistance in Am-Dafock, completing beneficiary verification and registration of 2,311 households (9,634 beneficiaries) and strengthening operational preparedness despite continued access constraints.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• The Central African Republic continues to face high levels of food insecurity and humanitarian need. More than 2 million people are projected to face acute food insecurity, including 262,000 people in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency).

• The country remains affected by a fragile regional environment. Spillover from the conflict in Sudan continues to drive refugee movements, displacement pressures and humanitarian needs, particularly in Vakaga Prefecture and other northeastern border areas.

• Security concerns persist in several areas, including northeastern CAR, where population movements, access constraints and insecurity continue to affect humanitarian operations.

• Humanitarian operations continue to face significant challenges during the rainy season, including deteriorated roads, limited access and logistical delays affecting the movement of relief supplies.

title: WFP Togo Country Brief, October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• Despite improving economic conditions, refugees, IDPs and host communities affected by the Sahel crisis, together with climate-affected households, remain vulnerable to food insecurity and malnutrition, requiring sustained humanitarian and development support.

• WFP school meals have resumed, aiming to reach 77,000 children in the Savanes and Kara regions during the 2026/2027 school year.

• Continued investment in resilience, food systems, social protection, and climate adaptation is critical to protect recent gains and strengthen long-term food security. WFP shares the Government’s vision around resilience and welcomes investments made in strengthening food systems; social protection; and climate adaptation. As a trusted partner, WFP remains committed to supporting these approaches to ensure strengthened agricultural communities and sustainable food security across the country.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Togo has experienced relatively strong economic and agricultural performance in recent years, with real GDP growth over six percent since 2023, supported by public investments and policy measures.

• Favorable harvests and market supply have contributed to generally adequate food availability with staple food prices remaining below the previous year and five-year average in August 2026, supporting food access, including for vulnerable households.

• However, localized climate-related shocks such as land degradation, soil erosion and irregular rainfall continue to constrain agricultural productivity and undermine resilience in affected areas.

• Additionally, in the Savanes region, the spillover effects of the Sahel crisis have led to an influx of over 55,300 refugees and asylum seekers and more than 13,400 IDPs with an additional 3,049 people estimated to be awaiting registration, according to the latest governmental data, increasing pressure on markets, services, and natural resources in areas hosting large numbers of displaced populations.

• Against this backdrop, WFP supports the Government in addressing immediate needs while strengthening longer-term resilience through an integrated approach combining emergency assistance, resilience-building and national system strengthening under the Country Strategic Plan.

title: UNHCR Nigeria Operational Update - January - June 2026
content: Nigeria hosts over 3.7 million internally displaced people, 140,000 refugees and asylum seekers, and 24,000 refugee returnees. Renewed insecurity and violence fuel a severe and deepening protection crisis, disrupting access to basic services and livelihoods. UNHCR works with partners to deliver protection, life-saving assistance, and durable solutions that build resilience and promote self-reliance

title: UNFPA Cameroon Situation Report: Humanitarian Crisis (1 - 30 September 2026)
content:
The humanitarian and protection situation in Cameroon deteriorated further in September amid persistent insecurity, flooding, and disease outbreaks. Escalating attacks by non-state armed groups in the border districts of Waza and Makary displaced more than 11,300 people. The violence was characterized by serious protection violations, including documented incidents of sexual violence against civilians. Displaced populations urgently require humanitarian assistance, particularly dignity kits and essential healthcare, including life-saving sexual and reproductive health services.

Torrential seasonal rains caused widespread flooding across the Logone-et-Chari and Mayo-Tsanaga divisions. Meanwhile, cholera and Mpox outbreaks in Cameroon’s Far North Region have intensified, with reported cholera cases exceeding 2,000 and significant transmission occurring in displacement settings, including Minawao refugee camp. These concurrent emergencies are placing additional pressure on an already overstretched public health system.

In September, UNFPA supported the delivery of sexual and reproductive health services across 22 health facilities in the North-West, South-West, and Far North regions, deploying 33 midwives to strengthen service provision. Through these efforts, 13,805 people accessed essential, life-saving sexual and reproductive healthcare services. In addition, 5,534 people received support through gender-based violence risk mitigation and response interventions, including case management, mental health and psychosocial support, and safe referrals to specialized services.

In 2026, UNFPA requires US$4 million to deliver critical reproductive health and protection services in Cameroon. As of 30 September 2026, US$1.6 million remained unfunded, highlighting the need for additional resources to sustain these essential interventions.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 90, as of 20 October 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Insecurity triggers population displacement in Ouham-Fafa
  • HIV prevention: more than 500 people screened in Mbomou

GENERAL CONTEXT

Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

  • On 16 October, a multisectoral needs assessment mission was unable to reach the locality of Nzako due to access constraints related to the poor condition of road infrastructure. Heavy rainfall recorded in recent weeks has significantly deteriorated the Bakouma–Nzako road, hampering the mobility of humanitarian actors. Approximately 20 km from Nzako, several vehicles in the mission convoy became stuck in the mud, immobilizing the convoy for nearly 24 hours. In the absence of conditions allowing traffic to resume under acceptable safety conditions, the team was forced to turn back. As a result, the planned multisectoral assessment in Nzako could not be carried out as scheduled, limiting the ability of humanitarian actors to comprehensively assess and respond to needs and to obtain an updated analysis of the situation in the locality.

Ouham-Fafa Prefecture – North-West

  • On 14 October, preventive population movements were reported from the villages of Bondili (located 114 km north-west of Batangafo) and Bode, where more than 900 people left their communities to move towards the Kambakota axis or seek refuge in the bush. These movements followed fears of reprisals after the killing of a civilian by armed elements. Access constraints and limitations on independent verification do not, at this stage, allow confirmation of the exact scale of the reported displacement. The situation remains of concern due to the persistent risk of reprisals, threats to civilian protection and the potential for further population displacement.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Health

Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

  • From 12 to 16 October, the French Red Cross, in collaboration with the Bangassou Health District, conducted an HIV and viral hepatitis screening campaign in the health centres of Maliko and Bangui-Ville, as well as Bangondé Hospital. A total of 586 people were screened. Among them, nine tested positive for HIV and 116 tested positive for hepatitis B and were referred to appropriate care and treatment services. The activity aimed to strengthen early diagnosis and improve access to health services for populations in the intervention area.

Protection

Bamingui-Bangoran Prefecture – North-East

  • From 12 to 15 October 2026, the Comité international pour l'aide d'urgence et le développement (CIAUD), through its mobile team, conducted protection monitoring activities in Bamingui-Bangoran Prefecture. A total of 11 protection incidents were identified and documented. All reported incidents involved cases of GBV. Girls were the most affected, accounting for eight of the 11 documented cases. In addition, a community awareness-raising session on the risks and consequences of early and/or forced marriage was organized in the Sultan1 neighbourhood. The activity reached more than 66 people with prevention and protection messages.

title: Attacks on Health Care in the occupied Palestinian territory (01-15 October 2026)
content:
Data collected by Insecurity Insight shows that at least 3,508 attacks on health care took place across the occupied Palestinian territory between 07 October 2023 and 30 September 2026. 95% of all incidents were attributed to Israeli forces. In Gaza, where 2,412 attacks on health care were recorded, health facilities were damaged 459 times, 785 health workers were killed and 399 arrested. In the West Bank, where 1,034 attacks on health care were recorded, health facilities were damaged 33 times, 13 health workers were killed and 200 arrested while ambulances and health workers were prevented from providing vital medical care to people in need over over 630 times.

In Gaza, 157 attacks on health care were recorded between the 10 October 2025 ceasefire and 30 September 2026, with 92% of these incidents attributed to Israeli forces. Health facilities including hospitals, health centres and medicine warehouses were reportedly damaged on 17 occasions. Nearly 90% of these 17 incidents were attributed to Israeli aircraft and drone strikes, artillery fire and gunfire. In one such incident, Israeli forces reportedly bombed medicine stores at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, destroying two of the hospital’s four medicine stores and damaging the remaining two. The strike also damaged the hospital’s outpatient clinic building and vital quantities of medicines and other supplies intended for patients. Two health facilities were deliberately set on fire by Israeli forces while in two other incidents, health facilities were damaged by gunfire from unidentified conflict parties. At least one damaged health facility was reportedly located within the so-called “Green Zone”, an area under Israeli control: Kamal Adwan Hospital was hit by an Israeli quadcopter drone strike that reportedly injured three hospital workers. In some incidents, health workers and patients were harmed. For example, Yemen Al-Saeed Hospital was reportedly hit and damaged by two Israeli missiles that struck the first floor of the facility in the evening, killing three Palestinians, including a woman, and injuring 16 others, including children. Two health facilities were reportedly damaged multiple times since the October 2025 ceasefire: both Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital and Yemen Al-Saeed Hospital were damaged twice.
