title: Eastern Facade Factsheet 08 October 2026
content:
Cameroon’s Eastern Façade, covering the East,
Adamawa and North regions, hosts most of the country’s Central African Republic refugees, many displaced for more than a decade.

More than 80% live in host communities. Funding cuts and pressure on services are deepening vulnerabilities. At the same time, 87.3% of refugees say they wish to remain in Cameroon, making inclusion, access to national services and self-reliance urgent priorities.

UNHCR is shifting from emergency assistance to durable solutions, prioritising refugee inclusion in national systems, local development and self-reliance.
Peaceful coexistence largely prevails despite mounting pressure on basic services and a decline in humanitarian funding

title: Education Factsheet January - August 2026
content:
Cameroon has strong policies for refugee inclusion in education, but funding gaps are keeping children out of class. Less than one in four refugee children are enrolled; more than 152,000 remain out of school; and secondary education is almost out of reach in key refugee-hosting areas.
Predictable donor financing is urgently needed to turn policy commitments into safe classrooms, trained teachers and real learning opportunities — especially for girls, children with disabilities and adolescents at risk of being left behind

title: Health Factsheet January - August 2026
content:
UNHCR Cameroon is supporting a gradual shift from direct health service delivery towards sustainable refugee inclusion in national health systems. This approach strengthens Government ownership, expands refugees’ access to public services and aligns with the Global Compact on Refugees, Cameroon’s National Health Sector Strategy 2016–2027, and the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework.

As national systems are increasingly taking the lead, targeted support remains critical to keep essential services for refugees with chronic and infectious diseases, pregnant women, malnourished children, referral patients and communities affected by public health emergencies.

title: Nepal Flash Flood 2026 Situation Report 7 (15 October 2026)
content:
A major flash flood entered Nepal through the Bhote Koshi River at approximately 9:00 AM on 26 August 2026, causing significant loss and damage across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts. Timure, Rasuwagadhi and Syabrubesi are among the worst affected areas, with impacts reported on communities, markets, roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure.

The cause of the flood remains under investigation, with authorities assessing the possibility of a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) or another upstream hydrological event. The Government of Nepal has mobilised security forces for search, rescue and relief operations and issued alerts for communities downstream along the Trishuli River corridor.

title: Weekly Bulletin on Outbreak and other Emergencies: Week 40: 28 September to 05 October 2026
content:
This Weekly Bulletin focuses on public health emergencies occurring in the WHO African Region. This week’s articles cover:

  • Diphtheria, Senegal
  • Lassa Fever, Nigeria
  • Humanitarian situation, Tchad

For each of these events, a brief description, followed by public health measures implemented and an interpretation of the situation, is provided.

A table is provided at the end of the bulletin with information on all new and ongoing public health events currently being monitored in the region, as well as recent events that have been controlled and closed.

Major issues and challenges include

Senegal: Diphtheria has re-emerged as a significant public health concern in Senegal after more than two decades without reported cases. Since the first confirmed case in July, transmission has spread across multiple regions and health districts, with the highest burden reported in Kédougou, Diourbel, Dakar,
Louga and Thiès. Cases in densely populated Dakar and Touba, a major religious centre with substantial population movement, increase the risk of further spread. Transmission appears to be driven by immunity gaps, with cases among schoolaged children, adolescents and adults suggesting waning or missed booster protection, while unvaccinated and children with unknown vaccination status indicate gaps in routine immunization and documentation. The high case fatality, particularly among unvaccinated young children, raises concerns about delayed care-seeking, referral, access to diphtheria antitoxin and quality clinical care.
Limited clinical familiarity may further delay recognition and treatment.

title: Yemen Situation: UNHCR Emergency Update - External Update #4 (12 October 2026)
content:
Highlights

  • Displacement inside Yemen continued to rise sharply, reaching close to 213,000 people between 1 August and 10 October, with Taiz hosting the largest share of those displaced. UNHCR is part of the inter-agency response under the Yemen Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP). In light of the recent escalation, UNHCR requires US$25 million to support an estimated 231,000 people with protection services, including monitoring, legal assistance and support for people at heightened risk, cash assistance, shelter and core relief items (CRIs).
  • A total of 4,003 people have arrived in Eastern Africa from Yemen, including 3,807 refugees in Djibouti and more than 196 people in Somalia.
  • Reportedly, some 20,000 Ethiopians have also recently arrived from Ethiopia to Djibouti. UNHCR remains ready to support the national authorities in ensuring access to asylum and appropriate protection procedures for persons seeking international protection.
  • UNHCR is deeply saddened by the deaths of least 139 people, including multiple children, following the capsizing of a boat carrying more than 305 Ethiopians off the coast of Djibouti travelling to Yemen late last week. With more than 80 people still missing, the number of deaths may grow. Our teams are working with IOM and government partners on the ground to assess protection needs and are providing counseling for survivors.

title: NCDC Lassa Fever Situation Report Epi Week 40: 28th September – 4th October 2026
content:
Highlights

• In week 40, the number of new confirmed cases decreased from 13 reported in epi week 39 of 2026 to 3. These were reported in Bauchi and Benue States (Table 3).

• Cumulatively, 268 deaths have been reported with a Case Fatality Rate (CFR) of 23.6% which is higher than the CFR for the same period in 2025 (18.6%).

• In total for 2026, 24 States have recorded at least one confirmed case across 119 Local Government Areas (Figures 2 and 3).

• Eighty-eight percent (88%) of all confirmed Lassa fever cases were reported from 5 states (Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo and Benue) while twelve percent (12%) were reported from 19 states with confirmed Lassa fever cases. Of the 88% confirmed cases, Ondo reported 36%,
Bauchi 23%, Taraba 12%, Edo 11% and Benue 6%.

• The predominant age group affected is 21-30 years (Range: 1 to 93 years, Median Age: 30 years). The male-to-female ratio for confirmed cases is 1:0.9 (Figure 4).

• The number of suspected and confirmed cases increased compared to that reported for the same period in 2025.

• No new healthcare worker was affected in the reporting week 40.

• National Lassa fever multisectoral multi-partner Technical Working Group (TWG) continues supporting the coordination of activities at all levels.

title: Nepal - Gorkha–Budhigandaki Flash Flood: Search, Rescue and Relief Response Situation Report #03 (13 October 2026) [EN/NE]
content:
NDRRMA prepared this report using information received from the District Administration Office and the District and National Emergency Operation Centers. It summarizes search, rescue and relief operations following the Budhigandaki flood in Gorkha and Dhading districts.

SITUATION OVERVIEW (BASED ON TECHNICAL REPORT)

At approximately 04:20 on 11 October 2026 (25 Asoj 2083), a snow avalanche at about 6,000 m elevation and a major landslide involving glacier ice and debris at approximately 5,500 m occurred in the upper reaches of Ungdilung Khola, Chumnubri Rural Municipality–6, between Chamar Himal and Syerang Himal. The area contains relatively weak rocks of the Tibetan Tethys Himalaya.

Smaller landslides were observed both before and after the principal failure. The mixed flow of snow, water and debris traveled south down the steep Ungdilung valley, rising as much as 300 m along the valley sides. At about 2,000 m elevation, large quantities of debris accumulated at the narrow confluence of Ungdilung and Syar Khola, repeatedly blocking and releasing the water flow. Similar temporary blockage may also have occurred at the Syar Khola–Budhigandaki confluence. These processes produced multiple flood surges downstream.

The unusually large volume of debris from Ungdilung Khola appears to have contributed more to flood height than the water impounded in Syar Khola. Mud-laden flooding first reached Salleri at approximately 04:30. The largest surge, with an estimated height of 20–25 m, swept away the hydropower camp at Salleri at approximately 06:30. It damaged buildings, especially at Jagat, and infrastructure including permanent bridges at Soti Khola and across the Budhigandaki.

About one hour before the highest surge, the flow in Syar Khola had stopped. Field observations indicate that water had accumulated for approximately 1.5 km upstream. Smaller surges followed the main surge.

Compared with typical floods, the flow carried an unusually high proportion of fine soil relative to sand and rocks, giving it the characteristics of a viscous mudflow. This is consistent with the soil-rich layered rocks and debris at the source area. A preliminary estimate by the Department of Mines and Geology indicated that the landslide released energy equivalent to that of a magnitude 3.5 earthquake.

title: Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda Weekly External Situation Report 22, Data as of 11 October 2026
content:
Democratic Republic of the Congo

The BVD outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to evolve, expanding both geographically and in
terms of the numbers of cases and deaths. The Dakwa Health Zone in Bas-Uélé Province has become the latest affected
health zone, bringing the total number of impacted health zones to 65 across seven provinces since the start of the
outbreak. Transmission remains highly heterogeneous across these regions. Since External Situation Report #21, a total
of 463 additional confirmed cases and 233 confirmed deaths have been reported. This increases the cumulative total
to 9066 confirmed cases, including 4381 confirmed deaths [crude case fatality ratio (CFR) 48.3%] as of 11 October 2026.
Ituri remains the principal focus of the outbreak, though its relative contribution is declining; it is currently for 73.8%
of cumulative confirmed cases. Substantial transmission persist in Nord-Kivu and Haut-Uélé.

National incidence remains high and fluctuating, with no sustained downward trajectory evident. Following rapid
expansion through July and August, the epidemic has entered a more heterogeneous phase characterized by repeated
declines and rebounds. This pattern reflects asynchronous transmission across provinces and health zones; declining
activity in established Ituri hotspots is being offset by persistent or renewed activity elsewhere, particularly in Nord-
Kivu, while sporadic detections continue to extend the geographic footprint. The overall trend suggest a shifting and
geographically fragmented epidemic than sustained contraction.

title: UNHCR Emergency Response: Earthquake in Panama – October 13 2026
content:
Situation

On 9 October, Panama experienced one of the strongest earthquakes in its history. With a magnitude of 7.5, an epicentre on the Azuero Peninsula, and more than 400 aftershocks recorded to date, the earthquake affected several provinces, causing severe damage to homes and critical infrastructure in communities across Panama's countryside.

As of 12 October, authorities reported over 3,000 affected homes, damage to more than 650 schools, at least 27 people injured, and hundreds displaced, evacuated, and nearly 600 staying in 14 temporary shelters. Among those affected are refugee families, as well as other vulnerable populations. The full extent of the losses has not yet been quantified, but the Government declared a state of emergency to mobilize up to USD 100 million for response efforts. President Mulino reported that more than 6,000 people have been affected and that the government is implementing recovery measures, including a housing reconstruction programme.

Heavy rainfall, rising river levels and landslides in affected areas have hindered the delivery of humanitarian assistance and the assessment of the most urgent needs. Several communities remain inaccessible, with no access roads, safe drinking water or electricity.

UNHCR joined the Government of Panama-led response and has mobilized over 33 metric tons of core relief items (CRIs) to date, including family tents, blankets, mosquito nets, kitchen sets, a rub hall and other essential supplies. The Agency remains in contact with authorities and community leaders, supporting efforts to address the most urgent needs, particularly for the most vulnerable.

title: Global Weather Hazards Summary, October 15, 2026 – October 21, 2026
content:
Global Overview: El Niño continues to strengthen. Long-term abnormal dryness and abnormal heat persist across areas of Africa, northern Central Asia, Central America, Hispaniola, and northern South America.

Africa Weather Hazards

Abnormal heat is forecast in the eastern Sahel and parts of Eastern Africa, while high risks of flooding with ongoing heavy rain in the horn of Africa.

1) Inundation in the Sudd wetlands of South Sudan persists.
2) Large 90-day rainfall deficits have led to abnormal dryness across Chad and large parts of Eastern Africa. As a result, deteriorated vegetation conditions, driven by drought, have been observed over western Sudan, southern and southeastern South Sudan, northern Uganda, and parts of Ethiopia's northern, eastern, and central regions.
3) Central Mali and central/eastern Liberia and southern Cote D’Ivoire are under Abnormal Dryness because of sustained below-average rainfall over the past 30 and 90 days.
4) Recent heavy rainfall has caused flooding in southern Ethiopia and parts of Somalia with more heavy rains ongoing.
5) The forecast heavy rainfall elevates flood risk in Guinea-Conakry, Sierra Leone, and western Liberia, as well as western Kenya during the next week.
6) Abnormal heat is forecast in southern Chad, eastern CAR, southern Sudan, South Sudan, and northwestern Uganda, along with eastern South Africa, as well-above-average temperatures are expected to persist for 3 or more consecutive days in this region during the next week.

title: UNICEF South Sudan Humanitarian Response Update (From Isolation to Assistance: UNICEF RRM - Lankien and Buong, Jonglei State), September 2026

title: Ukraine war situation update | 26 September – 2 October 2026
content:
Ukraine Conflict Monitor Update

Key trends

Russia intensified its strikes on civilians and critical infrastructure over the past week, with mass casualty incidents reported almost daily. Among the most deadly strikes, attacks in Kharkiv on 5 October, Pryluky on 7 October, and Kramatorsk on 8 October killed six, 22, and at least 32 civilians, respectively. Repeated mass casualty incidents point to a sustained threat to civilians and increase pressure on and danger to emergency responders across the country. Ukraine’s struggle to intercept faster, jet-powered Shahed drones compounds the threat as Russia has started intensifying strikes on civilian infrastructure ahead of winter. Although Russia has deployed fewer jet-powered drones on average per night so far in October than in September, it has increasingly dispersed them in smaller groups across the country, stretching Ukraine’s air defence and contributing to mass casualty incidents in multiple regions.
In Russia, Ukraine has expanded its strike campaign against Yandex data centers that host services ranging from online searches to transportation, entertainment, cloud services, and AI. A drone strike on 8 October disabled the company’s data center in Sasovo, while a subsequent attack on its largest facility in Kaluga disrupted services. The strikes were likely intended to counter Russia’s attack on Ukrainian data centers, weaken Russia’s technological capabilities, and increase economic pressure on Russia. Yandex was forced to operate its cloud infrastructure in emergency mode, indicating the scale of the damage. The disruption could have long-term consequences, as replacing high-tech hardware and restoring full capacity may take months, if it’s even possible at all.

Full update

title: WFP Eastern and Southern Africa Seasonal Outlook: Eastern and Southern Africa Regional Office (ESARO) - October 2026
content:
Highlights

• Above-normal rainfall and above-average temperatures are favoured across much of Eastern Africa during October to December 2026. Southern Ethiopia, central and southern Somalia and Kenya show the strongest wet signal, increasing extreme rainfall and flood risks.

• Much of central and southern Southern Africa is expected to receive below-normal rainfall and experience above-average temperatures during the 2026/27 rainy season. Dry spells could disrupt planting and crop development. Wetter conditions are favoured in some northern areas and along much of the Angolan coast.

• Food insecurity is expected to rise across the region as a result of this outlook: in Southern Africa, drought is likely to reduce maize harvests, push up staple prices and deepen the October 2027 to March 2028 lean season, while in Eastern Africa flooding threatens displacement and crop and livestock losses from October 2026.

• Preparedness actions are critical to limit how far seasonal rainfall impacts translate into food insecurity. These include early warning and close seasonal monitoring, anticipatory action for drought and floods, prepositioning of stocks, and early response planning with governments and partners.

title: Myanmar monthly food price report - August 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS:

  • Rice prices increased substantially in August 2026, with the national average rising by 5.2 percent monthon-month and 14.9 percent year-on-year. Regional price disparities persisted, reflecting differences in production conditions, market access, and transportation costs. The country-wide increase in retail rice prices was reportedly associated with flood-related concerns, supply disruptions, and transportation difficulties.
  • Export crop prices showed mixed movements. Maize prices declined month-on-month but remained substantially above year-earlier levels, while black gram and pigeon pea prices also remained elevated year-on-year. Green gram prices declined while chickpea prices increased. Vegetable prices generally increased in August. Chili and onion prices rose sharply, supported by constrained supplies and continued export demand, while garlic prices increased following a seasonal pattern. Potato prices rose more moderately.
  • Most animal-sourced food prices remained substantially above year-earlier levels. Chicken, eggs, mutton, beef, and fish prices increased year-on-year, with mutton prices remaining at record highs. In contrast, pig prices declined both month-on-month and year-on-year amid reports of swine disease and weaker pork demand in Yangon. Reports of livestock disease affecting poultry, pigs, and cattle also raised broader animal health concerns.
  • The conflict in Iran has led to a partial closure of the Strait of Hormuz — a major transit route for global oil and fertilizer trade — while fighting has also escalated in the Red Sea, another key shipping corridor. Together, these disruptions are raising concerns for Myanmar's agrifood system, which depends heavily on fuel for transportation, irrigation, mechanization, and processing. Fertilizer prices also remain substantially above last year’s levels, possibly reducing the profitability of fertilizer use and leading to lower application rates and agricultural production.
  • Flooding intensified during August, particularly in major rice-producing areas of Ayeyarwady and Sagaing. Flooding reportedly inundated approximately 97,000 acres in Ayeyarwady and affected more than 10,000 acres of paddy and other cropland in Sagaing. Meanwhile, strengthening El Niño conditions could bring additional risks from irregular rainfall, higher temperatures, and drought, potentially affecting agricultural production and food supply.
  • The outlook for Myanmar food prices will remain influenced by export demand, border trade conditions, input costs, and weather-related risks. Concerns over pulses production in India could support demand for Myanmar’s black gram and pigeon pea, while softer Chinese demand for green gram remains a concern. Changes in Thailand’s maize import arrangements and continued volatility in border trade stations could also affect agricultural market flows and will be important to monitor in the coming months.

title: Food Security Monitor - September 2026
content:
Global Market Updates

  • Global food commodity markets remained under upward pressure in September 2026 despite some month-on-month easing in grain and oilseed prices. The FAO Food Price Index rose by 1.5% from August and was 5.8% higher than a year earlier, driven by increases in cereals, vegetable oils, and sugar, reflecting Black Sea and Middle-East export disruptions, weather-related production risks, and tightening global supplies.

    While the International Grains Council’s Grains and Oilseeds Index declined by 3.4% during the month, it remained 19.5% above September 2025 levels, highlighting continued underlying market tightness. Wheat and maize prices eased from recent highs but remained significantly above year-earlier levels, while soyabeans recorded the strongest annual increase and rice continued to strengthen both monthly and annually.

    Overall, the data indicate that although short-term price corrections emerged in September, global food markets remain characterized by elevated prices, supply uncertainty, and persistent inflationary pressure across major grains and oilseeds.

  • Global fertilizer markets remained firm in September 2026, with phosphate fertilizers leading price increases, potash remaining relatively stable, and urea recovering after earlier declines. DAP and MAP prices continued to rise on sustained demand, while potash recorded modest gains under balanced market conditions.

    Urea posted the strongest monthly increase, signaling a stabilization of nitrogen fertilizer markets following significant volatility earlier in the year. Although the Hormuz crisis has so far had limited impact on fertilizer availability due to advance purchases, inventories, and domestic production, it has contributed to higher fertilizer, fuel, and transportation costs.

    Rising input costs are prompting farmers to adopt more efficient nutrient management practices and could eventually reduce fertilizer application rates and shift production toward less input-intensive crops. Consequently, the greatest risk to agriculture is not an immediate supply shortage but the gradual erosion of fertilizer affordability, which could weaken productivity, reduce output, and increase food security risks if elevated input costs persist.

  • Across Africa, fertilizer prices showed mixed trends in September 2026, with Rwanda recording the strongest and most sustained increases in both NPK and urea prices, while Malawi and Mozambique continued to experience notable longer-term price growth despite some recent easing. In contrast, Uganda and Zambia saw significant declines in several fertilizer categories, reflecting market corrections after earlier increases.

    Zambia’s expanding domestic fertilizer blending and granulation capacity is helping reduce prices, particularly for NPK fertilizers, but because the country still relies heavily on imported raw materials such as urea, DAP, and potash, fertilizer prices remain significantly influenced by global market conditions, exchange rates, and transport costs.

    West African markets were generally more stable, with Ghana experiencing sharp short-term declines in urea prices and Nigeria recording modest price reductions and overall market stabilization. Regionally, the data suggest that fertilizer affordability remains a concern in parts of East and Southern Africa, while price pressures have eased in several West African markets, resulting in increasingly divergent fertilizer cost and input access conditions across the continent.

  • As part of efforts to mitigate the impacts of the energy and fertilizer crisis, the African Development Bank Group has approved the Global Energy and Fertilizer Crisis Response Framework (GEFCRF), a one-year, demand-driven initiative backed by approximately USD 5.1 billion in additional financing to help African countries mitigate the impacts of the ongoing global energy, food, and fertilizer crisis. Triggered by rising commodity prices, supply chain disruptions, and trade bottlenecks linked to Middle East tensions, the framework aims to provide immediate relief while strengthening long-term resilience.

    Building on lessons from the Bank’s COVID-19 and emergency food production responses, the GEFCRF will support countries through four pillars: stabilizing macroeconomic conditions through rapid financing and policy support; securing food, energy, and fertilizer supplies while protecting vulnerable populations; safeguarding essential public spending and targeted social protection for women, youth, and other at-risk groups; and advancing reforms that reduce dependence on volatile external markets, strengthen regional supply chains, and enhance resilience to future shocks.

Food Commodity Prices Updates

  • Maize prices in Eastern Africa exhibited mixed trends between August and September when expressed in USD terms. Prices declined in South Sudan (-31.5%), Uganda (-4.3%), and Kenya (-3.2%) due to improved market supplies, stronger cross-border inflows, and increased regional trade, although South Sudan remained the most expensive maize market at USD 1,006/MT.

    Conversely, Ethiopia (+7.9%), Rwanda (+6.8%), and Tanzania (+4.6%) recorded price increases, reflecting tightening domestic supplies and sustained demand, with Tanzania remaining the lowest-priced market at USD 227/MT.

    However, local currency trends reveal more pronounced market pressures in some countries. Ethiopia continued to face significant inflationary pressures, with maize prices rising sharply and remaining 49-76% above six-month and year-earlier levels, while Rwanda also experienced moderate increases. In contrast, Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania recorded generally lower prices than six months and one year earlier, reflecting improved supplies and recent harvests, although South Sudan’s prices remained above historical levels despite the sharp monthly decline.

  • Rice prices across the region were relatively stable in USD terms, with modest increases in South Sudan (+4.0%), Tanzania (+3.9%), and Uganda (+0.7%), while Kenya (-1.8%) and Rwanda (-1.1%) registered slight declines. Kenya remained the region’s highest-priced rice market despite the decrease, whereas Tanzania remained relatively competitive.

    In local currency terms, trends were more varied. South Sudan experienced the strongest upward pressure, with rice prices increasing 5.6% month-on-month and remaining 27-40% above levels recorded three and six months earlier, reflecting persistent supply constraints and import dependence. Uganda and Tanzania also recorded moderate monthly increases, although Tanzania’s rise occurred within a broader medium-term downward trend.

    Meanwhile, Kenya and Rwanda continued to experience easing rice prices, with declines recorded across recent months; however, Rwanda’s rice prices remained over 20% above year-earlier levels, indicating that longer-term inflationary pressures have not yet fully subsided.

  • Maize prices in Southern Africa generally increased between August and September in USD terms, reflecting seasonal tightening and localized supply pressures. Malawi recorded the largest increase (+10.0%), followed by Zambia (+4.3%) and Mozambique (+1.0%).

    Although Malawi remained the highest-priced maize market when using the official exchange rate, prices converted using the parallel exchange rate suggest it was among the lowest-priced markets in the region, highlighting the influence of exchange-rate distortions on regional comparisons.

    In local currency terms, Malawi also recorded the strongest monthly increase (+9.9%), while Zambia (+4.4%) and Mozambique (+0.9%) registered more modest gains. However, despite these recent increases, maize prices in all three countries remained below six-month and year-earlier levels, indicating that improved harvests and better market supplies continue to support a broader medium- to long-term downward price trend.

  • Rice prices showed more varied movements across Southern Africa. In USD terms, prices increased in Malawi (+5.9%) and Mozambique (+2.3%), reflecting continued supply constraints, stronger demand, and higher import costs, while Zambia recorded a significant decline (-11.0%) due to improved market availability and easing domestic market pressures.

    Local currency trends mirrored these movements, with rice prices rising in Malawi and Mozambique but falling sharply in Zambia. Despite recent increases in Malawi and Mozambique, rice prices remained below levels observed six months earlier, reflecting broader market normalization.

    Zambia exhibited the strongest easing trend, with rice prices declining across all comparison periods, including three-month, six-month, and year-on-year intervals, pointing to sustained improvements in market availability and reduced pressure in the domestic rice market.

  • Maize prices in West Africa showed mixed movements between August and September in USD terms, with Mali standing out as the only market recording a substantial increase (+17.4%) as tightening supplies and reduced inflows strengthened prices.

    By contrast, maize prices declined in Togo (-7.3%), Niger (-5.0%), Ghana (-2.8%), and Burkina Faso (-2.1%), while Nigeria remained largely stable (+0.8%), reflecting improved market availability and easing supply pressures in several countries.

    Local currency trends indicate that although short-term movements were mixed, maize prices generally remained below year-earlier levels across the region. Mali experienced the strongest upward pressure, with prices rising sharply in key markets and recording positive medium-term growth, while Ghana, Niger, and Nigeria saw relatively stable monthly prices but still remained below last year’s levels. Togo recorded broad-based declines across all monitored markets and time periods, and Burkina Faso generally showed stable to declining trends, suggesting improved regional maize availability and continued market normalization.

  • Rice prices declined across all monitored West African markets in USD terms, reflecting improved supplies and easing market pressures. The largest declines were recorded in Nigeria (-18.3%) and Mali (-12.9%), followed by Togo (-5.2%), Niger (-4.3%), Ghana (-2.9%), and Burkina Faso (-2.0%). Despite the decline, Ghana remained the highest-priced rice market in the region.

    Local currency trends broadly mirrored the USD movements, with Nigeria recording the sharpest and most sustained declines across all comparison periods, indicating significantly improved availability and easing inflationary pressures. Togo also experienced widespread declines, while rice prices in Niger remained largely stable with modest medium-term increases.

    In Mali, local rice prices fell in most markets, although imported rice prices strengthened in some locations, highlighting divergent trends between domestic and imported supplies. Burkina Faso presented a mixed picture, with stable prices in most markets but notable increases in select locations, while Ghana’s rice prices remained broadly stable despite continuing to trend below year-earlier levels.

    Overall, regional rice markets showed clearer signs of easing than maize markets, supported by improved supply conditions and lower prices compared to a year ago.

Food Security Updates

  • East Africa’s food-security outlook remains highly uneven, shaped by conflict, production deficits, displacement, high prices and the contrasting effects of El Niño. Severe food insecurity persists in conflict-affected and drought-prone areas, particularly in Ethiopia and South Sudan, where below-average harvests, disrupted livelihoods and restricted market and humanitarian access are driving Crisis (IPC Phase 3), Emergency (IPC Phase 4) and, in parts of South Sudan, Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5) outcomes.

    At the same time, above-average October–December rainfall could improve water availability, pasture, livestock productivity, second-season crop production and agricultural labour opportunities in parts of Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania. These potential gains will be uneven and may be offset by flooding, waterlogging, crop and infrastructure damage, disease outbreaks and disrupted market access in flood-prone areas.

    The central policy challenge is therefore to manage a dual hazard: sustain drought recovery and production support where rainfall is beneficial while pre-positioning flood protection, market-continuity measures and humanitarian access in high-risk locations.

  • Southern Africa’s food-security outlook is expected to deteriorate through the 2026/27 lean season as household food stocks decline, purchasing power weakens and the risk of a strong El Niño production shock increases. Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia and Zimbabwe are likely to see Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes expand, with localized Crisis (IPC Phase 3) emerging among households that enter the season with limited stocks, low incomes and high dependence on markets.

    Current national maize availability and favourable recent harvests provide a temporary buffer in parts of the region, but this protection is uneven and may erode if the rainy season starts late, rainfall becomes erratic, temperatures remain above average and agricultural labour demand falls.

    Conflict in northern Mozambique, livestock disease restrictions, high fuel and transport costs and declining rural incomes will further reduce households’ capacity to absorb production losses. Preparedness should therefore focus on preserving grain-market stability, safeguarding planting and livestock assets, expanding water management and climate-resilient production, and pre-financing targeted assistance before stocks and incomes deteriorate further.

  • Food security conditions across West Africa remain mixed but continue to be heavily shaped by conflict, insecurity, climatic shocks, and high food prices. Severe food insecurity persists in conflict-affected areas of the Central Sahel and Lake Chad Basin, with Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes reported in parts of Mali and northeastern Nigeria, while Crisis (IPC Phase 3) conditions are expected to continue through early 2027 in insecure areas of Burkina Faso, Niger, northern Nigeria, and parts of Mali.

    Armed conflict and population displacement continue to disrupt agricultural production, market functioning, trade flows, and access to livelihoods, particularly in Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, and Nigeria. Across much of the region, delayed and erratic rainfall, prolonged dry spells, poor pasture conditions, and localized crop losses are expected to result in below-average agricultural and livestock production, further constraining food availability and incomes.

    Although the start of the harvest season is expected to improve food access and reduce prices in many areas, especially in Mali, Niger, and Togo, high staple food prices, reduced purchasing power, and ongoing insecurity continue to limit recovery for vulnerable households.

    In contrast, coastal countries such as Togo are benefiting from favourable production prospects and improved food availability, while northern Côte d’Ivoire faces increasing food security risks from cross-border insecurity, below-average rainfall, and declining cocoa incomes, highlighting widening disparities in food security outcomes across the region.

Update on El Niño Conditions

  • The 2026/27 El Niño is intensifying rapidly and is expected to remain strong through early 2027, creating sharply differentiated food-security risks across Africa. The most serious near-term concern is Southern Africa, where delayed and erratic rainfall, prolonged dry spells and above-average temperatures could reduce crop and pasture production and tighten regional maize supplies in 2027.

    In East Africa, impacts are likely to be mixed: enhanced October–December rainfall may improve water, pasture and second-season production in some areas, while flooding, waterlogging, crop damage and disrupted market access could worsen food insecurity elsewhere. In the Sahel, localized rainfall deficits may compound conflict, displacement and high prices.

    Governments and partners should therefore use forecast-based triggers to protect strategic food reserves, keep regional trade corridors open, pre-position agricultural and livestock support, expand irrigation and water management, and finance scalable social protection before the 2027 lean season.

Food Trade Updates

  • The AfCFTA Secretariat and Quest Ghana Limited have signed an agreement to develop a digital trade corridor aimed at more than doubling intra-African commerce from approximately $200 billion to $500 billion.

    The initiative will integrate a digital marketplace, minerals and commodities exchange, interoperable cross-border payments and logistics infrastructure, potentially reducing the more than $5 billion annual cost of intra-African trade payments. Supported by Seychelles, the project targets improved trade access for businesses, including SMEs.

  • Somalia has become the 50th State Party to the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) after depositing its instrument of ratification on 4 September 2026, securing full legal participation in Africa’s single market and enabling Somali businesses to benefit from AfCFTA preferences once they meet applicable rules of origin.

    However, ratification alone does not guarantee immediate preferential market access, as Somalia must still align its customs systems, implement AfCFTA tariff schedules, and fulfil outstanding regional trade commitments, including within the East African Community.

    Somalia’s accession reflects the broader shift in AfCFTA from agreement ratification to practical implementation, as countries work to address customs, tariff, standards, payment, and value-chain challenges that continue to limit intra-African trade. With support from the AfCFTA Secretariat, Somalia is now focused on translating its legal membership into tangible commercial opportunities for exporters and businesses across the continent.

  • On 21 September 2026, Afreximbank and the Africa Trading and Distribution Company (ATDC) signed a US$500 million Global Credit Facility to strengthen trade, logistics, and distribution networks across Africa, supporting the aggregation, transportation, warehousing, and movement of African goods.

    Operating initially in Egypt, Nigeria, Malawi, and Zimbabwe, ATDC will use the financing to expand trade corridors, improve market access, enhance supply chains, promote local value addition and import substitution, and accelerate implementation of the AfCFTA. The facility is expected to deepen regional value chains, increase the availability of raw materials and value-added products, boost intra-African trade, and improve the competitiveness of African exports in regional and global markets.

  • Zimbabwe has secured financing of approximately US$66.8 million to modernize the Chirundu One-Stop Border Post with Zambia under a public-private partnership, with construction expected to begin in October and be completed within 18 months.

    The upgrade will replace aging infrastructure and introduce advanced technology and operational systems to improve cargo processing, reduce congestion, and shorten delays along one of Southern Africa’s most important trade corridors linking the Copperbelt to ports in South Africa and Mozambique. Handling key commodities such as copper, cobalt, fuel, fertilizer, mining equipment, and agricultural products, the upgraded border post is expected to lower logistics costs, facilitate regional trade, and strengthen Zimbabwe’s role as a regional transport and logistics hub.

  • Nigeria has reduced the processing time for AfCFTA Certificates of Origin from over five days to just 24 hours through the digitisation and automation of registration, verification, and certification procedures, enabling businesses to access AfCFTA trade preferences more quickly and improve competitiveness.

    The country has also resolved eight non-tariff barrier cases, facilitated access to the AfCFTA Adjustment Fund, advanced a domestication bill for the agreement, and launched digital trade initiatives, while trade missions and business engagements have already generated export opportunities.

title: TCD: Food Insecurity - 10-2026 - Food crisis due to rainfall deficit
content:
Sources for data marked as Other

Estimates of the 2,990,000 people potentially affected by food insecurity are based on FEWS NET analyses. The figure of 294,800 displaced people is taken from data published by the Food Security Cluster on July 29, 2026.

Description

The 2026 agropastoral season in Chad is marked by a significant rainfall deficit, a late and irregular onset of the rainy season and an unusual extension of the lean season. In several regions of the country, rainfall remained below the seasonal average, affecting crop development, pasture regeneration and the availability of water resources. This situation led to a delay in agricultural and pastoral activities, while food stocks of producing households were already largely depleted and people were more dependent on markets to meet their food needs. Harvests, usually expected in September, were delayed until October in several areas, thus prolonging the period of vulnerability of rural households.

The provinces of Kanem, Barh El Gazal, Lac, Wadi Fira, Ouaddaï, Sila, Ennedi East, Batha, Guéra, Hadjer-Lamis, and Chari-Baguirmi are among the areas most exposed to the risk of food insecurity. In these provinces, households are facing a decrease in expected agricultural production, a deterioration in their livelihoods, and a gradual decline in their purchasing power. Fodder deficits observed in several Sahelian areas reduce the availability of pasture and increase the costs of feeding and maintaining livestock, further compromising pastoral activities.

The situation is aggravated by rising market demand, low food supply, trade disruptions and the lingering effects of regional security crises. Sudanese refugees, Chadian returnees, internally displaced persons, host communities, and poor agricultural and agro-pastoral households are among the most vulnerable groups. In the host provinces, pressure on natural resources, productive land, pastures, water points and basic social services is exacerbating humanitarian needs.

In the pastoral areas of Kanem and northern Barh E Gazal, the poorest households are particularly affected by the late pastoral season and low availability of fodder. Many households are already resorting to negative coping strategies, including the sale of productive assets, reducing the number of daily meals, or taking on debt to cover their food needs. In Lake Province, declining income from fishing and livestock farming, combined with persistent security constraints, further reduces household access to food and markets.

According to FEWS NET analysis, between 2.5 million and 2.99 million people could require food assistance, with a peak in needs expected during the lean season between July and September 2026. Humanitarian data also indicate that about 294,800 displaced people remain particularly food insecure due to their dependence on assistance and limited production and income generation capacities.

In order to mitigate the expected impacts of the rainfall deficit, the Government of Chad, with the support of the World Food Programme (WFP), OCHA and humanitarian partners, activated an anticipatory action mechanism in May 2026 in the provinces of Kanem, Barh El Gazal, Batha, Sila, Ouaddaï, Lac and Wadi-Fira. This intervention targeted 170,472 vulnerable people through early warning systems and advance cash transfers to protect household livelihoods before the crisis worsened.

Despite these efforts, the results of the Cadre Harmonisé 2026 estimate that more than 3 million people are facing acute food insecurity in Chad. The unfavourable evolution of the agricultural season, the deterioration of pastoral conditions, the increase in food prices and the vulnerability of displaced populations are likely to lead to a worsening of food consumption deficits and an increase in cases of malnutrition among children under five, pregnant and lactating women as well as the poorest households. Without a rapid scale-up of food security, nutrition and livelihood support interventions, the most affected provinces could experience a further deterioration of their humanitarian situation during the period 2026-2027.

Summary

The International Federation of IFRC Societies supported the Red Cross Society of Chad (CRT) in preparing for and coordinating to address food insecurity related to the 2026 rainfall deficit. This support included providing technical and strategic guidance to the teams, sharing documentation and analysis related to the El Niño phenomenon and its potential impacts on food security, as well as organizing working sessions to strengthen understanding of risks and response options.

Actions taken by RCRC

General

CTP/Basic needs

Summary

The ICRC supports agricultural and pastoral households in Lake Province through actions aimed at preserving their livelihoods and strengthening their resilience to shocks. Its support includes vaccinating livestock, improving access to water, distributing crop protection materials and carrying out paid community work for the development of market gardens. The ICRC also provides vegetable seeds, agricultural tools and cash transfers to enable beneficiaries to restart their productive activities. These interventions help protect crops and livestock, improve agricultural production and sustainably support the incomes and food security of vulnerable households.

Actions taken by National Society

General

Damage/Needs assessment

Other

Other

Cash & Voucher

Summary

In order to monitor the evolution of food insecurity and better guide humanitarian interventions, the Red Cross Society of Chad (CRT) participates in a community-based food security surveillance system based on sentinel sites. Through this mechanism, CRT volunteers and community members regularly collect data on the household food situation, livelihoods, access to markets, pasture conditions and adaptation strategies used by affected populations. Data is collected directly from communities through observations, community interviews and the monitoring of predefined indicators. This information is then transmitted and analysed in order to quickly identify signs of deterioration in food security, detect the most vulnerable areas and guide anticipatory response or humanitarian assistance actions. In particular, the CRT has collaborated with local authorities and technical partners to define monitoring sites and surveillance indicators in the provinces. The information collected also serves as an advocacy tool with national authorities, humanitarian partners and donors.

Actions taken by others

In addition to the efforts of the Government of Chad, several international partners and humanitarian actors have mobilized to respond to the effects of the rainfall deficit and limit the deterioration in food security. In particular, the Chadian authorities have set up a response committee and continued to monitor agricultural projects aimed at strengthening agricultural production, food security and the resilience of vulnerable households. Faced with the scale of the crisis, the Government has also called for increased mobilization of technical and financial partners to support a coordinated and sustainable response. The United Arab Emirates has made a significant humanitarian contribution in the form of food aid worth US$8.4 million, handed over to the National Office for Food Security (ONASA) to support populations affected by rainfall deficits and the risk of food insecurity. The World Food Programme (WFP), with the support of OCHA, UN agencies and the Government, activated an anticipatory action mechanism in the provinces most prone to drought. This intervention provided early warnings and cash transfers to 170,472 vulnerable people to protect their livelihoods before the food crisis worsened. With funding from the United Nations Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF), WFP also implemented targeted assistance to 56,952 people at high risk of drought in Kanem, Barh El Gazal and Batha provinces. Activities included advance cash transfers and awareness-raising to strengthen the food security of the most vulnerable households. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) has supported agricultural and pastoral livelihoods through the provision of agricultural inputs, improved seeds, production equipment and technical assistance to maintain production capacities despite the effects of drought. These actions are being implemented as part of the National Response Plan 2025-2026. For its part, OCHA coordinated the humanitarian response, monitored needs and mobilized resources, facilitating consultation between national authorities, UN agencies, non-governmental organizations and donors. The member organizations of the Food Security Cluster continued needs assessments, emergency food assistance, cash transfers and livelihood support in the regions most affected by the drought, particularly in areas hosting refugees, returnees and internally displaced persons.

title: Djibouti | sEAP Flood - Simplified Early Action Protocol: Activation (MDRDJ009), 12/10/2026
content:
Activation Overview

Djibouti Red Crescent National Society has activated it’s Simplified Early Action Protocol for Flood.

Djibouti seasonal forecast for October-December shows a rainfall impact related to the El Nino event. In line with this outlook ICPAC has released a weekly forecast that indicates a potential rainfall in the coastal zones including Djibouti, Tadjourah, obock, Arta and few areas of Ali Sabieh will be affected.

National Society has been monitoring the threshold and for the period of 13-20 October 2026 the agreed trigger which is total rainfall 50mm and above in Djibouti and its Suburbs is reached (as per the forecast it is in the range of 50- 100mm). 13 - 20 October 2026 - ICPAC

DRCS will target 2,500 people living in flood-prone areas who are expected to be severely affected, prioritizing low-income households; female- or child-headed households; large households with three or more children; households with children under five; and households with elderly members.

Anticipatory actions will be implemented in Djibouti among the communities living in Bouloas area within seven days to raise awareness of the forecasted flood event through early warning messages including dissemination through National media houses, sandbagging to protect shelters, strengthen community resilience by distributing and replacing roofing materials, promotion of hygiene to prevent health risks associated with stagnant water.

title: UNICEF Viet Nam El Niño Early Warning Situation Report No. 1 (June –19 August 2026)
content:
Situation Highlights

• On 24 July 2026, the Government confirmed that “El Niño 2026–2027 has taken shape,” increasing the risk of severe drought, water shortages and saltwater intrusion in Viet Nam.

• NOAA Global Outlook3 (13 August 2026): El Niño is further strengthening, with a >90% chance of a "very strong" event continuing through winter 2026-27, and during the October-December 2026 season, there is a 69% chance of a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950 (+2.5°C or more).

• Government planning scenarios: Under the high-risk scenario, El Niño reaches moderate-to-strong intensity and rainfall, and river flows could be 10–20 per cent below average. Under the very-high-risk scenario, El Niño becomes very strong and rainfall and river flows could be 20–40 per cent below average. These are probability-based scenarios, not certainties.

• Priority regions and impact window: The South-Central Coast, Central Highlands and Mekong Delta are assessed as very-high-risk regions. The most critical impacts are expected from late 2026 to May 2027, including prolonged drought, extreme heat, water shortages, reduced river flows, depleted reservoirs and saltwater intrusion.

• Children and essential services face rising risks from reduced safe water, food and livelihood insecurity, higher food prices and disruption to water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, health, nutrition, education, child protection and social protection services.

• Children most at risk: Children under five; pregnant and breastfeeding women; children with disabilities; children from poor and ethnic minority households; migrant children; and children in remote, coastal, drought-prone and water-insecure communities.

• No widespread El Niño-related humanitarian needs have been confirmed to date, making the current lead time critical for anticipatory action, risk communication, frontline readiness and continuity of essential services.

• Maintain multi-hazard readiness: El Niño does not remove the risk of typhoons, extreme rainfall, flash floods, landslides and urban flooding. Preparedness must therefore remain multi-hazard.

• Past El Niño events show the cost of delayed action and the value of preparedness: in 2015–2016, 2 million people lacked sufficient domestic water and 1.1 million were food insecure; earlier forecasting and community action helped reduce losses in 2023–2024. Preparedness financing is needed ahead of the anticipated February–May 2027 peak-impact period.

title: UNHCR Afghanistan: Monthly Protection Update (As of August 2026)
content: This monthly protection update for Afghanistan provides a comprehensive overview of UNHCR’s different protection programs, aiming to prevent, mitigate and respond to protection risks faced by vulnerable populations in the context of the current humanitarian crisis and in the absence of durable solutions. The data and insights presented are derived from an extensive protection analysis, collected through a variety of robust tools and systems. The activities include protection monitoring, household assessments, voluntary repatriation, returns monitoring, specialized support for persons with specific needs, community engagement, complaints and feedback systems, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), child protection, women protection, and civil documentation. This update aims to highlight key achievements, ongoing challenges, and the critical needs of the affected communities, ensuring a transparent and effective protection response.

title: Nepal: Rasuwa Flood Situation Report No. 11 (As of 12 October 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Recovery planning is accelerating as humanitarian partners and local authorities transition from emergency response towards early recovery.
  • Road access to Rasuwa has significantly improved following the opening of the Acrow Bridge at Betrawati, restoring a key humanitarian and logistics corridor.

title: WFP Pakistan Country Brief, October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• WFP is launching early recovery activities to support communities affected by floods and earthquake in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and GilgitBaltistan while advancing anticipatory action in Sindh to strengthen resilience against potential El Niño-induced drought.

• WFP Pakistan launched a ShareTheMeal campaign, aiming to provide 150,000 school meals for children across Pakistan, supporting access to nutritious food and improved school attendance and learning outcomes.

• Since 2024, the WFP-supported School Meals Programme in Balochistan has contributed to a 34 percent increase in girls' enrolment and an increase in attendance from 68 percent to 81 percent across supported schools.

title: Dengue Epidemiological Situation in the Region of the Americas - Epidemiological Week 37, 2026

This represents a decrease of 56% compared to the same period in 2025 and 63% compared to the average of the last 5 years. Figure 1 shows the trend of suspected dengue cases as of EW 37.

title: Shabelle River: Climate Update and Riverine Flood Risk Advisory (Digniin) - Deyr 2026 Flood Advisory No. 2 (13 October 2026)
content:
Observed Rainfall

Heavy rains have fallen over central Somalia and the lower part of the Shabelle catchment in Ethiopia since the start of October.

Satellite estimates for 1–11 October show above 100 mm over Hiraan, Galgaduud and the Gode–Kelafo area of Ethiopia, more than two times the normal amount for this time of year. The Ethiopian highlands, where the Shabelle starts, received less, about 25–75 mm.

River level

At Jowhar, the level rose by a further 0.20 m overnight to 5.37 m today, almost 1 m in 48 hours (4.38 m on 11 October). It is now 12 cm above the high flood risk level (5.25 m) and only 13 cm below bankfull (5.50 m). Levels are rising along the whole river:

Belet Weyne rose by 0.38 m to 3.98 m and Bulo Burti by 0.38 m to 3.90 m, both still about 2.5 m below their moderate flood risk level (6.50 m). Upstream at Deefow, near the Ethiopian border, the level rose by a further 0.45 m to 2.87 m, confirming that more water is coming from Ethiopia.

Moderate rains are forecast: 50–100 mm over most of Hiraan and Middle Shabelle (Belet Weyne, Bulo Burti, Jalalaqsi and Jowhar), with isolated falls of 100–150 mm. Over the Shabelle catchment in Ethiopia, rains will be lighter (mostly 10–50 mm), with only isolated areas getting 100 mm or more. Today, mostly light rain is expected along the river, with up to 50 mm just north of Belet Weyne and heavy rain (50–200 mm) along the Lower Shabelle coast.

With the river already above the high flood risk level at Jowhar, more water arriving from Belet Weyne and Bulo Burti and 50–100 mm of local rain forecast this week, the level at Jowhar is likely to reach bankfull (5.50 m) in the coming days. Flooding through the open river breakages between Jowhar and Balcad is likely to continue and spread into nearby farms and villages. Levels at Belet Weyne and Bulo Burti will keep rising but are expected to stay below the moderate flood risk level this week.

title: Juba River: Climate Update and Riverine Flood Risk Advisory (Digniin) - Deyr 2026 Flood Advisory No. 2 (13 October 2026)
content:

Moderate to heavy rains have fallen over the upper Juba catchment in the Ethiopian highlands since the start of October. title: Routes Monitor Key Updates - October 2026
content:
Highlights

1. Recorded movement indicators declined in August, particularly by sea. Compared with July, total departures fell by 26% and arrivals by 44%; however, the decline in arrivals should be interpreted cautiously because August data for Greece are not yet available. Maritime disembarkations decreased more moderately, by 3%, to 4,352. Between January and August, reported departures and arrivals were both 44% lower than during the same period in 2025, while maritime disembarkations were 41% lower. Despite the lower number of recorded movements, the protection toll remained severe: 2,050 people were reported dead or missing at sea between January and August 2026, only 6% fewer than during the same period in 2025.

2. The cumulative geographic composition continued to evolve. The Central Mediterranean and Western Africa Atlantic Routes represented smaller shares of reported arrivals, while the South and South-East Asia and Western Mediterranean Routes accounted for a larger share of movements recorded between January and August 2026. As August data for Greece are not yet available, findings related to the Eastern Mediterranean Route should be treated as preliminary.

3. Nationality patterns shifted on the Central Mediterranean Route in August. Bangladeshi nationals became the largest reported group, while arrivals of Somali, Sudanese, Tunisian and Pakistani nationals also increased. Algerian arrivals declined and accounted for a substantially smaller share than in July, resulting in a more diversified nationality profile. Nationality changes on the Eastern Mediterranean Route cannot be assessed reliably because August data currently include Cyprus but not Greece.

(*) Figures reflect data available at the time of publication and may be subject to subsequent updates or revisions. For the latest available data, please consult the Routes Monitor platform.

title: Ebola Outbreak, DRC and Region, Situation Report #14 (October 13, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • On May 15, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) declared an outbreak of Ebola virus disease (EVD), later confirmed to be caused by the Bundibugyo strain.
  • As of October 11, 9,066 confirmed cases and 4,381 confirmed deaths had been reported in the DRC.
  • On October 5, a case of imported EVD was confirmed in Kenya. The patient had traveled from the DRC through Uganda to Nairobi, where he died.
  • No EVD cases have been confirmed in South Sudan or the Central African Republic, but risk of cross-border transmission remains high due to transient populations and porous borders with the DRC.
  • In the DRC, the outbreak remains centered in Ituri province, but cases have also been confirmed in Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, North Kivu, South Kivu, South Ubangi and Tshopo provinces, indicating an uncontrolled spread of the disease.
  • Uganda has officially declared its outbreak to be over, though preparedness activities continue.

OUR RESPONSE

  • Across the region, our teams are providing case management, infection prevention and control, screening and triage, risk communication and community engagement, training and preparedness planning.
  • We are helping more than 110 facilities screen, identify and treat EVD.
  • Our supported sites in the DRC have conducted more than 1 million EVD screenings and provided treatment to 2,806 patients, including 828 confirmed cases.
  • We have so far trained 6,451 people in the DRC on EVD case management, response and transmission prevention.

With the support of the US Department of State, DG ECHO and other donors, International Medical Corps teams in the DRC, South Sudan and Uganda are actively responding to the outbreak and collaborating closely with ministries of health, key actors and response partners. International Medical Corps has used a hub-and-spoke model since the outbreak was declared to provide case-management support at designated treatment and transit facilities, strengthen IPC in referring health facilities, conduct screening and triage, support risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) in surrounding communities and train health workers on EVD response protocols.

title: Nigeria | Drought: Simplified early action protocol (sEAP №: EAP2025NG02)
content:
RISK ANALYSIS AND EARLY ACTION SELECTION

Prioritized hazard and its historical impact.

Nigeria is experiencing ecological disasters exacerbated by Climate Change with negative impacts on the welfare of millions of people. Drought and Desertification is one of the ecological disasters currently plaguing the country with a negative impact on ecosystem functions, reduce social, political and economic stability and can increase vulnerability to other natural disasters, such as heat waves and floods. The impact and incidence of droughts differ over space and time. While it is incontrovertible that droughts occur over the entire Nigerian littoral, the degree of vulnerability differs with the semi-arid regions in the north being more vulnerable to drought than the more humid regions in the south. Drought impacts on lives and livelihoods are more severe in the northern part of the country, spreading across the frontline states; Adamawa, Borno, Bauchi, Gombe, Jigawa, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi. Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. The droughts in Nigeria have a 30 year and 10-year cycle. The 30-year cycle droughts are usually regional, while the 10-year drought cycles are usually localized. Drought has occurred in Nigeria in 1883, 1903/1905, 1913/1915, 1923/1924, 1942/1944, 1954/1956, 1972/1973, 1982/1983 and 1991/1995 (FME- NDP, 2018). The impacts of drought can be extremely severe for the most vulnerable groups in the society (women, children and aged). The impacts may be grouped into Physical and ecological impacts; and socioeconomic impacts Since the 1970s, the term ‘the Sahel’ has been used as indicating those parts of West Africa where drought was followed by famine and where such a disaster could happen again. Drought is also precipitated with the issues of shortage of water and drying up of Nigeria’s climate has shown a very rapid variability in recent decades, particularly in the Sahel region (Ogunrinde et al. 2019). Drought events in this region are becoming more frequent due to increase in the evaporative demand of the climate, and this is very evident in the last few decades (Ogunrinde et al. 2020d). The long-term drought events in the Sahel region of Nigeria (SRN) started around the 1970s and have since become a recurring decadal event and there are projections of it becoming more intense and frequent as the twenty-first century progress (Ogunrinde et al. 2020d; Brooks 2004; Agnew and Chappell 1999). Several studies on drought show that there has been an increase in the occurrence of extreme weather events, such as decrease in precipitation in the range of about 3–4% per decade from the mid to the end of the twentieth century. Notably, as a result of the reduction in precipitation, some monumental drought events were recorded between 1971 and 1972, 1983 and 1984, 1993, 2007, and 2011. According to the Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative (2022), Nigeria ranks 154th place out of 185 countries reflects high vulnerability to climate change and extremely low readiness – 14th-worst in the world, to confront the threat. In Nigeria, the direct and indirect impacts of droughts have been very enormous with respect to environmental degradation, large scale crop failure and loss of livestock, as well as human displacement and migration, diseases outbreak and death. The cumulative effects of drought gave been expressed in increasing levels of poverty and environmental degradation which will retard the country’s ability to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (FME NDP, 2018). Droughts exacerbate poverty, undermine economic development, and can lead to conflicts over scarce resources. Droughts accelerate desertification and soil degradation, making land unsuitable for agriculture and grazing.

title: Aid in Danger Bi-Monthly News Brief (01-15 September 2026)
content:
Aid in Danger News Brief

The impact of drones on aid operations
In 2025, incidents where drone-delivered explosives impacted aid operations increased by 235%, from 23 recorded incidents in 2024 to 77. In these incidents, aid workers were killed or injured while aid assets and humanitarian supplies were damaged or destroyed, including in attacks on distribution sites and convoys transporting supplies. These incidents occurred amid over 1,800 recorded drone-related incidents affecting aid operations and critical civilian services such as healthcare, education, food and water systems and IDP or refugee settlements areas - a 131% increase compared to 2024.

In 2025 a growing number of aid workers killed by drones
In 2025, at least 28 aid workers were killed by drone strikes, a 65% increase from 2024 and the highest annual toll since 2021, when Insecurity Insight documented an aid worker killed by a drone. Almost a third of aid workers killed or injured were employed by local non-governmental organisations (LNGOs), which deliver frontline assistance despite having more limited financial resources than UN agencies and larger international organisations. Aid workers were killed by drones whilst carrying out their duties, particularly when travelling in convoys delivering critical aid supplies or moving between project sites. Aid workers were also killed in drone strikes at aid compounds or residences, and at aid distribution points.

title: Ethiopia Drought 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRET042)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

01-09-2026

What happened, where and when?

El Niño-driven drought conditions have severely suppressed the June-September 2026 Kiremt rainfall, causing onset delays of up to 4 weeks across Northern Eastern and Southeastern Ethiopia. The NS EOC reports highlighted moisture deficit critically resulted to crop failure, drying of water points, livestock deaths, and livelihood loss with a widespread impact in Oromia (West & East Hararge), Northern Amhara, and a part of Tigray. The impacts severely affected the community; already their livelihood depleted due to Belg rainfall shortages in these locations. Accordingly: 250,035 hectares of crop land damaged in west Hararge, North Gonder, Tigray and some woredas in Southeastern Ethiopia. 28,629, livestock death recorded across West Hararge, North Gonder and a part of Tigray, and more then 319 water points are either completely or partially dried out across these regions posing significant risk for both human and animals.

The 1 September 2026 trigger date does not represent a single meteorological event, but rather the point at which multiple drought indicators confirmed that the situation had evolved from seasonal stress into a humanitarian crisis requiring response. By this date, ERCS had received repeated alerts from Branch EOCs, confirming severe rainfall deficits across Oromia, Amhara and Tigray, following consecutive failures of the Belg and Kiremt seasons. These alerts were subsequently validated by the respective Disaster Risk Management Commissions (DRMCs). The assessments confirmed significant humanitarian impacts, including crop failure affecting more than 250,000 hectares, the death of over 28,000 livestock, the drying of more than 319 water points, and widespread deterioration of food security and livelihoods affecting over 3.5 million people. ERCS therefore considers 1 September 2026 as the operational trigger date, marking the point at which the scale, severity and geographical spread of the drought impacts justified activation of a DREF response.

title: Panama: Earthquake in Azuero & Veraguas - Situation Report No. 03 (as of 12 October 2026, 14:30)
content:
KEY POINTS

  • As of 12 October, authorities report some 1,250 affected homes, more than 800 people in shelters and 27 people injured following the magnitude 7.6 earthquake on 9 October. There are no reports of deaths or missing people.
  • Fearing further aftershocks, many families are sleeping outdoors or staying with relatives. More than 350 aftershocks have been recorded so far. In Herrera, some families lack regular access to water and a safe place to sleep.
  • Several hospitals are still treating patients in tents or car parks, and at least three health centres are out of service. In Tonosí, 11 townships remain without water or power.
  • The bridge over the Oria River remains closed, but aid is reaching communities in Tonosí by air and road. Heavy rain is forecast for the worst-hit areas and could hamper access.
  • As assessments continue to pin down needs, UN agencies and their partners have delivered tents, shelter items and health supplies as part of their ongoing support for the Government’s response.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

On 9 October at 12:56 p.m., a magnitude 7.6 earthquake struck Panama, according to the Institute of Geosciences of the University of Panama (IGC-UP). The United States Geological Survey puts it at 7.7. The epicentre was in Veraguas, near the border with Los Santos, 39 km north-west of Tonosí, at a depth of 4 km. By the morning of 12 October, IGC-UP had recorded more than 350 aftershocks. They are getting weaker, but IGC-UP says they could continue for weeks, possibly for close to a month. The last major earthquake on this fault system, a magnitude 6.9, struck in 1913. Soil type partly explains why Chitré and Penonomé suffered more damage than areas closer to the epicentre.

Impact: According to the Government’s preliminary count as of 12 October, some 1,250 homes are affected, mostly in Los Santos, Veraguas, Coclé and Herrera. Not all of them will need rebuilding, and the Ministry of Housing is assessing which ones need repairs. The earthquake also damaged 16 bridges, churches and public buildings, and affected 29 health facilities and 619 schools. Twenty-seven people are injured, and there are no reports of deaths or missing people.

Some 478,000 people live in areas that felt very strong shaking or stronger, and around 41,000 live where moderate to heavy damage is expected, according to the Pan American Health Organization/World Health Organization (PAHO/WHO).

More than 800 people remain in shelters, mostly in Veraguas, Colón and Los Santos. Many others are staying with relatives or friends or sleeping outdoors for fear of aftershocks. In Búcaro, Los Santos, residents have left their homes, many of which were destroyed, and are staying at the entrance to the village. Rain has already disrupted care in tents outside Anita Moreno Hospital, and swollen rivers and landslides are delaying access to some communities.
