title: UNICEF Viet Nam El Niño Early Warning Situation Report No. 2 (20 August - 12 October 2026)
content:
Highlights

  • El Niño is intensifying and expected to persist into early 2027. Viet Nam is preparing for a severe, prolonged event, with humanitarian risks expected to rise from late 2026 and peak during the January - May 2027 dry season.
  • Children and vulnerable households face growing risks of water insecurity, food and livelihood losses, higher costs, and disruption to essential WASH, health, nutrition, education, child protection and social protection services.
  • Those most at risk include children under five, pregnant and breastfeeding women, children with disabilities, ethnic minorities, migrants, and communities in remote, coastal, drought-prone and water-insecure areas.
  • A critical window for early action remains. No widespread humanitarian needs have been confirmed. Priorities include risk communication, frontline readiness, continuity of essential services and multi-hazard preparedness for typhoons, extreme rainfall, flash floods, landslides and urban flooding.
  • Prevention can reduce future humanitarian and recovery costs. Every US$1 invested in disaster risk reduction can save up to US$15 in recovery costs, while less than 1% of humanitarian funding supports anticipatory action.
  • UNICEF is working with Government counterparts, development partners and the Viet Nam Red Cross to strengthen local preparedness, risk communication and the positioning of essential supplies.

title: WFP Jordan Country Brief, October 2026
content:
IN NUMBERS

78,000 people assisted in September 2026 (50% female) - estimate

USD 1.2M cash transferred in September 2026

USD 42.4M required in the next six months (October 2026 – March 2027)

230,000 Syrian refugees returned to Syria (December 2024 – September 2026)

KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • In September, WFP provided food assistance to 78,000 refugees in camps only, at reduced transfer value. In parallel, WFP started preparations to temporarily reinstate its reduced monthly assistance for a prioritized group of the most vulnerable refugee households in host communities from October.
  • In partnership with the Higher Food Security Council, WFP supported the launch of Jordan’s first national food waste awareness campaign, “Appreciate It, Don’t Waste It” (قدّرها ولا تهدرها), to promote responsible consumption and reduce food waste nationwide.
  • WFP and the Ministry of Education resumed the school feeding programme, reaching 510,000 students in refugee camps and host communities with healthy meals and fortified date bars.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Jordan is an upper-middle-income country with a population of 12 million, 63 percent of whom are below the age of 30. Jordan is also a resource-poor, food-deficit country with dwindling energy and water resources and limited agricultural land.

• Jordan remains one of the world’s largest refugeehosting countries, accommodating more than 3 million refugees. This includes Palestinian and Syrian refugees, with 329,700 Syrian refugees registered with UNHCR as of September, in addition to smaller numbers of other nationalities.

• Jordan’s recent political reforms have contributed to strengthening the resilience of its economy. Nevertheless, ongoing regional conflicts have had a considerable impact on the country and have intensified pre-existing economic challenges. Unemployment remains a structural challenge, reaching 16 percent across population (21 percent across Jordanians only) in the second quarter of 2026, with women accounting for 30 percent of those unemployed.

• Building on achievements under its Country Strategic Plan (2023–2027) in previous years, WFP continues providing unconditional food assistance to vulnerable refugees, alongside technical assistance to strengthen national social protection programmes and systems. It prioritizes education and nutrition activities while advancing resilience interventions. In parallel, WFP Jordan, together with the Government plays a pivotal role in coordinating and facilitating the delivery of food assistance into Gaza and Lebanon.

title: WFP Ukraine Country Brief, September 2026 [EN/UK]
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • WFP assisted 280,900 people through its emergency response programmes across seven frontline regions of Ukraine in August.
  • WFP and FAO are supporting Ukraine’s procurement of grain sleeves to protect harvested crops and expand temporary storage.
  • According to the Government of Ukraine, recent attacks have destroyed approximately 90 percent of national retail-chain storage facilities.
  • In August, WFP recorded eight security incidents affecting WFP and cooperating partner assets or equipment.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• In August, the aerial strike campaign against Ukraine evolved into combining a variety of weapon types in multi-phase attacks extending across day and night periods, disrupting transportation networks, rail operations, and civilian movement.

• The list of potential targets expanded to border crossings, ports, energy, fuel, transport, metallurgy, and water systems in Ukraine, generating cascading humanitarian and supplychain disruptions and increasing operational constraints beyond the frontline. An increased use of higher speed jet-powered drones additionally reduces warning times and shelter response windows.

• According to government reporting, recent attacks have destroyed approximately 90 percent of national retail-chain storage facilities. While national food availability remains sufficient, continued degradation of commercial storage and distribution capacity could increase humanitarian food assistance requirements, particularly in frontline areas and major population centres.

Black Sea:

• Since late July 2026, Black Sea grain exports have halted due to escalating attacks and war-risk insurance constraints. Rising transport costs and market volatility contributed to a 13 percent increase in global wheat prices since January 2026, with implications for WFP procurement costs.

• In response, WFP, FAO, and INGO partners are supporting the Government of Ukraine in the procurement of grain sleeves to protect harvested crops and expand temporary storage.

• WFP is leveraging its rapid procurement, and logistics capacities and has placed an initial order for 1,780 sleeves, expected to arrive in September. With export and storage capacity disrupted, up to 11 million mt of Ukraine’s harvest could remain stranded.

title: WFP Palestine Emergency Response External Situation Report #98, 12 October 2026 (Reporting period: 1-30 September 2026)
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Funding constraints are already forcing WFP to reduce the cash transfer value in Gaza for 75,000 families, and to scale back assistance in the West Bank from 400,000 to 200,000. WFP is shifting to more targeted assistance, prioritizing the most vulnerable. Unless more funding is received, WFP will be forced to make even further cuts next month.
  • As winter approaches, displaced families in Gaza face heightened risks from flooding and harsh weather, while funding shortfalls and access constraints continue to limit winter preparedness and strain humanitarian response efforts.
  • Aid throughput into Gaza declined in September due to disruptions across key supply corridors. All humanitarian cargo continued to use the sole operational entry point at Kerem Shalom, increasing pressure on the crossing and contributing to multiple returns and longer offloading times.

SITUATION UPDATE

• As winter approaches, humanitarian concerns are mounting across Gaza, following the severe challenges of winter 2025/26. Displaced people remain highly exposed to flooding, harsh weather and deteriorating living conditions in overcrowded displacement sites and damaged shelters. Winter preparedness efforts are constrained by funding shortfalls, access restrictions and shortages of critical supplies, heightening risks of disease outbreak and worsening humanitarian needs.

• According to WFP Palestine Market Monitor of September, markets in the Gaza Strip remain relatively stable, although price volatility and supply constraints amongst some commodities persist, underscoring the need for sustained commercial and humanitarian inflows. In the West Bank, recurring checkpoint closures, settler attacks, high unemployment and elevated fuel prices continue to deepen people’s economic hardship. Food insecurity remains widespread and severe in Gaza with 1.4m people (67% of the population) facing acute food insecurity. Dietary diversity remains significantly below preconflict levels.

• In the West Bank, restrictions on access to agricultural land, settler-related violence, and settlement expansion continue to undermine agricultural livelihoods across the West Bank, where farming remains a key source of income and resilience for many rural communities. Ahead of the 2026 olive harvest, farmers face land attacks, crop theft and damage to agricultural assets. These pressures are compounded by worsening economic conditions, with unemployment rising to 28 per cent in Q2 of 2026, more than double pre-conflict levels, while declining incomes and reduced purchasing power are increasing household vulnerability.

title: ACAPS Briefing Note: Democratic Republic of Congo - Mpox outbreak affecting Kasaï province (13 October 2025)
content:
CRISIS IMPACT OVERVIEW

• On 16 September 2026, provincial authorities announced an mpox outbreak in Kasaï province, initially covering five health zones (7Sur7.cd 17/09/2026; mediacongo. net 17/09/2026). By 1 October, 1,017 cases and more than 24 deaths had been reported across all 18 of the province’s health zones (Actualite.cd 01/10/2026).

• The declaration of a provincial mpox outbreak in Kasaï comes five months after the Government announced the end of a national mpox emergency designation; on 2 April, the Government announced a shift from emergency response to resilience, promoting community vigilance given the risk of resurgence (MSPHP 08/04/2026). The end of the emergency designation did not mean that transmission had ceased throughout the country, and available reporting does not establish whether the Kasaï outbreak is a result of continued local transmission or a new introduction into the province.

• Earlier media reporting from 1–2 September quoting health sources identified Kambangoma and Mukwandjanga in Luebo health zone as the main affected locations, approximately 20km from the health zone coordination office. Authorities in Luebo were awaiting laboratory results from the National Biomedical Research Institute, indicating reliance on diagnostic support outside the health zone at that stage (ACP 01/09/2026; Radio Okapi 02/09/2026). The sources reviewed do not establish whether provincial testing arrangements have subsequently changed.

• Hospital staff reported limited equipment and response resources from the outset. Suspected cases included infants aged two to three months. There were also reports of concerns about obtaining food and lodging during hospital care discouraging patients from seeking treatment (ACP 01/09/2026).

• On 4 October, national health authorities deployed Rapid Intervention Teams to Tshikapa to support the Kasaï Provincial Health Division, particularly in Luebo. The mission focuses on epidemiological surveillance, the investigation and early detection of suspected cases, case management, and community awareness, while also reinforcing the operational capacity of local health teams (CongoCroissance 05/10/2026).

• Kasaï is facing a simultaneous measles outbreak and suspected cases of yellow fever, increasing pressure on surveillance and health response capacity (WHO 31/08/2026; Beto 23/09/2026). At 9 October, no cases of Ebola had been reported in the province (CDC 09/10/2026).

• On 26 September, an mpox case was confirmed in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province; by 29 September, there were five confirmed cases reported in Rwampara and Aru health zones of the province (MedAfrik Info Instagram 26/09/2026; mediacongo. net 01/10/2026; Reuters 25/09/2026). Earlier reports dating from July indicate nearly 4,000 cases confirmed in Sud-Kivu since the start of the year (mediacongo.net 23/07/2026). The available reporting does not establish whether cases in Ituri, Kasaï, and Sud-Kivu are linked to the same transmission chains.

title: Sudan Monthly Update - September 2026
content:
Key developments

  • During September, the operational environment in the conflict affected regions of Sudan was highly complex and volatile, marked by localized ground clashes, intensified military activity, drone strikes, and severe weather conditions that placed increased pressure on forcibly displaced and host communities. In Blue Nile State, an escalation of violence triggered renewed internal displacement, heightened protection risks, and UN personnel had to adopt alternate and remote working modalities in line with common UN security guidance. In parts of Kordofan and the Darfur States, persistent ground fighting, drone attacks, and intercommunal tensions are consistently affecting civilians, humanitarian service delivery and damaging basic civilian infrastructure. Despite growing access and security challenges, UNHCR continues to adapt operational models to sustain critical protection and assistance services.
  • Attacks on humanitarian operations and civilians continued to pose severe challenges. On October 3, 2026, an airstrike struck two WFP-contracted aid trucks in South Kordofan, just one day after an explosive device incident occurred in Dilling. The WFP noted that these events significantly hindered the delivery of essential food assistance to vulnerable populations. Further compounding the violence, an attack on a displacement site in Blue Nile State on October 10 resulted in a reported 30 civilian casualties.
  • Seasonal strong winds, heavy rainfall, and flooding caused extensive structural damage to shelter, sanitation, and educational facilities in Kassala and Gedaref States. In Northern State, adverse weather in Merowe resulted in localized structural damage and one fatality, while a fire at the Al-Afad internally displaced persons (IDP) gathering site some 100 family shelters.

title: WFP Nepal External Situation Report, 13 October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• Following the 11 October floods, WFP dispatched 100 kg fortified biscuits and government relief items to Gorkha district.

• During the second round of food assistance, WFP distributed 34.2 mt of food to 955 households (4,107 people), provided 0.52 mt of specialized nutritious foods to 634 students and reached 4,108 households so far with multi-purpose cash transfers in Dhading, Nuwakot and Rasuwa.

• The Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster received and stored 1,747.3 m³ of humanitarian cargo and dispatched 393.3 mt of partner relief items through logistics hubs in Kathmandu and Nuwakot.

Situation Overview

• Only six weeks after the devastating floods in Rasuwa, flash floods triggered by a landslide dam outburst on the Budhi Gandaki River on 11 October caused significant damage across parts of Gorkha and Dhading districts. According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), five people are missing and 302 people have been rescued.

• NDRRMA reports that the floods swept away two motorable bridges and two suspension bridges, creating significant access challenges, damaged three hydropower projects and affected more than 550 households. Schools, homes and other critical infrastructure also sustained damage across the affected areas.

• WFP will participate in a joint UN multi-sector needs assessment to inform the humanitarian response and identify priority needs following the Budhi Gandaki floods.

title: Mental Health in South Sudan: The Invisible Burden
content:
Mental health is an essential component of health and well-being, influencing how people think, feel, and function throughout their lives. People affected by conflict and displacement, survivors of gender-based violence, people living with chronic disease such as HIV/TB, persons with epilepsy and other neurological conditions, people with substance use disorders, and people facing food insecurity and chronic poverty are some of the groups at a higher risk of developing mental health disease.

Mental health conditions contribute to disability, reduced productivity, poor physical health outcomes, and increased demand for health and social services. Drawing on emerging findings from the South Sudan Annual Health Sector Performance Report 2024/25 and the 2025 Health Statistical Abstract, this knowledge product examines the status of mental health services in South Sudan and the implications of limited service availability, workforce capacity, and utilization for health system performance and universal health coverage.

title: WFP Dominican Republic Country Brief, October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• WFP strengthened national emergency preparedness capacities by supporting a Humanitarian Protection and Gender in Emergencies workshop for Civil Defense shelter coordinators, enhancing knowledge on protection, gender-sensitive approaches, gender-based violence prevention and response, and inclusive shelter management.

• WFP provided cash assistance to flood-affected beneficiaries in Puerto Plata, prioritizing femaleheaded households, helping vulnerable families meet immediate needs while facilitating the identification of beneficiaries for subsequent UNHCR non-food assistance.

• WFP facilitated a Cuban technical mission to enhance disaster preparedness and risk management capacities and specialized QGIS training to strengthen institutional capabilities in climate and geospatial data analysis for evidence-based decision-making and emergency response.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• The Dominican Republic, like other Small Island Developing States in the Caribbean, is highly exposed to severe weather events such as hurricanes, flooding, and droughts, which disrupt livelihoods, damage infrastructure, and strain food systems.

• Ecosystem degradation further reduces natural protection against extreme events. Around 25 percent of households are highly vulnerable to climate shocks, disproportionately affecting poor and hazard‑prone communities. Territorial inequalities leave rural and border provinces with fewer opportunities and higher poverty rates, while 53.4 percent of employment is informal.

• Global food price volatility, dependence on remittances, and localized migration pressures compound these risks, intersecting with persistent micronutrient deficiencies and the double burden of malnutrition disproportionately affecting women, children, and excluded groups. These vulnerabilities are exacerbated by global market instability linked to the Middle East crisis, driving food price volatility, energy cost increases, and supply chain disruption, raising concern for national food security and household resilience.

• WFP’s strategy links national planning with local action to address recurrent shocks systemically. Evidence and data guide interventions, building government capacity so central decisions translate into community protection. Climate services and risk management tools are embedded in social protection, enabling anticipatory action. Pre‑positioning and disaster risk finance ensure rapid response when systems are strained. Platforms such as ANACAONA and the DR–Haiti corridor exemplify collective resilience.

title: Earthquake in Panama | UNFPA Flash Update (9 - 11 October 2026)
content:
On 9 October 2026, a magnitude 7.6 earthquake struck Panama, prompting the Government to declare a National State of Emergency on 10 October. Preliminary reports indicate that 27 people sustained minor injuries, while at least 820 homes and 29 health facilities have been affected.

Aftershocks are continuing, with 200 already recorded, posing a risk of further damage to already weakened structures, including health facilities. Health service delivery has been disrupted by damage to several health centres and hospitals. In response, the Ministry of Health has established six field hospitals to help maintain the continuity of essential healthcare services.

Women and girls face heightened risks due to displacement and barriers to accessing healthcare, water and sanitation, and protection services.

UNFPA is actively engaged in the United Nations Emergency Response Group and is coordinating with national authorities and government counterparts through the Office of the United Nations Resident Coordinator. These efforts aim to support a coordinated response to the earthquake and ensure that sexual and reproductive health as well as protection needs of women and girls are adequately addressed within the humanitarian response.

title: Myanmar Flood-Landslide 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRMM025)
content:
Description of the Event

Crisis Category Supporting Document

Date of event

30-09-2026

What happened, where and when?

In late September 2026, a low-pressure system over the North Andaman Sea and Mon-Tanintharyi coastal areas intensified into a depression, resulting in strong monsoon conditions across southern Myanmar. The system brought heavy rainfall, strong winds, flooding and landslides, with significant impacts reported in Tanintharyi Region, particularly in Launglon, Dawei, Thayetchaung and Tanintharyi Townships.

By 30 September, the system had moved north-northwestwards across Myanmar, bringing additional rainfall to areas already affected by several days of heavy precipitation and increasing the risk of flooding, landslides and damage to houses and infrastructure. On 6 October 2026, the Department of Meteorology and Hydrology (DMH) officially announced the withdrawal of the southwest monsoon from the entire country.

The hazard is expected to continue affecting low-lying flood-prone communities, riverine areas, coastal settlements and landslide-prone hilly terrain, particularly across southern and western parts of Tanintharyi Region. Launglon Township remains the area of greatest concern due to the severity of flooding and landslide impacts. Given the saturated ground conditions and damaged infrastructure, there remains a risk of additional localized flooding, further slope instability and secondary landslides during the immediate response period.

The humanitarian impact has increased significantly since the onset of the event. A Rapid Needs Assessment conducted by the Myanmar Red Cross Society (MRCS), in coordination with local authorities, indicates that approximately 49,371 people and 7,629 houses have been affected across four townships: Dawei, Launglon, Thayetchaung and Tanintharyi. An estimated 9,032 people were temporarily displaced and accommodated in 24 evacuation centres. The most severe impacts were reported in Launglon Township, where more than 400 households (approximately 2,560 people) were affected and over 400 houses were destroyed. A total of 25 deaths and 11 injuries were also reported.

Floods and landslides have damaged roads, bridges, water sources and other critical infrastructure, limiting access to essential services and humanitarian assistance. Rapid assessments conducted by MRCS identified food, emergency shelter, essential household items, water-source rehabilitation, emergency sanitation support and access to healthcare as priority needs. While food and drinking water are currently available in many accessible locations through support from local authorities, community-based organizations and private donors, shortages persist in isolated villages where access remains restricted.

According to weather forecasts issued by DMH, isolated heavy rainfall was forecast for Tanintharyi Region, with warnings issued for communities living in flood-prone and landslide-risk areas. Although DMH announced the withdrawal of the southwest monsoon from Myanmar on 6 October 2026, the combination of saturated soil conditions, damaged drainage systems and ongoing recovery challenges is expected to maintain an elevated risk of recurrent flooding and landslides throughout the immediate response period.

title: WFP Nigeria Country Brief, September 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• WFP provided nutrition integrated assistance including emergency food assistance, malnutrition supplementation and livelihood assistance to 1million people in August.

• WFP and its partners facilitated a series of workshops to strengthen fortified rice production and regulatory capacity in Nigeria. Participants included representatives from rice mills, key regulatory institutions and government agencies.

title: WFP Sao Tome and Principe Country Brief, September 2026

title: WFP Lao People's Democratic Republic Country Brief, October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• The Ministry of Health signed public-private partnership agreements with two private millers to enable the production and distribution of fortified rice for government-led programmes. The partnerships also create opportunities for the private sector partners to expand production and commercialise fortified rice in the domestic market.

• WFP presented its new Country Strategic Plan (2027-2031) to Executive Board members and Member States during the Informal Executive Board Consultation. The strategy is expected to receive final approval at the Board’s second regular session in November.

• In September, WFP supported a government-led inter-agency rapid assessment across six flood affected provinces and began verifying and registering families for food assistance in Luang Namtha province.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• The Lao People's Democratic Republic is a landlocked, least developed country with a population of 7.8 million. As of 2024/2025, about 15 percent of the population lived below the national poverty line of USD 1.10 per day. Poverty has declined by over half in the past two decades. The 2024 Global Hunger Index rates the country's hunger as “moderate.”

• Climate change is a major challenge for rural populations, as the country is vulnerable due to its low adaptability and heavy dependence on climate-sensitive natural resources. Changing climate patterns, limited access to markets and varied livelihoods further worsen the situation in remote upland areas, where over 20 percent of households are food insecure (national average: 10 percent). Chronic malnutrition affects every third child under five, while micronutrient deficiencies are high and overnutrition is on the rise in urban areas.

• WFP has been present in Lao PDR since 1976, supporting national efforts to improve food security, nutrition, and resilience. It operates through a main office in Vientiane Capital and three field offices in Oudomxay, Xiengkhouang, and Champassak provinces.

title: UNHCR Romania Ukraine Refugee Situation Weekly Update #217 - 12 October 2026
content:
Highlight

On 5 October, UNHCR partner Project Voyager received the UNHCR “Hope Away from Home” award for initiatives that help refugees build a new beginnings in Romania for its Jobs4Ukraine project at the 24th edition of the Civil Society Gala. Projects shortlisted for the award were assessed by a joint panel comprising of IOM, UNHCR, UNICEF and WHO. Project Voyager also won second prize in the Economic and Social Development category, and the Social Impact award. The Jobs4Ukraine initiative helps refugees from Ukraine access employment through career counselling, training courses, workshops, recruitment events and direct connections with empoyers. Held annually, the Civil Society Gala celebrates civic engagement in Romania. Initiated in 2002 by The Institute, a non-governmental organization supporting creative and civic initiatives, the event recognizes outstanding projects, campaigns and programmes led by civil society organizations.

title: VNM: Flood - 10-2026 - Heavy rainfall caused flooding #3 (2026-10-12)
content:
Description

According to local authorities, heavy rainfall on 10–11 October caused localized flooding, landslides and transport disruption in parts of Central Viet Nam, particularly Quang Tri, Da Nang and Lam Dong. One flood-related death was confirmed in Dan Hoa, Quang Tri. Floodwaters have generally receded, although some local roads and low-water crossings remain affected. In Da Nang, landslides affected two road sections in Nam Tra My, temporarily disrupting traffic. In Tra Giap, landslides affected three households, prompting local authorities to assist residents in moving away from dangerous areas. No casualties were reported in these incidents.

According to the National Centre for Hydro-Meteorological Forecasting (NCHMF), localized heavy rainfall remains possible across Central Viet Nam, particularly from southern Quang Tri to Da Nang and in eastern areas from Quang Ngai to Dak Lak and Khanh Hoa. The forecast issued on 12 October indicated rainfall of 20–40 mm, locally exceeding 80 mm. Flash-flood and landslide warnings were issued for Da Nang, Quang Ngai and Dak Lak, with a further warning issued for parts of Dak Lak on 12 October.

River levels in North Central Viet Nam are generally receding. However, further heavy rainfall may trigger flash floods and landslides in vulnerable areas.

title: Serbia: Extreme Winter Condition and Floods - DREF Final Report (MDRRS016)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

09-01-2026

What happened, where and when?
Since 4 January, severe winter weather conditions, including heavy snowfall, strong winds and low temperatures, have affected several parts of Serbia, causing partial collapse of the electricity distribution network and widespread, prolonged power outages. These outages severely disrupted heating, water supply and access to essential services, particularly in rural and hard-to-reach areas. The situation further deteriorated on 7 January, when additional heavy snowfall coincided with a sharp drop in temperatures to severe sub-zero levels. The most affected municipalities included Loznica, Valjevo, Osečina, Ivanjica, Vladimirci, Krupanj, Lučani, Mali Zvornik and Majdanpek, where heavy snow accumulation caused restricted access to communities, disrupted transportation and prolonged electricity cuts due to damage to power infrastructure.

Additionally, as a consequence of heavy precipitation, rivers in Kosovo and Metohija began to overflow. Note: All references to Kosovo in the present document should be understood in the context of United Nations Security Council resolution 1244 (1999). On 7 January, the Ibar river overflowed, followed by the Sitnica river on 9 January, causing localized flooding in the municipalities of Kosovska Mitrovica, Zvečan, Kosovo Polje and Lipljan. Flooding affected residential areas, agricultural land and critical infrastructure, posing risks to livelihoods, health and safety of the population.

The Emergency Situations Sector of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Seriba announced a state of emergency due to snow in 11 municipalities (Loznica, Osečina, Prijepolje, Vladimirci, Mali Zvornik, Valjevo, Majdanpek, Krupanj, Sjenica, Lučani, Ivanjica) as a result of severe winter weather.

The State of emergency was declared in 11 municipalities:
Loznica 5/1/2026
Osečina 5/1/2026
Prijepolje 5/1/2026
Vladimirci 6/1/2026
Mali Zvornik 6/1/2026
Valjevo 8/1/2026
Majdnapek 8/1/2026
Krupanj 8/1/2026
Sjenica 9/1/2026
Lučani 10/1/2026
Ivanjica 10/1/2026

The state of emergency still remains in 10 municipalities. In response to immediate needs, the Red Cross of Serbia provided emergency assistance to over 400 households, including food and hygiene parcels, blankets, sleeping bags, drinking water, candles, and Primus stoves. However, the evolving situation, remaining unmet needs, and depletion of contingency stocks require continued support and reinforcement of operational capacities through DREF assistance.

title: THA: Flood - 09-2026 - Heavy rainfall caused flooding #4 (2026-10-09)
content:
Description

According to DDPM report, as of 06:00 on 9 October 2026, flooding continued in 22 provinces, including Bangkok, affecting 109 districts, 927 subdistricts and 6,934 villages. According to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (DDPM), a total of 1,145,352 households (3,183,726 people) had been affected.

The flooding was caused by the influence of a monsoon trough, unstable weather conditions and accumulated water in low-lying areas along rivers. Flood levels were receding in several provinces, while water levels remained stable in others. Water levels were reported to be rising in Chachoengsao Province.

The highest reported impacts included Bangkok, with approximately 329,000 affected households; Pathum Thani, with 246,818; Samut Prakan, with 223,346; and Ayutthaya, with 61,365. DDPM reported fatalities in several affected provinces, including 19 in Prachin Buri, nine in Samut Prakan and five in Suphan Buri.

The Thai Meteorological Department forecasts unstable weather, thunderstorms, strong gusts and isolated heavy to very heavy rainfall across several regions during 9–13 October 2026. Continued rainfall may trigger flash floods, river overflows and landslides, particularly in low-lying and flood-prone areas. Authorities are advised to closely monitor the situation and prepare for potential further impacts.

title: Nepal - 25-28 September Heavy Rainfall Situation Report #1 (28 September 2026) [EN/NE]
content:
Brief Summary

A low-pressure system originating over the Bay of Bengal resulted in heavy to very heavy rainfall across various parts of Nepal from 25 to 28 September 2026. The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) and the Center for Hydrology and Water Resources Research (CHWRR) initiated continuous monitoring and analysis of the development, movement, and potential impacts of the weather system from 23 September 2026 . Through the Flood Forecast Bulletin issued on 24 September 2026, advance information was disseminated regarding the potential risks of heavy rainfall, flooding, and landslides.

On the same day, the Hon. Minister for Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation and the Hon. Minister for Home Affairs visited the Flood Forecasting Information Center and were briefed on the prevailing risk situation. To further strengthen preparedness and early warning measures, from 25 September 2026, the flood forecasting lead time for major rivers was extended from 3 days to 5 days, while the forecasting lead time for flash floods in smaller rivers and streams was increased from 24 hours to 48 hours.

title: UNICEF Panama Situation Report No. 2 (Earthquake), 11 October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • The 7.5-magnitude earthquake on 9 October damaged homes, educational facilities, health facilities, and water and transport infrastructure. Damage and needs assessments are ongoing, with significant impacts confirmed in Veraguas, Los Santos and Herrera provinces. No fatalities have been reported.
  • Children’s access to education has been significantly affected, with 419 educational facilities reported damaged nationwide and classes suspended on 12 October while safety inspections continue.
  • UNICEF deployed emergency personnel together with implementing partners to Coclé, Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos provinces to conduct initial needs assessments. Initial field reports identify needs related to access to safe water, shelter, health and psychosocial support, as well as visible infrastructure damage.
  • UNICEF is supporting the response led by national authorities and coordinating with other United Nations agencies. Work is focused on assessing children’s needs in water, sanitation and hygiene, education, health and protection, and on preparing operational support and emergency supplies based on verified needs.

title: UNHCR Facilitated Return of Syrian Refugees - Lebanon, 30 September 2026
content:
Since January 2025, 694,392 Syrians known to UNHCR have returned to Syria and consequently been inactivated from UNHCR's records. This includes refugees confirmed to have returned1 and those inactivated due to prolonged absence and loss of contact2 . Among the 694,392 Syrian returnees, 86% (597,552) returned spontaneously to Syria; this includes 11 % (65,500) who returned under duress in late 2024 and remained in Syria; 23% (140,000) identified by the General Security Office (GSO) while crossing through an Official Crossing Point (OCP) without a Repatriation Form; 6% (35,903) identified as returning due to force majeure after 2 March 2026; and 60% (356,149) who were inactivated due to prolonged absence or loss of contact, or whose return was confirmed by UNHCR through interviews with family members. The spontaneous departure figures reflected in the chart indicate the date of inactivation from UNHCR's database, rather than the date of departure, which explains the high number of inactivations in December 2025 following the completion of the presence verification.

By the end of September 2026, 14% of the 694,392 Syrians who had returned, representing 96,840 individuals, had been assisted by UNHCR: 79,548 under the voluntary repatriation programme and 17,292 under the Return due to Force Majeure (RFM) programme. The RFM programme was implemented between 1 April and 30 June 2026 in response to the escalation of hostilities in Lebanon to provide humanitarian assistance to refugees returning to Syria without a viable alternative for safety. Among those assisted under the RFM programme, 72% returned to their areas of origin in Syria, 19% were women, 59% were children. Almost all (96%) returned in complete families.

title: World Vision Situation Report #2: Humanitarian Response to Flooding (09 October 2026)
content:
Cambodia experienced significant flooding throughout September 2026 due to prolonged heavy rainfall and tropical weather disturbances, affecting 10 provinces, 53 districts and cities, 255 communes/sangkats, and approximately 73,922 households nationwide. The floods damaged homes, agricultural land, and public infrastructure, while continued rainfall poses ongoing risks to vulnerable communities, particularly in Battambang and Banteay Meanchey provinces.

In response, World Vision Cambodia launched a 90-day Flood Emergency Response Plan (October–December 2026) to address urgent humanitarian needs through an integrated multi-sectoral approach, including food assistance, nutrition, WASH, shelter and non-food items, protection, and education support. The response targets more than 20,000 people across the most affected areas.

To date, World Vision Cambodia has reached 3,169 people, including 1,798 children, and supported 898 households with emergency food and hygiene assistance valued at USD 35,922.73. The response has prioritized vulnerable groups such as young children, pregnant and lactating women, and persons with disabilities. Child protection awareness and community feedback mechanisms have also been integrated to ensure safe, accountable, and people-centered assistance.

Working closely with government authorities, local disaster management committees, humanitarian partners, volunteers, and youth, World Vision Cambodia continues to coordinate relief efforts while appealing for USD 800,000 to meet the growing needs of flood-affected communities across eight districts in Battambang and Banteay Meanchey.

title: Nepal Flood 2026 - DREF Operation Update #02 (MDRNP022)
content:
As of 2 October 2026, CHF 13.04 million in confirmed multilateral hard pledges recorded against the CHF 18 million IFRC Secretariat Emergency Appeal (approximately 72% per cent). Continued funding is required to sustain the response and scale up early recovery interventions.

On 26 August 2026, an ice-and-rock avalanche occurred in the upper Lhende Khola watershed, around 20 km upstream of the Rasuwagadhi border point. The avalanche triggered a debris flow and severe flooding downstream along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli–Narayani river system. The flooding caused widespread erosion and sediment deposits and damaged settlements, agricultural land, productive assets and critical infrastructure. The most serious humanitarian impacts happened in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, although impacts were also reported further downstream along the river corridor.

The extent of infrastructure damage continues to affect access and recovery efforts. According to the Government-led Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA)3, around 69 km of road was damaged, including 55 km classified as completely damaged. The assessment also identified damage to 37 motorable bridges and 68 trail-bridge spans. Of the motorable bridges assessed, 33 were reported washed away. Damage to roads and bridges, as well as electricity, water-supply and communication networks, has disrupted essential services, economic activities and access to affected communities. Access remains difficult in some locations, particularly in Rasuwa, where relief supplies continue to be airlifted to communities that cannot be reached by road because of damaged roads and bridges.

According to the latest Government statistics4, dated 1 October 2026, 1,453 people had been reported dead, 5,179 remained reported missing, and 13,795 had been rescued. The number of people reported missing still requires further verification and reconciliation. In the context of the access barriers and the ongoing assessments, the Government RDNA also cautions that figures for deaths, missing people and rescues should not necessarily be treated as separate or mutually exclusive counts.

According to the Nepal Red Cross Society (NRCS) Situation Report5, displacement has decreased as families continue to leave collective accommodation, but considerable temporary shelter and recovery needs remain. NRCS reported that 1,107 people were staying in 21 holding centres across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading as of its latest update. In the very beginning, there were around 33 holding centers, which are gradually decreasing, depicting movement of people to alternate places. Thus, the number of people staying in these centres does not represent the full displaced population. Some affected families are staying with relatives or host families, while others have moved to different forms of temporary accommodation. The Government has also announced monthly cash support for displaced families choosing to live outside holding centres, providing NPR 15,000 (CHF 82) per month for households of up to four members and an additional NPR 2,000 (CHF 10.75) for each additional household member, for up to six months or until alternative accommodation is arranged. As displacement becomes more dispersed, continued household-level verification remains important to understand which families can safely return home and which will require temporary accommodation, reconstruction support or possible relocation. IFRC-supported ongoing emergency response efforts have distributed shelter items, including NFI sets, mattresses, blankets, etc., to approximately 9,905 people and the operation plans to prioritize emergencies and transition shelter going forward. The IFRC shelter coordination surge supports coordination among humanitarian partners in affected areas. Collectively, 51 actors have provided shelter and essential household items to around 23,000 people (5,900 households), against 25,709 people initially targeted in holding centres. Most households have since moved to temporary sites. By 2 October, basic services and access had largely been restored, except in some hard-to-reach areas of Rasuwa District.

More than a month after the disaster, the response is increasingly moving from immediate lifesaving assistance towards restoring essential services, temporary and transitional shelter and early recovery. This transition is already visible through household assessments, temporary site development and work to rehabilitate damaged water-supply systems, while emergency assistance continues in locations where access remains constrained. Humanitarian needs nevertheless remain, particularly among displaced families and communities that are difficult to reach. Unstable slopes, accumulated sediment, obstructed channels, continuing rainfall and the possibility of further flooding exacerbate the challenges for the affected people. Continuing rainfall is also affecting temporary shelter conditions and has already interrupted some shelter works, increasing the importance of adequate weather protection, sanitation, protection services and winterization as seasonal conditions change.

title: UNICEF Panama Situation Report No.1 (Earthquake), 9-10 October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • On 9 October 2026, a magnitude 7.5 earthquake struck Panama, causing damage to homes, schools, health facilities, roads, bridges, and water supply infrastructure, particularly in Veraguas, Coclé, Los Santos and Herrera provinces. On 10 October, the government declared a state of emergency following the earthquake.
  • According to the National Emergency Operations Centre (COE), 27 people sustained minor injuries, with no fatalities or missing persons reported as of 10 October. The number of affected children and families remains unknown.
  • The Ministry of Education (MEDUCA) reported 419 affected educational facilities nationwide, raising concerns about school safety, access to water and sanitation, and continuity of learning.
  • The Ministry of Health (MINSA) reported 20 affected health facilities. Evacuations and temporary adjustments to patient care were reported, potentially affecting access to essential health services for children and families.
  • Damage to roads and bridges restricted access to several rural communities. Although water production has reportedly been restored at major treatment facilities, the situation in affected rural areas remains under assessment. Approximately 300 people were preventively evacuated from Isla Caña, while eight families were accommodated in a temporary shelter in Penonomé.
  • UNICEF is supporting the Government-led response and assessing priority needs affecting children and families. Initial efforts are focused on WASH, education, health and child protection, including assessing water and sanitation services in affected communities, schools, health facilities and temporary shelters. UNICEF is preparing to provide emergency supplies and support the rapid restoration of essential services, prioritizing isolated and displaced communities as needs are confirmed.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 314: Week 1 - October 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Market Overview

During the 1st week of October, national average prices recorded generally modest week-on-week movements, while several key food commodities remained elevated compared with last year and their longer-term averages. Rice, wheat, cooking oil, sugar and salt prices remained above their corresponding annual levels, while elevated fuel and fertilizer prices continued to add pressure to transportation, production and supply-chain costs. Meanwhile weak labour availability and subdued purchasing power continued to constrain household access to food.

Food Categories:

National average food prices recorded limited week-on-week movements, although notable annual and longer-term price disparities persisted across commodities.

• Wheat and Wheat Flour: Wheat grain prices increased marginally by 0.6% during the week, while high-price wheat flour remained unchanged and low-price wheat flour declined by 0.2%. Compared with last year, wheat grain and low-price wheat flour were both 10% higher, while high-price wheat flour was 6% higher.

• Rice: Rice prices declined during the week, with Palawi and Sholae falling by 1.9% and 1.7%, respectively. Despite these weekly declines, Palawi remained 17% and Sholae 31% above last year's levels, while both varieties remained substantially above their three-year averages, by 19% and 20%, respectively.

• Other Staples: Weekly movements in cooking oil, pulses, sugar, salt and bread remained limited. Cooking oil and sugar prices were 12% and 10% higher than last year, while salt was 4% higher. In contrast, pulses and bread remained 12% and 3% below their respective annual levels.

• Vegetables: Potato prices declined by 4.1% during the week, while onion fell by 3.1% and tomato by 0.2%. Despite the weekly decline, potato remained 25% above last year's level and 23% above its three-year average. In contrast, tomato and onion prices were 55% and 6% lower year-on-year, respectively.

Non-Food Categories:

Terms of Trade (ToT): Purchasing power remained constraint for both labour-dependent households and pastoralists, as declining income and higher prices limit their access to food.

• Unskilled Labour ToT: The nominal unskilled labour ToT stood at 9.9 kg of low-price wheat flour, representing a 13% decline from last year and 12% below the three-year average. The continued deterioration indicates sustained pressure on labour income relative to food prices.

• Labour Availability and Wages: Unskilled labour availability remained at 2.0 days per week, 14% below last year and 21% below the three-year average. Unskilled labour wages also declined by 5% year-on-year, contributing to a 25% decline in the real unskilled labour ToT compared with last year and 30% below the three-year average.

• Pastoralist ToT: A pastoralist could exchange a one-year-old female sheep for 260 kg of low-price wheat flour, 12% below last year's level and 7% below the three-year average, indicating continued pressure on the purchasing power of livestock-dependent households.

• Fertilizers and Agricultural Inputs: DAP prices increased marginally by 0.3% during the week, while urea prices declined by 1.8%. Despite these limited weekly movements, DAP and urea remained 10% and 24% higher than last year, respectively. Improved seed and animal feed prices remained below last year, by 8% and 5%, respectively.

title: Nepal - Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Flood: Search, Rescue and Relief Update (Reporting Period: 26 August – 3 October 2026) [EN/NE]
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

On 26 August 2026 (10 Bhadra 2083), a severe flash flood travelled through the Lhende Khola–Bhotekoshi–Trishuli–Narayani river system. It was caused by an ice and rock avalanche, rather than monsoon rainfall. A hanging glacier and rocky mass covering approximately 2.0 km2 broke away at an altitude of about 5,200 metres on the northern side of Langtang Lirung in Rasuwa district and struck the Lhende Glacier at 3,800 metres. The resulting avalanche and subsequent flow down the Lhende Khola generated the flood. The impact produced a strong seismic signal of magnitude 5.2, recorded at 08:37.

Travelling at approximately 188 km/h from its source, the flood covered 20 km within seven to eight minutes and reached the Nepal–China border at Rasuwagadhi at 08:45. It destroyed the hydrological stations at Syafrubesi at 08:50 and Betrawati at 09:20.

title: Nepal - Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi Flood: Search, Rescue and Relief Response Situation Report #12 (13 September 2026) [EN/NE]
content:
Highlights

• The Government of Nepal has decided to provide immediate cash relief for temporary accommodation and livelihoods to families with completely destroyed and uninhabitable homes across 15 local levels in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading,
Tanahun, and Gorkha, with NPR 15,000 per month for families of up to four members and an additional NPR 2,000 per additional member, for up to six months, exclusively for those opting for self-arranged temporary accommodation instead of holding centers.

• Similarly, if any family opts not to avail of the aforementioned cash relief facility, an alternative option has been provided wherein the government itself will arrange temporary housing until permanent housing is constructed; to collect the necessary details regarding this, forms have already been dispatched to all concerned local levels.

• The government has completed the preliminary damage and loss assessment, while the Post- Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA) process is currently underway, based on which necessary resources will be secured to accelerate reconstruction and rehabilitation efforts.

• A total of 339 patients received treatment across 19 health facilities, of whom 271 have been discharged, 32 remain under treatment, 32 were referred to other hospitals, and 4 individuals passed away during treatment.

• According to respective districts information, 825 affected persons are currently taking shelter in 9 holding centers in Rasuwa District, 1,613 in 22 holding centers in Nuwakot District, and 94 in 2 holding centers in Dhading District. In total, 2,532 affected persons are currently taking shelter across 33 holding centers.

• Three Shelter Cluster partner meetings have been successfully conducted, finalizing both the ‘Rehabilitation and Shelter Management Action Plan 2083’ and the Detailed Damage Assessment (DDA) Action Plan.

• In collaboration with the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction (DUDBC) and partner organizations, various prototype options for 1-room, 2-room, and 3/4-room emergency transitional shelters have been prepared and discussed.

• For the first time in Nepal following the Bhote Koshi floods, live monitoring of river conditions has been initiated under the leadership of the Center for Hydrology and Water Resources Research (CHWRR) by installing a CCTV camera in Timure, approximately 70 meters above the river level. Its live feed is connected to CHWRR’s 24/7 operated flood forecasting service.

title: Nepal - Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi Flood: Search, Rescue and Relief Response Situation Report #11 (12 September 2026) [EN/NE]
content:
Highlights

• Key findings from the ‘Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA)’ report prepared by the Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment Team under the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA):

 Total Disaster Effects: Total physical damage and economic loss is estimated at NPR 40,828.91 crore (USD 2,695.33 million).

 Total Recovery Needs: A total budget of NPR 72,331.52 crore (USD 4,774.99 million) is estimated for sustainable reconstruction and recovery.

 Sectoral Breakdown of Damage and Recovery Needs:

 Infrastructure Sector: Total damage and losses stand at NPR 19,004.39 crore (USD 1,254.58 million), with recovery needs estimated at NPR 47,357.19 crore (USD 3,126.30 million) (most severely affected sector in terms of both damage and needs).

 Productive Sector: Total damage and losses stand at NPR 15,037.42 crore (USD 992.70 million), with recovery needs estimated at NPR 5,077.49 crore (USD 335.19 million).

 Social Sector: Total damage and losses stand at NPR 6,787.10 crore (USD 448.05 million), with recovery needs estimated at NPR 10,354.99 crore (USD 683.59 million).

 Cross-Cutting Sector: Recovery needs are estimated at NPR 5,187.34 crore (USD 342.44 million).

 Most Affected Sub-Sector: The Infrastructure Sector specifically the Hydropower and Energy Sector emerged as the most impacted, incurring NPR 15,104.45 crore (USD 997.13 million) in damage and loss, and requiring NPR 39,062.30 crore (USD 2,578.71 million) for reconstruction.

• A total of 339 patients received treatment across 19 health facilities, of whom 269 have been discharged, 34 remain under treatment, 32 were referred to other hospitals, and 4 individuals passed away during treatment.

• According to respective districts information, 839 affected persons are currently taking shelter in 9 holding centers in Rasuwa District, 2,502 in 25 holding centers in Nuwakot District, and 93 in 2 holding centers in Dhading District. In total, 3,434 affected persons are currently taking shelter across 36 holding centers.

• Nepal Police deployed a medical team from Nepal Police Hospital, Maharajgunj, to Nuwakot and established a Level 1 hospital at the Chamber of Commerce and Industry building in Bidur, Nuwakot. To date, essential health services have been provided to a total of 1,382 flood-affected individuals, comprising 226 patients (117 males, 49 females) treated directly at the Level 1 hospital, 805 individuals reached across various holding centers, and 351 individuals across various holding centers in Rasuwa.
